23001-by-the-sea-1887:
Heman White Chaplin sketches a tidy man in By the Sea, a story dated 1887. James, with his easy collar and wristbands, always seemed fresh from the ironing-board. Keeping James clean costs no effort at all, Mrs. Parsons says in her funny little way. He picks his way round like a pussycat and never gets a spot on him, nowhere.

Chaplin wrote of New England coastal folk in dialect as fine as lace. A character like James, neat to a fault, becomes a whole study of village values. Little happens beyond talk, weather, and small errands by the sea. The pleasure is in the voice. Chaplin's ear for shore speech made his stories favorites of the magazines, and this one shows the gift plainly.
23002-saint-patrick-1887:
Heat hangs over the city in Saint Patrick, Heman White Chaplin's story dated 1887. Soulless faces loll in open ground-floor windows. Few customers sit in the barrooms, and policemen stroll listlessly with little to do. At nightfall comes the change, the scrape of fiddles and the stamp of boot-heels from the dance halls.

An Irish saint's day in an American city gives Chaplin his crowd and his music. The story moves between the day's dull weight and the night's release, watching immigrants at leisure. Chaplin usually wrote of fishing villages, and the urban setting stretches his range. Dance halls, saloons, and patrolmen fill the frame. The piece survives as a vivid slice of Irish-American city life in the Gilded Age.
23004-in-madeira-place-1887:
An old street musician carries a war in In Madeira Place, a sketch by Heman White Chaplin dated 1887. Nobody watching her slow round would guess her past. She once marched in Napoleon's armies and stood in the ranks at Waterloo. Since music goes with war, she also bears a worn accordion.

Kneeling by a flagged park path, she lifts a wrinkled, hopeful face. Now and then a passerby drops a copper into her hand. Chaplin builds a whole life from that kneeling figure, glory shrunk to a busker's pitch. His sketches often work this way, one overlooked person, closely seen. The Napoleonic detail startles, and it is meant to. Empires end, this piece says, in old women playing for pennies.
a-professor-of-alchemy-denis-zachaire-18: A Professor of Alchemy, dated 1887, is a short life of Denis Zachaire, the sixteenth-century French alchemist. Zachaire became famous for his own tale of the alchemical quest. In it, a gentleman spends his fortune chasing the philosophers' stone. The copy here comes through the University of Glasgow Library and its Ferguson collection. The piece belongs to the nineteenth century's revival of interest in the old adepts: a Victorian sketch of a Renaissance seeker after the stone.
appletons-cyclopaedia-american-biography:
James Wilson and John Fiske edited Appletons' work, and Volume One appeared in 1887, covering Aaron to Crandall. The whole set holds more than 15,000 lives. It was America's great national book of lives of the nineteenth century.

Entries sketch presidents, generals, inventors, clergy, and artists from the colonial age to the editors' own day. Portraits and facsimile signatures enliven the pages. The editors aimed for a complete record of notable American lives in one alphabet. Family historians and scholars still consult Appletons' for people found in no other reference work of the period. The entries run short, plain, and full of dates that are hard to find elsewhere now.
arxiv-2509-00387:
Jinluan Yang, Ruihao Zhang, Zhengyu Chen, Fei Wu, and Kun Kuang propose a unifying adversarial perturbation method for graph neural networks in 2025. Such networks learn from graph data, but they are vulnerable to attacks on node features and graph structure. Adversarial training hardens them by training under perturbations, yet past work is confined to specific data sets and network types.

Their method, PerturbEmbedding, integrates perturbation and training in one frame. It perturbs embeddings rather than only raw features or structure, which broadens its reach. The aim is resilience to attacks plus better generalization across graphs. A unified method could make graph models safer to deploy in fraud, social, and molecular tasks.
arxiv-2509-00587:
Vaibhav Mehta and one co-author, Justin Hsu, develop a Hoare logic for symmetry properties of programs. Hoare logic is a classic system for proving program correctness with conditions before and after code, and many natural properties state that a program behaves the same under a symmetry.

Mehta and Hsu design a syntax for group actions, the formal way symmetries act, with standard constructions and a natural notion of entailment, when one claim follows from another. Their logic puts group actions where pre- and post-conditions usually sit. A prototype tool, SymVerif, checks handcrafted benchmarks and even uncovered an error in a published model of a dynamical system, showing the approach can catch real mistakes.
arxiv-2509-00687:
Chen Su, with three co-authors, Yuanhe Tian, Yan Song, and Yongdong Zhang, improves multimodal time series forecasting, predicting future values from past series plus text. Text can help, but it may not fully or accurately capture what the history shows, which makes performance unstable.

Su and his co-authors propose a text reinforcement model that generates strengthened text fixing weaknesses in the original wording. A reinforcement learning scheme rewards each reinforced text by its effect on forecast performance and its relevance to the task, guiding the model toward higher quality text. Extensive experiments on a real-world benchmark across domains show the approach beats strong baselines and prior studies.
arxiv-2509-00887:
Takuya Miyamoto, writing alone, studies Hasse-Schmidt derivations in positive characteristic. These are sequences of operators that extend ordinary derivations. The lifting problem asks when such structures can be raised to richer settings. Miyamoto first studies that lifting problem in depth. He works out when lifts exist and when they do not.

He then applies the results to locally trivial deformations of algebraic schemes. Such families look unchanged in small neighborhoods. As a use case, he builds an algebraic curve with a striking trait. Its deformation functor fails Schlessinger's condition H1. That condition is a standard test in deformation theory. The counterexample clarifies limits of the classical theory in this setting.
arxiv-2509-01387:
Links between documents at the level of single sentences matter for tasks such as tracing how news frames a story or how a review answers a paper. Serwar Basch, Ilia Kuznetsov, Tom Hope, and Iryna Gurevych introduce ABCD-LINK, a framework to build such link data from scratch in any domain. Hand annotation is slow, so bootstrapping is used to grow data with machine help.

The framework first generates and validates semi-synthetic linked documents, then uses them to benchmark and shortlist linking methods. The best methods are finally applied to natural text pairs with humans in the loop. In peer review and news domains, joining retrieval models with language models won a seventy-three percent human approval rate for suggested links, more than double strong retrievers alone. All code, data, and protocols are released.
arxiv-2509-01587:
Federated learning trains one model from many clients without moving their private data, but a single model fits diverse clients poorly. Maciej Krzysztof Zuziak, Roberto Pellungrini, and Salvatore Rinzivillo work on clustered federated learning, where clients are grouped so each cohort gets a more personal model. The hard part is knowing when and how to form those groups.

Their algorithm, OCFL, is clustering-agnostic, meaning it does not assume a set number or shape of groups in advance. It computes cosine distances between clients' gradients and watches a temperature measure that signals when the shared model begins to converge. That signal picks the earliest suitable moment to cluster, in a single shot. The authors present the method as a practical answer to a subfield whose basic settings still differ from standard federated learning.
arxiv-2509-02087:
Heyang Peng, Seid Koudia, and Symeon Chatzinotas check the safety of a key sharing scheme sent through open air. The scheme lets two sides share a secret key with no need to trust the gear that reads it. Air churn blurs the light spin state and cuts the rate of secret keys. Their joint channel model folds those harms into closed forms with three terms.

Beam spread, drift, cuts at the rim, and sparkle all fold into those three terms. Churn maps to random twists with known laws, which yield a key rate in closed form. The model stays true in clear, cloud, and haze air in their checks. Sims on a ground to space link back the model with good fit. The work aids live link tuning for world scale key nets.
arxiv-2509-02187:
Matthew de Courcy-Ireland, Matthew Litman, and Yuma Mizuno study orbit divisibility on Markoff-like surfaces over prime fields. Markoff surfaces tie three variables in a classic cubic relation with rich orbit structure. Their family adds off-diagonal terms to that template. Orbits are the sets reached by the natural Vieta moves on solutions.

For a typical surface in the family, every nontrivial orbit has size divisible by the prime. That extends a theorem known for the Markoff surface itself. Special parameters provably force at least two or four orbits instead of the expected one. Cayley cubic surface parametrizes those exceptional cases and dictates solution counts modulo the prime. The proof elaborates a recent argument from the literature.
arxiv-2509-02387:
Rye Stahle-Smith and Rasha Karakchi present a 2025 computer security paper on malicious bitstreams, the files that configure FPGA chips in reconfigurable devices. A hostile file can block service, leak data, or hide covert attacks.

Their detector studies the bitstream bytes directly, so no source code or circuit layout is needed. Samples came from public benchmarks, rebuilt for a Xilinx PYNQ-Z1 board, giving a small set of benign and malicious files. Byte frequency features were compressed and rebalanced to handle uneven classes. Among the classifiers tried, Random Forest scored best on the macro F-score. The trained model was deployed on the board itself, showing that live screening can run on modest hardware.
arxiv-2509-02487:
Mayur Sawant and Abdelhamid Tayebi present a 2025 control theory paper on steering a state on a sphere to a target point while avoiding forbidden regions. The unsafe zones are star-shaped, meaning each has a centre that can see its whole interior.

Their feedback law switches behaviour by distance to danger. Far from unsafe regions, the state follows the shortest spherical path toward the target. Near a region, it first heads toward the antipode, the far side point, of a chosen interior point. The authors prove the target is almost globally asymptotically stable, so nearly every start ends there. Simulations on two- and three-dimensional spheres support the theory. The work suits attitude control problems where pointing directions must dodge keep-out zones.
arxiv-2509-02587:
Emmanuel Fleurantin, Jeremy L. Marzuola, and Christopher K. R. T. Jones present a 2025 mathematical physics paper on Schrödinger operators, the equations governing quantum particles in a potential, when that potential acts at two very different spatial scales at once.

The radial potential splits into a fixed part plus a second part that spreads out and weakens as a small parameter shrinks. The authors show the count of positive eigenvalues, the allowed energy levels, simply adds the counts from each scale treated separately. No cross terms appear in the total. Their proof mixes dynamical systems methods with an argument that separates the scales. The framework suits physical problems where a tight inner structure sits inside a broad outer field.
arxiv-2509-02687:
U. Burgaz and twenty co-authors wrote a 2025 astronomy paper using Type Ia supernovae, exploding white dwarfs used as cosmic distance markers, to probe why their brightness depends on host galaxy mass. That dependence, the mass step, is usually corrected with one universal value.

The team splits nearly three hundred supernovae from the ZTF survey by silicon line velocity into high- and normal-velocity groups. Normal-velocity events show a strong mass step, while high-velocity events show one consistent with zero. The split is sharpest near galaxy centres, likely older, metal-rich regions. Both groups show a step tied to host colour. The authors warn that a universal correction could bias cosmology, and suggest refined classes or environment-based factors.
arxiv-2509-02787:
Brian Lins and Aljoša Peperko present a 2025 functional analysis paper on the joint spectral radius, a quantity measuring the long-run growth rate of products drawn from a family of maps. Their maps preserve order and scale homogeneously on a cone, a setting beyond ordinary matrices.

The authors prove the Berger-Wang formula in this setting: for bounded, equicontinuous families on a polyhedral cone, the joint and generalised spectral radii coincide. That equality anchors stability analysis for switched systems built from such maps. They also give conditions ensuring the generated semigroup stays bounded when the generalised radius equals one. Notions of joint and generalised spectral subradii are extended to homogeneous maps on wedges, widening the theory's reach.
arxiv-2509-02887:
Ramya M Anche and 11 co-authors modeled a 2025 Arizona test bench that practices blocking starlight inside a vacuum chamber. The bench uses a vortex coronagraph, a mask that twists starlight away from a detector. Knowing what limits its performance matters before similar gear flies in space.

Their computer model follows light through the whole setup, end to end. It folds in measured flaws, such as mask imperfections, surface errors, and unwanted reflections. The team ran the model at two visible colors of light and at several bandwidths, meaning ranges of colors at once. Results show which flaws eat most into contrast, the gap between star brightness and the dark zone. That guides where engineers should improve the hardware.
arxiv-2509-03087:
Emin Ablyatifov and Georgy Lukyanov modeled in 2025 how a government's reputation shapes its ability to raise money over time. In their setup, a fiscal authority picks taxes and audit effort without knowing key facts. An executive who does know more then chooses whether to deliver public programs or divert the funds.

Reputation is the public's running belief about that executive, updated from what happens each period. A trial mandate can act as an experiment: delivering today gives up rents but preserves future access. The authors prove a dynamic threshold result showing such trials can be wise even when any tax looks bad in a one-shot view. Long-run versions show learning can freeze entirely when mandates drop to zero. Computed equilibria show fiscal capacity that depends on history.
arxiv-2509-03187:
Xiaoxiao Xu and 5 co-authors proposed a 2025 recommendation framework that handles numeric features more honestly. Recommenders rank items for users, and numeric inputs like price or age should often act monotonically: raising the number should never flip the output the wrong way. Ignoring that pattern hurts both accuracy and the ability to explain a ranking.

Their framework, shortened to CCSS, works in two stages and can wrap around many model types. First it synthesizes counterfactual samples, copies of real cases with one numeric trait altered. Then it contrasts those samples during training so outputs respect the expected order. Tests on a public dataset and a large industrial one favored the approach. It now serves hundreds of millions of users in a live system.
arxiv-2509-03287: Mouna Chegaar and Á. P. Horváth wrote a 2025 functional analysis paper on fractional Bessel-Sobolev spaces, function spaces that blend smoothness measured through Bessel operators with fractional order. They first prove that a Bessel version of the K-functional, a device measuring how well a function splits into smooth parts, matches a spherical modulus of smoothness. With those spaces defined, they state how the fractional Bessel-Sobolev and Bessel B-potential families embed into each other. Applying it, they characterize removable sets for a certain fractional differential operator.
arxiv-2509-03387:
Leonardo Bellinato Giacomelli and 5 co-authors designed a one-dimensional system in 2025 where topology and superconductivity meet. Strongly interacting fermions, particles that both exclude each other and interact heavily, host many striking phases that remain hard to reach. Their platform uses ultracold magnetic lanthanide atoms. The atoms sit in a one-dimensional optical lattice, a row of light-made wells.

The atoms' large magnetic moments let the team engineer a t-J model. That is a standard model of strong interaction, here with hopping, spin coupling, and onsite interaction each tunable on its own. Analysis and numerics uncovered several many-body phases. Among them were superconducting and topological ones. With attractive onsite interaction, the two traits coexisted in a single exotic state, a topological triplet superconductor. A practical plan to prepare and detect all the phases, using current techniques, is also outlined.
arxiv-2509-03487:
Jigang Fan and five co-authors introduce SafeProtein in a 2025 research paper on safety testing for protein foundation models. Those are large artificial intelligence models trained on protein data, used to understand and design proteins. Systematic red-teaming, or deliberate attack testing, had been missing for them.

SafeProtein mixes multimodal prompt design, using varied input types, with a heuristic beam search to build attack prompts automatically. A companion benchmark, SafeProtein-Bench, supplies hand-built test data and a scoring protocol. Tests achieved repeated jailbreaks of leading models, with attack success reaching high rates for one major model. The results expose biological safety risks in current systems. They also point toward stronger protections for future frontier models.
arxiv-2509-03587:
Marija Tomašević and one co-author argue that quantum effects prevent naked singularities during critical gravitational collapse in a 2025 research paper. Critical collapse sits at the edge between a dispersing cloud and a forming black hole. Classically it can leave a singularity exposed, with no horizon hiding it, challenging the cosmic censorship idea.

Working with tractable Einstein-scalar models, the authors add one-loop vacuum polarisation, a quantum correction from empty space itself. Regularity picks out one special quantum state for that correction. Its stress-energy carries a growing quantum mode that rivals the classical unstable mode and shifts the collapse threshold. A trapped surface then forms, giving the would-be singularity a horizon and leaving a minimum black hole mass. For primordial collapse, that shift strongly changes predicted black hole numbers, and the mass gap cuts off the lightest ones.
arxiv-2509-04087:
Michelle Dargasz and twenty-eight co-authors watch proteins move inside crowded liquid mixtures in a 2025 physics paper. Cells are packed with large molecules, and that crowding changes how proteins drift and meet. The team studied ferritin, an iron-storing protein, mixed with sugar and two bulky carbohydrate crowders named dextran and Ficoll. A powerful X-ray laser in Europe tracked motion on millionths-of-a-second scales.

Crowders pull proteins together at short range while pushing at longer range, through what scientists call depletion forces. Past a threshold crowder level, a loose middle-range order appeared and flickered quickly. Extra crowding first sped protein motion, then slowed it as the liquid thickened. Simple thickness alone could not explain the behavior.
arxiv-2509-04187:
Shin-ya Koyama and one co-author, Arshay Sheth, study a sign imbalance in modular forms in a 2025 mathematics paper. Chebyshev's bias is the tendency of one side to win a counting race more often than fair odds suggest. Here the race concerns signs of Fourier coefficients, the numbers that build up cuspidal newforms, a central family in number theory. Whether positive or negative signs lead turns out to hinge on one quantity.

That quantity is how strongly the form's L-function, a related analytic object, vanishes at the center of its critical strip. The main result ties the bias direction completely to that vanishing order. Worked examples compute the order explicitly, and confirm a super-positivity property proposed by Yun and Zhang.
arxiv-2509-04387:
Xihui Zhao and two co-authors rebuild the fluid theory of cosmic rays from first principles in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Cosmic rays are fast charged particles that push on gas across galaxies, yet their transport mixes tiny plasma physics with huge scales. Two-moment methods track both ray density and flow, but older versions omit some transport processes and suffer numerical instabilities from streaming terms. The new framework adds pressure anisotropy, meaning direction-dependent push, and Alfvén waves traveling both ways along magnetic fields.

The theory became a module inside the Athena++ simulation code. Benchmark tests check its wave behavior, including a newly mapped cosmic-ray acoustic instability. A time-step guideline tames the streaming instabilities, giving modelers a sturdier tool.
arxiv-2509-04487:
Håkon Kolderup, writing alone, generalizes a beloved arithmetic party trick using symmetry in a 2025 mathematics paper. The classic 1089 trick reverses a three-digit number, subtracts, reverses again, and adds, always landing on 1089. Kolderup replaces digits with permutations, the rearrangements counted by the symmetric group, inside its group ring over the integers. Any pair of zero divisors there, elements whose product is zero, generates a new trick, he proves.

The n-digit numbers split into regions defined by linear inequalities. On each region the zero divisors act as constants, so the trick's outcome is forced. Many classical-looking tricks may hide inside this single algebraic pattern, the result suggests.
arxiv-2509-04687:
Image labelling rules can run very long, and machine segmentation often breaks them. Vanshika Vats, lead author with two co-authors, present a training-free multi-agent setup for guideline-consistent segmentation in a 2025 paper. General-purpose vision-language models do the work inside a repeating Worker and Supervisor loop.

The Worker produces a segmentation mask, and the Supervisor checks it against the retrieved guidelines. A light reinforcement learning stop rule decides when the loop should end, balancing quality and resource use. Tested on the Waymo and ReasonSeg datasets, the method beats strong baselines. It also generalises without task-specific retraining.
arxiv-2509-05087:
Could throwing charged particles into a spinning black hole destroy its horizon and expose a naked singularity? Shauvik Biswas, lead author with two co-authors, use that question to test modified gravity in a 2025 paper. In general relativity, Wald showed extremal black holes cannot be overcharged this way, a protection called weak cosmic censorship.

Beyond general relativity, the protection may fail. The authors examine generic rotating black hole solutions outside the Kerr-Newman family and map where absorption could overcharge them. Regions where censorship fails become direct, physically motivated bounds on how far gravity may deviate from Einstein's theory.
arxiv-2509-05187:
Fast forecasts for how matter clumps across the universe are the goal of Charalampos Anastasiou and four co-authors in a 2025 cosmology paper. Surveys of large-scale structure, meaning galaxies spread over huge distances, need theory that can be tested against many possible universes quickly.

Their method compares each new case with a reference case and breaks the small difference into fixed building blocks. Loop integrals, the hard part of the two-loop calculation, are computed once in advance and stored. Combining those stored pieces with case-specific weights gives the dark matter power spectrum, a measure of clumping by scale. The released integrals support analysis of galaxy lensing signals.
arxiv-2509-05287:
Finding a hidden object inside moving fluid from partial measurements is the problem Mourad Hrizi and two co-authors study in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. The flow follows the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations, and velocity data exist only in a small region of the domain.

First the authors show the object can in principle be identified from such data. They then frame the search as shape optimisation, balancing a fit measure against a penalty on the object's perimeter, and prove a best shape exists and is stable. A fast, non-iterative method based on topological derivative recovers the shape. Ocean simulations with realistic Mediterranean depth and conditions test the method.
arxiv-2509-05387:
Salt water creeping through a charged channel under a concentration gradient is analysed by Evgeny S. Asmolov, Elena F. Silkina, and Olga I. Vinogradova in a 2025 fluid physics paper. The resulting flow, called diffusio-osmosis, moves toward higher or lower concentration depending on conditions in the channel.

The authors derive one equation for the total flow rate in channels with uniform surface charge and thin charged layers near the walls. It shows the flow depends only on surface charge and the concentration drop between the ends. Their theory also explains flow and ion flux directions, a bent concentration profile along the channel, and a slip velocity that varies strongly and can even alternate.
arxiv-2509-05487:
Links between points in clouds of charged particles, at special parameter values, get an exact form from Christopher D. Sinclair and Jonathan M. Wells in a 2025 random matrix theory paper. These beta-ensembles describe spread values of random arrays, or particles pushing apart through a log-shaped force.

When the parameter beta is the square of an even integer, the authors express each correlation function through a hyperpfaffian, a higher analogue of a determinant-like quantity. The building blocks come from integrals of Wronskians of polynomials chosen to suit the ensemble's weight, extending the skew-orthogonal family. For circular ensembles they give exact formulas, including the two-point function at one chosen value for small systems.
arxiv-2509-06187:
A locksmith trying keys under uncertainty inspires a new family of decision problems in a 2025 paper led by Ramiro N. Deo-Campo Vuong with four co-authors. In the Keychain Problem, each round offers only a subset of keys, one might open the lock, and a Bayesian prior rates each key. The cost counted is opportunity cost: rounds where the right key was on the chain but a different one was chosen.

The authors compute Bayes-optimal play through reductions to matching theory. With a known chain order the problem becomes maximum weight bipartite matching; with a sampled order it becomes a new laminar matching problem, then a combinatorial auction problem. Letting the locksmith choose the order makes it hard in the NP sense. The reductions also feed results for online matching.
arxiv-2509-06287:
Adaptive experiments can quietly break the statistics used to judge them, warn Yongyi Guo and Ziping Xu in a 2025 paper on contextual bandits. Valid inference needs policy convergence, the settling of how likely each action is, given context. The authors show a popular algorithm, LinUCB, may never converge when its reward model is misspecified, as linear stand-ins for complex systems usually are.

They propose and analyze a broad class of algorithms sure to converge even when the model is wrong. On that base sits an inference framework built on an inverse-probability-weighted Z-estimator, with proven asymptotic normality and a consistent variance estimator. Simulations give robust, data-efficient confidence intervals, beating existing approaches that only work for offline policy scoring.
arxiv-2509-06487:
Jets switched on and off within days in a black hole system, according to a 2025 astronomy paper by Francesco Carotenuto and five co-authors. The system, MAXI J1348-630, pairs a black hole with a normal star. Steady jets appear in its hard X-ray state and vanish in the soft state, while separate blobs fly out during changes between states.

Radio telescopes MeerKAT and ATCA caught a bright radio flare during a mostly soft phase in 2019, just as the NICER X-ray telescope saw flickering grow stronger. Two fast blobs were launched soon after. The authors suggest a short-lived steady jet briefly woke during a swing toward the hard state, then shut down before the blobs left. They also tentatively link the blob launch to a drop in X-ray flickering, a clue to how jets and the hot corona interact.
arxiv-2509-06587:
Algebraic invariants of symmetry groups for a family of groups built from graphs are computed by Marcos Escartín Ferrer in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. Right-angled Artin groups are defined from graph data, and their automorphism groups capture all their symmetries. The first L2-Betti number is a numerical invariant that can detect rich structure.

Ferrer computes that number for the automorphism and outer automorphism groups of arbitrary such groups, and characterizes exactly when it is nonzero. He also studies algebraic fibring, the existence of maps onto the integers with well-behaved kernels, for the pure symmetric automorphism groups. For outer automorphism groups without non-inner partial conjugations, a virtual version is analyzed. In the transvection-free case, vanishing of the invariant matches exactly the cases where the outer group virtually fibres, tying two kinds of structure together.
arxiv-2509-06687:
Self-driving boats on narrow inland waterways are steered safely in a 2025 control paper by Sajad Ahmadi and two co-authors. Automated surface vessels could cut road congestion and emissions, but canals bring tight channels, dense traffic, and water disturbances. Many existing navigation methods lack the robustness or precision such places demand.

The proposed planner combines robust model predictive control, which plans ahead while allowing for uncertainty, with control barrier functions, which mathematically fence off unsafe states. Channel banks and obstacles enter the design directly as safety constraints, so avoidance is built into steering rather than added afterward. Simulations under realistic conditions show the vessel staying safe and adapting better than leading alternatives. The authors present the method as a step toward dependable autonomous shipping on inland routes.
arxiv-2509-06787:
Seven infant stars forming together inside one disk are reported by Shanghuo Li and seventeen co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. Multiple star systems shape cluster dynamics and stellar evolution, and they seed later events from X-ray binaries to gravitational-wave sources. How the largest multiples form was poorly understood.

The septuple protostellar system sits in a Keplerian disk in the high-mass star-forming region NGC 6334IN, with close separations of a few hundred astronomical units. Stability analysis shows the surrounding disk is dynamically unstable, pointing to disk fragmentation as the birth mechanism. Earlier studies typically found only two or three members forming this way, in both low- and high-mass regions. Seven members offer strong observational evidence that a fragmenting disk can build extreme high-order multiples, confirming a long-standing theoretical idea.
arxiv-2509-06887:
Search software rebuilt as one generative system is presented by Jiahui Chen and twenty co-authors in a 2025 information retrieval paper. Traditional search engines chain recall, pre-ranking, and ranking modules, and that complexity blocks overall gains. Generative recommendation suggested an alternative, but earlier attempts trained the item tokenizer and the generator separately, causing mismatched goals.

UniSearch, built for Kuaishou Search, joins a search generator with a video encoder in one end-to-end architecture. The generator produces semantic identifiers of relevant items for a query, while the encoder learns item embeddings and their token forms. Joint training lets the parts improve each other. A preference optimization step adds a reward model and real user feedback. Industrial-scale experiments and online A/B tests in short-video and live search showed strong results, including a standout improvement in live search.
arxiv-2509-07387:
Wei Liu and 3 co-authors study how hospital networks can move nurses from sites with spare staff to sites facing shortages in a 2025 paper. The practice, called internal travel, grew during the COVID-19 pandemic. It needs advance notice and short secondments, and demand forecasts from old data prove unreliable when conditions change fast, which limits plain sample-based planning.

The authors frame the problem as a stochastic dynamic program, a model that decides step by step under uncertainty, guarded by a sample robust optimization approach. A linear decision rule turns the model into a tractable linear program a computer can solve. Connectivity between hospitals has the largest effect, cutting cost, redeployments, and travel distance. Its benefits, though, depend on matching how long secondments last to the shape of the network.
arxiv-2509-07487:
Masaki Nakagawa, writing alone in 2025, studies the statistics of homoclinic bursting to help predict extreme events. Bursting is a pattern of quiet phases broken by sudden spikes. It shows up in neurons and in other nonlinear systems. Homoclinic bursting follows a special geometric route. Its behavior can be captured by maps with infinitely many modes, called infinite-modal maps. The statistics of these maps were poorly known.

Nakagawa computes bifurcation diagrams and Lyapunov exponents, which measure how fast nearby paths split apart. He also computes the spread of burst heights and of the gaps between bursts. He derives formulas that match these statistics, using a randomization theory of the maps. A method to fit the map's parameters from data makes the theory usable in practice. It even works on data whose parameters drift over time. The work grounds the prediction of extreme events in the mechanism that produces them.
arxiv-2509-07687:
Solving partial differential equations again and again for new settings is slow, so engineers train neural surrogates instead. Sebastian Schaffer and Lukas Exl present PILNO in a 2025 research paper. PILNO is a neural operator, a model that learns the mapping from equation inputs to solutions. It works directly on point cloud data and ignores any fixed grid.

The design pairs low-rank kernel approximations with an encoder-decoder structure for fast, one-shot predictions. Training adds a physics-informed penalty, so the model's outputs respect the equation and its boundary conditions. The authors test it on function fitting, the Poisson equation, and parameterized Darcy flow, a model of fluid moving through porous material. PILNO stays efficient in high-dimensional parameter spaces. It offers a flexible surrogate for design and control problems needing many fast solutions.
arxiv-2509-08087:
Victor Garcia and 2 co-authors argue that health AI needs more than test scores in a 2025 paper. Language models now help with many tasks in medicine. Yet a model that tops a test may act quite differently in a real clinic. Scores on fixed tests are still the main way teams judge these tools. That habit has clear flaws.

Fixed tests can be gamed by training on the test itself. Gains then fail to spread to new tasks or new wards. The authors say sound review starts with the real clinical task. What will the tool do, where, and for whom? They set out steps for judging health tools in that grounded way. Patient care should rest on bedside proof, not on league tables.
arxiv-2509-08287:
Simulations that can converge to the wrong answer while looking healthy get a new warning light from Anosh Joseph and Arpith Kumar in a 2025 computational physics paper. The complex Langevin method attacks the sign problem, which blocks ordinary simulation of quantum field theories with complex actions. Existing checks watch drift behaviour but never test whether configurations carry the correct statistical weight.

Configurational temperature, built from gradients and curvature of the action, tests exactly that weight. In one-dimensional PT-symmetric test models it reproduces the expected value within a few percent or better. A diagnostic aimed at the actual failure mode could rescue results across nuclear and particle theory, where complex Langevin is often the only available tool.
arxiv-2509-08387:
Endless data streams can be published with privacy that varies by user, show Leilei Du and 5 co-authors in a 2025 data privacy paper. Streams feed event monitoring, but releasing them raw leaks individual behaviour. W-event privacy protects each person inside a sliding time window while keeping collected statistics accurate, yet earlier work forced one privacy level on everyone.

Personalised w-event privacy lets different users demand different protection strengths within the same infinite stream. A mechanism is designed so each user's data is estimated under their own requirement. People genuinely differ in privacy comfort, and uniform rules either overprotect the relaxed, wasting accuracy, or underprotect the cautious, breaking trust.
arxiv-2509-08587:
Cell adhesion holds because many molecular bonds share a pulling force, but how far that sharing reaches changes everything. Yannick Lüdemann, Stefan Klumpp, and Komal Bhattacharyya model bond clusters in a 2025 research paper. Earlier models assumed the load is shared either only locally or across the whole cluster. Their model distributes load over a characteristic length scale, decaying exponentially with distance.

The local and global pictures emerge as the two limiting cases of the new model. The authors derive approximations that yield analytical rupture conditions. Stochastic simulations validate those conditions. Two failure routes appear. All bonds can tear loose above a critical force. Or a critical crack, a wide gap of open bonds, can spread both ways. The framework helps explain how biological materials stay strongly attached under load, from cell surfaces to tissue interfaces.
arxiv-2509-08687:
Whether stars are born with the same mass distribution everywhere is one of astrophysics' open questions, and dwarf galaxies are the testing ground. M. V. Legnardi and 10 co-authors use the James Webb Space Telescope to probe the Small Magellanic Cloud's outskirts in a 2025 research paper. Ultra-deep images let them count stars far fainter than before.

The team measured the fraction of unresolved binary systems from the color-magnitude diagram. That fraction matches values in Milky Way clusters and field stars of similar age and mass. Combining the luminosity function with the best-fitting stellar model gave the mass function down to the lowest limit yet reached for this galaxy. Its slope falls below the canonical Salpeter value. The result adds evidence that the birth mass distribution does vary in sparse, metal-poor environments.
arxiv-2509-08887:
Sergio Martínez-González studies whether dusty clumps survive in supernova ejecta in a 2025 paper. A reverse shock can crush dense, cold clumps blown out by the explosion. Whether supernovae create or destroy dust depends on that contest.

Cloud crushing times are compared with cooling times across a large grid of densities, dust ratios, and shock speeds. When dust is abundant enough, gas-grain collisions cool the clump faster than it is crushed. Such clumps can survive even fast shocks and gain cold mass. Strong cooling can shield dust and pass it into interstellar space. The predicted survival zone matches dusty globules seen in the Crab Nebula.
arxiv-2509-09187:
Iskra Velkovska and 1 co-author introduce a test method for radiation hardness of silicon sensors for ATLAS in a 2025 paper. The High Granularity Timing Detector needs over twenty-one thousand sensors based on low gain avalanche diodes. Production quality control must check each wafer fast.

Their method uses the transient current technique in the interface region between two devices. It extracts gain layer voltage, gain versus bias, leakage current, and effective interpad distance. Capacitance and charge collection measures on the same samples calibrate the results. Acceptance criteria for wafer radiation hardness in the project are defined from those calibrations.
arxiv-2509-09387:
Mohamed Bal-Ghaoui and 1 co-author presented MetaLLMix in 2025, a framework meant to pick deep learning settings and pretrained models without long trial runs. Choosing hyperparameters usually costs expert time and heavy computing. Earlier language model approaches, the authors note, leant on costly outside services and gave weak explanations for their choices.

MetaLLMix instead joins meta-learning with explainable tools and local, lightweight language models. Past experiment results feed in together with SHAP explanations, and a judge model checks replies for form and completeness. Trials on eight medical imaging sets found strong results at far lower cost, with much shorter response times and the quickest training on most sets.
arxiv-2509-09487:
Two-dimensional turbulence organizes itself into great coherent vortices, and how tightly those vortices are packed at birth steers everything after. Snehanshu Maiti, Shishir Biswas, and Rajaraman Ganesh study that steering in a 2025 research paper. Earlier simulations showed the initial vorticity packing fraction decides the late-time statistical equilibrium. The team now follows the moving tracers, not just the flow field.

They track tracer spread and motion statistics through the onset, development, and late coherent stages. Higher packing speeds the onset of turbulence. In the middle stage, transport shifts from slower-than-diffusion to faster as packing grows. Late behavior splits between tracers trapped orbiting a vortex and tracers riding a translating vortex pair. The two viewpoints, Eulerian equilibrium and Lagrangian transport, tell one consistent story. For mixing predictions in thin fluid layers, the initial packing is a number worth knowing.
arxiv-2509-09587:
Kuang-Hung Chou and 2 co-authors show that parity-time symmetry creates a distinct kind of quantum critical point in a 2025 physics letter. Critical points can carry topological character, a theme called symmetry-enriched criticality. The authors solve parity-time symmetric free fermion models exactly and uncover critical points that are topologically nontrivial in a non-Hermitian sense, complete with sturdy boundary modes.

Such a point cannot be deformed into a trivial one without breaking the symmetry or passing a multicritical point. Entanglement entropy at these points also gains a quantised imaginary piece, set by the boundary mode count and steady under disorder and interactions. The authors link that term to a boundary free energy idea and trace the effects to a mass inversion special to non-Hermitian settings.
arxiv-2509-09687:
Pharmaceutical researchers searching a digital library often want the story entities tell together, not a list of documents. Hermann Kroll and 4 co-authors demonstrate narrative pattern mining in a 2025 research paper. The setting is PubPharm, Germany's specialized information service for pharmacy. It already offers keyword search, chemical structure search, and graph-based discovery workflows.

The new function lets users explore context-relevant entities and their interactions as narrative patterns across the biomedical literature. Instead of retrieving papers, the searcher browses the web of drugs, targets, and effects the papers collectively describe. Five domain experts were interviewed to judge the prototype's usefulness. The authors report the demonstration as a step toward discovery-oriented library services. For fields drowning in publications, tools that surface the plot may matter as much as tools that fetch the text.
arxiv-2509-09787:
Nojan Sheybani and 6 co-authors defend split learning against cheating clients in a 2025 security paper. In split learning, small devices keep the first and last layers of a network while a server runs the heavy middle, so sensitive data stays home. A malicious client can still poison the shared model by sending rigged gradients that plant a backdoor, and forcing clients to run a defence honestly is itself a hard problem.

ZORRO answers with interactive zero-knowledge proofs. Each client must prove it actually ran the client-side defence correctly, producing a checkable record that its local training stayed clean, without giving up privacy. Earlier defences leaned on the server or piled work onto it; this design shifts verified responsibility to where the risk begins.
arxiv-2509-09887:
Ricardo Tolentino and 2 co-authors characterise a crystal source of entangled photon pairs spanning visible and near-ultraviolet light in a 2025 optics paper. The device is periodically poled lanthanum borogermanate, and the team measures both its second harmonic generation and its spontaneous parametric down-conversion output. A Hanbury-Brown-Twiss setup times the pairs, while a specialised spectrometer camera records their colours.

One working grating, with a poling period just over two micrometres, emits temperature-tunable pairs centred near green light, its two photons sliding across a band on either side. Pair rates passed a million per second per milliwatt, with a strong coincidence-to-accidental ratio. The authors present the crystal as a stepping stone toward waveguided entangled sources reaching into the ultraviolet.
arxiv-2509-10187:
Simcha van Collem and 2 co-authors build the basic objects of domain theory in a 2025 paper. The work sits at the border of logic and computing. Domains give programming languages a firm meaning. They also model effects such as partiality and nondeterminism. Their frame starts with algebras over directed complete partial orders. A signature lists the operations for such an algebra. It also lists the order laws those operations must obey.

The freest such algebras are then shown to exist. They are built as quotient inductive-inductive types. Such a type builds three things at once. It builds a type and a relation on that type. It also builds the equations the type must meet. Known constructions fall out as cases. Joined sums are one case. Smash products and free domains are others.
arxiv-2509-10387:
Eleonora Zari and nineteen co-authors present a motion map of young stars in the Milky Way's disc. It is the first map at this scale, and it appears in this 2025 paper. The data cover roughly fifty thousand hot young OB stars. They come from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey V. Spectra, distances, and Gaia motions combine into full three-dimensional velocities. The map reaches out to about five kiloparsecs.

Radial motions dominate the story. Flows run inward and outward in turn. They stay coherent across kiloparsec scales. Their strength is around thirty kilometers per second. Older red giants show far weaker flows. The patterns line up only weakly with spiral arms. The youngest stars do trace density enhancements, though. Many causes could contribute. Spiral dynamics, the galactic bar, and resonances are candidates. So is the ringing of an old disturbance. The full survey should sharpen the answer.
arxiv-2509-10987:
Kai S. Shimagaki and five co-authors extend a classic approximation for evolving gene pools in this 2025 paper. Tracking a population's full genotype distribution means tracking every correlation among alleles at different sites, an impossible bookkeeping job. Quasi-linkage equilibrium simplifies by assuming those links are weak. It breaks under strong selection, strong gene interactions, or feeble recombination, though.

Their extended scheme lets correlations, organized as cumulants, evolve up to any chosen order. Higher orders are assumed to settle instantly. The gradient of average fitness drives the resulting equations, through a matrix born of competition among genotypes, which can be read and interpreted. Keeping just second-order cumulants already captures dynamics with third- and fourth-order gene interactions, which the standard theory misses. The scheme can also infer fitness from sequences sampled over time. That last use may matter most in practice.
arxiv-2509-11087:
Omkar Shailendra Vengurlekar, Adithya Pediredla, and Suren Jayasuriya present this 2025 imaging paper. It concerns synthetic aperture sonar. That technique builds three-dimensional pictures of underwater scenes from sound echoes.

Standard methods treat each point in the scene the same way. They assume sound scatters equally in all directions. Real echoes depend on direction, so results can blur. The new method, SH-SAS, stores the scattering field in a smarter form. A small neural network predicts how each point responds from each angle. Training uses raw echo timing signals directly. The system beat earlier approaches on simulated and real sonar data. It won on both picture quality and shape accuracy. Tests covered sonar used in air and underwater.
arxiv-2509-11187:
Android malware that hides its code is the target of this 2025 cybersecurity paper. Doan Minh Trung and six co-authors wrote it. Attackers also tweak malware to fool detectors. Single-view detectors tend to break under such tricks. They look at strings, images, or call graphs alone.

Their system is called DMLDroid. It fuses three views of an app at once. Permissions and intents form tables. The code file becomes an image. API calls become sequences drawn from graphs. A dynamic weighting scheme balances the views. On a standard malware dataset, the fused detector scored near the top. It held up under code obfuscation. It also held up under adversarial attacks.
arxiv-2509-11487:
Rashid Mushkani wrote this 2025 paper with no co-authors. It proposes a civic remedy for biased AI city pictures. Text-to-image models now picture urban futures for planners and the public. They can amplify harms against whole groups. Single users have little power to get such images fixed.

Mushkani frames a remedy called collective recourse. Communities file structured visual bug reports. Reports move through report, triage, fix, check, and closure. Four fix kinds sit inside the image stack. They run from counter-prompts and negative prompts to dataset edits and reward tweaks. A mandate score weighs severity, volume, fair spread, and evidence. In a synthetic run of hundreds of reports, prompt fixes landed fast but recurred most. Dataset and reward fixes were slower yet lasted longer.
arxiv-2509-11687:
Di Jin and 5 co-authors build a fake news detector that keeps its knowledge current in a 2025 paper called DYNAMO. News events develop suddenly, and authenticity labels can shift as facts emerge, so detectors need the latest updates rather than a frozen snapshot.

Retrieval-based methods often fetch content of doubtful credibility or drown in noise. DYNAMO instead maintains a news-specific knowledge graph that updates continuously. A large language model serves two roles: judging news authenticity and verifying the correctness of newly extracted knowledge. A tree search procedure decomposes complex stories and verifies them step by step. Verified real news then feeds new knowledge back into the graph. Experiments on two real-world datasets gave the best performance among compared methods.
arxiv-2509-11787:
Pascal Joos, Islem Bouzenia, and Michael Pradel set an AI agent on warning lists developers ignore. This 2025 software engineering paper treats static analysis tools. They flag bugs, vulnerabilities, and code smells. Triage by hand is tedious. Warnings pile up and code quality rots.

Their system is CodeCureAgent. It works as an agent, not a fixed script. It calls tools to search the codebase for context. Each warning is classified. False alarms are suppressed. Genuine ones get code edits. A three-step check approves each patch. The project must build. The warning must vanish with no new ones. The test suite must pass. On a thousand SonarQube warnings from over a hundred Java projects, plausible fixes came for nearly all. Most inspected fixes were correct.
arxiv-2509-11987:
Fractional derivatives, which remember the past instead of reacting only to the present slope, enter optimization dynamics in a solo-authored 2025 paper by Tumelo Ranoto. The work extends the classic Nesterov accelerated flow, a second-order system famous for speeding convex minimization.

Ranoto's system pairs the usual damping term with a fractional-order gradient, interpreted through the Caputo, Riemann-Liouville, and Grünwald-Letnikov definitions. Attention centers on weak damping, the borderline case where the ordinary flow can fail to settle. There, the memory in the fractional term steadies the motion and convergence returns. The author builds fractional Opial lemmas and Lyapunov functionals with memory to prove weak convergence toward minimizers, plus explicit faster rates when the function is strongly convex.
arxiv-2509-12087:
Translating code between languages breaks most often at third-party libraries, and Pengyu Xue with thirteen co-authors build a benchmark to expose exactly that weakness in 2025. Practical programming leans on such libraries for over ninety percent of its work, yet earlier translation benchmarks barely cover them.

TransLibEval holds two hundred real-world tasks across Python, Java, and C++, each deliberately built around libraries for data processing, machine learning, web development, and more, with thorough tests. Seven recent language models were tried under direct, intermediate-representation-guided, and retrieval-augmented strategies. Scores collapsed compared with library-free translation, falling by more than sixty percent on average, and nearly five thousand failed GPT-4o cases revealed a flood of library reference errors earlier benchmarks had hidden.
arxiv-2509-12387:
Mohamed Zayaan S, writing alone in a 2025 paper, proposes Causal-Symbolic Meta-Learning, a framework meant to learn from very few examples. Modern deep learning finds patterns well but often relies on spurious correlations, links that do not reflect real causes. That weakness harms generalization and forces training on massive datasets.

The framework has three parts. A perception module turns raw inputs into clean symbolic representations. A causal induction module discovers the causal graph behind those symbols, and a reasoning module uses that graph to predict. By meta-learning a shared causal world model across many tasks, the system aims to adapt quickly to new tasks, including questions about interventions and counterfactuals. A new physics-based benchmark, CausalWorld, is introduced for testing.
arxiv-2509-12887:
Nayan Sharma, Ranjit Kumar Singh, and Ajay Tripathi present a simple vector magnetometer in a 2025 paper. A vector magnetometer measures not just a magnetic field's strength but also its direction. Their method determines the azimuthal angle, the direction in the plane, using the ground-state Hanle effect, a change in atomic light response caused by a magnetic field.

The approach exploits phase matching of laser beams and the symmetry of the system's Hamiltonian, its energy description, which provides a phase-independent frame. As a proof of concept, experiments used a specific transition in rubidium atoms with three laser beams and observed the predicted dependence of resonance signals on phase. Without active phase control in the setup, the key features were still validated. The team also measured two components of their laboratory's stray field.
arxiv-2509-13287:
Nandan Sriranga, Haodong Yang and two co-authors detect targets in 2025 with paired passive radars that share compressed reads. One delay-Doppler cell is the focus. An unknown source sends a low-rank waveform, as in OFDM.

Each receiver whitens noise and projects onto the source subspace. Cross links form the core measures. Receivers swap and mix those measures to save bandwidth. Only a subset forwards sums to a fusion hub via shared channel. Weights are set from hub measure moments to lift detection. The scheme trades bandwidth for joint gain.
arxiv-2509-13387:
Delaram Golpayegani and 4 co-authors uncover AI governance themes in European Union policies in a 2025 paper. Policies and guidelines aiming to ensure AI systems are safe and trustworthy have proliferated, creating a fragmented governance landscape. The EU is a key actor, through its expert group's guidelines for trustworthy AI and the adoption of the EU AI Act in 2024.

EU policies are expected to be aligned, but they may differ in scope, emphasis, degree of normativity, and priorities. The authors leverage qualitative thematic analysis of key EU documents, including the AI Act and the ethics guidelines. They further employ quantitative topic modelling with BERTopic to enhance the results and expand the sample to EU AI policy documents published after 2018. The combined approach aims at a broad understanding of EU AI governance.
arxiv-2509-13487:
Prompt2DAG, a 2025 systems paper by Abubakari Alidu, Michele Ciavotta, and Flavio DePaoli, turns plain-language requests into executable Apache Airflow pipelines, the step-by-step workflows that enrich raw data. Building such pipelines by hand takes deep engineering skill, so the team tests whether large language models can draft them reliably instead.

Four generation styles, direct prompting, model-only, hybrid, and template-based, were compared across many experiments with thirteen language models and five case studies. The hybrid style won, succeeding in just under four fifths of runs and scoring best on reliability, structure, and executability. The authors argue reliability, not raw code quality, separates the methods, and that hybrid generation is the practical path.
arxiv-2509-13587:
Taichi Uyama and 37 co-authors report the discovery of a brown dwarf companion to a nearby M dwarf star in a 2025 paper. Brown dwarfs are objects between planets and stars in mass. Direct imaging, photographing a faint companion beside its bright star, is one way to find them, and the Subaru and Keck telescopes provided the observations here.

The companion was imaged around the nearby mid-type M dwarf designated LSPM J1446+4633. Combining radial velocity monitoring, direct imaging, and Gaia proper motion acceleration in orbital fitting yielded a dynamical mass estimate and a semi-major axis for the companion. Flux variability was also suggested by two imaging epochs. The authors identify the object as an intriguing late-T dwarf for future atmospheric studies, with the advantage of a constrained dynamical mass and a system accessible to many observation techniques.
arxiv-2509-13787:
Abdulkafi Sanad introduces new graph measures for hypergraphs in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. Zagreb indices summarize a graph's structure in numbers built from vertex degrees. Chemists use them to predict molecular properties. Hypergraphs extend graphs by letting one edge join many vertices at once. That matches how real molecules and reactions group atoms.

Sanad defines first and second Hyper-Zagreb indices for hypergraphs. He proves bounds for them across several families. The families include hypertrees, weak bipartite hypergraphs, and uniform hypergraphs. In a uniform hypergraph, every edge has the same size. He also pins down which hypergraphs hit the bounds exactly. A final application shows the indices at work in models that link a molecule's structure to its drug effect.
arxiv-2509-13987:
Ozer Ozturk and three co-authors measure the price of differential privacy in federated learning in a 2025 paper. Federated learning keeps client data local and shares only trained models, yet attackers can still run inference attacks on those models to reconstruct pieces of the training data. Privacy noise is the standard shield, but its cost in accuracy is rarely mapped carefully.

The team applied differential privacy through randomized response, a technique that flips answers with a set probability, inside a federated setup aggregated by an association-based classification algorithm. As the privacy parameter epsilon shrank, meaning stronger privacy, accuracy fell and class predictions grew lopsided. Stronger privacy, they conclude, is not automatically the practical choice; the balance must be tuned deliberately.
arxiv-2509-14287:
Elham Sadeghi and four co-authors propose PrIVAE in 2025 for designing biological sequences such as DNA, RNA and peptides. Designers want sequences with rich target traits, not just a yes or no label. Examples include glow colour, stability and strength against microbes.

PrIVAE is a variational autoencoder, a model that squeezes sequences into a compact code and rebuilds them. Its code is trained to keep the layout of the trait space. Nearby codes mean nearby traits. The trait space is treated as a curved surface and sketched with a neighbour graph. That link lets users search the code space for sequences with a desired mix of traits. Such control matters for new materials, sensors and antimicrobial drugs.
arxiv-2509-14387:
Marco Mingione and three co-authors build a flexible model in 2025 for air pollution risk in Bergen, Norway. Several pollutants move together over time and respond to hidden weather like conditions. A good model must track levels, links and how long each regime lasts.

Their framework mixes a hidden semi Markov process for the unseen conditions with a vector autoregression for the pollutants. Time varying factors can shift both average levels and regime durations. Fitting uses maximum likelihood with a tailored expectation maximisation algorithm. A penalty term selects which time lags matter and curbs overfitting. Tests on simulated data and the Bergen record assess the method. City risk forecasts gain a model that respects both chemistry links and weather persistence.
arxiv-2509-14787:
Qixuan Li and four co-authors present COMPASS in a 2025 robotics paper. COMPASS helps a robot arm explore and manipulate objects inside tight, cluttered spaces. Such spaces are hard because the robot sees only part of the scene, and safe motions are difficult to plan. The framework works in stages, sensing first and acting with what it learns.

A near-field scan first builds a local collision map to lower the risk of bumps. A utility function then picks viewpoints that are informative and also useful for later grasping. Finally, a constrained optimization step produces manipulation poses that respect nearby obstacles. On a new benchmark with four difficulty levels, COMPASS raises manipulation success well above exploration-only methods in simulation. Tests on a real robot confirm the design.
arxiv-2509-14887:
Hoang-Son Nguyen and Hoi-To Wai ask whether standard graph learning still works when some nodes of a network stay hidden, in a 2025 signal processing paper. Many tasks need the network's wiring, inferred from signals measured at its nodes. Hidden nodes can corrupt that inference, and earlier work added explicit fixes to the learning objectives.

Nguyen and Wai show the plain methods are already tougher than expected. For signals that are smooth, low-pass filtered versions of graph signals, naive learning recovers the true connections among the observed nodes. Their proof extends the restricted isometry property, a tool from compressed sensing, to the Dirichlet energy used in smoothness-based learning. Experiments on synthetic and real data back the theory, suggesting practitioners may not always need hidden-node corrections.
arxiv-2509-14987:
Md Talha Mohsin proposes a healthcare framework that pairs blockchain records with explainable AI in a solo 2025 paper. Health networks face two trust problems at once: patient data must be shared safely, and AI advice to clinicians must be understandable. The proposed BXHF framework addresses both inside one design.

Blockchain storage keeps records tamper-proof and auditable, while explainable AI methods produce predictions that clinicians can inspect and justify. Security and interpretability requirements enter a single optimization pipeline, giving trust at the data level and at the decision level. A hybrid edge-cloud layout supports federated computation across institutions, so hospitals can analyze data jointly without giving up privacy. Example uses include cross-border research networks and rare disease detection, where both safeguards matter most.
arxiv-2509-15387:
Stephan Huckemann writes a short treatise, in German, on the Star of Bethlehem. Many writers have tried to explain the star named in the Bible. Kepler linked it to a rare meeting of Jupiter and Saturn, with Mars joining, like one he saw in 1604. Huckemann sets out the old ideas of the sky that sit behind that claim.

The treatise walks through physics, astrology, and star lore from the time of Christ to the early modern age. It shows how Kepler could count back to a triple meeting of the two planets in the year 7 BC. It also touches the shift from an Earth centered sky to a Sun centered one. An epilogue turns to the questions this raises for faith.
arxiv-2509-15487:
Dingshan Deng leads a team that models the disk of gas and dust around the young star IM Lup. Such disks are where planets form, so knowing where their mass sits matters. This disk is large and heavy, yet past models found far less of a key gas than expected. The team test whether a fuller model can settle that puzzle.

Their tool, DiskMINT, now lets gas and dust spread in unlike ways across the disk. It solves for gas heat, height, and the fate of a key carbon gas as light breaks it or frost traps it. Fit to many light measures, the model gives a gas mass that matches a motion based estimate. The outer disk proves dust poor, which may block a step toward planet growth.
arxiv-2509-15587:
Tsz Ting Chung leads a team that tests how well language models reason with logic. Logic skill is a core sign of smarts, yet popular tests mix many skills at once. Such mixes can give a false read on pure logic. Tests also skew toward few languages and odd spreads of questions.

Their new test, DivLogicEval, uses plain sentences built from varied statements in surprising ways. It rests on classical logic, so each item has a firm answer. They add a scoring rule that damps bias and chance in model replies. Their runs show how much true logic each item needs. They also rank popular models on the test. The work gives a cleaner gauge of logic skill.
arxiv-2509-15687:
Elena Farahbakhsh Touli and Talha Bin Masood compare tree shaped summaries of data. Merge trees track how features join as a threshold rises, and they are core tools in topological data study. A distance called interleaving measures how alike two such trees are. Exact distances are known only when labels overlap; unlabeled or disjoint cases stayed hard.

Their fast method assigns labels mainly to the leaves of each tree to guess how the trees line up. They also improve an older method. Both run in time that grows modestly with size. The tools suit real data with few or no labels. A test on time varying electron density shows the use case.
arxiv-2509-15887:
Remo Garattini and Athanasios Tzikas ask whether a spinning, charged wormhole can be held open by a quantum effect. The Casimir effect gives an energy that can, in theory, support a tunnel between distant places. Past work covered still wormholes and uncharged spinning ones. The pair add electric charge and an outside electric field.

They work out the heat based stress the tunnel needs to satisfy Einstein's equations. A simple case has steady spin as seen by a non turning observer. There the tunnel keeps the shape of the known still charged case, under set constraints. A second case lets spin fade with distance from the throat. That damping kills an unrealistic drag at far range.
arxiv-2509-16187:
Translating code from one language to another is only safe if the new code behaves just like the old. Ali Reza Ibrahimzada and four co-authors build MatchFixAgent, a system of cooperating AI agents that checks translated code for equal behavior and repairs it when needed. The system works across languages and does not lean on weak test suites.

Against four prior translation tools, it gave a verdict on nearly every pair tested. Where it disagreed with prior checks, its verdict proved right more often than not. It also fixed about half of the faulty translations, far above the prior rate.
arxiv-2509-16487:
What makes a chatbot good at dialogue is rarely measured piece by piece, since most scores blend all traits into one. Zixun Chen and four co-authors score the Pythia model family on many fine-grained dialogue traits drawn from language theory. They vary model size and add fine-tuning on conversation data, then watch each trait move.

Size alone changed most scores only mildly, while fine-tuning lifted them fast until they leveled off. Many scores moved in lockstep, especially when one judge model produced them all, which casts doubt on how separate the traits really are. Extra checks on word use help explain the pattern.
arxiv-2509-16587:
M. Leok, C. Sardón, and X. Zhao build a shared frame for motion on special geometric spaces in a 2025 math paper. The spaces extend classic tools for systems with several time scales at once. The team lay out the basic geometry first. They then derive new results on systems that can be solved in full.

They also sort out special coordinates that make such systems easier to read. A theory for multi-time systems follows, built in two ways. To show the frame at work, they model a nerve-cell system with three time scales. The example ties abstract geometry to a real biological rhythm.
arxiv-2509-16687:
Uzzwal Kumar Mallick and co-authors model antibiotic dosing in a 2025 health paper. Taking too little of a drug can let bacteria adapt and resist it. Taking too much can harm the body and its helpful microbes. The team build a math model that weighs dose size, bacteria, resistance, and the immune system together.

Their results show underdosing raises the risk of resistant strains through mutation. Overdosing weakens immune defense by harming good microbes. Both errors speed the rise of resistance, in their model. The authors stress tight control of dose plans. Such models could help doctors think through trade-offs before resistance takes hold in a patient or ward.
arxiv-2509-16787:
Rui Han and Moises Gomez Solis study transport in near-periodic systems in a 2025 math paper. Ballistic transport means a wave packet keeps spreading at a steady rate. For systems that are almost periodic, past work left open how fast the near pattern must settle for ballistic motion to survive. The pair take up that open problem.

They show that a fast, exponential rate of settling is enough. The gap between the true system and its periodic cousins must shrink at that rate. The result gives a clear test for this class of matrices. Such matrices model electrons in layered and quasicrystal materials.
arxiv-2509-16987:
Vyron Kampourakis and co-authors measure Wi-Fi use in industry in a 2025 paper. Factories once kept control systems cut off from outside networks. That air gap is fading as wireless gear spreads to the shop floor. New Wi-Fi standards meet factory speed needs, but they raise security worries.

Field data show Wi-Fi adoption growing across industrial sectors. Many sites still run weak or outdated security settings. Those settings directly expose critical infrastructure to attack. The team offer their dataset as a reference for future work. Plant managers can use the findings to audit their own wireless setups before an intruder finds the gaps.
arxiv-2509-17187:
Lalith Bharadwaj Baru, Kamalaker Dadi, Tapabrata Chakraborti, and Raju S. Bapi tackle fuzzy borders in medical scans in a 2025 arXiv paper. Outlining a lesion is hard when its edge is unclear, and human raters often draw distinct masks for the same scan. A good tool must respect the image structure, trace weak edges, and still show the range of fair readings.

Their method, called the Segmentation Schrödinger Bridge, is the first use of that bridge idea for this task. It models how image and mask evolve together and uses a new loss to keep outputs varied. The team also proposes an index that scores both the spread and the agreement among raters. On three scan data sets, the method reached the best scores reported so far.
arxiv-2509-17587:
Saveliy V. Skresanov, writing alone, answers a group theory question posed in the Kourovka notebook in 2010. His 2025 arXiv paper asks about commutators, the elements of a group built from a standard four-factor product. MacHale's problem asks whether a finite group with more than two elements can have exactly one element that is not a commutator.

The answer turns out to be yes. Skresanov gives an infinite series of such groups, so the example is not a one-off curiosity. The smallest group in his construction is huge, with billions upon billions of elements, which hints at why the question stayed open. The paper settles the existence question in full. It also gives group theorists a new family to probe for how commutator sets can sit inside a group.
arxiv-2509-17887:
Daniel Perniok defines a new class of algebras tied to Coxeter and Dynkin shapes. His 2025 paper aims to widen a known class past quiver path algebras. Quivers are arrow graphs, and their path algebras are a standard way to build such objects.

Perniok builds two tilting objects over the squid algebra, by two routes. The end algebras of both match his new class. That match places the new class in the same derived group as the squid and canonical algebras. He also checks the rank group and a pairing form, and proves finite type in the domestic case.
arxiv-2509-18387:
Fast table tennis balls smear into streaks on camera, which makes them hard to track. Thomas Gossard, Filip Radovic, Andreas Ziegler, and Andreas Zell tackle that blur in this 2025 paper. Older labels mark the ball at the streak's front edge. That choice skews the data and throws away speed clues hidden in the blur.

The team instead labels the ball at the center of its streak and records blur traits as extra data. They release a new data set built on that rule. Across many models, the new labels improved detection scores. Their model, BlurBall, reads several frames at once and estimates both ball position and blur traits. It reached top results for ball detection. Using blur, not fighting it, also made path forecasts more reliable for live sports analysis.
arxiv-2509-18687:
Turbulent flow in three dimensions is hard to measure fully; lab setups often capture only a few planes. Yaxin Mo and Luca Magri present a neural method that rebuilds the full flow from such sparse views in this 2025 paper. Their network trains with no ground truth at all. Inputs are velocities on three planes plus pressure on a fourth.

The network shares its parameters along directions where the flow is uniform. That sharing cuts memory and uses data efficiently. On a standard test flow with clean data, both their network and a rival rebuilt time-averaged fields and the energy spectrum well. Their network could even infer structures far from the measured planes. With noisy data, its test error tracked its training error, a sign of good generalization. The authors aim the method at real experiments.
arxiv-2509-18787:
AI agents need a directory: a place to find what other agents can do and where they came from. Luca Muscariello, Vijoy Pandey, and Ramiz Polic describe the AGNTCY Agent Directory Service in this 2025 paper. The service supports discovery across mixed multi-agent systems. It rests on an open schema framework for agent records.

Records are stored by content address, sorted by layered taxonomies, and signed for proof of origin. A two-level map splits capability indexing from content location, run over a distributed hash table. Existing container infrastructure handles artifact delivery, and a signing system supplies provenance. The design is schema-driven, so new agent kinds, from prompt agents to tool servers, can join. The paper sets out the architecture, storage and discovery layers, and security traits. It also places the service among other emerging agent registries.
arxiv-2509-18887:
The Nordic power market's system price anchors hedge contracts across the region. Yousef Adeli Sadabad and four co-authors build a full framework to explain and forecast that price in this 2025 paper. Good forecasts need the right drivers, and drivers hide in tangled, correlated data. Their pipeline starts with finding those drivers in an interpretable way.

A feature algorithm joins clustering, seasonal decomposition, and a seasonal time series model to name the drivers. A principal component step, tuned to the forecast task, then untangles correlated inputs. A final selection and shrinkage step blends a subset of forecast models with optimal weights. On historical Nordic data, the blend beat every single input model, robustly and by clear margins. It also beat a top transformer forecaster while using simple parts. Cost stayed comparable to standard methods.
arxiv-2509-18987:
Translating speech straight into text in another language skips the step of writing the speech down first. Abderrahmane Issam and three co-authors attack the gap between how speech and text are stored inside such systems. Past methods lined up the two forms word by word, but the tool for that is missing for many languages. A cheaper method based on nearest matches gives sloppy alignments.

The team adapts dynamic time warping, a classic method for lining up two sequences that unfold at different speeds. Applied during training, it matches speech and text forms more accurately. Their system reaches results on par with past work while running much faster. It also beats past methods in most low-resource language pairs, where training data is scarce.
arxiv-2509-19087:
Satellite images that see beyond visible light can identify ice, water, and crops far better than ordinary photos. Ganesh Mallya and six co-authors ask whether a general-purpose AI model, trained only on normal images, can read such multi-spectral data with no extra training. Specialist models for this data are costly to build and maintain. Big general models, meanwhile, cannot take the extra bands as input at all.

Their training-free approach reshapes the spectral data into a form the general model can use, and adds written instructions carrying expert knowledge. They test it with the Gemini 2.5 model on standard land cover and land use benchmarks. The method scored strong zero-shot gains there. The authors argue that specialists in remote sensing can now tap large general models for new sensor data with little setup.
arxiv-2509-19387:
Absence epilepsy announces itself in brain recordings as spike-and-wave discharges, and spotting them in days-long EEG recordings by hand is slow and error-prone. Antonio Quintero Rincon and three co-authors build a light automated detector for those events. A moving-average filter first strips the fast wiggles of normal background activity.
