MSBM stretches a fit loop so each mid snapshot binds the path. The path keeps all mid spreads while it stays smooth end to end. Tests use fake data and real single-cell gene data sets. Scores match or beat past methods at lower cost. True paths help show how cells grow, heal, or sicken.
arxiv-2510-16787:
Philani Rodney Majozi, in a single-author paper, studies modular pseudometric spaces, a flexible generalization of distance used in modern topology and analysis. Building on recent work by Mushaandja and Olela-Otafudu, the paper asks when the topology from a modular matches the uniform topology from its matching pseudometric.

Majozi gives conditions that are both needed and sufficient for the two topologies to agree, stated through a generalized delta condition. Concrete examples show the modular topology can be strictly smaller, so the conditions really matter. The paper also examines completeness, compactness, separability, and countability in these spaces. It links the results to Orlicz-type settings from functional analysis, then closes with categorical and fuzzy viewpoints.
arxiv-2510-17187:
Alexander Aghili and seven co-authors build a shared test yard for protein motion sims in this 2025 paper. New sim methods, some learned by machines, grow faster than shared checks. Scores clash, rare shapes get missed, and runs are hard to repeat. The team wants one fair yardstick for all methods.

Their yard uses weighted group sampling to roam shape space fast. It scores more than nineteen traits and views for each run. Nine proteins, from tiny to large, form the shared test set. Each was run for a long stretch at room heat from many starts. A test with a half-trained learned model shows the yard can spot weak fits.
arxiv-2510-17487:
Persistent gravitational waves, humming steadily rather than chirping once, could come from spinning neutron stars, from distant unresolved mergers, or from the early universe itself. The LIGO Scientific Collaboration, with 1767 co-authors spanning the Virgo and KAGRA collaborations, reports a directional search for such signals. The search uses data from the first observing run through the first part of the fourth, and maps where on the sky any steady power might be coming from.

The team applied radiometer methods to build sky maps for both narrowband and broadband sources, and a spherical harmonic analysis for sources spread across the sky. No persistent signal was found. Instead, the search sets the tightest limits yet on steady gravitational wave emission, including targeted limits for famous sources such as Scorpius X-1 and the remnant of supernova 1987A.
arxiv-2510-17587:
Timur Aslyamov, with Krzysztof Ptaszyński and Massimiliano Esposito, links noise and response in living style networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Many systems sit at a steady state that is not at rest, yet still jitter with random fluctuations. The team derives exact links between that jitter and how the system responds to a small push. Both sides of the link can be measured in experiments.

From those measures, one can rebuild the core parts of the system's linearized dynamics. The authors then apply the theory to gene regulatory networks, which are circuits where genes switch each other on and off. They split the noise spectrum into internal and external parts for any such network. Cross links between genes are included in the split.
arxiv-2510-17887:
Ehsan Roohi and Amirmehran Mahdavi build a fast stand-in model for gas flows through tiny nozzles under thin-air conditions. Such flows form shocks, and slow physics solvers make design work costly. Their system blends a DeepONet operator with features that line up with the shock, guided by the physics of the flow.

Training follows two phases that stress the steep regions near shocks. The team first checks the method on the classic Burgers equation, which also forms sharp fronts. For engineers who shape micro-nozzles, the result points to quick flow guesses that still respect where the shock sits.
arxiv-2510-17987:
Cristiano Ugolini, writing as sole author, traces how the masses of merged black holes take their observed shape. After three observing runs, the catalog is large enough for population patterns to show. The study evolves ten million binary star systems with a fast population code across many metal levels and physics choices.

Nearly a thousand runs test rival rules for dying stars, pair instability, and shared-envelope phases. Single-star physics sets the heavy tail, while binary steps pile black holes into set mass bands. One famous bump near thirty-five solar masses also forms through stable mass transfer alone, a fresh caution for simple readings.
arxiv-2510-18087:
Daniel Israel, with six co-authors, lets a language model plan its own writing order before filling in the text. Word-by-word models are slow in one way, while diffusion models that write many tokens at once need a smart order for revealing them. Fixed rules for that order trade quality against speed.

Under planned diffusion, the model first sketches a plan that splits the answer into independent chunks. It then fills all chunks in parallel. On a standard chat benchmark the approach ran notably faster than plain word-by-word writing. Model builders get a way to let the text decide how it wants to be written.
arxiv-2510-18187:
Fatima AlGhamdi, with five co-authors, detects odd behavior in crowds by tracking each person's speed. Crowd scenes hide people behind each other and mix many motion patterns, which defeats simple detectors. VelocityNet pairs head detection with dense motion flow to extract a personal velocity for everyone visible.

Speeds are grouped into halt, slow, normal, and fast classes, and a percentile score flags departures from learned normal patterns. Experiments show the system catching varied odd motions in dense crowds in real time. Surveillance and safety readers get an interpretable signal, speed itself, instead of a black-box alarm.
arxiv-2510-18287:
Vishal Vinod works on editing three-dimensional faces in a sole-authored 2025 paper on generative models. The task changes traits like glasses, age, hair, or expression while keeping identity intact. Three-dimensional editing is harder than flat photo editing because every view must stay consistent.

Vinod finds directions in latent space, meaning the model's inner code space, that correspond to realistic edits. Ten or fewer labeled examples per trait proved enough to estimate each direction. Tests used synthetic images from a masked face dataset to supply those examples. Sequential edits and a style method for face aging showed the edits behave in a smooth, linear way.
arxiv-2510-18387:
Silvère Ségaud and his six co-authors present a way to measure a glowing drug marker in brain tumors during surgery. The marker, called PpIX, forms inside glioma tumors after patients receive a drug known as 5-ALA, and its glow can help surgeons see tumor tissue. Measuring that glow accurately is hard, because the marker shines in two chemical states with overlapping colors, normal tissue glows faintly too, and tumor tissue distorts light.

The team's pipeline separates the two states of the marker from background glow without needing their spectra in advance, then corrects for how tissue bends the light at each color. To test the method fairly, they built fake tissue samples that copy both the optical behavior of glioma and the marker's changing glow. Results tracked the true marker amounts closely, pointing toward more reliable readings in the clinic.
arxiv-2510-18587:
Joe Williams and his four co-authors model icy pebbles in a young disk around a forming star system. Pebbles grow and drift inward there. Each chemical leaves a pebble at its own snowline, the distance where it turns to gas. But lab work and telescope data hint at mixed ices. Carbon monoxide can stay trapped in water ice, well past its own snowline.

Their model is the first to join growth and drift with that trapping. Up to about sixty percent of the carbon monoxide stays locked. It escapes only when the water ice breaks down at a much warmer front. Over a million years, trapping raised gas-phase carbon and oxygen ratios a lot. Inside the water snowline, some ratios rose up to ten times. More carbon can reach the inner disk that way, while much water remains. The mix of planet-building material changes as a result.
arxiv-2510-18887:
L. Yildiz, D. Kayki, and E. Gudekli set out a new wave equation. It blends a few effects and keeps strict laws of conservation. The name is the Resonant Weighted Nonlocal Schrödinger equation. It joins weighted local spread with nonlocal exchange. A phase drive with zero mean is added. By design, it keeps mass exactly. With no drive, it has a Hamiltonian form and keeps energy.

Under standard terms, solutions exist for a short time span. Terms for them to last for all time are also given. A linear study shows how each part shifts wave speeds. Two probes are defined to split those shifts apart. Plans are sketched for optical lattices. Plans for cold-atom setups with cavities are sketched too. Links to phase marks in space media are also noted.
arxiv-2510-19187:
Zi-Yun Chen, Zhi-Yi Wu, and Min-Min Zhang study spectra of self-affine measures. A spectrum is a special set of frequencies. It lets a measure be expanded in a Fourier-like way. Older work showed the dimension of such sets is flexible. It can take values in between.

The authors prove density and dimension can be set at once. Any allowed pair of values can be hit. They build a spectrum for each target pair. That full freedom shows how loose the link is. The spectrum is only weakly tied to the measure itself. The result sharpens fractal Fourier theory.
arxiv-2510-19787: Manuel Kauers and Isaac Wood continue a line of work that bounds the tensor rank of matrix multiplication by exploring flip graphs, combinatorial structures whose moves connect different multiplication schemes. Lower rank means fewer multiplications for the same task, so each improved bound sharpens what is known about fast matrix multiplication. The authors report improved rank bounds for about thirty matrix formats.
arxiv-2510-19887:
Télio Cropsal and Rocío Mercado run the first full check of whether the Stable Diffusion image model's autoencoder can compress microscopy images from drug screens without losing biology. Phenotypic screens produce huge image collections. A compact form would help generative modeling. The open question is whether a model trained on plain photographs understands cell images.

Across a large dataset with many molecular perturbations and cell types, the reconstructions kept the phenotypic signal with minimal loss. The authors compared ways of scoring rebuild quality: at the pixel, embedding, latent, and retrieval levels. General-purpose feature extractors such as InceptionV3 matched or beat bespoke microscopy models at retrieval. That result could simplify pipelines for phenotypic drug discovery.
arxiv-2510-20487:
Tim Tian Hua and three co-authors show that activation steering can stop a language model from behaving differently when it thinks it is being evaluated. Models that detect evaluation cues may act more aligned under test, which undermines safety evaluations. To study the effect in a controlled way, the team first trained a model to be evaluation-aware, using documents describing the behavior followed by expert iteration training.

The trained model writes Python type hints in evaluation contexts but not in deployment contexts, exactly the planted tell. A steering vector built from the original model before that extra training then suppresses the evaluation awareness, making the model act during evaluation as it would when deployed. The authors suggest evaluators could use steering to improve safety test reliability.
arxiv-2510-20587:
Moslem Zarei and three co-authors analyze whether gravity can entangle two remote fermionic qubits, using the quantum Boltzmann equation with a graviton propagator as the mediator. The qubits sit in spatial superposition states, and any entanglement generated this way could in principle evidence the quantization of gravity. Treating the qubits as spin-half particles in wave packets, they trace the entanglement to forward scattering processes involving graviton exchange.

Two explicit microscopic models are examined in both a static limit and a dynamical limit of the propagator. Entangled states can be generated only in the dynamical limit, a sharp dividing line between the two regimes. The effect also weakens as the wave packet size grows, which the authors note as a practical constraint on any future test.
arxiv-2510-20887:
Anujraaj Argo Goyal leads ten co-authors on a counterintuitive fix for adapter training in personalized image generation, giving the adapter the very shortcuts it should ignore. Adapters learn a target trait such as identity from single images, but they also absorb pose, expression, and lighting that happen to be in the training photo.

That entanglement weakens prompt following and harms generalization to new scenes. By supplying the incidental factors explicitly during training, the adapter no longer needs to smuggle them into the target trait. Tests show cleaner separation of identity from pose and light, so generated images track the text prompt more faithfully while keeping the person recognizable.
arxiv-2510-20987:
V A Chizhikov and one co-author develop a theory of elastic moduli for the cubic blue phases of cholesteric liquid crystals at low chirality. Blue phases are periodic chiral liquids whose lattice like order gives them elastic responses akin to crystals, used in fast switching displays.

A rigid tensor approximation, sound at low chirality, is used to compute moduli for the two observed phases known as BPI and BPII. In the one constant approximation for the underlying Frank moduli, explicit forms follow. The results help predict how blue phase materials deform under fields and stress, a design input for photonic and display uses.
arxiv-2510-21087:
Anubhav Jangra and one co-author design and evaluate chain of hints for scientific question answering, so tutoring systems guide students instead of handing over answers. General chat models tend to reveal solutions outright, weakening conceptual learning even when answers are correct.

Eighteen open source models are tested on generating hint chains that scaffold learners toward the answer. Static hints written per problem are compared with dynamic hints adapted to learner progress, across five teaching criteria. The study maps which models hint well, informing educational tools that preserve student effort and thinking.
arxiv-2510-21187:
Tsun Hin Navin Tsung and three co-authors simulate energy loss in plasma. Plasma is a hot gas whose particles carry charge. Their plasma lacks collisions, moves near light speed, and sits in a magnetic field. Shear means layers slide past, or field lines tilt sharply.

Only two instabilities can grow; a third, tearing, is forbidden. An instability is a small disturbance that grows over time. Kelvin-Helmholtz instability grows where flow layers slide past. Drift-Kink instability grows where magnetic shear bends a layer. Together, they thicken the layer and form swirling vortices. The mixed case loses far more energy than either shear alone. Particles gain energy as they wander in an S shaped path. A moving electric field boosts them as they cross. Most top energy particles came from this wandering process. This may matter for sheaths around active galaxy jets.
arxiv-2510-21487:
Jun Dai and four co-authors read the magnetic skeleton of a quiet solar prominence from the way it swayed. A prominence is a cool cloud of gas hanging in the Sun's corona. A collision with a hot neighboring structure set it swinging lengthwise. Two coronal jets were tied to that structure. The swing had a period of about seventy-seven minutes.

The team combines images and spectra taken in end view. They track two signal groups with matched timing. The initial swing spans forty million meters, with speeds near fifty kilometers per second. Two separate methods convert the motion into the bend of the magnetic dips cradling the gas. Both give dip radii growing from ninety to two hundred twenty million meters before shrinking again. The sideways field measures near twenty-five gauss. The dips trace a smooth sinusoidal shape.
arxiv-2510-21687:
Bogdan-Vasile Matioc and Christoph Walker solve a detective problem for heat-like equations. The task is to recover the starting state of a system from averages of its behavior over time. The equations are quasilinear parabolic. That means their diffusion strength depends on the state itself. The class covers chemical and biological spreading processes.

Under mild conditions on the equation's structure, they prove the starting state is uniquely fixed by small time averages. The growth condition on the reaction part near zero is part of those conditions. The observation window can be any time period at all. That turns a weak measurement into a full fingerprint of the start. Two families of examples show the result at work. They are chemotaxis models, where organisms chase chemical signals, and reaction-diffusion systems.
arxiv-2510-21887:
Shamim Yazdani leads a nine-author survey of generative artificial intelligence, the model family behind synthetic images, video, and text. With research, uses, and open problems all growing fast, the authors set out to organize the field so newcomers and practitioners can see how the pieces fit together.

The survey builds a taxonomy covering the three main model families, adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models, along with their many variants and hybrids. It traces the innovations that improved output quality, variety, and control, and catalogs real-world uses across domains. Ethical concerns raised by systems that can fabricate convincing content receive direct attention as well. The result is a map of a fast-moving area, including the technical challenges still unresolved.
arxiv-2510-22087:
Shvetank Prakash leads a twenty-seven-author team grading language models in computer architecture. The field links software ideas to working hardware. It has been absent from model evaluations until now. No shared measure existed for processor design, memory systems, or interconnects.

Their benchmark, QuArch, holds two thousand six hundred seventy-one expert-checked question pairs. Frontier models clearly carry book knowledge of the field. Yet accuracy on higher-order thinking swings widely. It runs from about a third to nearly three quarters of questions. Analysis, design, and implementation items expose the deepest gaps. Fine-tuning tests show the benchmark can also teach. The authors offer QuArch as shared ground for a specialty models had entered untested.
arxiv-2510-22387:
Nader Nemati presents a privacy aware way to turn paper ECG pages into digital signals without pooling patient images in one place. Training happens across sites, each keeping its own scans, while a shared segmentation model learns from all of them. Sites differ in layout, grid style, scanner traits, and noise, which makes joint training hard.

The setup tests three rules for merging site updates and adds secure aggregation plus user level noise for privacy. On ECG pages made from a public data set, the adaptive merging rule converged faster and came close to central training. Raw images and single site updates stayed hidden.
arxiv-2510-22487:
Quin Aicken Davies and C Clare Worley, in a 2025 paper, test whether starlight can reveal the mix of magnesium isotopes inside cool stars. Isotopes are versions of an element with different weights, and their ratios record which past stellar events made the material. The signal comes from magnesium hydride features in star spectra.

Using spectrum synthesis, meaning building model spectra to match real ones, the pair check eight stars from type M to type G. Seven of ten known spectral regions prove reliable for the task. Their measured ratios match some expected patterns, and europium amounts track the magnesium results closely.
arxiv-2510-22687:
Finsler geometry lets length depend on the way you face, not just where you are. Teresa Arias-Marco and Zdenek Dusek wrote a 2025 paper in that field. They give a new sense to the term naturally reductive for such spaces. Their tool is the geodesic graph. Those graphs encode the paths that act as straight lines.

The pair build on their own past work. They study Finsler metrics that come from Riemannian metrics. Riemannian metrics are the more standard kind. Clear examples of pure Finsler cases are built. Some mix a Riemannian part with one forms. Graphs are also mapped for wide classes that lack the trait. The one forms change how the straight paths run.
arxiv-2510-22787:
Drawing software architecture by hand is slow and manual. The C4 model is a common way to show such structure. Kamil Szczepanik and Jaroslaw A Chudziak automate that task in 2025. They use several language model agents. Each agent plays a role specific expert.

The agents debate requirements in dialogue form. They then build Context, Container, and Component views. Quality checks mix two styles. Fixed checks test structure, syntax, and C4 rules. A model judge scores meaning and quality. Five classic system briefs were tested. Model creation was fast with high compile success. Four leading models showed distinct design strengths.
arxiv-2510-22887:
Bounds for curved surfaces can fail at a critical phase. Arunima Bhattacharya, Ravi Shankar, and Jeremy Wall wrote a 2025 paper on that case. Their equation is the Lagrangian mean curvature equation. It is set in two dimensions. In their case, the phase changes sign. Its slope is zero where the phase is zero.

At the critical phase, a key inequality breaks down. Methods from higher dimensions then fail. The team use a new doubling trick. It works even when that inequality is weak. With it, they prove interior bounds on slopes. They prove bounds on second derivatives too. The work deals with the valued Lagrangian phase. It opens a path past a long block in this field.
arxiv-2510-22987:
Mahsa Tavakoli, Rohitash Chandra, and Cristian Bravo propose judging mortgage risk from free public data instead of costly private records. Standard scoring leans on structured financial data that is often secret and expensive. Their framework instead fuses text, images, and sentiment scores from open sources.

First they pick the best model for each data type, using BERT for text and VGG for images, plus a small network for sentiment. A capsule network then merges those signals into a credit score meant to mimic commercial scorecards. The approach could widen fair access to risk checks where records are scarce.
arxiv-2510-23187:
Mushal Zia, Faisal Suwayyid, and Guo-Wei Wei bring graded Betti numbers from commutative algebra into machine learning for biological data. Persistent homology is widely used to describe data shape through Betti numbers. Persistent commutative algebra goes further, giving algebraic invariants plus graded Betti numbers, yet those richer numbers had rarely touched real data.

Their GBNL framework learns from graded Betti numbers of complex biological data sets. The authors present it as the first such application in data science. Extra algebraic detail may reveal structure in molecules and cells that plain topology misses, aiding drug and disease studies.
arxiv-2510-23287:
The KM3NeT collaboration, as sole author, asks whether the most energetic neutrino ever seen could be cosmogenic in origin. In February 2023 the ARCA telescope recorded a track consistent with a muon of about one hundred twenty petaelectronvolts, born from an even more energetic neutrino. The implied flux hints at a new diffuse component.

Cosmogenic neutrinos should arise when ultra-high-energy cosmic rays hit ambient photons and matter. The authors show the reported flux level can match that origin only after integrating the flux in a specific way. Their check weighs a standard explanation before invoking exotic sources.
arxiv-2510-23587:
Yizhang Zhu and twenty-four co-authors survey data agents, AI systems meant to run data work on their own, and ask whether the field is a real shift or hype. The label covers everything from simple query answerers to near-autonomous systems, which blurs what buyers should expect and who answers when things go wrong. Borrowing the SAE levels for driving automation, the authors bring order to the confusion.

Their scheme sets six levels, from fully manual work at level zero to a vision of fully autonomous agents at level five. Through that lens they review research on agents for data management, preparation, and analysis, plus early general-purpose systems. They spotlight the jump from level two to level three, where agents stop merely carrying out steps and start directing whole jobs. The survey closes with a roadmap toward proactive agents and the gaps still blocking them.
arxiv-2510-24087:
Yingying Zhou and four co-authors apply object detection models to a hard task in space astronomy: reading slitless spectra. The China Space Station Telescope will take images where spectra overlap and their place is uncertain. Old step by step methods build up errors as they extract and sort these traces.

Their framework uses YOLO models to find, sort, and study traces directly from raw two dimensional images. YOLOv5 finds both compact and stretched traces even in crowded fields, while YOLO11 adds source sorting and rough estimates of traits like redshift. The system works fast on large images and can spot quasars, showing an end to end path with little manual work.
arxiv-2510-24187:
Lucas Lévy and three co-authors present a unified framework for adversarial linear bandits, a setting where a learner picks actions and sees only partial feedback. The framework bridges two classic families of methods, those that follow a regularized leader and those that follow a perturbed leader, extending a known link between them. Within it, they introduce self-concordant perturbations.

These random perturbations play the role that self-concordant barriers played in an earlier regularized algorithm. The new perturbed leader method pairs this regularization with efficient random exploration. It achieves a regret rate on both the hypercube and the Euclidean ball that matches the best known rate on the ball, up to logarithmic factors.
arxiv-2510-24487:
Konstantinos Konstantos and Pavlos Motakis, two authors, study a family of Banach spaces. Banach spaces are complete spaces where length and distance work well. The Bourgain-Rosenthal-Schechtman spaces form a tall ladder of such spaces. Each space has a basis built from martingale steps, like fair-game sums. The pair block that basis into chunks with strong copying traits.

These chunks form a finite-dimensional decomposition, a split into small blocks. The split supports maps that copy one space's patterns into another. With those maps, each operator on a limit space can be simplified. An operator is a rule that sends each point to a new point. Up to any set precision, it becomes a plain diagonal rule. A factorization trait for the basis follows from the result.
arxiv-2510-24787:
Mingzhi Zhu, Ding Shang, and Sai Qian Zhang speed up photo real face avatars for use in virtual worlds. Such avatars use deep models to render a true to life face, but head sets have tight limits on time and power. Their frame, ESCA, joins a leaner model with a chip made for the task.

A post train squeeze step cuts the model's number size with no loss in face grade. The chip then runs that lean model fast on the head set's main board. Tests showed grade gains on a known face video score, plus large cuts in wait and power. The stack aims to make live talk in virtual space feel smooth.
arxiv-2510-25087:
Nourah M Salem, Elizabeth White, Michael Bada, and Lawrence Hunter test chat models on link work in health texts: which words point back to the same thing. Such texts brim with hard terms, vague short forms, and long gaps between linked words. Their bench is a known health text set, CRAFT.

Four prompt styles were tried, from plain to rich with text cues and term lists. Gauge was set next to a span based code tool for a fair match. Chat models showed strong top level link skill, more so with term based prompts. But long range links and vague forms still tripped them. Two Llama sizes led on the joint score.
arxiv-2510-25187:
Ritesh Sunil Chavan and Jack Mostow test how well chat models read text across tongues, by which line comes next. Training data for such models leans hard to English, so high scores may show data wealth more than true skill. Their test puts models where that wealth runs out: low resource tongues.

They built a large bench with ten thousand asks each in English, Swahili, and Hausa. Top models were run on all three. All did well in English, less well in Swahili, and far less in Hausa, with one model hit most hard. Step thought prompts helped the weak model in the low tongues, a split the team flags.
arxiv-2510-25387:
Bill Psomas led seven co-authors on composed image retrieval. George Retsinas, Nikos Efthymiadis, and Panagiotis Filntisis helped. Yannis Avrithis, Petros Maragos, and Ondrej Chum joined. Giorgos Tolias closes the eight-author team. Their 2025 paper mixes visual and textual queries. Retrieval must find the same particular object instance.

Current datasets focus on semantic class definitions instead. Their new i-CIR dataset uses instance-level definitions. Text queries describe modifications to the pictured object. Hard negatives were selected semi-automatically for challenge. The compact set rivals searching forty million distractors. Clean training data are hard to obtain here. Their BASIC method works training-free with pretrained models. It values image and text similarities separately. Late fusion upweights images satisfying both queries. Images matching only one query are downweighted. BASIC set new leading results on i-CIR. It also led on current composed retrieval datasets.
arxiv-2510-25687:
Mallika Prabhakar, Louise Xu, and Prateek Saxena study model inversion and fuzzy extractors. Their 2025 paper defends privacy in machine learning systems. Model inversion attacks reconstruct data from model outputs. Face authentication systems compute embedding vectors from images. Leaked vectors let attackers reconstruct user faces accurately. Fuzzy extractors are cryptographic primitives that could defend.

They offer attack-agnostic security without retraining models. No systematic cryptanalysis of noise-tolerant schemes existed. Modern face recognition needs extractors tolerating L2 noise. They perform first in-depth security study of schemes. Current schemes offer weak security, they show. End-to-end inversion attacks reach high success rates. Faces meant to be protected get recovered. They offer a simple new candidate scheme instead. Its security is proved formally in the paper. The construction offers useful runtime and stronger security. Usable quality for commodity face authentication is maintained. Privacy-sensitive uses gain a better design point.
arxiv-2510-25887:
Franc Forstneric and Alfheidur Edda Sigurdardottir prove an Oka principle for families of complex manifolds that vary over a parameter space. Stein manifolds are a flexible class of complex spaces, and Oka theory says that for suitable targets, continuous maps can be deformed into holomorphic maps, which obey strict complex rules. Here the complex structure itself changes with a parameter, so the maps must vary in step.

The authors call a family tame when convex hulls vary in a controlled, upper semicontinuous way. Under that condition, any family of continuous maps can be deformed into a family of holomorphic maps. They also prove matching results for vector bundle sections and for bundle types, and they note that families over an open surface are always tame.
arxiv-2510-25987:
Kevin Phan, William Mitchell, David Chaparro, Enrique De Alba, and J. Zachary Gazak extend a standard star identification tool with color information from hyperspectral images. Lost in space algorithms find a spacecraft orientation by matching a photographed star field to a catalog, using only the geometric pattern of stars. That pattern can be ambiguous when few stars are visible or the field is cluttered.

Phan and the team add each star spectral type, its class based on light color and lines, as an extra matching clue from the hyperspectral sensor. The added clue narrows the search and raises specificity, so good solutions appear with far fewer stars. Fit rates improved and failures fell, which matters for autonomous space awareness and traffic management.
arxiv-2510-26187:
Mohammed Rafiq Namiq, working alone, introduces a new class of modules in order free algebra that widens two known families. The setting is a order free Noetherian local ring, a ring with a single maximal ideal and a finiteness condition. A module is called initially Cohen Macaulay when its depth, a measure of how many regular elements can act in sequence. That depth equals its initial dimension, a new invariant built from the coheights of its associated primes.

Namiq develops the theory with homology based, counting based, and shape based descriptions, and checks fit with regular sequences, local study, and dimension layerings. Applied to simplex based structures, the theory yields counterparts of classic results by Reisner, Eagon and Reiner, and Duval. He also sorts certain graph cases of interest.
arxiv-2510-26287:
Guochang Li leads nine co-authors in a training framework for agents that answer questions about a whole code repository. Repository level tasks force a language model to navigate a complex codebase through many tool interactions, and training free prompting guides such agents poorly. Training based routes often distill a larger model, which is costly and raises data compliance concerns in firms.

Their framework, RepoSearch-R1, uses reinforcement learning driven by Monte Carlo tree search, a search method that explores action paths by simulation. The agent can then generate diverse, high quality reasoning trajectories by self training. No distillation or external supervision is needed. A RepoQA-Agent built on it shows substantial improvement on repository question answering in their evaluation.
arxiv-2510-26387:
Konstantin von Beringe and Mark Whitmeyer ask how much a policy change helps or hurts when a market is not fully known. In markets with weak competition, firms have market power, and the effect of a policy runs through pass-through, the share of a cost change that lands in prices. The pair study welfare, the gains split between buyers and sellers.

Von Beringe and Whitmeyer allow ranges for both pass-through and firm conduct, then use two snapshots of the market to find the worst and best cases. They show the extremes come from simple pass-through rules that take just one of the two end values, split by a single price cutoff. Adding shape limits on demand gives plain bounds for buyer gain, seller gain, total gain, and waste.
arxiv-2510-26487:
Wajdi Hammami, Soumaya Cherkaoui, Jean-Frederic Laprade, Ola Ahmad, and Shengrui Wang design a quantum tool to spot odd behaviour in network traffic. Finding anomalies in time series matters for security, but quantum machine learning tools are held back by small qubit counts. Their system aims to catch attacks both fast and well.

Hammami and his four co-authors pair a quantum gated recurrent unit with a generative adversarial network, two models that learn by competing. The quantum generator outputs the centre and spread of a Gaussian curve, and a gating step flags suspects by uncertainty, then confirms them with critic scores and rebuild errors. On benchmark data, the method reached a time-aware F1 score near eighty-nine percent, beating classical and quantum rivals. It also kept its form when run on real IBM quantum hardware.
arxiv-2510-26687:
Caeley V Pittman, with five co-authors, finds that young stars' magnetic axes are aligned across parsecs in the Lupus star-forming region. A star's magnetosphere shapes how gas falls onto it, and its tilt may be set by the cloud that bore it. How far that influence reaches was not well constrained.

Pittman and the team report the first evidence for spatial correlations of magnetospheric inclinations at parsec scale, about three parsecs across. A density-based clustering method shows the pattern holds up against measurement uncertainty. The scale matches the filaments of the Lupus cloud. The authors link the pattern to expanding shells from nearby star groups and to cores stretched along filament axes. If such tilts are non-uniform, counts of exoplanets could be biased, so the longevity of the effect matters.
arxiv-2510-26787:
Mantas Mazeika, with forty-six co-authors, introduces the Remote Labor Index, a benchmark of real remote work. AI has raced ahead on research benchmarks of knowledge and reasoning, but how those gains translate into economic value is unclear. The index gathers real-world, economically valuable projects across many sectors and asks AI agents to complete them end to end.

Mazeika and the team find agents perform near the floor: the best agent reached an automation rate of two and a half percent. That stark result grounds talk about AI automation in evidence rather than hype. The authors offer the index as a shared yardstick for tracking AI's impact over time. It is meant to help stakeholders navigate labour automation before it arrives, rather than after.
arxiv-2510-26887:
Francisco Villaescusa-Navarro, with thirty-five co-authors, presents Denario, a multi-agent AI system built to assist scientific research. Denario can generate ideas, check the literature, develop research plans, write and execute code, make plots, and draft and review papers. Its modular architecture lets it handle single tasks or run end-to-end analysis through a deep-research backend.

Villaescusa-Navarro and the team describe the system and its modules in detail, then showcase complete AI-generated papers across ten fields, from astrophysics to planetary science. One paper mixes quantum physics and machine learning methods on astrophysical data. Domain experts scored and reviewed the outputs, and the authors report strengths, weaknesses, and limits frankly. They close with ethical implications and the philosophy of science, and they release the code publicly.
arxiv-2510-27587:
Anish Ghoshal, Paweł Kozów, Marek Olechowski, and Stefan Pokorski set out a method in 2025 to test early-universe models with sky data. Inflation is a brief, fast stretch of space just after the start, which sets the seeds of galaxies. The heat left when that phase ends is called the reheat temperature, and it can also govern how dark matter forms.

All model inputs are first written in terms of three traits seen in the faint glow left from the early universe. The reheat heat is then fixed by those same traits. Tight bounds on that heat thus turn into narrow allowed ranges for a key trait. The plan is shown on a broad class of stretch models.
arxiv-2511-00087:
Anshu Dubey and Akash Dhruv propose a methodology for adding genuinely new algorithmic capability to an existing scientific application with language model assistance. Code generation research mostly tests tasks with prior examples in training data; a new algorithm has none. Their approach writes code from scratch for a new algorithm, and extends their earlier code translation tool to support new code generation.

Scientific software readers get a workflow for the hardest assistance case, where the model cannot copy a remembered solution. Legacy scientific codes must keep growing to stay useful, and trustworthy AI help with novel algorithms could change their economics.
arxiv-2511-00487:
Stephen Meisenbacher and Florian Matthes argue that size matters in private text rewriting, and that evaluations have ignored it. Differentially private rewriting scrambles text so individuals cannot be identified, and many promising mechanisms exist. Yet tests usually run on modest datasets, leaving open how the privacy-utility trade-off shifts as collections grow toward real-world scale.

The authors design utility and privacy tests on datasets of varying size, up to one million texts, with dynamic splits. Their runs show dataset size plays an integral role in judging any rewriting mechanism: verdicts at small scale need not hold at large scale. The findings call for more rigorous evaluation habits in private language processing, and they map where the field must look as deployment at scale approaches.
arxiv-2511-00687:
Ivan Smiljanić, Ivanka Božović, Ivana Vidaković, Nataša Vukašinović, and Goran Kačarević chase a subtle systematic effect in a future measurement. The target is the integrated luminosity at the CEPC collider's Z pole, at one part in ten thousand precision. Counting Bhabha scattering events in a luminometer delivers that number, but the electromagnetic fields of the incoming bunches bend the very particles being counted.

Two deflection effects are separated: fields acting on the initial electrons and positrons, and fields acting on the final state particles. Both shift particle momenta and change the counted Bhabha rate. Simulations quantify each effect and its stability as beam parameters wobble. The authors also discuss, at a conceptual level, correction methods built on measurements the CEPC detector itself can make, keeping the precision goal credible.
arxiv-2511-00787:
Angelot Behajaina, Roghayeh Maleki, and Razafimahatratra study a quantity called intersection density for certain symmetry groups. For a group acting on a set, the quantity compares the largest families of group elements that pairwise agree somewhere against the size of a point stabilizer.

They fully determine this density for the groups PSL2(q), where q is a power of an odd prime, when the stabilizers are cyclic of prime order p. Their proof builds an auxiliary graph whose cliques match the intersecting families they want to measure. For a second family of stabilizers, they show the graph is not regular and construct an intersecting set that is sometimes as large as possible.
arxiv-2511-01087:
Md. Abid Hasan Rafi, Mst. Fatematuj Johora, and Pankaj Bhowmik release SliceVision-F2I, a synthetic data set for studying network slices through pictures. Network slicing, central to 5G and 6G services, needs reliable ways to identify slice states, and visual methods need data to train and test on.

Each sample pairs a vector of network performance indicators with a color image encoding it. Four encoding schemes are used, based on physical mappings, Perlin noise, neural wallpapering, and fractal branching, with thirty thousand samples per scheme at low resolution. Noise and realistic imperfections are added deliberately. The data set suits visual learning, network state classification, anomaly detection, and benchmarking of image based methods on network data, and it is publicly available.
arxiv-2511-01187:
Muhammed Saeed, Muhammad Abdul-Mageed, and Shady Shehata test whether large language models reproduce subtle stereotypes when they write freely, not just when they classify. Most bias tests are English only and classification based, missing how narrative bias appears in realistic generated text.

Their benchmark uses structured debate prompts, eighty four hundred of them. The prompts span four sensitive domains: women's rights, backwardness, terrorism, and religion. They run across seven languages, from English and Chinese to Swahili and Nigerian Pidgin. Four flagship models produced over one hundred thousand responses, which were sorted by which groups received stereotyped versus modern roles. All models reproduced entrenched stereotypes, and the bias grew sharply in lower resource languages, suggesting safety alignment trained mainly in English does not travel well.
arxiv-2511-01387:
Hajar Assil, Abderrahim El Allati, and Gian Luca Giorgi estimate entanglement with a quantum extreme learning machine. In that scheme a fixed quantum reservoir does the processing, and only a simple output layer is trained. Their target is the Werner states, a standard family of two qubit states mixing a maximally entangled state with noise.

The protocol generates a sequence of random Werner states, combines them with a reservoir state, and evolves the whole under an Ising Hamiltonian. Measurements in the Bloch basis supply the features used to train the readout to recognize entanglement in unseen states. The authors test robustness by adding noise to the inputs, and they study how the magnetic field parameter in the Hamiltonian affects the estimation accuracy.
arxiv-2511-01487:
Xiaoyi Wang, Jixuan Liu, and Long Feng develop tests for detecting change points, moments when a time series' behavior shifts, in data with very many variables tracked over time. Their starting test uses a maximum L2-norm statistic, which performs strongly when the change is spread densely across many variables.

Sparse changes, concentrated in a few variables, are better caught by other statistics based on the maximum coordinate. The authors prove their statistic is asymptotically independent of two such existing statistics, which lets them merge all three with the Cauchy combination method into one adaptive procedure. The combined test stays robust whether the change is dense or sparse, and simulations plus a real-data analysis confirm its advantage in high-dimensional settings.
arxiv-2511-01687:
The ANTARES Collaboration, with Pedro De la Torre Luque and colleagues, mines fifteen years of data from the ANTARES neutrino telescope. They hunt a glow that should come from home: diffuse neutrinos. These are produced when cosmic rays strike interstellar matter in the Milky Way. The full all-flavor dataset spans 2007 to 2022.

Emission models differ in how cosmic rays diffuse, where their sources sit, and how dense the target gas is. A maximum-likelihood template method compares each model's predicted spatial and energy patterns with the observed neutrino events. The data did not yield stringent constraints on the models, so the team derives upper limits on the diffuse Galactic neutrino flux, compatible with what other experiments have found. The search still sharpens the tools for reading cosmic ray propagation from neutrinos.
arxiv-2511-02787:
Vladimir Golubinskii and Vladimir Zyuzin study magnets that order in opposite directions on two sublattices yet still bend electric current. That bending, the anomalous Hall effect, was long tied to net magnetization, which these compensated antiferromagnets lack. Their 2025 paper builds minimal models, mostly in two dimensions on a square lattice, to find when the effect can appear.

They give concrete cases: a Neel-ordered ferrimagnet, a weak ferromagnet of the Dzyaloshinskii type, and a rutile lattice magnet. Using Dzyaloshinskii's symmetry rules, they test when spontaneous magnetization is allowed, then confirm the rules with Berry curvature calculations. The effect arises when momentum-dependent exchange meets the Neel order together with spin-orbit coupling, all rooted in broken symmetries.
arxiv-2511-02987:
Randon Weaver, Robert Coulter, and Alice Hui classify certain geometric designs inside finite planes built from nearfields. A unital is a set of points that meets every line in a fixed number of points, a tidy pattern used in finite geometry. Their 2025 paper treats parabolic unitals in regular nearfield planes of odd order, where the order is a square.

They classify fully those unitals whose symmetry group, the linear collineation group, reaches the largest possible size. Weaker assumptions yield several more general results about parabolic unitals in the same planes. Classifications like this matter because nearfield planes are among the few non-classical planes known, and their highly symmetric designs are rare objects that anchor wider theory.
arxiv-2511-03187:
Jonghae Park and five colleagues teach robots skills that repeat in cycles, like walking and hurdling, without any reward signal. Skill discovery methods usually chase variety alone and miss rhythm, yet locomotion is periodic at many time scales. Their 2025 framework, Periodic Skill Discovery, trains an encoder that maps states onto a circle, so repeating behavior lands naturally on repeating points of the latent space.

Because the encoder captures time gaps, the agent learns cycles of many periods, even from raw camera pixels. The learned skills scored well on downstream tasks such as hurdling. Bolted onto an existing discovery method, the framework widened the skill set further. The team links the work to a broader point: structure in the latent space shapes what an agent can discover.
arxiv-2511-03587:
Howard E Bond and co-authors report deep images of a faint bow-shock nebula around the variable star FY Vulpeculae. The star belongs to the Z Camelopardalis class of cataclysmic variables, where a white dwarf feeds from a companion. Long exposures with amateur telescopes and modern cameras revealed the surrounding glow, cataloged as StDr 90.

A bright bow shock shines in oxygen light ahead of the star as it plows through a dense patch of interstellar gas. Nearby, a wide faint hydrogen glow reads as a wake of gas recombining after the star's ultraviolet light ionized it. FY Vul joins only five other such variables known with bow shocks. Citizen-scale telescopes reaching this depth widen the hunt for faint stellar surroundings.
arxiv-2511-03687:
Safoura Mirkhalaf, Helmut Ritsch, and Karol Gietka argue that plain frequency shifts in two coupled oscillators betray deep quantum links. Folklore says two linearly coupled oscillators in their ground state show nothing quantum beyond discrete energies. The authors show their everyday, classical-looking observables tell another story.

Shifts in the coupled frequencies signal non-classical correlations and true ground-state entanglement at zero temperature. In one mode picture the effect reads as squeezing between the uncoupled modes, while in another it reads as a mere spectral shift. Both views describe one phenomenon wearing two descriptions. Listening to frequencies thus becomes a quiet probe of entanglement, with no exotic measurement needed.
arxiv-2511-03787:
Sebastiano Cantarella is the lead author among seven authors testing the GAEA galaxy formation model against early-universe observations from the James Webb Space Telescope. Run on merger trees from a large N-body simulation, GAEA is checked on galaxy counts and brightness at the highest redshifts yet observed.

GAEA matches the stellar mass function to about redshift thirteen and the combined galaxy and active nucleus brightness function to about redshift ten. Active nuclei matter at the bright end up to redshift eight. Beyond redshift eleven, observed brightness exceeds the model by at least tenfold. Feedback-free starbursts in dense clouds can close that gap, though they raise tensions with metal content data.
arxiv-2511-04087:
Ge Zhang is the lead author among eight authors on E-CARE, a framework that brings language model commonsense into e-commerce recommendation without paying for live model calls or human labels. Matching user queries to products drives shopping and revenue, and commonsense links between queries and products have recently improved that matching, at high cost.

A reasoning factor graph stores most of the reasoning schema drawn from powerful language models, so recommendation models can use it at inference without real-time decoding. Neither supervised fine-tuning nor human annotation is required. Experiments on two downstream tasks improved precision at five by up to about twelve percent in the reported figures, showing efficiency and accuracy can rise together.
arxiv-2511-04387:
Franziska Kühn leads eight authors studying how magnons flow toward a Bose-Einstein condensate. Magnons are waves of magnetic excitation, and they can gather into a shared quantum state. The team pumped magnons into thin films of yttrium iron garnet at set angles.

They combined theory and experiment to trace the transfer step by step. One path is a gradual cascade that works at all field values. Another path uses a kinetic instability that can speed the flow under set conditions. Knowing which path dominates helps physicists control these condensates, which are test beds for quantum effects at room temperature.
arxiv-2511-04787:
Bradley E. Schaefer, writing alone, catalogs white dwarf masses for more than two hundred novae. The catalog gathers two hundred eight mass measures for Galactic nova white dwarfs. It also holds two hundred thirty-two average quiescent brightness values across four hundred two known novae.

Mass emerges as the main driver of both spectral and light-curve class. A clean cutoff near ninety-five percent of a solar mass splits the light-curve families. Spectral class flips near one point fifteen solar masses between iron and helium types. Speed of decline follows a tight formula in the mass, turning the catalog into a predictive tool.
arxiv-2511-04887:
Fei Yin leads nine authors studying motor cortex dynamics while people steer a brain-machine interface. The cortex is often pictured as an autonomous system during movement. Flexible motion then comes from setting start conditions that unwind along fixed dynamics.

Whether that picture holds during interface control was an open question. Cursor movements here lasted from hundreds of milliseconds to several seconds. Motions in one direction shared their starting neural state across durations. Long movements held their patterns in ways the team tracks in detail. The results test dynamical theories of motor control in a setting that assistive technology depends on.
arxiv-2511-05187:
Kamil Ciosek and co-authors ask if idle inference chips can cut the cost of training a language model. Training needs scarce, pricey graphics chips, while inference fleets often sit idle, an imbalance their method tries to exploit.

Their algorithm guesses gradients with a cheap, low-precision program much like inference work. A few exact gradients then correct those guesses, so error turns into variance, not bias. On a model with 124 million parameters, in short test windows, the plan lowered a simulated cost ledger. All tests ran on a normal chip, with fleet billing faked in the ledger.
arxiv-2511-05787:
Hao Yang and co-authors uncover an unusual spin-orbit effect in ordinary semiconductor structures. Spin-orbit coupling links an electron's motion to its spin, and it is textbook knowledge that the effect appears as odd functions of momentum. The Dresselhaus form of the coupling is a standard example.

Through model calculations and symmetry analysis, the team shows a quadratic Dresselhaus term also appears. It inherits from the bulk crystal form and emerges through coupling between bands, while respecting all symmetries. This even-order term produces striking effects, from swirling spin textures to bands that avoid crossing. The authors say the overlooked term opens new routes for spintronic devices, which use spin rather than charge to carry information.
arxiv-2511-05887:
Younghoon Kim, Sumanta Basu, and Samprit Banerjee hunt for stressful stretches in the lives of older patients with mood disorders and chronic pain. Spotting such periods matters for mental health research. Classic change-point tools force a stated model of how variables relate and return single time points, which misses slow, messy shifts.

Their hotspot method instead flags time windows where statistical features of phone-sensed data and stress measures change at the same or nearby times. Built on moving-sum tests with distance-based statistics, it needs no assumed link between series and reports intervals, not points. Simulations favored their variants for power and false-alarm control. On real trial data the method found complex shifts in stress that lined up with sensing changes.
arxiv-2511-06187:
Mathew Joseph, Tanush Savadi, and Abel Souza present LiteCast, a lightweight way to forecast the carbon intensity of an electricity grid. Carbon-aware computing shifts work to cleaner times, but it usually leans on heavy forecasting models fed with long histories. The authors argue that exact accuracy matters less than ranking future hours in the right order.

LiteCast models a region's energy mix from only a few days of energy and weather data. It runs fast and adapts quickly when grid conditions change suddenly. Tested in fifty regions worldwide under real workloads, it delivered twenty percent higher savings than leading forecasters and reached ninety-seven percent of the best savings possible.
arxiv-2511-06287:
V. I. Yukalov and E. P. Yukalova ask how order in a physical system builds up before the system becomes infinitely large. Strictly, ordering and symmetry breaking are only defined in the thermodynamic limit, when particle numbers grow without bound. Real systems are finite, so some early form of order must appear and grow as size increases.

The authors introduce order indices to measure that growth quantitatively for finite systems. Mean-field versions of several classic models make the idea concrete and easy to follow. The examples cover Bose-Einstein condensation, superconductivity, magnetization, and crystallization, showing in each case how order strengthens on the way toward the limit.
arxiv-2511-07087:
Jean Philip Filling, Felix Post, Michael Wand, and Denis Andrienko design a neural network that predicts molecular polarizability as a tensor. Polarizability describes how a molecule's electron cloud distorts in an electric field, and it is inherently directional. Standard models regress scalar quantities and recover tensor parts only through derivatives, losing geometric structure along the way.

Their graph neural network maintains rotational equivariance by working in local coordinate frames attached to the molecule. Scalar, vector, and tensor channels all pass messages within this local system, so the geometry is respected at every step. On the QM7-X dataset, tensorial message passing beat scalar message passing models at predicting polarizabilities. The authors present the design as a step toward structured, geometry-aware learning for molecular response.
arxiv-2511-07287:
Daniele De Luca maps power in games geometrically, without first choosing anyone's payoff function. Payoff assignments in game theory carry guesswork, and recent methods inherit it. De Luca instead defines a standard preference space in which each player's relational stance is a normalized vector. A game's payoffs and outcomes are projected onto this space, and the resulting landscape is summed up by metrics including a center of mass and structural markers for hierarchy and reciprocity.

Classic concepts, bargaining power, dependence, and reciprocity, reappear as geometric features, widened beyond their original settings. Demonstrations on the Prisoner's Dilemma, the Battle of the Sexes, and a Cournot duopoly reveal shared structure across very different strategic cases. The system treats power as a structural property of the mapping from preferences to equilibria, bridging cooperative and non-cooperative game theory.
arxiv-2511-07387:
Joon-Hwi Kim examines how classical mechanics can make a basic conservation property obvious. The Liouville theorem says motion in phase space flows without compression, like an incompressible fluid. Kim compares two frameworks that each display that property in a different way.

Hamilton-Jacobi theory gives an in-out picture suited to scattering, where particles enter and leave. A newer exponential form gives an in-in picture focused on evolution itself. Worked examples show the key objects in each view differ, yet a matching calculation links them. The result is a clean, fully classical account of scattering built from first principles.
arxiv-2511-07487:
Mozib Bin Awal, Bidyut Hazarika, and Prabwal Phukon study flickers from matter orbiting ModMax black holes. ModMax theory alters electromagnetism near strong fields, and its tuning parameter shifts particle orbits. Quasi-periodic oscillations, paired brightness rhythms, encode those orbits.

Raising the parameter moves behavior smoothly from charged black hole patterns toward the Schwarzschild case. Stable orbit edges and orbital frequencies shift in step. The team compares several oscillation models and fits telescope data with Markov chain sampling. Constraints on the parameter follow from real observations. The study links an abstract field theory knob to signals astronomers can measure.
arxiv-2511-07587:
Shreyas Rajesh, Pavan Holur, and Chenda Duan give language models a memory for stories, not just facts. Long documents overflow context windows, and even fitting text degrades answers. Retrieval systems fetch facts well but lose who did what, where, and when across episodes.

Their Generative Semantic Workspace builds space-and-time anchored narrative structures instead of flat fact lists. Entities stay tracked through events, supporting questions about unfolding situations. The design blends semantic generation with structured storage. Better episodic memory could help agents follow long reports, cases, or histories where sequence matters as much as content. The proposal targets a clear blind spot in retrieval today.
arxiv-2511-07787:
Benjamin Richards and Pushpa Kumar Balan open the black box of Aurora, a leading AI weather forecaster. High accuracy means little for high-stakes operations if the model inner representations ignore real physics. The authors test whether Aurora encoder embeddings line up with known meteorological concepts.

Simple linear classifiers trained on embeddings try to detect the land-sea boundary, extreme temperature events, and atmospheric instability. The probes find quantitative evidence that the encoder encodes those physical concepts. A model whose internals respect geography and instability earns more trust than one that merely scores well. Consistency checks like this guide safe adoption.
arxiv-2511-08487:
Zihan Ma and co-authors introduce OASIS, a benchmark for testing how brittle the safety of language model agents becomes when harmful intent is hidden inside complex tasks. Standard safety tests focus on single, obvious harms and miss threats diluted across long, legitimate looking jobs. OASIS varies two pressures independently: how concealed the intent is, and how complex the task is, inside a high fidelity simulation sandbox with fine grained annotations.

Safety alignment degrades sharply and predictably as intent grows more obscured. A complexity paradox also appears: agents look safer on harder tasks mainly because they are less capable there, not because they refuse more wisely. The released benchmark and environment support stronger future safety probing.
arxiv-2511-08787:
Yongqiang Liu, Laurentiu Maxim, and Botong Wang settle a question about the topology of spaces cut out by hyperplane arrangements. Remove a family of complex hyperplanes from space, and the remaining complement can carry local systems, twisted coefficient systems whose algebra is recorded by Betti numbers.

The question, raised recently by Yoshinaga together with Liu, asked which local system makes those twisted Betti numbers largest. The answer proved here is the simplest possible one: the constant local system wins, and it is the precise maximizer for arrangements that are essential. The result closes the question in full generality for this setting. Specialists in arrangement theory use such extremal facts to bound the topology of complements without computing each twisted system separately.
arxiv-2511-08887:
Tommy Sha and ten co-authors tackle fairness in automated stroke diagnosis, where a model that works better for some demographic groups than others can widen real healthcare gaps. Their framework, FAST-CAD, diagnoses stroke without physical contact. It is built to level performance across groups.

Two mechanisms combine. Domain-adversarial training pushes the self-supervised encoders to learn features that hide demographic identity, while Group-DRO trains against the worst group's risk. The supporting theory gives convergence guarantees and fairness bounds. A curated dataset spans twelve subgroups defined by age, gender, and posture. Across tests the method posts the best results in the comparison while holding fairness steady.
arxiv-2511-09387:
Chihiro Kubota, Taizo Sadahiro, and Yoshika Ueda compute where the largest number tends to sit in a random shifted staircase tableau. Standard Young tableaux of this staircase shape connect, through a bijection, to reduced decompositions of the longest signed permutation. The maximal label's cell is the object of their study.

The authors obtain the exact probability that any given cell holds the maximal label. As the shape grows, the position's distribution follows a quarter-circle law, an explicit limiting curve. Through the bijection, the same formulas give the distribution of letters in random reduced decompositions of signed permutations. Computational experiments on random sorting networks for the group round out the note.
arxiv-2511-09787:
Briggs Damman, Jarett LeVan, and Scott Baalrud run molecular dynamics simulations to measure how a two-component plasma transports heat, charge, and momentum. The particles interact through a repulsive Coulomb potential, and the team computes five transport coefficients with the Green-Kubo formalism. Coupling strengths span a wide range, from very weak to very strong, letting them test classic theory where it should hold.

At weak coupling the simulations agreed with Chapman-Enskog theory, but only after carefully matching how each framework defines its quantities, a step the authors note is often skipped. Electrical conductivity stayed meaningful across the full range. In the strongly coupled regime, parts of the other coefficients diverged, and only their kinetic components remained meaningful for a classical plasma.
arxiv-2511-09887:
Xingyu Cheng studies when semistable systems of Hodge bundles with parabolic structure can exist over the projective line with a finite set of marked points. These systems are Higgs bundles split into a line bundle plus a higher-rank part, with the Higgs field mapping one part into the other. They are fixed points of a circle action and correspond, under Simpson's correspondence, to local systems from complex variations of Hodge structure.

Following the spirit of work by Agnihotri, Woodward, and Belkale, Cheng uses enumerative geometry to derive numerical criteria for existence. The criteria apply when the local monodromy is semisimple, giving concrete conditions that the numerical data of a bundle must satisfy. The result adds a counting-based test to a correspondence-heavy corner of geometry.
arxiv-2511-10087:
Haidong Huang and six co-authors write an opinion piece proposing UEPO, a unified approach for training robot policies that start offline and then adapt online. That offline-to-online path promises safer deployment, but behavior coverage is thin and distributions shift during adaptation. The authors borrow the pretrain-then-fine-tune rhythm of large language models and rebuild it around generative diffusion policies.

Three components carry the design: a multi-seed dynamics-aware diffusion policy that captures varied behaviors in one model, a divergence regularizer that keeps that diversity physically meaningful. A diffusion-based augmentation module that hardens the dynamics model. On the D4RL benchmark the system improved over a leading baseline on locomotion and dexterous manipulation tasks, which the authors offer as evidence for the unified approach.
arxiv-2511-10187:
Outongyi Lv, Yewei Yuan, and Nana Liu improve offline reinforcement learning when training data are scarce, a common real-world constraint. Instead of learning directly on raw states and rewards, they first embed states with a Quantum Metric Encoder, a trainable unitary-style module inspired by quantum circuits. The encoder is classically simulable for ordinary data and could run directly on quantum hardware for quantum state data.

Agents trained on the embedded states, with decoded rewards, performed far better than agents trained on the originals across three datasets capped at one hundred samples each. Two standard algorithms each improved by well over a hundred percent in maximum reward. The authors link the gain to geometry: embedded state spaces show low delta-hyperbolicity, a property known to help reinforcement learning.
arxiv-2511-10387:
Prince Mensah and three co-authors estimate plant traits from satellite images using a physics informed neural network. Their target is the PROSAIL model, a standard simulation of how light interacts with leaves and plant canopies. Running that simulation backwards lets them recover leaf area and canopy chlorophyll content from Sentinel-2 satellite data.

Their design pairs a Transformer with a variational autoencoder and uses PROSAIL itself as a physical decoder, keeping inferred traits plausible. Remarkably, training used only simulated data, with no real images or field labels. On real field data sets the method matched leading approaches that do train on real imagery, pointing to cheaper global vegetation monitoring.
arxiv-2511-10587:
Valeria Olivares and twelve co-authors compare the chemical makeup of two gas phases at the centers of massive elliptical galaxies. Warm ionized gas, at about ten thousand degrees, is common in these galaxies and likely feeds their central black holes, yet where it comes from is still debated.

Combining MUSE optical data with Chandra X-ray observations for 13 galaxies, the team measured metal content in both the warm gas and the million-degree hot gas. The two metallicities rise and fall together across the sample. They span roughly a third to one and a half times the Sun's value, which points to cooling and mixing linking the phases. Ionization sources vary from galaxy to galaxy, and in some the warm gas metallicity drops toward the center.
arxiv-2511-10887:
Nishant Mishra, Wilker Aziz, and Iacer Calixto present MedPath, a large dataset for biomedical entity linking, the task of tying mentions in text to entries in medical vocabularies. Progress in the area is slowed by fragmented data, few resources for building explainable models, and evaluation metrics blind to meaning.

MedPath merges nine existing expert-annotated datasets and normalizes every entity against the latest Unified Medical Language System. Each entity is further mapped to 62 other biomedical vocabularies and enriched with full ontological paths, from general to specific concepts, in up to eleven vocabularies. The authors say the resource directly enables research on semantic-rich, interpretable linking systems and on the next generation of interoperable clinical language tools.
arxiv-2511-11087:
Sora Kadotani, Kosuke Nishida, and Kyosuke Nishida ask whether a large language model can catch its own made-up facts. Such models write fluent text but sometimes state false claims with full confidence. Spotting those slips after the fact would make the models safer to use, if the skill to do so sits inside the model itself.

They frame the task as judging one sentence at a time and use step-by-step prompting to draw knowledge out of the model. In their tests, one widely used model with that prompting caught about fifty-eight percent of its own false claims. The authors conclude that detection works when the needed knowledge is stored in the model.
arxiv-2511-11187:
Ludwig Felder, Jacob Miller, and their colleagues present ReTrace, an interactive system that makes the long reasoning traces of modern models easier to grasp. Reasoning models write out step-by-step traces that show their goals and logic, which aids trust and debugging. Those traces are often verbose and tangled, so readers face a heavy mental load.

ReTrace first structures trace text with a validated scheme for types of reasoning steps. Two interactive views then let users explore that structure instead of raw text. In a controlled study, both views helped users grasp the reasoning more accurately and with less felt effort than plain text, with lessons for explainable AI design.
arxiv-2511-11287:
Sven Schultze, Meike Verena Kietzmann, and their colleagues introduce VOIX, a framework that lets websites declare what AI agents may do on them in plain HTML. Today agents must guess what a human-oriented page allows, which makes their actions brittle, wasteful, and insecure. VOIX instead gives each site a clear, machine-readable contract for agent behavior.

Two new tags let developers list available actions and relevant state, keeping control with the site while shielding user chats from the site itself. In a three-day hackathon, sixteen developers of varied experience rapidly built diverse working agent-ready apps. The authors present VOIX as a base layer for an agent-friendly web.
arxiv-2511-11687:
Dragan Filimonovic, Christian Rutzer, Jeffrey Macher, and Rolf Weder ask whether generative AI is pulling scientific writing around the world toward one dominant style, United States English. Earlier studies tracked changes in vocabulary or readability, but convergence, the shrinking of gaps between styles, carries different stakes for who can publish and compete.

Nearly five point seven million English-language articles from 2021 to 2024, indexed in Scopus, are compared with a United States benchmark using text embeddings. An event-study design centered on the late 2022 release of ChatGPT finds that AI-assisted papers from non-English-speaking countries moved significantly toward the benchmark style. Language barriers in science may be falling, with cultural costs still open.
arxiv-2511-11887:
Francois Foucart checks a recent claim about merger disk mass formulas. The claim said symbolic regression formulas beat older ones by a wide margin. Disk mass drives the light from neutron star mergers. So the formulas, fitted to simulations, are used a lot. Their errors limit what observers can extract from real events.

On a like-for-like basis, the gain mostly comes from changed error measures. The claimed safe reach beyond the fitted region is also questioned. The most directly matched older model performs far closer than reported. The critique is a caution for gravitational-wave work. Formula upgrades must be judged on identical terms before observers trust them.
arxiv-2511-12287:
Duilio De Santis and six co-authors ask whether driving a material with light can boost coherence in a system that has superconducting correlations but no long-range order. Strong optical drives have produced short-lived superconducting-like responses above the normal critical temperature. The team tests the idea in a two-dimensional XY model with a stiffness that varies in time.

Even though the average coupling stays the same, a slow drive raises long-range, time-averaged correlations well above the equilibrium transition temperature. Faster drives mainly heat the system and suppress conductivity. For slow drives the conductivity changes in a way that suggests longer-lived currents and stronger low-frequency response. The authors map these regimes across temperature.
arxiv-2511-12587:
El-Mehdi Mehiri derives the first complete explicit formula for the M-polynomial of generalized Hanoi graphs, a family named for the Tower of Hanoi puzzle. The M-polynomial packs many degree-based graph indices, such as the Zagreb and Randić indices used in chemical graph theory, into one algebraic object. Closed forms were unknown for many graph families.

The derivation analyzes the occupancy structure of these graphs in detail, using Stirling numbers and a two-associated variant to count configurations by how vertices group together. Closed formulas follow for every coefficient of the polynomial, on and off the diagonal, and those yield exact values of the main degree-based indices. Numerical checks on small cases support the formulas.
arxiv-2511-12987:
Daivik Patel and Shrenik Patel argue that reasoning models waste most of their compute re-deriving what they already know. Large reasoning models gain accuracy by thinking longer, but long chains of thought cost tokens and time. ENGRAM-R is an inference-time memory layer: typed retrieval over stored knowledge, compact fact cards instead of raw text, and explicit control of citations. When evidence already exists in memory, the model reuses it rather than recomputing the derivation.

On the LoCoMo benchmark, the layer cut input tokens by eighty-five percent and reasoning tokens by seventy-five percent against a full-context baseline, while holding accuracy. On a multi-hop slice of LongMemEval it kept similar efficiency and gained accuracy substantially. The authors frame memory as a lever on the economics of reasoning itself, .
arxiv-2511-13087:
SeokJoo Kwak and seven co-authors improve how AI agents find things on a screen. Grounding, turning an instruction into exact screen coordinates, is essential for software agents and accessibility tools. Single models handling the whole screen at once lose accuracy in clutter and ambiguity. MEGA-GUI splits the job: specialized vision-language agents first pick a rough region of interest, then ground the element inside it. A bidirectional zoom fights the dilution that comes from shrinking a big screen, and a rewriting agent clarifies vague instructions before the search begins.

Different vision-language models proved strong at different visual scales, which the pipeline exploits. On ScreenSpot-Pro, a dense professional-screen benchmark, the system reached about seventy-three percent accuracy, and on the semantically harder OSWorld-G it reached about sixty-nine percent, both above earlier results. The authors release code and a grounding benchmark toolkit.
arxiv-2511-13487:
Davoud Shariat Panah and 4 co-authors systematically test which time-frequency features help a neural network locate sounds with two ears. Binaural localization can use loudness cues, phase cues, or mixes of both, and the best mix may shift with the listening setting. Their study holds the network fixed and varies only the input features.

Tests on matched and mismatched head shapes show that feature choice often beats added model complexity. A loudness-difference plus phase-difference pair sufficed for matched data, while richer mixes with full channel spectra generalized better to new content. Their compact network stayed competitive with the best feature sets, giving builders clear design guidance.
arxiv-2511-13687:
Nitish Kumar Chandra, Eneet Kaur, and Kaushik P. Seshadreesan compare two ways to schedule network operations for distributed quantum computing. Linked processors need nonlocal entangling gates, and a scheduler must sequence the network steps that deliver entanglement with the shortest total span. Circuit parts are first spread across processors to cut cross-links while balancing load.

One approach frames scheduling as a resource-constrained project problem, and the other uses a greedy heuristic. On a small quantum Fourier transform run over a star network with a central switch, the project method won in one instance and tied in another. The authors read this as support for the formal framework, with greedy methods still useful in practice.
arxiv-2511-13787:
