Huijie Guo and 5 co-authors probe what makes self-supervised representations transfer to new tasks, and how to improve that transfer. Transferability means features learned on one objective still serve another, but task conflict during training can quietly damage it. Their approach builds several self-supervised tasks inside each training batch so transfer can be modeled directly.

Evidence and causal analysis show task-level detail helps, yet conflict still drags results down. Their Task Conflict Calibration method extracts causal factors for each task, weights samples per task, and recalibrates representations inside a two-stage optimization loop. Across multiple downstream tasks, calibrated models consistently transferred better than standard self-supervised training.
arxiv-2511-13987:
Antonio Manuel Martínez-Heredia, Dolores Godrid Rodríguez, and Andrés Ortiz García review AI agents for music analysis and test them in teaching settings. Their survey traces the field from rule-based systems through deep learning, multi-agent designs, and retrieval-augmented generation. They then evaluate educational uses through two concrete cases.

One case brings generative AI platforms into secondary classrooms to build analytical and creative skills. The other designs a multi-agent system for symbolic music analysis with modular, explainable workflows. Results show the agents improve pattern recognition, compositional parameterization, and feedback over older automated methods. The authors also flag open problems: transparency, cultural bias, and fair ways to judge hybrid human-machine work.
arxiv-2511-14187:
Pengcheng Shi segments the aorta in medical scans with a learning scheme modeled on how humans build understanding. The aorta and its branches suffer dissection, aneurysm, and plaque, and detailed three-dimensional maps guide minimally invasive repairs. Branched vessels create severe class imbalance, and many methods ignore the anatomical hierarchy among the parts.

A curriculum strategy learns simple, dominant structures first and rare branch classes later, using a new fractal softmax built for hierarchical labels. The loss improved overlap scores markedly over a strong nnU-Net baseline, and the test score beat baselines clearly. A two-stage inference scheme also ran up to five times faster, aiding clinical use.
arxiv-2511-14387:
Richard D. Ball, Amedeo Chiefa, and Roy Stegeman refit the part-level maps of the proton while owning up to small, power-linked fixes. The maps say how the proton's push is split among its quarks and gluons. Two fixes count here: higher twist terms in deep smash tests, and first-power fixes in jet data from the LHC. Both are small, but both can skew the fit if skipped.

With a theory error method, the team finds the fixes and their linked doubts at the same time as the maps. The match to data gets better, in part since low-share smash data and low-push jet data are weighed less. Shifts in Higgs yields and in the strong force strength are small but real, and the math sits on firmer ground.
arxiv-2511-14487:
Trung Hieu Giang and Cristinel Mardare prove an improved existence result for rigid elastic plates. A plate counts as rigid when any displacement with zero strain must itself be zero. The authors work with the nonlinear Kirchhoff-Love model for such plates. Past results needed the plate to be clamped on its whole boundary.

They show a solution exists for any applied forces and boundary conditions in this rigid case. They also give sufficient conditions on the data that ensure rigidity. Together the results greatly extend the earlier theorem by Rabier. The work clarifies when this nonlinear plate model can be trusted to have a solution.
arxiv-2511-14587:
Andrew Knightly and Kimball Martin count newforms with prescribed local components at ramified primes. Newforms are basic building blocks in the theory of modular forms. At some primes their local behavior can be supercuspidal, a rich and rigid type. The authors fix that behavior at a chosen set of primes and count how many newforms match.

Their formula expresses the count through the trace of an Atkin-Lehner operator. It depends only on weight, level, attached quadratic extensions, and root numbers. The formula becomes fully explicit for one prime or for all primes dividing the level. The result makes a deep counting problem computable in concrete cases.
arxiv-2511-14787:
Khwahish Kushwah, Caio V. P. de Brito, and Gabriel S. Denicol derive equations for a hot two-part plasma moving near light speed with electrical resistance. Such plasmas appear in heavy-ion collisions and in some astrophysical settings, and their flow couples charge drift with shear stress. The authors start from kinetic theory rather than guessing the flow equations directly.

Using the Boltzmann-Vlasov equation with a fourteen-moment approximation, they obtain coupled equations for the charge current and the stress. In gentle conditions the result matches the standard relaxation form used in practice. Strong electric fields break that match in a controlled way, delaying current peaks and stirring stress even without a flow pattern.
arxiv-2511-15687:
Marek Lewicki and Ville Vaskonen compute gravitational wave spectra from strongly supercooled first order phase transitions while tracking cosmic expansion across the shift. Supercooling can trap the universe briefly in thermal inflation before radiation domination returns. Past spectra often froze the background metric during that change. The authors evolve it explicitly throughout.

Spectral shape stays largely unchanged, apart from a causality driven tail on large scales. Peak amplitude and rate, however, depend more weakly on shift rate than standard scaling predicts for slow transitions. That weaker dependence matters when inferring early universe settings from future wave detections. Planned space detectors will probe exactly this signal class. Accurate templates must include background evolution to avoid biased conclusions.
arxiv-2511-15987:
Phu Khanh Huynh, Francky Catthoor, and Anup Das design a scenario aware control plane for segmented ladder buses in neuromorphic chips, implemented on programmable hardware. Neuromorphic tiles exchange spikes that are sparse and bursty in time. A dynamic segmented bus offers simplicity and energy speed for that traffic. Its control plane must stay streamlined, or the benefits vanish.

Scenario awareness lets control adapt to activity patterns without heavy overhead. The design targets minimal power during idle periods and fast handling of bursts. Field programmable implementation shows practical feasibility. Scaling behavior is central: control must grow gently as networks enlarge. The methodology guides future interconnect design for large neuromorphic systems where communication energy dominates total budgets during sparse activity.
arxiv-2511-16087:
Vincent Fan and Regina Barzilay introduce AssayMatch, a data selection method for molecular activity models in drug discovery. Model quality rests on training data. Yet public bioactivity sets merge assays run under varied protocols, which adds noise. Rather than train on all data, AssayMatch builds smaller, more uniform training sets tuned to the test set at hand, whose labels are unknown in real campaigns.

Data attribution scores how much each training assay helps performance. Those scores fine-tune language embeddings of text assay descriptions, so they capture assay fit, not just word likeness. At test time, the tuned embeddings rank all training data for selection. Tests show the gain from picking data by fit rather than by volume.
arxiv-2511-16387:
Hongjie Dong, Hongjie Li, and Longjuan Xu analyze what happens when waves meet two nearly touching subwavelength resonators, modeled by the two-dimensional Helmholtz equation with high-contrast material parameters. Such close pairs concentrate wave energy in the narrow gap, and both the resonant frequencies and the field growth need precise estimates.

The authors show the configuration supports two subwavelength resonant modes whose frequencies follow distinct leading-order asymptotic laws. Those laws differ markedly from the three-dimensional case, a contrast the paper makes explicit. They also quantify how fast the field gradient blows up in the gap between the resonators as the spacing shrinks. The estimates matter for designing acoustic and electromagnetic devices that exploit extreme field concentration.
arxiv-2511-16587:
Amartya Mukherjee and Jun Liu strengthen the theory of differentially private stochastic gradient descent, the standard algorithm for training models with formal privacy guarantees. Most analyses show convergence on average or with high probability; what a single training run does in the long run was less clear.

The authors prove almost sure convergence of the method along individual trajectories, in both nonconvex and strongly convex settings, under standard smoothness assumptions and decaying step sizes. The analysis extends to private momentum methods, the stochastic heavy ball and Nesterov acceleration, using careful energy constructions. The results show that, despite the noise privacy injects, private training remains pathwise stable, giving practitioners a firmer foundation for relying on it.
arxiv-2511-16787:
Hossain Shaikh Saadi, Faria Alam, Mario Sanz-Guerrero, Minh Duc Bui, Manuel Mager, and Katharina von der Wense describe the winning entry to a shared task on writing Python code from Bangla instructions. Their system splits the job between two agents that pass work back and forth. One agent writes a first program from the Bangla prompt.

A second agent then runs the test cases, and only the failed cases move on for repair. Using the error traces, the current program, and the failed tests, it writes a fixed version. The loop earned first place in the BLP-2025 task with a top score on the main pass measure. And the team has released its code in public for others to inspect and reuse.
arxiv-2511-17087:
Alena Vishina and seven co-authors report the first magnetization measurements on single crystals of DyCo5, a compound of dysprosium and cobalt studied for magnetic materials research. They measured the crystals in fields up to 14 tesla and at temperatures up to 600 kelvin. The two elements form two magnetic sublattices that pull against each other, which makes the material's overall behavior hard to predict.

The measurements turned up features not reported before, including strong directional response and a dip in spontaneous magnetization near the compensation point, where the two sublattices cancel. Three kinds of theory, combined, reproduce the data across the full temperature range, from the high-field saturation to how the moment changes with heat. The agreement gives researchers a firmer grip on how rare-earth and cobalt magnetism interact.
arxiv-2511-17187:
Daniel Benedicto Orenes and five co-authors study how a cold, dense cloud of atoms gives off light just after a strong drive is switched. When atoms act together, early decay can run faster or slower than for lone atoms, and the balance shifts as the drive moves from weak to strong. The team combines lab work with computer runs to track that shift.

They watch two kinds of signal: the light leaving the cloud at set angles, and the total share of excited atoms. At some angles the light flips from the slow shared mode to the fast one as drive strength grows, while the total population shows no such flip. The split between readouts is the key lesson for anyone probing shared decay.
arxiv-2511-17387:
Yusuf Baran Ates and Omer Morgul work on making two-legged robots walk more like people. Human-like walking is hard to learn because balance shifts sharply at each step and ground varies. Their approach pairs a gait generator, trained on human motion and tuned to the rhythm of steps, with a learning controller that sets joint torques through trial and error.

Training used only flat ground and mild slopes, yet the learned walkers handled steeper ramps and rough surfaces in tests. The authors suggest that rhythm-based motion priors drawn from people give the controller a strong head start, so natural and steady walking can be reached with modest training cost. The work is a step toward service robots that move safely among people.
arxiv-2511-17587:
Yuxuan Hu and eight co-authors improve how chat systems pick the right sticker in reply to a message. Stickers carry emotion and implicit intention at once, and earlier selection methods modeled those two signals separately, which mispicks whenever a sticker's emotion and intention point in different directions. Their framework is the first to model emotion and intention jointly, aligning both within each modality and across the visual and textual channels with a dual-level contrastive scheme.

A fusion module then integrates the two signals progressively: emotion guides which intention knowledge gets selected, attention fuses the guided streams, and a similarity-adjusted matching step makes the final choice. On two public sticker selection datasets, the method consistently beat the state of the art, with better reading of both emotional and intentional cues. The work treats a playful corner of online communication with appropriate seriousness.
arxiv-2511-17987:
Jinping Wang and three co-authors improve task arithmetic, a cheap way to edit a pre trained model by adding or subtracting the weight change from fine tuning on a task. The method is efficient, but it can get stuck and leave performance on the table.

They generalize task vectors into difference vectors drawn from the path optimization took, then use them as directed nudges in an iterative scaling algorithm. Merged multi task models can even beat separately fine tuned ones in their tests. The same idea yields a fine tuning method for single tasks, with few added parameters and strong results on supervised and unsupervised tests.
arxiv-2511-18187:
Sristy Sumana Nath, Banani Roy, and Munima Jahan study the missing links between software release notes and the work they describe. Notes should connect to pull requests, commits, and issues so teams can trace why changes shipped, yet in open-source projects the links are often skipped or broken. Their survey of GitHub projects found nearly half of release artifacts lacked such links, and about one in eight links were broken.

The team analyses what information notes carry and how it lines up with the linked artifacts, then builds a benchmark of three and a half thousand checked link cases. On that base they test language model approaches that forge the links automatically for three kinds of artifact pairs. Practitioner views shape the study, keeping the problem grounded in daily maintenance work.
arxiv-2511-18787:
Bhuvan Sachdeva and three co-authors study task transfer in vision language models: fine tuning a model on one perception task, such as depth or counting, can unpredictably help or hurt others. Specialized perception still lags behind humans, so knowing these interactions matters for efficient training.

They introduce a normalized metric for the change in performance after transfer and use it to score each task's breadth and strength of influence. Across three open models and thirteen perception tasks, a transfer graph reveals groups of tasks that aid each other and risks of negative interference. The metric can guide which data to train on next.
arxiv-2511-18987:
Donghu Kim evaluates a dynamic mixture of experts approach for lifelong learning. In that setting, a network must keep adapting to changing data without forgetting old skills or losing the ability to learn new ones. Brains sustain that plasticity partly by growing capacity, which artificial methods imitate unevenly, often at high parameter cost or only when told the task identity.

Mixture of experts models, which route inputs to specialized sub networks, offer a more efficient route. Kim benchmarks the dynamic version in continual and reinforcement learning settings against existing network expansion methods, testing how well growing and specializing experts handle severe distribution shifts over time.
arxiv-2511-19487:
Ben Shaw and four co-authors generalize a trick from random forests: trees that send two cases to the same leaf mark them as close, giving a proximity measure. Such proximities help with outlier hunting, filling missing values, and visualization. Their catch is that they only work as well as the forest behind them, and forests are not ideal everywhere.

A distance-based model called the Proximity Forest had already carried the idea to time series. The generalized version extends it to every setting where supervised distance-based learning applies. It also adds a regression variant. As a meta-learner, it can give imputation skills to any pretrained classifier. Experiments show distinct gains over random forests and nearest neighbors.
arxiv-2511-19787:
Dmitry A. Ryndyk, Olga Guskova, and Marina Saphiannikova model, atom by atom, how light bends films of azo-polymers. These plastics carry dye-like azo units that shift under polarized light, and the whole film deforms in response. Earlier models skipped the molecular detail, leaving the link between structure and motion unclear.

Using a fully atomistic force field for the first time in this setting, the team mimics light with an orientation potential that redistributes the azo units relative to the polarization. The simulations resolve how single chromophores behave and how the polymer matrix answers as a whole, bridging molecular motion and film-scale deformation.
arxiv-2511-20287:
Hlushchenko, Bratchenko, and Chechkin quantify the jitter shaking magnetic bits on racetracks. Their 2025 paper studies skyrmion motion under noise. Skyrmions are tiny swirling spin textures for memory. Racetrack devices shuttle them with electric currents. Speeds above fifty meters per second are required.

Fast driving also amplifies spin-current noise strongly. Thermal jiggling adds a second, equilibrium noise source. A stochastic Thiele equation frames the analysis. Diffusion coefficients come out for both noise types. Mean-squared displacements quantify the random wandering. Micromagnetic simulations checked the analytical results. Spin-current noise dominates in typical racetrack structures. That holds all the way to room temperature. First-passage times were computed along and across the track. Their spread measures timing errors in devices. Random slips threaten data detection reliability. Error budgets for high-speed memory get firmer numbers. Design rules can now price in the noise.
arxiv-2511-20387:
Li and colleagues test how nuclear matter resists squeezing using particle flows. Their 2025 paper models gold-gold collisions recorded by the HADES experiment. Colliding nuclei spray protons in preferred directions. Those patterns, called anisotropic flows, encode the matter's stiffness. The team simulated them with a transport model. A new Skyrme-based force law supplied the nuclear forces.

The collisions ran at a beam energy of 2.4 GeV. Directed, elliptic, triangular, and four-sided flows were all computed. Flows proved strongly sensitive to how the force depends on momentum. How stiff symmetric matter is also mattered greatly. The elliptic flow's momentum pattern responded to higher-order stiffness terms. Skewness and kurtosis values of the state equation played roles. Cross-section changes in the medium modestly affected directed flow. High-density symmetry energy had limited effect on the flows. The study tells future combined analyses which parts cannot be skipped.
arxiv-2511-20587:
Kadry and colleagues steer AI-generated anatomy with local control boxes. Their 2025 paper presents Anatomica, a guidance framework for diffusion models. Such models can synthesize 3D maps of organs as voxel grids. Plain generation cannot promise a structure sits at the right size or place. Virtual trials and training data need that control.

Box-shaped control domains slice out local substructures during generation. Penalty functions push the sample toward target traits inside each box. Size, shape, and position are steered through voxel moments. Counts of parts, loops, and voids are enforced via persistent homology. Constraints compose freely across regions and coordinate systems. A latent diffusion version decodes only parts of the structure at once. That partial decoding makes guidance cheap enough to run live. Many anatomical systems were tested with strong control results. Synthetic datasets for machine learning workflows are the payoff.
arxiv-2511-20687:
Irina Tezaur and five colleagues present in 2025 a way to glue engineering simulations of different fidelities without shared meshes or clocks. High-fidelity simulations of solid parts are accurate but slow. Building a mesh for one complex component can take weeks. Reduced order models run far faster, solving a small learned stand-in for the physics. Stitching such models to full models, or to each other, has been awkward.

The team couples local models with the overlapping Schwarz alternating method. That method passes solutions back and forth across overlapping subdomains until they agree. Their reduced models come from operator inference, which learns the stand-in equations from simulation data alone, without opening the source code. On complex three-dimensional solid-dynamics problems, the mixed couplings ran up to 106 times faster than full-to-full coupling. The authors argue the same plug-and-play stitching should extend to other engineering equations.
arxiv-2511-21087:
Ziyun Zeng, Hang Hua, and Jiebo Luo present in 2025 MIRA, an agent that edits images the way a human would: one small step, a look, then the next step. Diffusion editors given a complex instruction often drift, mangling referring expressions or compositional relations. MIRA instead runs a perception-reasoning-action loop, issuing atomic edit instructions and checking the visual result before continuing. It plugs into editors rather than replacing them.

Training used MIRA-Editing, a set of 150,000 multimodal tool-use examples, with supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO reinforcement learning. Paired with open-source editors such as Step1X-Edit, Qwen-Image-Edit, and Flux.1-Kontext, MIRA lifted semantic consistency and perceptual quality. The combinations matched or beat proprietary systems including GPT-Image and Nano-Banana on complex instructions. Reasoning about edits with feedback, the authors argue, closes the gap between open and closed editors.
arxiv-2511-21287:
Ivan Guo, Severin Nilsson, and Johannes Wiesel give a dynamic picture of a generalized transport problem in a 2025 probability paper. Classical optimal transport asks the cheapest way to reshape one distribution into another, and the Benamou-Brenier formula recasts that cost as the energy of a continuous flow over time. The authors work in weak optimal transport, where the cost can depend on the whole conditional distribution, not just pairs of points.

Guo and his coauthors extend the Benamou-Brenier formula to this weak setting and show that the barycentric transport problem of Gozlan and Juillet has a matching dynamic analogue. They then study a martingale relaxation of the problem, where the flow must also be a martingale, a fair-game process whose expected future equals its present. That relaxed problem ties neatly to the known martingale Benamou-Brenier formula of Backhoff-Veraguas, Beiglböck, Huesmann, and Källblad.
arxiv-2511-21487:
Mircea Bejan, Pieter Claeys, and Jiangtian Yao track an invisible fuel of quantum computing as it spreads, in 2025. The fuel is magic, technically nonstabilizerness: the extra resource, beyond stabilizer operations, that makes quantum circuits impossible to simulate classically and powers error correction. In Clifford circuits, the circuits studied here, total magic is conserved, but no physical observable measures where the magic sits at any moment.

Bejan and his coauthors borrow a trick from stabilizer error-correcting codes: a bookkeeping frame they call the bipartite magic gauge, which lets the spatial distribution of magic be inferred indirectly. They define two operational length scales for how far injected magic has spread. Simulations show both scales first grow ballistically, at two distinct speeds set by the entanglement velocity, like ripples racing outward. After that opening sprint, the magic delocalizes across the whole system, a transport picture that may guide future error-correction design.
arxiv-2511-21787:
Park and colleagues introduce Dynamical Implicit Neural Representations, or DINR, a way for a neural network to store a signal such as an image or a 3D field. Normal implicit representations pass coordinates through a fixed stack of layers and tend to blur fine detail, a weakness called spectral bias. DINR instead lets the network's internal features change steadily over time, like a moving system rather than a single snapshot.

The team backs the idea with theory about learning capacity and training behaviour, then tests it across four datasets on images, field reconstruction, and compression. The dynamical versions beat their static counterparts throughout, and on a turbulence dataset they cut reconstruction error by 48.0 percent and 88.7 percent for the two base designs tested. On a complex cloud dataset the error fell by about 97 percent compared with the static version.
arxiv-2511-21887:
Jin and colleagues present UniArt, a system that generates movable, jointed 3D objects, like opening drawers and swivelling chairs, from a single ordinary image. Such assets are essential for robot training and simulation, but hand-building is slow, and earlier staged generators caused part mismatches. UniArt instead uses one diffusion model with a unified representation encoding shape, texture, part segmentation, and joint parameters together.

A reversible joint-to-voxel embedding ties articulation information spatially to the volumetric geometry, so motion and structure are learned coherently instead of drifting apart. The system also treats joint-type prediction as an open-set problem, meaning it is not limited to a fixed list of joint categories and can generalize to unseen object types. On PartNet-Mobility, covering seven categories from refrigerators to microwaves, UniArt achieved state-of-the-art mesh quality and articulation accuracy, clearest under open-set evaluation.
arxiv-2511-21987:
Courtney-Barrer and colleagues use interferometry to investigate why the red giant RT Pav pulsates on a long secondary period. A third of evolved stars show such cycles, explained either by a dusty companion or by an oscillatory convective mode in the star itself.

Observations spanning 1.5 to 5.0 micrometres were timed for greatest predicted companion separation. Binary models sometimes fitted best on paper, but their fitted companion positions jumped inconsistently between wavelengths and instruments. Significant detections above three sigma appeared in only two of the four wavebands tested, unlike a real dusty companion. Gaia data also cap any companion's mass below what the light variations would need. By contrast, a convective dipole pattern with a temperature contrast near 200 kelvin reproduced both the surface appearance and the light curve, supporting an intrinsic, photospheric origin for the cycle.
arxiv-2511-22087:
Inui and Ryu, roboticists in Korea, soften virtual fixtures, the haptic guides that steer a teleoperator's hand along safe paths but often fight the user, pushing back whenever the operator deviates. They model shared control as a two-player game between human and robot assistant and add an entropy regularization controlled by a single softness parameter, tau. Zero recovers the classic hard fixture, while larger values shrink the robot's authority and align it with the operator's own input.

It was tested with twelve users on a six-degree-of-freedom haptic device in a 3D tracking task. Moderate softness around tau of 2 to 3 kept tracking error indistinguishable from a classic fixture while sharply reducing controller-user conflict, lowering NASA-TLX workload scores, and raising users' sense of agency. A composite balance score peaked in that same range, suggesting a practical dial for personalizing assistance.
arxiv-2511-22287:
Feingold, Kaduri, and Dekel are computer vision researchers at the Weizmann Institute. They generate an edited photo set at once while keeping shared content consistent across it. Photo albums and catalogs show the same object from many viewpoints. Today's image generators edit one picture at a time. So the shared element drifts in appearance between shots. Their Match-and-Fuse method is zero-shot and training-free. It models the set as a graph whose edges trigger joint generation of image pairs on one shared canvas, fusing internal features guided by dense pixel correspondences from the source images.

Joint pairwise generation compounds into global coherence across sets of 2 to 15 images, from photographs to hand-drawn sketches, with no masks or supervision. The team reports state-of-the-art consistency and quality, plus a new consistency metric aligning with human judgments, targeting uses like product ads and concept art.
arxiv-2511-22387:
Chakraborty, Ghosh, and Samanta study the cops and robber game on large random graphs. Cops and a robber move along a network's edges; the cops win by landing on the robber's vertex, the robber by evading forever. The question is whether size alone tips the game toward one side. Such games also model robotic search and other pursuit-evasion problems.

The team connects the game to logic. They show that whenever either player's winning condition can be written as a certain kind of first-order formula, that player wins for almost all large random graphs. This holds in the sense of the zero-one law. A first-order formula is a statement built from simple relations and quantifiers. So the outcome is usually no close contest but a near-certainty decided by the winning condition's shape. The analysis also sharpens the known link between games and logic.
arxiv-2511-22687:
Shi and colleagues redesign the multi-stage compression at the heart of neural speech codecs. Codecs compress speech into discrete tokens for transmission and speech language models, and residual vector quantization stacks quantizers, each encoding what the previous stage missed. In practice the stacking trains unstably and decomposes the signal poorly, hurting reconstruction. The authors' PURE Codec guides the stages with a pre-trained speech enhancement model, ordering them by entropy.

The first stage reconstructs low-entropy, denoised speech embeddings, the signal's clean backbone, while later stages encode residual high-entropy components, the detail and noise. This unfolding of residual entropy improves training stability. In experiments, PURE consistently outperformed codecs on reconstruction and on downstream text-to-speech driven by speech language models. The advantage held particularly under noisy training conditions, where ordinary codecs struggle most, suggesting entropy ordering is a useful organising principle for learned audio compression.
arxiv-2511-22787:
Kim and colleagues test whether vision-language models keep cultures straight when they share one picture. In globalised scenes, foods and settings from different countries appear together, yet each keeps its cultural identity, which humans read effortlessly. The team built CultureMix, a food question-answering benchmark of 23 thousand diffusion-generated, human-verified images mixing foods and backgrounds from over thirty countries across four subtasks. They evaluated ten vision-language models on it.

The models consistently failed to preserve cultural identities in mixed settings. They leaned heavily on background cues, accuracy dropping 14 percent when cultural backgrounds were added to food-only baselines, and predicted inconsistently for identical foods across contexts, treating new cultural elements as distractors. Of three robustness strategies tried, supervised fine-tuning on a culture-mixing dataset substantially improved consistency and cut background sensitivity. The authors call culture mixing a missing benchmark for models deployed in culturally diverse environments.
arxiv-2511-22987:
Wouters and colleagues improve how scientists extract information from gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime, recorded when neutron stars collide and merge. The standard analysis weighs the signal against prior assumptions. But those assumptions are usually left deliberately blank, ignoring what nuclear physics and telescope observations already say about how neutron stars behave, such as their maximum possible mass.

They encode that knowledge into neural priors, prior distributions learned by a neural density estimator called a normalizing flow from equation-of-state constraints and neutron star population models. Applied to three real recorded events, GW170817, GW190425, and GW230529, the informed priors gave narrower, sharper constraints on source properties than blank priors. They consistently pointed to higher luminosity distances. For the loud event GW170817, they also supported classifying the source and choosing between equation-of-state models straight from the wave data itself.
arxiv-2511-23387:
Sukhorukov and colleagues build the Hierarchical AI-Meteorologist. A language-model agent system that turns tables of numerical weather forecasts into explainable written reports people can check. Instead of treating a forecast as one flat time series, the system reasons at three scales at once, hourly for local dynamics. Six-hourly for smoothed patterns, and daily for persistent trends, then writes a single coherent narrative from the combined view.

Alongside the narrative, the agent extracts a few keywords naming the dominant weather events. And those keywords act as anchors for validating the report's consistency with the underlying data from OpenWeather and Meteostat. Across four case studies in Cork, Manila, Chennai, and Da Nang. The system correctly flagged and justified a hazardous rainfall and wind episode in Da Nang while avoiding false alarms elsewhere, and the hierarchical context reduced bias toward noisy hourly rows.
arxiv-2512-00187:
Simulating how particles shower through a detector is essential in high-energy physics, but it is also a bottleneck. Lorenzo Valente studies fast electromagnetic shower simulation in a 2025 study, focusing on transfer learning across detector geometries. Standard Monte Carlo tools such as Geant4 are accurate but computationally prohibitive.

Machine learning surrogates are faster, yet most are tied to one geometry and need full retraining for each design change. Valente examines whether a model can carry knowledge from one geometry to another. If transfer works, detector designers could test new layouts quickly instead of rebuilding simulations from scratch each time. Particle detectors are redesigned often, which makes reusable simulation especially valuable. The point lands for teams who plan the next round of test beams. Each new plan can reuse what was learned from the last one in the lab.
arxiv-2512-00587:
Mean field games model crowds of rational agents, each reacting to the average behavior of all. Antonio Siconolfi investigates first-order mean field games in a generalized form in 2025, comparing differential and variational approaches. The games play out on a torus, a periodic domain.

The classical formulation couples a Hamilton-Jacobi equation for optimal choices with a continuity equation for the crowd's density. The variational approach instead uses fixed points of a multivalued map on probability measures over trajectories. Showing how the two views relate strengthens the theory behind models of traffic, economics, and crowd motion. The torus removes boundary effects, letting the comparison focus on the equations themselves. The work is pure math, and its worth is in the bridge it builds. Two ways to pose the same crowd game are shown to be two sides of one coin.
arxiv-2512-00687:
Ruofan Jiang wrote a 2025 paper in arithmetic geometry on p-adic monodromy and unlikely intersections. The setting is ordinary abelian schemes in characteristic p, a world where numbers are measured by divisibility by a prime p. Their moduli spaces catalog whole families of these objects at once.

Jiang studies these spaces through three conjectures from characteristic p geometry, tied to Mumford-Tate groups, Ax-Lindemann type results, and André-Oort type results. Unlikely intersections are special overlaps that should happen only for good reasons. Results at this level help map the hidden order inside families of geometric objects.
arxiv-2512-01387:
Sanjeeva Rao Prattipati, Reetanjali Moharana, and Sourav Dutta hunt for bursts like a famed 2017 event. That event paired gravitational waves with a short gamma-ray burst. It came from two neutron stars merging. Wave rates hint more such bursts hide in past records.

The team scans Fermi-GBM records for bursts with traits like that event. They look in both mega and giga energy ranges. Finds would add cases where light and waves came from one merger. More cases sharpen rates for mergers and for the heavy elements they forge. Each added case also helps separate true merger bursts from look-alike bursts made by other violent events in deep space.
arxiv-2512-02587:
Marcelino Agúndez asks how much trust to place in computed air compositions for distant planets. Chemical models predict what exoplanet atmospheres hold, and telescopes check those predictions against real spectra. How wrong the model abundances might be has rarely been measured.

Agúndez runs a sensitivity analysis with a state of the art atmosphere model. Six well observed planets serve as test cases, from hot giants to a small sub-Neptune world. Knowing the uncertainty on each gas helps astronomers judge whether a claimed detection, or a mismatch, means new chemistry or just model noise. Error bars of this kind turn a bold claim about a far world into a claim that can be checked.
arxiv-2512-03287:
Wearable sensors can track what a person is doing. Dario Fenoglio and co-authors study activity recognition with head-worn sensors in this 2025 work. Such tracking helps in health and elderly care, where daily habits matter.

Classic systems send user data to a central server, which raises privacy concerns. The authors use federated learning, where models train on each device and share only updates. They also use signals at several frequencies. Private, on-device learning could let health tools work without gathering raw personal data. Head-worn sensors suit daily life, since glasses and earbuds already sit where motion is rich.
arxiv-2512-03887:
Deep research agents promise reports that go far beyond a single search, but users rarely control how hard the agent works. Saurav Prateek introduces the Static Deep Research Agent in a 2025 artificial intelligence preprint. Instead of a fixed pipeline, the agent follows a configurable tree-shaped workflow that users can tune before the run starts.

Two knobs, Depth and Breadth, set how deep and how wide the investigation goes, trading report quality against the cost of language model calls. Supervisor, independent, and worker agents divide the labour, chasing subtopics in parallel across multiple hops. On the DeepResearch Bench, judged by a reference-based evaluation framework, one mid-range configuration earned a solid score. Raising either knob deepened the research and lifted the score further. All code, outputs, and benchmark results are openly released, making the trade-offs transparent for other builders.
arxiv-2512-04087:
Students far from home who struggle emotionally often cannot find words for distress in a second language, and pictures might say it faster. Sui He and Shenbin Qian test that idea in a 2025 preprint on neuroscience and computing. Twenty Chinese international students at British universities wrote descriptions of their own mental distress, which were then expanded into images by a generative model.

The descriptions were elaborated by GPT-4o under four persona prompt templates drawn from counselling practice, producing four hundred images. Students rated how well each image helped them express what they had written. Prompt design mattered: the illustrator persona earned the highest ratings. The team releases the full dataset, one hundred text descriptions with images and human helpfulness scores. They describe it as the first public resource of its kind for evaluating image generation in mental health communication.
arxiv-2512-04687:
Philippe Balbiani, Çigdem Gencer, and Tinko Tinchev prove that intuitionistic modal logic LIK4 is decidable. Intuitionistic logic drops the classical rule that every claim is either true or false, suiting reasoning where proof must be built step by step. Modal logic adds operators for necessity and possibility. LIK4 names one system that joins the two traditions, with its own axioms for how the modal operators behave. Their 2025 arXiv note announces the decidability result.

A logic is decidable when a fixed procedure can always settle, in finite time, whether a formula counts as a theorem of the system. Without such a procedure, even basic questions about the logic can stay open forever. Proving decidability for LIK4 gives logicians firm ground: automated checkers can, in principle, test any claim in the system. The note adds one more settled case to the map of modal logics.
arxiv-2512-04887:
Aleksandra Łopion, Pierre-Maurice Piel, Thomas Kliewer, and co-authors show how to read the layered magnetic state of the crystal CrSBr with light alone. This van der Waals magnetic semiconductor couples its magnetic order tightly to how it reflects light. Stacks of its layers can settle into many magnetic arrangements, not just two. Their 2025 arXiv paper realizes a purely optical, contact-free, non-destructive readout of those configurations through magneto-reflectance.

A field along the easy axis drives the stack from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic order through a cascade of intermediate states. The number and stability of those states scale with layer thickness. Pairing CrSBr with the antiferromagnet MnPS3 tunes them further. An optical multilayer model decodes the reflectance into the magnetic layout. Reconfigurable magnetic layers that report their state in light could serve low-power memory and sensing.
arxiv-2512-05887:
Sairam Vaidya, Marcel Böhme, and Loris D'Antoni make compiler fuzzing work for languages too new and small to have test corpora. Extensible frameworks like MLIR let teams mint domain specific dialects quickly. Each dialect needs automated test generation without hand built seed files. Their tool, Germinator, refuses the trade by mining the dialect itself.

Dialect grammars, which encode structure and type rules, can often be extracted automatically from the specification. Germinator feeds them to a pretrained language model, which writes representative seed programs from the full dialect space. Those seeds bootstrap a coverage guided fuzzer. Across six MLIR projects spanning ninety one dialects, the seeds lifted line coverage by margins from a tenth to more than double, over grammar based baselines. The campaign found eighty eight previously unknown bugs, forty of them confirmed, including twenty three in dialects that had no automated test generator at all.
arxiv-2512-06087:
Zohra Mehri and Abdelâali Boudjemâa study a droplet of quantum fluid lost in a maze of disorder. A quantum droplet is a self bound puddle of ultracold atoms. Place one in a speckle potential and ask how it spreads. The authors track its width, profile, and diffusion for small and large droplets.

The transport is anomalous and tunable. With disorder strength, it superdiffuses or subdiffuses. Past a critical strength, Anderson localization traps the whole droplet. Localization lengths are computed. The results are testable in cold atom laboratories. A switchable droplet is a probe of localization physics.
arxiv-2512-06187:
Young-ho Cho, Harsha Nagarajan, Deepjyoti Deka, and Hao Zhu teach a neural network to stand in for a power grid's defender. The worst attack can then be computed before it happens. The problem is a two level game: an attacker maximizes blackouts; the operator redispatches. Exact solution is prohibitive.

A reformulation collapses the game to one level, with a neural surrogate for the defender's value. Spectral clustering keeps the surrogate sparse and scalable. On standard test systems it found near optimal worst cases in under a minute. Fast surrogates make worst case analysis routine.
arxiv-2512-06487:
Nina-Elisabeth Nemec and three co authors use the Sun as a test bench for a bias that haunts the study of planets around other stars. When a planet crosses its star, the depth of the dip at each color reveals its atmosphere. Starspots and bright faculae on the star's face can fake or mask that signal, and for distant stars no one knows where those features sit.

The team fed real spot and faculae maps into a solar model and computed how the Sun's apparent size shifts with color. Simple methods that ignore how brightness fades toward the limb understate the effect, most of all for faculae, which dominate near normal solar activity. Between quiet and active Sun, the shift could swamp the fine noise floor of the Webb telescope for a Jupiter sized transit, though not for an Earth sized one. Careful faculae treatment is a must.
arxiv-2512-06787:
Ofek Glick and four co authors generate industrial control charts with large language models. Sequential Function Charts are a standard graphical language for programming factory controllers, spelling out steps and transitions of a workflow, with text code embedded inside. Language models handle the textual dialects of this standard well, but the graphical charts resist them, and naive output often fails to run in real industrial tools.

Their framework, LLM4SFC, first recasts each chart in a reduced structured form that keeps the topology and the inline code while cutting verbosity. Fine tuning and retrieval of worked examples align the model with chart conventions. Generation is then constrained live, pruning illegal tokens as they arise, so the output obeys the chart format by construction. On a data set of real charts from manufacturing projects, the system reliably produced charts that parse and run, bridging graphical and textual control languages.
arxiv-2512-06887:
Ricardo Alonzo Fernández Salguero reviews the reviews on whether charging for carbon actually cuts the emissions heating the planet. His umbrella review gathers systematic reviews and meta-analyses on carbon taxes, emissions trading schemes, voluntary carbon markets, and forest protection programs such as REDD+. Study selection followed strict PRISMA rules, and the quality of each review was graded with a standard appraisal tool.

The evidence gives a split verdict. Taxes and trading schemes do cut emissions by a moderate amount, though the size of the cut varies widely by place and sector. Weak prices and too many free allowances blunt their force. Offsets fare far worse: doubts about whether projects add anything new, last long enough, or merely shift emissions elsewhere lead to broad over-counting of their benefit. Fernández Salguero concludes that firm carbon pricing is necessary but not enough, and that offset markets need deep reform.
arxiv-2512-07087:
Matthew Bolan and a large team of collaborators, including Terence Tao, report on the Equational Theories Project, a mass online effort to map how simple algebraic laws imply one another. The objects are magmas, sets with a single binary operation, and the laws are short equations such a operation might obey. With thousands of such laws in play, the implication graph between them holds tens of millions of possible edges, each needing a proof or a counterexample.

The project settled every single edge. Human contributors and automated provers worked in tandem, and every result was checked in the Lean formal proof assistant, so the map is not just believed but verified. Along the way, participants found new constructions of magmas obeying specific tricky laws, and answered side questions such as what changes when only finite magmas are allowed.
arxiv-2512-07687:
Sujoy Nath, Arkaprabha Basu, Sharanya Dasgupta, and Swagatam Das wrote this 2025 paper on a trust problem in multimodal models. Models that read images and text can describe scenes fluently. They also hallucinate, inventing content the picture does not contain.

Most checks for hallucination lean on outside language models as judges. Those judges can hallucinate too. The authors propose a different signal: look inside the model. Their hypothesis is that hallucination leaves measurable irregularities in layer dynamics. The shifts are not only a matter of input distribution drifting. Layer-by-layer analysis of specific internal assumptions exposes the trouble. Their method, HalluShift++, builds on an earlier text-only detector. It widens that approach from plain language models to multimodal ones. Internal representation shifts become the core evidence for flagging bad output. The goal is a detector with no external judge.
arxiv-2512-07787:
Nawaf Mohammed wrote this 2025 paper in mathematical finance on Value-at-Risk, a standard risk measure. Value-at-Risk can reward diversification at some confidence levels. At other levels, the same measure penalizes spreading risk instead.

Mohammed studies the two extreme regimes for one-sided risks. In the first, diversification always helps, at every level at once. He shows several conditions collapse into one there: universal sub-additivity, exact additivity, and co-monotonicity. No finite-mean assumption is needed for that equivalence, a sharpening of recent work. In the second regime, diversification always hurts, and a dominance condition rules. He factors that condition into two weaker, checkable parts.  The other concerns each risk's distribution. A striking corollary follows for mixed cases between the extremes. Any such vector must contain at least two infinite-mean risks. Bounded risks can never be strictly one-sided.
arxiv-2512-07987:
G. Garcia-Segura wrote this 2025 astrophysics paper on the glowing shells dying stars leave behind. Planetary nebulae expand as a fast wind sweeps up slower earlier ejecta. Predicting their motion usually means heavy numerical simulation.

Garcia-Segura instead derives new analytical solutions for that expansion. The formulas allow the wind's mechanical power to vary with time. They also fold in the common envelope scenario of binary evolution. In that scenario, a companion spirals inside the star's shared outer layers. A database of real nebulae is then compared against the solutions. A large share of them fit the common envelope picture better. Fast and slow expanders alike line up with that binary story. Single giant-star models succeed only in a narrow speed band. Their reach covers just the moderate expansion velocities in the sample. Binary interaction, the solutions suggest, shapes most planetary nebulae.
arxiv-2512-08187: Kazuhide Matsuda, a number theorist in Japan, posted a short research paper on arXiv in December 2025 about two classic functions of complex analysis, the eta and theta functions. Powers of these functions carry multiplier systems, which are characters that record how the functions change under modular transformations. Matsuda determines the kernels of those multiplier systems for all integer powers, completing a basic piece of the theory of these functions.
arxiv-2512-08387:
M Schultheis, L Serrano, B Thorsbro, and colleagues, astronomers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about the Milky Way nuclear star cluster. This dense cluster sits at the galactic center, inside a nuclear stellar disc, and together they rule gravity in the inner few hundred parsecs. How the cluster formed, and whether it grew from inside out or by swallowing smaller clusters, remains debated.

The team reanalyzed low resolution infrared spectra of the cluster with an improved line list built for cool giant stars. Cross checks against high resolution spectra pinned the measurement errors down tightly. Their clean sample covers over a thousand giant stars. Most are metal rich, but about a fifth form a metal poor group, recording more than one formation channel. Mapping metal content revealed a clear gradient, richer toward the center, which the authors say favors inside out formation.
arxiv-2512-08487:
Amandine Boucart, Sonia Fliss, and Laure Giovangigli, applied mathematicians in France, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. They study how sound waves scatter from an object coated with a thin layer of randomly placed tiny particles, all far smaller than the wavelength. Simulating every particle directly is costly, and the answer depends on the exact random layout, which no one can fully know.

Their solution replaces the messy coating with an equivalent boundary condition. A multiscale expansion produces it, with coefficients from corrector problems on unbounded random domains. Assuming the particles follow a stationary, well mixed random process, they prove those problems have exactly one solution. They then give error bounds for the model, and simulations illustrate the theory. The work turns a costly random microstructure problem into a clean boundary problem engineers can solve.
arxiv-2512-08787:
Zeyu Huang and coauthors study how members of a university community understand and build collective memory together. Collective memory, the shared memories and impressions that shape a group culture, grows only through ongoing member contributions. Past work often views it from a broad social angle, with less focus on how individual members see it or act on it.

The team ran a two week field study on a campus with close to forty participants, using two mobile systems as observation anchors. One was a location based narrative and exploration tool drawn from prior design work. The other was a standard online forum that reflects current practice. A core tension emerged between looking back to reflect and documenting the present as history for the future. That tension shaped story focus, expectations, and how people drew inspiration. Design lessons for community platforms follow from the findings.
arxiv-2512-09187:
Mrinal Agarwal and coauthors present WOLF, a benchmark to measure deception in language models. Deception is central to multi agent reasoning: a good system must hide facts with care while detecting misleading behavior in others. Most evaluations reduce deception to static classification, missing its interactive and evolving nature.

WOLF places role based agents, such as villager, werewolf, seer, and doctor, in a scripted state machine with strict night and day cycles, debate turns, and majority voting. Every statement is a study unit, rated for honesty by its speaker and by peers for how false it seems. Deception is classified by a standard taxonomy covering omission, distortion, fabrication, and misdirection,. Across many runs and thousands of statements, werewolves deceive in a sizable share of turns, while peer detection shows high precision but only moderate accuracy. Doubts about werewolves rise across rounds, while doubts about truthful roles stay flat.
arxiv-2512-09287:
Yi Liao, Xiao-Dong Ma, and Xiang Zhao study an exotic possibility in particle physics: a nucleon, a proton or neutron, decaying into three leptons. Such decays would break baryon number, a rule that ordinary physics keeps exact. Earlier work by two of the authors covered one class of contributions to these decays and found them strongly suppressed.

This paper handles the other class, the contact contributions, which come from higher-dimensional operators in the low-energy effective theory of particle interactions. The authors build a complete basis of the relevant operators, then translate them into the language of chiral perturbation theory to compute decay rates. Comparing with existing experimental data, they place strict limits on the operators. They also work through one complete ultraviolet model to show how it connects with their framework, aiming to guide searches at upcoming large neutrino experiments.
arxiv-2512-09587:
Francesco Scarano, Angelo Paduano, and Francesco Avallone use simulations to explain how acoustic liners dissipate noise when air flows across them. Liners, perforated panels over cavities, quieten aircraft engines and ventilation systems. In service they sit under grazing turbulent flow, and how that flow changes their absorption was not understood.

Their lattice-Boltzmann simulations model a liner cavity under grazing flow with sound waves at various pressure levels and frequencies, and with waves traveling either way. They identify two dissipation mechanisms: viscous losses in the shear layer along the orifice walls, and vortex shedding, quantified through Howe's energy corollary. Without grazing flow, both flow phases dissipate equally. Grazing flow reshapes the topology, pinning a vortex that confines the acoustic motion to the orifice's downstream half. Viscous losses rise at low sound levels, while vortex shedding switches sign between phases, generating sound on outflow. Net dissipation drops with grazing flow.
arxiv-2512-09787:
Felipe S. Quintino, Pushpa N. Rathie, and three coauthors develop a general family of probability distributions for positive, lopsided data. Real datasets are often asymmetric, with a long tail on one side, and fitting them well matters. The family they study has support on the positive numbers only. It also serves as a unified frame for limit results in extreme value theory, the study of rare extremes. The authors derive several mathematical properties of the class.

A strength of the construction is how many familiar models it contains as special cases. The Generalized Gamma, Inverse Gamma, Weibull, Fréchet, half-normal, modified half-normal, Rayleigh, and Erlang distributions all fall inside it. That means results proved once for the general class apply across this whole list. To show practical value, the authors test their analytical models on real life datasets and report how the fits perform.
arxiv-2512-10087:
Igor Rivin presents a software suite for studying ideal polyhedra in hyperbolic space, and reports two surprises it uncovered. Ideal polyhedra have all vertices at infinity, and Rivin's variational theory tells which ones exist. The software checks whether a combinatorial type can be realized and searches for the shape of maximum volume. Across a thorough software study, the largest volume polyhedra kept showing dihedral angles that are rational multiples of pi. Nothing in the setup predicts that pattern.

The second phenomenon concerns random configurations. Their volumes track a Beta curve closely, and the mean scaled volume settles near a simple constant as the vertex count grows. The author supplies complete data for small vertex counts: positions, triangle meshes, and verified rational angle structures. An interactive implementation is public. The rational angle phenomenon is the kind of empirical regularity that demands a theorem.
arxiv-2512-10487:
Vyron Kampourakis and co-authors propose a standard way to judge cyber ranges, the practice grounds where security teams train against realistic attacks. Ranges matter most for critical infrastructure, where exercises join information and operational technology. Yet judging whether a platform is suitable and effective has varied from buyer to buyer.

Their framework sets out criteria covering technical fidelity, training and assessment strength, scalability, and usability, then weights them with the Analytic Hierarchy Process, a structured decision method based on pairwise comparisons. A large language model plays a panel of experts from several fields, making the comparisons consistent and repeatable without gathering real experts each time. The output is a numbered score for each platform, meant to guide providers and users and expose where a range needs improvement.
arxiv-2512-10587:
Maxim Dvornikov reviews how quantum field theory handles massive Dirac neutrinos as they move through matter and fields. Neutrinos are famously elusive, and their oscillations can shift when matter or magnetic fields are present, so a careful quantum treatment matters for making sense of experiments. His review, written for the Lomonosov Conference, works through two backgrounds in detail.

First comes ordinary matter, then a magnetic field acting on neutrinos with anomalous magnetic moments. In both cases he derives operator-valued wavefunctions that respect the canonical anticommutation rules, and checks that the field's total energy and momentum come out in the proper forms. Using the exact solution of the Dirac equation in a magnetic field, he also builds the neutrino propagator for that background. The results support field-theory work on neutrino oscillations in real settings.
arxiv-2512-10687:
Manon Kempermann and co-authors argue that safety testing for language models asks the wrong question. Standard evaluations hunt universal dangers, but millions of people ask chatbots for personal advice on money and health, where whether an answer harms depends on who is asking. A tip that is fine for a wealthy user can be reckless for someone in debt or poor health.

The team gave finance and health advice from GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4, and Gemini 2.5 Pro to evaluators judging it for user profiles of varying vulnerability. Identical answers scored far worse once evaluators knew the user's circumstances, especially for the most vulnerable. A second study found that letting users disclose the context they naturally would share did not close the gap. Welfare safety, they conclude, needs its own method, and they publish code and data.
arxiv-2512-10787:
Moshe Lahmy and Roi Yozevitch fix a failure mode of retrieval-augmented generation on questions that need several hops. If the first retrieval misses a bridge fact, later reasoning stalls. Corrective systems usually respond by adding more context, but a fatter context dilutes: distractors crowd out the evidence that matters. Their controller, SEAL-RAG, follows the opposite rule, replace, don't expand, under a fixed retrieval depth.

SEAL cycles through search, extraction, assessment, and looping. It extracts entities on the fly to build a live list of what is missing, fires targeted micro-queries for the gaps. And ranks entity-first so gap-closing evidence swaps into the fixed slots, pushing distractors out. Against faithful reimplementations of Basic RAG, CRAG, Self-RAG, and Adaptive-k on HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA, it improved answer correctness and evidence precision substantially while keeping costs predictable.
arxiv-2512-12287:
Ahmad Zafarani and five co-authors present RealDrag, a benchmark for drag based image editing, in a 2025 paper. In drag editing, a user pulls a point in a photo to a new spot, like moving a smile wider. Judging such tools has been unreliable, since no data set gave the correct final image to compare against.

RealDrag supplies over 400 human labeled samples from varied videos, with source and target images, pull points, edit masks, and captions. The team adds four new scores that check pixel match, kept areas, and meaning. They test 17 top models, revealing clear trade-offs, and plan to release the data and tools in public.
arxiv-2512-12687:
Marwa Ennaceur introduces almost periodic Banach-Malcev algebras in a 2025 math paper. Malcev algebras are non-associative algebras tied to Moufang loops, structures that soften group rules. Almost periodic functions, from Bohr's theory, nearly repeat their values in a regular way. Ennaceur joins the two by requiring adjoint orbits of the algebra to be compact in a relative sense.

That condition yields a spectral description: the spectrum of each adjoint operator lies on the imaginary axis. Orbit closures stay uniformly bounded, and a continuous calculus exists for such derivations. Compact Malcev algebras, above all the imaginary octonions, give finite size examples whose Moufang loops carry flows that repeat exactly. A case study treats actions on eigenspaces of the Malcev Laplacian. The paper is a work of pure math, with proofs rather than lab tests.
arxiv-2512-12887:
Han Liu and a large team revisit how 2D foundation models, large pre-trained image models, can be adapted to classify 3D medical scans. Sorting such scans is a core task in modern clinics. Foundation models promise a faster path to new tasks, but the team finds the field has weak spots.

They name three pitfalls in current research: bias from the data regime used, poor choices in how models are adapted, and too narrow a set of test tasks. Their study takes a fresh look at scaling these models to 3D tasks with those flaws in mind. The goal is a more honest guide for clinical image work.
arxiv-2512-13187:
Aida Abiad and Jan Meeus extend a classic eigenvalue bound on graph coloring to graphs where distance matters. Hoffman's bound uses the eigenvalues of a graph's adjacency matrix to lower-bound its chromatic number, the fewest colors needed so neighbors differ. Their version covers distance-k coloring.

The new bound also lower-bounds a quantum version of the distance coloring number. It depends on a polynomial that can be chosen freely, so they propose linear programming methods to pick it well. The bound proves sharp for some graph classes. They also extend it to the vector chromatic number in the distance setting, unifying several older bounds.
arxiv-2512-13287:
Lucy Arditi and Anna Lisa Varri build equilibrium models for star clusters that rotate while being pulled by the tides of a host galaxy. Globular clusters often spin at a rate that does not match their orbit, a state called asynchronous rotation. Realistic models of that state were lacking.

Their three-parameter family extends truncated King models with a new asynchronicity parameter that couples tidal and rotational effects. A matched asymptotic expansion solves the governing equations globally. The resulting clusters stretch toward the galactic center and flatten toward the orbital plane, more so as asynchronicity grows. The models offer a base for later, fuller simulations.
arxiv-2512-13387:
Arkadeb Pal and co-authors study BiCrTeO6, a layered honeycomb magnet that shows two magnetic changes and multiferroic behavior. Low-dimensional honeycomb systems are prized for exotic states that emerge when spin, lattice, and charge effects compete. The team probed this compound with a wide battery of methods.

Measurements found antiferromagnetic changes near 16 and 11 kelvin, strong magnetic-electric coupling, and electric order at the lower transition. Diffraction showed a structural change at that point, with symmetry lowering that likely triggers the electric order. Disorder between chromium and tellurium sites adds relaxor behavior above the changes, making the material a rich test case.
arxiv-2512-13787:
Marie Hein, Benjamin Nachman, and David Shih study the look elsewhere effect in machine learning searches for new physics. Anomaly detectors can scan high-dimensional data with little theory bias. Searching in many directions at once, though, dilutes statistical power and can distort significance values.

Training and testing on the same data gave badly miscalibrated p-values, since the detector overfits random fluctuations. Splitting data in half gave perfect calibration but lower sensitivity. Early stopping also helped calibration, possibly at a sensitivity cost. K-folding struck the best balance between the two. Tests used Gaussian variables and the LHC Olympics collider benchmark. The findings guide how anomaly searches should report the strength of a claimed signal.
arxiv-2512-13887:
Xinfeng Gao, Olivier Pfister, and Stefan Bekiranov put the Koopman-von Neumann approach on continuous-variable photonic quantum computers. That scheme rewrites classical physics in Hilbert space, with a wave function and linear operators like quantum physics. Unlike Liouville's equation for a probability density, it evolves a classical wave function with position and momentum operators that commute.

On quantum hardware, this offers a route to model classical dynamic systems with unitary time change and quantum linear algebra tools. The authors aim at both sampling and computing hard nonlinear dynamics. They show the approach on two problems: the harmonic oscillator and a 1D partial equation for nonlinear dynamics. The nine-page paper argues this use can work on photonic hardware.
arxiv-2512-13987:
Neelesh Rampal and co-authors compare generative machine learning methods for downscaling daily precipitation over New Zealand. Downscaling turns coarse climate model output into fine-scale detail. Machine learning is cheap and can make large ensembles, but deterministic methods smooth fine structure and understate extremes.

They compare GANs, flow matching, and diffusion models in several configurations, judging spatial structure, distributions, means, extremes, calibration, and climate change signals. Higher-order solvers let diffusion and flow models use far fewer steps with minor skill loss, easing their cost. All three families performed competitively on most metrics. Diffusion and flow matching gave higher fidelity and better calibrated ensembles, while GANs were under-dispersive. Most methods understated end-of-century extreme precipitation change signals.
arxiv-2512-14087:
Yang Yang, Risa Shinoda, Hiroaki Santo, and Fumio Okura present GaussianPlant, a method to reconstruct both the look and the inner structure of plants from multi-view images. Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting renders plant appearance well for novel views, but it does not capture branching structure. That structure matters for plant phenotyping and growth analysis.

GaussianPlant uses a hierarchical representation that separates structure from appearance. Structure primitives model branches as cylinders and leaves as disks, with their branch or leaf identity optimized in a self-organized way. Appearance primitives, bound to each structure piece, render the plant as in standard splatting. Joint optimization with a re-rendering loss gives high-fidelity appearance plus accurate structure, enabling extraction of branch structure and individual leaves.
arxiv-2512-14287:
Yunnuo Xu and five coauthors design a robust scheme for low Earth orbit satellite links in a 2025 paper. Fast moving satellites make fresh channel data at the transmitter hard to get, which hurts multi user downlink performance.

Their scheme pairs OTFS modulation, which describes fast changing channels in a stable delay Doppler domain, with rate splitting multiple access, which is robust to interference and imperfect channel data. They handle real effects like fractional delays, Doppler shifts, and rectangular pulse shaping. A compact input output relation is derived, and a weighted minimum mean square error algorithm maximizes the ergodic sum rate. Simulations show the scheme improves sum rate and robustness across user layouts and channel data quality.
arxiv-2512-14387:
Fabio DiFonzo and four coauthors examine real time control of water systems in a 2025 paper. The test case is river flow control in hydropower cascades. Flow there is governed by the nonlinear shallow water equations, a set of hyperbolic partial differential equations.

Real software would need to solve mixed integer problems under those equations. It would also need to handle possibly non smooth dynamics and run fast enough for day to day choices. Theory on control to state maps under changing boundary conditions is still thin, and forecast errors add more strain. Rather than claim a full solution, the authors map the math, methods, and computing pieces a real system would need. Their framework highlights open problems and next steps.
arxiv-2512-14487:
Yu. Kozitsky, once a student of Ihor Yukhnovskii, looks back fifty years at his teacher's theory of critical points. Yukhnovskii studied the three-dimensional Ising model by integrating layer by layer over collective variables. The method rivaled the epsilon-expansion approach that later won Kenneth Wilson a Nobel Prize, reaching similar answers through a quite different route.

Kozitsky argues the work deserves a wider frame than his fellow students once gave it. He places the theory inside the rapid reshaping of quantum field theory and statistical physics during the late twentieth century. The article weighs what the method explained, where its insight ran deeper, and how it influenced later work.
arxiv-2512-14887:
Massimiliano Fadda and four coauthors improve a system that maps political viewpoints in news coverage. News outlets shape public debate through the topics they pick and the voices they quote. The team's earlier pipeline first found the range of views on a topic with human help, then sorted claims into those views.

The upgrade fine tunes large language models to do the sorting, and enriches each claim with facts about the actors it names, drawn from Wikidata. Tested on a benchmark about the UK immigration debate, each upgrade helped on its own. Together they worked best, above all with models that can read long inputs. The work gives media scholars a sharper way to judge whether coverage offers a fair spread of views.
arxiv-2512-15487:
Mats Ehrnstrom and Mark Groves prove that a full dispersion water wave model has fully localized solitary waves in a 2025 paper. The Kadomtsev Petviashvili equation models gravity capillary waves under strong surface tension. Its fully localized lumps, which decay to zero in every direction, were known for the standard version.

The full dispersion version keeps the exact dispersion relation from the water wave problem instead of an approximation. The authors recast it as a perturbation of the standard equation and apply a variant of the implicit function theorem. That yields a family of symmetric, fully localized solitary waves for the sharper model as well.
arxiv-2512-15687:
Zhenwen Liang and co authors present G2RL, a gradient guided reinforcement learning method for language model reasoning, in a 2025 paper. Reinforcement learning improves reasoning, but common exploration tricks, such as entropy bonuses, reward surface variety without regard to how a sample would actually change the model. Exploration and learning can thus pull apart.

For each response, G2RL builds a feature from the model's final layer sensitivity, cheaply taken from a standard forward pass. Samples that would push the policy in novel gradient directions earn a bounded reward boost, while redundant ones are damped. On math and general reasoning tests with Qwen3 models, G2RL beats entropy based and embedding based baselines on pass rates.
arxiv-2512-16187:
Giedrius Zlabys and five co-authors explore patterned quantum landscapes in a paper posted to arXiv in 2025. They study particles moving through a row of sharp barriers whose heights vary in a repeating spatial pattern. Tuning how fast that pattern repeats reshapes the energy spectrum into a fractal shape like Hofstadter's butterfly.

Within certain regimes, the system carries current in a topological way, protected by whole-number invariants called Chern numbers. The authors connect their setup to the classic Hofstadter model and confirm the topology by tracking how wave packet centers drift. Slowly changing the pattern steers the transport in a controlled fashion. They also propose a lab realization using three-level atoms controlled by light. Such engineered lattices could serve as flexible test beds for topological quantum transport.
arxiv-2512-16287:
Yehor Tereshchenko, Mika Hamalainen, and Svitlana Myroniuk test AI translation for dying languages in a 2025 paper posted to arXiv. Translation research mostly covers big languages. Low-resource ones are left understudied. The team compares OpenAI GPT models at translating between Finnish and four Uralic languages. Some models reason step by step, and some do not.

The languages are Komi-Zyrian, Moksha, Erzya, and Udmurt. All four are endangered. The test material is a parallel corpus of literary texts. Beyond quality, the authors measured the refusal rate. That is how often a model declines to try at all. Reasoning models refused 16 percentage points less often than the others. Scores also varied a lot across model designs. The results help researchers and language communities judge whether modern models can support work to preserve these languages.
arxiv-2512-16387:
Kazuki Nakazawa, Terufumi Yamaguchi, and Ai Yamakage study exotic electrical responses in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their material is Cu2WSe4, a layered compound. Its crystal has a gyrotropic twist, but it is not truly chiral. Physicists now explore orbital effects, tied to electron orbits, as counterparts of spin effects.

The team computed the Edelstein effect, where current creates magnetization. They also computed two nonlinear Hall effects. In the Edelstein response, the orbital part dominates the spin part. The nonlinear effects are governed mainly by the Berry curvature dipole. That dipole is a geometric property of the electron bands. Spin-orbit coupling plays only a minor role here. Orbital degrees of freedom are essential instead. The orbital signals in both effects track the crystal's chirality closely. They could serve as a practical chirality indicator.
arxiv-2512-16587:
Julius Koschnick tests a well known claim about the start of modern economic growth. Joel Mokyr argued that growth took off in the 1700s. In his view, pure knowledge and hands-on know-how began to feed each other then, during the Industrial Enlightenment. That claim had never been tested head on.

Koschnick builds two new text-based measures. One gauges how fresh a publication is. The other gauges how ideas spill between the two kinds of knowledge. Using English data from 1600 to 1800, he finds the feedback loop turned positive in the late 1700s. The shift also tracks with gains in the real economy, seen through patents.
arxiv-2512-16887:
Julián López and coauthors present SiCoBioNa, an open-source simulator for pedestrian evacuations based on the Social Force Model. Evacuation planning needs tools that capture how people push, follow goals, and squeeze around obstacles in enclosed spaces.

The software gives a friendly graphical interface where users set pedestrian traits, room layouts, and start positions with no modeling background. The force model covers goal-driven motion, person-to-person effects, and wall effects. Output comes as both numbers and visuals, so users can compare layouts and spot jams. Its modular build makes it a reusable research tool and a practical aid for safety planning.
arxiv-2512-17387:
Sravani Gunnu, Shanmukha Guttula, and Hima Patel built CIFE, a test of whether code-writing AI follows orders, not just whether its code runs. Real developers demand more than working code: they set rules on style, safety checks, and error handling. Old benchmarks mostly ran the code and counted passes, missing every broken rule.

CIFE holds 1,000 Python tasks, each carrying about 7 stated rules drawn from 13 kinds of constraint.
