The team graded 14 leading models with a combined score that weighs working code and rule keeping together. The best models met over 90 percent of rules one by one. Yet when every rule in a task had to hold at once, success fell to between 39 and 66 percent.
arxiv-2512-17587:
Francesco Martinelli, Anouk Droux, and Claude Ederer measure what really sets the strength of spin splitting in altermagnets. These magnets split electron energies by spin without any net magnetization, a prized trick for future devices. Theorists had guessed the split is governed by multipoles, lopsided patterns in the charge and magnetism around each atom, but the link rested on symmetry talk alone.

Using first-principles calculations on two model crystals, SrCrO3 and LaVO3, the team dialed multipoles up and down and watched the split respond. No single lowest multipole ruled the split. Several multipoles of similar strength added their effects together. Describing altermagnetism fairly, they argue, takes a multi-part order parameter, not a single number.
arxiv-2512-17687:
Jin Lei builds a fast stand-in for one of nuclear physics' slowest calculations. When a loose deuteron nucleus strikes a target, it can stretch and break apart mid-flight, and the CDCC method tracks all those coupled paths at great cost. Exploring how the answer shifts across 18 uncertain input settings the honest way would take prohibitive computer time.

The emulator learns from a library of full runs, compresses them into a small basis of key patterns, and answers new settings by quick projection onto that basis. It runs about a hundred times faster. On deuterons hitting nickel-58 at 21.6 MeV, its scattering predictions missed the full model by under 0.1 percent. Bayesian fitting and honest error bars for reaction theory are now affordable.
arxiv-2512-17787:
R Ruffini and a large team look back over fifty years of gamma-ray burst research and restate their group's reading of the field. Gamma-ray bursts are the brightest explosions known, and the team's BdHN model explains the strongest class as a collapsing star feeding a newborn black hole beside a neutron star companion. Two record events, GRB 190114C and GRB 220101A, anchor the account.

The review walks through the seven episodes they use to dissect such a burst, from first flash to TeV glow, and offers fresh reasoning about the highest-energy light. Bolder threads run alongside: the Crab supernova may itself hide a burst, and Sagittarius A, our galaxy's central black hole, may help unmask dark matter's particle, which they call the X fermion. Read it as a school of thought's manifesto, claims included.
arxiv-2512-17887:
Mateja Bošković, Rafael A. Porto, and Matthias Koschnitzke study clouds of ultra light particles that may gather around spinning black holes. When two black holes orbit each other, a companion can stir or drain such a cloud. Those effects could leave marks on the gravity waves the pair emits.

Their framework handles tilted and stretched orbits and tracks both sharp and smooth changes in the cloud. Some orbits hover in a floating state while they drain the cloud early, pushing the pair's path more oval. Tilt can even make flat orbits unstable at certain mass ratios. Future detectors like LISA could read these trails as signs of new particles.
arxiv-2512-18087:
Meysam Ghanbari leads a five author team adding a watch layer to outdoor light based networks. Rooftop optical links beam data through open air at high speed, but open beams can be tapped or abused. Their system locates users by reading the light pattern that lands on a grid of small detectors.

A physics based model does the first pass, and a light learning step cleans up device quirks. In matched tests the hybrid beat a plain deep learning method on accuracy while training faster and cheaper. Adding more detector cells helped up to a grid near 60 by 60 or 80 by 80. Live position checks against network logs could flag odd use, like a hidden listener.
arxiv-2512-18387:
Francesca Ballatore, Lorenzo Scolaris, and Chiara Giverso model immunotherapy for glioblastoma, a fast and deadly brain tumor. Their math couples tumor growth with an infusion of killer T cells, the immune soldiers that hunt cancer. Cells spread, multiply, and drift toward a signal the tumor itself gives off.

A stripped down version of the model first finds the infusion level where the tumor can be wiped out, and that level matches clinical patterns. The full model then runs on scans of a real patient's brain, rebuilt in 3D from MRI and fiber maps. Where the tumor sits and how hard the cells are dosed decide the outcome, a case for plans shaped to each patient's scans.
arxiv-2512-18587:
Marios Papamichalis and Regina Ruane tackle a practical question in network science: when several models fit the same network, how should their predictions be combined? Each estimates a graphon, the function giving the chance two nodes link. Their 2025 paper introduces Bayesian predictive synthesis at the graphon level. Models act as agents, a prior weights their link probabilities, and the posterior returns one graphon with credible intervals.

The test case is a union of overlapping mechanisms, where a pair links if any mechanism links it. Weights forced to sum to one cannot reproduce a union. Free or nonnegative weights do far better, and a noisy-OR rule matches the union exactly. On six standard networks, combining adds under one percent once a benchmark flaw is corrected. On the Amazon and YouTube multiplex networks, though, synthesis beats every competitor, including spectral estimation, blockmodels, random forests, and node2vec.
arxiv-2512-19387:
Yueyao Chen, Kai-Ni Wang, Dario Tayupo, and Arnaud Huaulm'e steady the automatic reading of surgical video. Workflow recognition labels each frame with the current phase of an operation, feeding context-aware help and skill scoring. Two flaws plague current systems: labels jitter between frames, and look-alike phases get confused.

Their framework, DSTED, runs two paths. A memory path passes forward only high-confidence past features, judged by several reliability checks. A prototype path refines shaky frames by matching them against learned class prototypes built from hard cases. A confidence gate blends the paths. On a hysterectomy dataset, the method set a new best accuracy and F1 score.
arxiv-2512-19787:
Jaewon Yoo leads a fifteen-author white paper for a new telescope, K-DRIFT. The KASI Deep Rolling Imaging Fast Telescope was built to catch the faintest light in the sky. Its strength is dim, spread-out glow inside galaxy clusters. Chief among these is intracluster light. That is the glow of stars torn from galaxies, adrift between them.

To compare where that glow sits and where dark matter sits can show how clusters form. The paper also lists other faint game. It names dim structures in the brightest cluster galaxy, ultra-diffuse galaxies, and tidal debris. Each is a clue to how galaxies change in dense homes. Plans for viewing, for computer models, and for machine learning are laid out. Links with other sky surveys, across many wavelengths, are weighed as well.
arxiv-2512-20087:
Guang-Yao Xiao and five co-authors join three data kinds to unmask dark companions of eclipsing binaries. A third body tugs the pair's orbit. That shifts the eclipse times. Hipparcos and Gaia astrometry track the wobble on the sky. Together, they give the companion's true mass and tilt, not just lower bounds. The method is shown on two systems.

For V Puppis, a massive B-type pair, the old five-and-a-half-year signal fails to confirm. A fourteen-year period fits instead. The outer body weighs about 7.7 solar masses. It is a strong stellar-mass black hole candidate. For the contact binary CY Arietis, the companion's true mass is near two-thirds of a solar mass. That backs the white dwarf idea from past work. Both outer orbits lie near edge-on, a hint of coplanar birth.
arxiv-2512-20187:
Mohamad Maassarani classifies a family of rings and algebras built from simpler pieces. Each building block has only two idempotents, zero and one, and blocks are combined by taking products of powers. He determines exactly when two such products are isomorphic and describes their automorphism groups, which split into products of wreath products.

The results are then applied to algebras generated by a single element over a perfect field. Maassarani shows any such algebra is either a polynomial ring or a finite product of truncated polynomial rings over field extensions. He classifies these algebras completely and computes their automorphism groups in matrix terms. Algebraists get a full inventory of a basic building-block class.
arxiv-2512-20287:
Wanting Sun, Shunan Wei, and Donglei Yang count special vertex subsets in highly regular graphs. Take a regular graph on a multiple of r vertices. A clique factor is a set of disjoint cliques of size r covering chosen vertices. The question is how many vertex subsets induce a subgraph containing such a factor.

The authors prove that, for large enough graphs of the stated regularity, the number of good subsets is at least a constant times two to the number of vertices. In other words, a positive fraction of all subsets works, in an exponential sense. The theorem confirms a conjecture of Draganić, Keevash, and Müyesser for large cases, closing a problem about cyclic subsets in regular Dirac-type graphs.
arxiv-2512-20587:
Furkan Semih Dündar, Xerxes D Arsiwalla, and Hatem Elshatlawy derive quantum logic gates from rewriting systems. In the Wolfram model, multiway systems track every possible way a string can be rewritten, forming a branching graph of computations. The authors restrict attention to cyclic strings with a neighbourhood constraint, called Leibnizian strings.

Such strings mimic a system of fermions: occupation numbers of character neighbourhoods follow a Fermi-Dirac distribution. The strings form a module with a symmetric bilinear form, supporting a discrete path integral and an S-matrix whose entries are transition amplitudes. Those matrices explicitly represent the CNOT, pi-over-eight, and Hadamard gates, and circuits built from them. Nondeterministic rewriting, with causal structure added, thus encodes genuine quantum circuits.
arxiv-2512-21687:
Yoshiki Fukusumi derives a formula for how anyons transform when they pass through a domain wall. Anyons are exotic particle-like excitations in two-dimensional topological phases, and domain walls separate regions in different phases. Tracking how anyons change across a wall is central to classifying topological order and the phase transitions between orders.

The formalism rests on ring homomorphisms between the commutative fusion rings of the two sides, structures described as symmetry topological field theories. It assumes the Verlinde formula holds for those rings. Combined with setting-specific data, the formula classifies the allowed anyon transformations. Through known links, it describes massless renormalization group flows between conformal field theories and series of measurement-induced phase changes. Fukusumi connects the ideal structure of the massless flow to modules in the massive theory, enabling Nambu-Goldstone-style arguments for generalized symmetries. Orbifolding extends the results to richer models.
arxiv-2512-22287:
Zikun Guo, Adeyinka P. Adedigba, and Rammohan Mallipeddi generate fake device power data so energy teams can work without exposing real households. Non-intrusive load tracking, which infers device use from a home's total use, needs labeled data that barely exists. Earlier generative models treated every appliance alike, ignoring that kettles switch in bursts while fridges run nonstop, and training often turned unstable.

Their Cluster Aggregated GAN routes each appliance to a branch matching its behavior. Bursty devices are clustered by activation pattern, with a dedicated maker per cluster so rare modes get capacity too. Continuous appliances go to an LSTM-based generator with sequence compression for stability. On the UVIC smart plug dataset, the system beat baselines on realism, diversity, and training stability.
arxiv-2512-22387:
Bhanu Prakash Vangala, Ali Adibifar, Ashish Gehani, and Tanu Malik test whether code written by AI agents runs. They took three leading coding agents, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Gemini, and had them build 300 projects from 100 standardized prompts in Python, JavaScript, and Java. Each project was then launched in a clean environment with only operating system packages plus whatever dependencies the model itself specified.

Only about sixty-eight percent of the projects executed out of the box. Python fared best at roughly eighty-nine percent, while Java managed just forty-four percent. The team separates claimed, working, and runtime dependencies, and found actual runtime needs expanded more than thirteenfold beyond what models declared. Hidden dependencies, they conclude, are the reproducibility gap.
arxiv-2512-22487:
Jungyeul Park and Chulwoo Park settle a design question for Korean syntax databases: what should count as the basic terminal unit in a constituency treebank? Korean words are morphologically rich. Using morphemes as terminals blurs the line between word-internal structure and phrase structure. It also clashes with resources built on the eojeol, the space-delimited word unit of Korean writing.

The authors argue for eojeol-based constituency representation, with morphological segmentation and fine-grained part-of-speech detail kept in a separate, non-constituent layer. Under explicit normalization assumptions, the Sejong, Penn Korean, and KAIST treebanks can all be compared over one shared eojeol backbone. Their outlined annotation scheme preserves interpretable trees, supports alignment between constituency and dependency resources, and gives future Korean parsers a surface-form terminal layer.
arxiv-2512-22787:
Zhou Yang, Edward Dougherty, Chen Zhang, Zhenhe Pan, and Fang Jin reconstruct how COVID-19 spread through China, aiming to learn which public health responses actually slowed transmission. They gather case reports from local health commissions, the Chinese CDC, and official government social media accounts. Natural language processing plus manual checking turns those reports into transmission and tracking chains showing who likely infected whom and where cases traveled.

Combined with population movement data from Wuhan, the chains reveal strong regional differences, with larger cities recording more infections, plausibly driven by social activity. Most symptomatic people reached a hospital within five days of symptoms starting, and close contacts of confirmed cases arrived even sooner. Early infections traced mainly to travel involving Hubei Province, while later spread was increasingly linked to everyday social activities, a shift that matters for planning future responses.
arxiv-2512-22887:
Shunrui Li and Yang Liu offer a new route to the Atiyah-Singer index theorem, one of the central results linking analysis and topology. The index theorem is traditionally derived through supersymmetric physics, where paired bosonic and fermionic contributions cancel neatly. Li and Liu show the same structure arises directly from ordinary quantum statistics, with no supersymmetry assumed.

Their bridge is a correspondence: the grand partition functions of non-interacting boson and fermion systems are exactly the Chern characters of certain vector bundles, the geometric objects the theorem counts with. They extend the correspondence to infinite dimensions by building a framework of spectral-sheaf pairs. Inside it they state a generalized index theorem that identifies the topological index with a regularized product over a spectrum. The authors present quantum statistics itself as a sufficient foundation for these topological invariants.
arxiv-2512-22987:
Sebastian Buhai studies how reputation forms when evidence is kept in a sealed record, revealed only at a final moment. In the protocol analyzed, the record's existence, its public custodian, and its review dates are all visible, while the contents stay sealed until terminal disclosure. At each review, the holder may pass the record along, disclose it, or retain it, and retention itself carries information.

A holder who retained the record evidently chose not to act. Each retention therefore rules out the states where acting would have been chosen. That censoring yields an exact Bayesian updating rule for the public. Under interval strategies, the public belief is captured by finitely many support points, and a compact benchmark verifies equilibria in the Markov perfect Bayesian sense. With two certified routes for one record, retention on one route constrains the other, creating network value pairwise analysis would miss.
arxiv-2512-23087:
Yingru Li and co-authors diagnose a quiet source of instability in reinforcement learning for large language models: the training engine and the inference engine compute slightly different probabilities for the same model. That mismatch matters unevenly across the vocabulary. The authors prove the divergence bound shrinks for high-probability tokens but stays significant for rare tail tokens, which then inject biased errors that compound across a sequence.

Their remedy, Dynamic Vocabulary Pruning, restricts the learning objective at each step to a dynamically chosen safe vocabulary that excludes the tail. The trade is deliberate: accept a small, bounded optimization bias to remove large, destabilizing errors, instead of correcting errors after the fact. Experiments show training stays stable under the pruned objective, and the authors derive strict bounds on the bias the pruning introduces. The result is a recipe for steadier large-model reinforcement learning on high-throughput stacks.
arxiv-2512-23587:
Christopher Burger, Karmece Talley, and Christina Trotter test whether large language models can police their own kind in computing classrooms. With students able to generate code and essays with AI, educators need detection methods they can trust. The study asks GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini to identify AI-generated text in computing-specific material, including under deceptive prompts designed to evade detection.

The models proved unstable judges. Default AI text was easy for them to spot, but they misclassified human-written work at rates reaching about a third of cases. Deceptive prompting degraded them badly; in one test, Gemini's output completely fooled GPT-4. The authors conclude these models are currently too unreliable for high-stakes academic misconduct decisions. The paper was accepted to the Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences.
arxiv-2512-23687:
Juan Gutiérrez and Sagartanu Pal study a graph editing problem called minimum subgraph complementation. Complementing a set of vertices toggles every edge and non-edge inside the set. Given a graph and a target family, the task is to find the smallest set whose complementation pushes the graph into the target family. The yes-or-no version is well studied and often NP-complete; the optimization version had barely been touched.

The authors give polynomial-time algorithms for several nontrivial cases, including transforming between bipartite, co-bipartite, and split graphs, and turning bipartite regular graphs into chordal ones. Complementing toward graphs of fixed degeneracy is polynomial when the input is a forest. They also settle connectivity targets: reaching a disconnected graph, or a 2-connected one, can each be optimized in polynomial time for arbitrary inputs.
arxiv-2512-23887:
Maria Chudnovsky, Jadwiga Czyżewska, Marcin Pilipczuk, and Paweł Rzążewski prove a structural graph theory result in a long-running series on the tree-independence number. A measure of how far a graph is from being treelike when independence is taken into account. This seventh installment excludes a star: the graphs considered contain no fixed star as an induced subgraph, and no fixed planar graph as an induced minor.

Under those two exclusions, the authors show the tree-independence number grows at most polylogarithmically in the size of the graph, a very slow bound. The theorem is a weakening of a conjecture by Dallard and co-authors, who expected an even stronger conclusion; proving the weaker polylogarithmic version is a step toward the full conjecture. Results like this one typically feed algorithms, since small tree-independence number makes many hard problems on such graph classes tractable.
arxiv-2512-24587:
Sunay Joshi, Yan Sun, and Hamed Hassani address test-time filtering as a way to control several risks in generative AI systems at once. A filter compares behavior scores with estimated thresholds and changes outputs that break the bounds. Users may rank some risks above others, so thresholds must respect stated priorities while holding finite-sample guarantees.

Two dynamic programming algorithms exploit the sequential structure of the problem. One gives a direct finite-sample procedure, and the other uses data exchangeability for its guarantee. Readers deploying generative systems get a principled way to enforce multiple limits together, rather than tuning each risk in isolation.
arxiv-2512-24787:
Yunsheng Pang, Zijian Liu, Yudong Li, and Tencent colleagues present HiGR, a hierarchical generative system that recommends a whole slate of items at industrial scale. Generative recommenders using semantic identifiers struggle with slates: identifier spaces tangle planning, long autoregressive decoding is slow, and token goals ignore whole-list quality. HiGR splits the job into high-level list planning and finer generation.

That hierarchy bridges semantic planning and detailed item choice for a single display. Readers in recommender systems get a design aimed at production scale at a major platform. The key lesson is to judge a slate as a whole, not as isolated tokens.
arxiv-2512-24987:
Justin McInroy and Abdul Wajid Mir guide readers through the two-generated axial algebras of Monster type, non-associative algebras generalizing the Griess algebra. Their symmetry group is the Monster, the largest sporadic simple group. Two-generated algebras are the building blocks for the whole class and were recently classified by several authors. Twelve infinite families appear, plus the exceptional Highwater algebra and its cover.

Properties of each family are detailed, since the sorting alone left their behavior poorly understood. Algebra readers get a reference for working with these objects. Such guides turn a bare sorting list into usable knowledge about identities, ideals, and automorphisms.
arxiv-2601-00387:
Somnath Bhattacharjee, Markus Bläser, Pranjal Dutta, and Saswata Mukherjee study whether adding up very many small algebraic circuits can force the total size to explode. The question echoes a famous open conjecture about the permanent polynomial. Their 2026 paper, an extended version of a 2024 conference paper, ties the question to the Shub-Smale tau conjecture, a deep claim about how hard it is to write down integers.

Assuming that conjecture, the team proves an exponential lower bound for such sums. Their tools come from parameterized complexity, and they also prove a matching lower bound for a weighted parameterized class. Further results link that class to a collapse of a counting hierarchy, and a related class is described through permanents.
arxiv-2601-00787:
Jonathan Simkin and seven co-authors test, in 2026, whether a cancer registry AI can move between provinces in Canada. Registries log each cancer case, mostly from pathology reports written in prose. A transformer model, BCCRTron, was built for the British Columbia registry. The team retrained it, and a second medical model, on reports from Newfoundland and Labrador.

The training sets held about one hundred four thousand reports for a first task. That task asks if a report shows cancer at all. Both models kept high scores after modest retraining. The team then merged the two models with a cautious rule: a flag from either one counts. That merge caught almost every cancer, and cut missed cases to twenty-four. The missed count was half that of either model alone. Only model weights crossed province lines, so patient data stayed home.
arxiv-2601-01287:
Wu and Konstantinidis argue that how well a system follows the rules could serve as a fair measure of trust online. Most trust scores rest on user ratings or narrow service measures, which are easy to sway. Laws such as European and United States health privacy rules give firmer standards, but checks usually end in pass or fail.

Their engine turns written duties into a form a computer can check, then scans event logs for breaches. Each breach is scored by how much data it touched, how long it lasted, and how serious it was. Tests on fake hospital data gave graded scores that showed far more detail.
arxiv-2601-01687:
Outlining organs and tumors in three-dimensional medical scans is essential for diagnosis and surgery, yet labeled 3D scans are scarce and patient anatomy varies widely. Abdur Fayjie, Pankhi Kashyap, Jutika Borah, and Patrick Vandewalle propose FALCON, a segmentation framework that learns from very few examples and transfers across medical domains.

FALCON first learns general segmentation skills from ordinary photographs, slice by slice, then adapts to medical images with adversarial fine-tuning and extra attention to boundaries. Guided by a few support examples, it adjusts to each patient's anatomy. Across four benchmarks it earned the best boundary accuracy scores while matching leading methods on overlap, using far less labeled data, no augmentation, and much less computing power.
arxiv-2601-01887:
Fine-tuning a safety-aligned language model on new data can quietly strip away its safety training, and the usual fix needs many safety examples and costs model quality. Jiawen Zhang and six co-authors report a surprise: a single safety example can fully restore alignment.

The recovery worked regardless of how many harmful examples the fine-tuning used or how large the model was, and it converged within a few epochs across five safety-aligned models and multiple datasets. The authors trace the effect to the low-rank structure of the safety gradient, which makes the correction cheap to apply. One-shot patching could make repairing fine-tuned models far less expensive for developers.
arxiv-2601-01987:
Quantum sensors promise extreme precision but noise erodes their advantage. Ran Liu and eight co-authors harness quantum Zeno dynamics. This effect confines a system's evolution to a protected subspace. The team uses it to shield the measurement itself. Strong interactions between particles are added during the encoding stage. Earlier Zeno schemes faltered at that stage.

The test platform was nuclear magnetic resonance. There, the scheme reached near-optimal precision scaling. It did so while suffering amplitude damping. Both parallel and step-by-step settings were tested. Computer tests indicate the approach scales well. It also combines well with other control methods against broader noise types. The experiment moves Zeno protection from a single-particle curiosity toward a practical strategy for robust quantum metrology.
arxiv-2601-02087:
Photonic quantum computing builds large entangled graph states by fusing small clusters, but fusions fail often, and naive repeat-until-success wastes enormous resources. Korbinian Staudacher, Bhilahari Jeevanesan, and Tobias Guggemos develop protocols that adapt to failure, reusing leftover graph states instead of discarding them.

Graph-theoretic analysis guides the fusion networks. Each protocol is treated as a Markov process. The expected number of fusion attempts becomes a first-passage calculation. Polynomial algorithms can optimize it. The ordering of fusions is part of the search. Against simple repeat-until-success, overhead falls by orders of magnitude. Against leading protocols, it falls by up to forty percent. The biggest gains sit at realistic fusion success rates. Those run between fifty and seventy-five percent.
arxiv-2601-02187:
A superconducting diode passes current freely one way and resists it the other. No magnetic fields or ratchet shapes are needed, if the material's kinetics are nonlocal. Yuriy Yerin and Iman Askerzade build a fractional-order Ginzburg-Landau theory. It covers Josephson junctions made from fractal superconductors. An off-center layer separates them.

The one-way effect emerges from two ingredients. A Lifshitz invariant term interacts with fractional kinetics. Those kinetics encode the fractal geometry and its memory effects. Two versions give analytic solutions. One uses fractional integrals. The other uses fractional derivatives, handled through an energy-based principle. A compact current-phase relation and a diode efficiency map come out. An exact solution confirms near-ideal one-way flow. Tuning the fractional orders attains it. Everything reduces to the standard junction when the orders become integers.
arxiv-2601-02287:
Yue Zhao, Poshak Gandhi, and seven co authors search for fast moving X ray sources that may hide a black hole or neutron star in a binary system. Such pairs can be kicked to high speed when a star explodes. The team matched X ray catalogs from Chandra, XMM-Newton, Swift, and eROSITA against the Gaia DR3 star catalog.

Using Gaia positions and motions, they compute how fast each source moves compared with normal disk rotation, allowing for the unknown motion along the line of sight. They keep only sources very likely moving faster than two hundred kilometers per second, and bright in X rays compared with visible light. That cut leaves a sample of more than two thousand sources. Most normal contaminants are removed by that cut, so the list is a strong starting point for follow up.
arxiv-2601-02487:
Yashvardhan Tomar, Philip F. Hopkins, and Kyle Kremer challenge an optimistic claim about active galactic nuclei, the bright centers of galaxies where gas falls onto a supermassive black hole. It has long been argued that the accretion disk there boosts rates of binary capture, gravitational wave mergers, and other encounters between embedded stars and compact objects. Almost all of that work assumed a very thin disk.

Real disk models can be much thicker, whether supported by radiation, magnetism, or turbulence. The authors show that rates for processes set by gravitational cross sections fall steeply as disk thickness grows, scaling with a high inverse power of the thickness ratio. Thick disks therefore suppress captures and mergers far below thin disk estimates. The title's verdict is that thick disks leave thin hopes for an AGN boost.
arxiv-2601-02887:
Hui-Qiang Shang and four co-authors calculate how CP violation shows up in rare decays of the Lambda b baryon, a heavy particle made of three quarks. CP violation, a slight imbalance between matter and antimatter behavior, is one of the clues to why the universe holds more matter than antimatter. The team focuses on decays into an excited nucleon plus a light meson, handled through final-state rescattering.

Unlike the standard cutting method, their approach computes both the absorptive and dispersive parts of the rescattering diagrams. They predict branching ratios, several kinds of CP asymmetries, and decay asymmetry parameters for a list of channels. These two-body decays feed four-body final states whose asymmetries the LHCb experiment at CERN can measure, giving the predictions a near-term test.
arxiv-2601-02987:
Wingwa Fu and Takayuki Okatani present LAMS-Edit, a framework for editing images with diffusion models while keeping the unedited content intact. Text-guided editing always balances two pulls: apply the requested change, and preserve everything else. Real photos add a further step, since they must first be inverted into the model's latent space before editing can begin.

LAMS-Edit reuses the intermediate states of that inversion during generation, mixing latent representations and attention maps from both passes at every step, with schedulers controlling the blend. Combined with Prompt-to-Prompt editing, the framework supports precise edits within region masks and style transfer through LoRA adapters. Extensive experiments show it balances content preservation against edit strength better than the alternatives tested.
arxiv-2601-03087:
David Hartmann and five co-authors make fairness auditing of black-box language models cheaper. Such models show systematic biases across demographic groups, and outside auditors can only probe them through costly queries. The authors frame auditing as estimating a fairness metric under uncertainty, and introduce BAFA, an active auditor that plans its queries instead of sampling blindly.

BAFA keeps a set of surrogate models consistent with the answers seen so far and computes uncertainty intervals for the fairness metric. It then picks the queries that narrow those intervals fastest. On two standard fairness case studies, BAFA reached tight error targets with up to forty times fewer queries than stratified sampling, with steadier performance over time and lower variance between runs.
arxiv-2601-03487:
Nicholas W. Hackney, Joel T. Clemmer, and Gary S. Grest simulate bent rod particles that form liquid crystals, materials whose order sits between liquid and solid. Curved rods favor bent patterns, but pure bend cannot fill flat or three-dimensional space evenly, so the material must mix in twist and splay. The team used molecular dynamics with a bonded particle model whose rods have adjustable elasticity.

For rods of middle curvature, rising density moved the system from disordered to a nematic twist-bend state, then to a layered splay-bend state. Those steps match earlier work on rigid rods. Softer rods shifted the points where ordering begins. Understanding how particle shape drives these states helps scientists design soft materials with planned optical and mechanical behavior.
arxiv-2601-03787:
Sara Najem and Amer E. Mouawad present a new algorithm for the graph isomorphism problem, deciding whether two networks are secretly the same structure with renamed nodes. The problem is fundamental across mathematics, chemistry, and network science, and highly regular graphs defeat many classical methods. Their approach builds candidate matches between vertices using spectral and geometric information, especially vertex curvatures.

Every candidate answer is verified explicitly, so non-isomorphic graphs are never wrongly declared identical. The method does not yet guarantee success on all inputs, but it correctly resolved every tested instance in deterministic polynomial time, including many graphs known to be hard. The results suggest enriched spectral methods are stronger than previously understood, hinting that this old problem may yield to geometric ideas.
arxiv-2601-04087:
Matteo Barigozzi, Diego Fresoli, and Esther Ruiz compare how well two standard tools recover hidden factors from many variables at once. Principal components treat the true factors as fixed, while a Kalman filter treats them as random over time. Knowing the error in recovered factors matters when factors are read directly or used to summarise predictors.

For finite numbers of variables, the three authors show principal component factors carry larger mean square error than Kalman filter factors. The gap holds whether the random factors are independent over time or correlated. They also study what happens when leftover parts are wrongly assumed to share one variance or to be uncorrelated. Simulations show how the errors affect confidence intervals built around the factors.
arxiv-2601-04287:
Ben Carvell and three co-authors introduce online action-stacking, a wrapper that lets reinforcement learning policies issue realistic air traffic control instructions, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Training agents on tiny action sets is easier, but real controllers give compound clearances, not single nudges, so learned policies often speak the wrong language for the job.

Their agents train with simple heading or level steps plus a penalty that discourages chatter, so commands come in short bursts. At run time, action-stacking compiles each burst into one proper clearance. Trained with proximal policy optimisation in the BluebirdDT digital twin, the agents handle route following, climbs and descents. two-aircraft conflict avoidance, issuing far fewer instructions than a damped baseline while matching a policy trained on a much larger action space.
arxiv-2601-04787:
In crystals with a handed twist, a shaking magnetic field can drive an electric response called the gyrotropic magnetic current. Koushik Ghorai and 2 co-authors complete the theory of that current in a 2026 paper. Known parts came from changed band energies and a spin-driven displacement effect. Their question is whether orbiting electron motion adds a missing piece.

Using a density-matrix formulation, a bookkeeping method for quantum states, the authors include both direct field coupling and spin-Zeeman interaction. They derive the equations of motion under an oscillating field and uncover an orbital counterpart to the known displacement current. Completing the picture helps predict how such crystals respond in sensitive magnetic and optical devices.
arxiv-2601-04887:
Sofiene Lassoued's 2026 paper, written with 4 co-authors, takes on scheduling inside flexible manufacturing systems. Beyond the classic job shop problem, their setting adds automated guided vehicles moving materials and tools shared between machines, two complications that interact in messy ways. A plan must coordinate jobs, vehicles, and tools together rather than each in isolation.

The authors combine coloured-timed Petri nets, a formal modelling tool for timed processes, with actor-critic reinforcement learning that uses action masking. The Petri net structure supplies valid-action limits, keeping the learner from proposing impossible moves. Smarter intralogistics scheduling helps factories change products quickly without wasting vehicle trips or leaving machines idle waiting for shared tools.
arxiv-2601-05387:
Zachary D. Hartman and 17 co-authors share speckle shots of stars on the list for a next great scope in a 2026 paper. The scope is the Habitable Worlds Observatory, a planned craft that aims to take direct shots of Earth-like worlds round near stars. That aim needs a survey of a hun-dred or so bright, near stars. Teams must know which of those stars have a mate, since a hid-den mate can block or spoil a shot of a world.

Speckle shots freeze the blur of the air and reach fine scale. The team share such shots for stars on the first draft list, from fresh runs and from old files. This is part one of a run of works to pave the craft's road. To know which stars are lone and which are twinned helps set the craft's needs ere steel is cut.
arxiv-2601-05487:
Huanxiang Lin and 5 co-authors propose EvidFuse, a 2026 framework for writing data reports where text and charts stay consistent. Many automated systems draft text and charts in separate stages. That split can freeze the evidence early, so later claims cannot draw on new visual analysis.

EvidFuse instead builds evidence during writing. An analysis agent with exploratory data tools and raw table access works beside a writer agent that plans and drafts the report. The writer can request fine-grained analysis whenever the narrative needs it, and new evidence then constrains the next claims. In judge-based and human evaluations, EvidFuse ranked first for chart quality, chart-text alignment, and overall usefulness.
arxiv-2601-05887:
Victor Mayoral-Vilches and 8 co-authors add a game-theoretic guidance layer in 2026 to AI agents that perform penetration testing. Automated security testing now runs thousands of actions per hour, yet it lacks the strategic intuition human experts bring to competitive attack and defense. Their system, Generative Cut-the-Rope, supplies that intuition inside the agent's reasoning loop.

It pulls attack graphs out of the agent's working context, finds Nash equilibria with effort-weighted scoring, and hands the model a short digest of the results. Across real-world exercises it reportedly matched most expert graph structure far faster and cheaper than manual analysis. In a cyber range, success rates more than doubled, while a shared digest let a combined purple agent beat both solo and separately guided teams.
arxiv-2601-06087:
Research and engineering roles in AI are merging, writes Deepak Babu Piskala in a 2026 paper. Large neural networks and language models need both deep inquiry and heavy systems work. The once-clear line between scientist and engineer titles has collapsed inside leading AI organizations.

Piskala synthesizes public job descriptions, hiring criteria, and company narratives into an AI Roles Continuum. Research Scientists, Research Engineers, Applied Scientists, and Machine Learning Engineers sit at overlapping positions, not in separate boxes. Shared skills now include distributed systems design, large-scale training, careful experimentation, and publication-minded inquiry. Treating roles as fluid shortens the path from research to production. The paper maps competencies to roles and discusses hiring and career implications.
arxiv-2601-06287:
Joseph Heyward and 7 co-authors summarize the third Perception Test challenge in a 2026 report. Held as a workshop at a major computer vision conference, the challenge benchmarks video models on multimodal perception. Two guest tracks covered image understanding and a video generation physics test.

This edition emphasized unification: competitors had to use single approaches rather than task-specific pipelines. Five consolidated tracks covered video question answering, merged object and point tracking, merged action and sound localization, grounded video QA, and hour-long video QA. One track recast classic perception tasks as multiple-choice video questions that video-language models can answer natively. The results highlight how hard diverse perception remains for current models under unified interfaces.
arxiv-2601-07087:
Dylan Sam and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers when should we introduce safety interventions during pretraining?. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Ensuring the safety of language models in high-stakes settings remains a pressing challenge.

As aligned behaviors are often brittle and easily undone by adversarial pressure or downstream finetuning. Prior work has shown that interventions applied during pretraining, such as rephrasing harmful content, can substantially improve the safety of the resulting models. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07387:
F. Bolis, E. Sobacchi, and F. Tavecchio wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on jets from blazars. A blazar is a galaxy whose jet points near our line of sight. The jet shines by synchrotron radiation, light from fast charges that spiral in a magnetic field. That light is polarized, which means its waves lean one way more than others.

The team asks how that lean shifts over time. Data at many bands show the lean angle swing by large amounts. The angle is called the electric vector position angle, or EVPA. Swings show up in light we can see and in X-rays. More often, both the strength of the lean and the EVPA jump in a way that looks random. The paper weighs what such jumps tell us about the jet. Shifts in the lean can trace how the field in the jet twists and churns.
arxiv-2601-07487:
J. W. Moffat examines a puzzle in cosmology in this 2026 preprint: radio galaxies seem unevenly spread across the sky. Wide-area surveys report a number-count dipole, an excess in one direction, larger than expected. The measured amplitude is three to four times the purely kinematic value predicted by the standard cosmology model. Reported significance reaches up to 5.4 sigma.

An effect that strong demands an explanation, either in the data or in theory. Moffat turns to modified gravity, a family of theories that change Einstein's gravity rules. He asks whether such a change can produce the observed excess. Readers get a compact case study in how an odd survey result can test the foundations of cosmology.
arxiv-2601-08087:
Kristen Dage and twelve co-authors look inside three nearby open star clusters. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses observations across many wavelengths to find results of close stellar encounters. Dense clusters force stars to interact, and those interactions leave unusual products behind.

The three clusters span very different ages. IC 2602 is about 30 million years old, NGC 2632 is about 750 million years old, and M67 is about 4 billion years old. Comparing young, middle-aged, and old clusters shows how interaction products change over time. Readers get a tour of hidden cluster life, from fresh systems to ancient ones.
arxiv-2601-08287: Jiaman He and co-authors link personality traits to eye movements during interactive search. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that personality shapes how people engage, behave, and decide while seeking information. Few studies have tied personality to observable search behavior, though. The team builds a multimodal time-series model that joins eye-tracking data with gaze missingness. Missingness means periods when the user's gaze is not captured at all. Treating absence as signal may reveal traits that gaze position alone would miss, with uses in adaptive search design.
arxiv-2601-08687:
Marco Tonnarelli and three co-authors present Data Product MCP for chatting with enterprise data. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts from computational data governance, which aims to enforce policies and legal duties efficiently. Natural language processing and agentic AI offer ways to improve how organizations share and use data.

Many barriers remain in current practice. Today's tools demand technical skills and multiple roles to discover, request, and query data. A chat interface over governed data products could let staff ask in plain language. Governance rules would still gate what can be shared. The work targets firms where data access delays, not data scarcity, slow decisions.
arxiv-2601-08787:
F. Dai and V. Temlyakov survey how to rebuild a smooth curve or field from a few sample points. Such rebuild work sits at the heart of data squeeze, signal work, and learn theory. A good rebuild uses few points, yet stays close to the true field at all points. The survey maps what is known on how close we can get.

They tie best rebuild error to two known gauges. One is how well short sparse sums can near the field. The next is the width of the class the field comes from. Those ties tell us when a rebuild plan is as good as it can be. A reader gets a map of a wide field in one place, with the key open asks marked.
arxiv-2601-08987:
Mohammad Waquas Usmani, Susmit Shannigrahi, and Michael Zink guard 3D video streams with a rights lock that is light to run. A 3D stream sends point clouds, vast sets of dots that form a scene. Locking all dots costs much time and power. Pirates need just a clear view to steal worth, so a light lock may still block them.

Their frame is called ABE-VVS. It locks just a picked set of dot places, based on who may view the stream. The rest of the dots flow free, so lag stays low. The locked dots blur the view past use for a thief. A reader in stream work gets a rights plan that trades full lock for speed.
arxiv-2601-09087:
Schuyler Van Dyk and nine co-authors name the star that blew up as the supernova SN 2025pht. The burst was of Type II-Plateau, a class from huge red stars. The host galaxy is NGC 1637, near by space scale. Old sky shots from two space scopes caught the star long past its death, in a span of more than two decades.

The star looks to be a red supergiant, huge and bright. It was wrapped in much dust, the most dust the team has seen for such a case. Dust hid part of its light, so its true size took care to gauge. A reader in star death work gets a rare pre burst view of the star that died.
arxiv-2601-09287:
Dafne Lozano-Paredes and four co-authors build a warn tool for a fast grid talk rule with no built in guard. The rule is the GOOSE protocol, used in power sub stations. It sends trip and state notes in a flash, to guard gear. A foe who can join the net can send fake GOOSE notes that look rule true. Old guards miss such fakes, and marked attack data is thin.

Their tool learns the shape of sound GOOSE talk with an auto code net. Talk that breaks that shape is flagged. They add a why layer, so staff can see what trait set off the flag. A reader in grid safety gets a guard that can learn with few attack marks.
arxiv-2601-09587:
Samuel A. Federman and a large team peer at jets from newborn stars with the James Webb Space Telescope. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports observations within 2,000 astronomical units of three deeply embedded protostars. The targets are the low-mass Class 0 protostars B335 and HOPS 153, plus the intermediate-mass HOPS 370.

Webb's infrared eyes, from 2.9 to 27 microns, show the jets' shapes and motions. Class 0 is the youngest phase, when the star is still wrapped in its birth cloud. Jets this close to the source reveal how infalling material gets expelled. Those flows shape the mass the star finally keeps.
arxiv-2601-09687:
Yi Huang and Sankar Das Sarma explain a striking experiment on electrons in bilayer graphene. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats strong localization in two-dimensional systems under a strong magnetic field. A scanning tunneling study had found three distinct quantum phases in the lowest Landau level.

The three phases are a fractional quantum Hall liquid, a hexagonal Wigner crystal with long-range order, and a random localized solid with no order. Which phase appears depends on the filling factor. Disorder, often treated as a nuisance, helps create the localized phase. The paper works out how strong fields and disorder together produce this strong localization.
arxiv-2601-09887:
Rostyslav Hnatyshyn and four co-authors help materials scientists see atoms move. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents LAMDA, a visual tool for atomic displacements in molecular dynamics simulations. Modern materials research runs in silico, generating huge simulations of atomic motion.

Listing the basic patterns in how atoms shift is key to knowing how a material's traits will change. The space of possible transitions is vast, and high-throughput runs flood experts with data. LAMDA supports visual exploration of the movement patterns. Better tools for seeing atomic shifts could speed the design of new materials for real use.
arxiv-2601-09987:
Guglielmo Grimaldi, Matthew Headrick, Veronika Hubeny, and Pavel Shteyner study bounds on how much parts of a system can share. In holography, shared load can be read from cuts on a weighted graph. The least cut sets the bound. Bounds of this type are called HEIs.

The team built a new frame to sort these bounds. They use it to prove traits that all such bounds share. Two traits deal with which bounds beat which. One trait gives a full test for when a bound counts at all. The frame turns a loose set of bounds into a clear class.
arxiv-2601-10387:
Christina Lu and co authors map the role space of language models. A model can play many roles. Yet it slips back to one base role: the helpful Assistant. That role is set by late train steps. The team ask how that role sits in the model's state space.

They pull out state paths for a range of role types. Each path marks one stock role, from sage to rogue. The base role sits at a set place in that map. The team then test ways to keep it there. Shifts in role can change how a model acts. A firm base role is a safety aim.
arxiv-2601-10687:
S M Rayeed and a large team of co-authors built a dataset of ground beetles that spans a continent. Trait databases for ecology lean hard toward vertebrates and plants. Groups like ground beetles, rich in species, are left thin. Yet these beetles are trusted signs of ecosystem health, since their numbers shift with changes in the land.

The dataset pairs high-resolution images of the beetles with checked measurements of their body traits. Such traits let ecologists compare species and sites on equal terms. With images and traits together, the data can train vision models as well as serve field studies. It helps close a data gap that has limited work on insect diversity.
arxiv-2601-11287:
Markus Bink, Marten Risius, Udo Kruschwitz, and David Elsweiler demo a search helper. Their 2026 preprint was made for the ACM SIGIR meeting. Many users search poorly and judge sources with weak care. The risk is worst in high-stakes fields such as health.

Users also tend to rate their own digital skill too high. The team's helper sits inside normal search result pages. It weaves expert search moves into the page flow itself. No separate app or new habit is asked of the user. The design is then put to a test with real users. The aim is better queries and sharper checks on what is found.
arxiv-2601-11387:
Greta Warren, Jingyi Sun, Irina Shklovski, and Isabelle Augenstein test AI fact-check help. Their 2026 preprint asks what evidence does for such help. Much past work honed the explanations AI gives users. The role of the evidence itself is oddly under-studied.

The team varies three things in a study with non-experts. One is the type of explanation shown with a claim. One is how sure the AI says it is. The third is whether the AI advice is right or wrong. Users then judge the truth of claims themselves. They also judge the AI system's calls on those claims. The design shows when evidence earns its place in the loop.
arxiv-2601-11587:
Yuyan Huang and five coauthors support city carbon planning with grounded AI. Their 2026 preprint joins multi-agent planning with retrieval. Urban carbon governance needs many kinds of evidence at once. Emission inventories and statistical yearbooks are two such kinds.

Policy texts, technical measures, and academic findings add more. Planners must merge them into cross-departmental action plans. LLMs can assist, but factual reliability is a barrier. Evidential traceability is the other barrier in pro use. The team's support grounds each claim in retrieved sources. Multi-agent planning splits the governance task by role. Plans that cite their evidence are easier to defend.
arxiv-2601-11987:
Berkani Khaled presents a graph method for chest X-ray diagnosis that can explain its calls. Feature maps from a convolutional net are recast as graphs of image patches. Each node holds both look and place data, and edges link near patches.

Anatomical priors, facts about chest form, guide the graph. That guide should make the calls more clear to a doctor. A tool that shows its grounds can earn more trust in clinics. The work joins graph thought with known body form for X-ray reads.  Clear grounds help a doctor judge each call with care.
arxiv-2601-12187:
Rafał Filipów, Adam Kwela, and Paolo Leonetti study sets of Ramsey-limit and IP-limit points for sequences. They work in an uncountable Polish space. The Hindman ideal holds all sets of whole numbers that are not IP sets.

For each sequence, they define its set of IP-limit points via finite sums. Ramsey-limit points add a second, stricter notion. The team sort how these sets can look. Such sorts link combinatorics on numbers to topology of limit sets.  The sets are tied to sequences in the space X.  Such limit sets show how wild a sequence can act in a space.
arxiv-2601-12287:
Bijun Fan, Chao Zhang, Liang Zheng, and Shusu Shi model open charm hadron output in proton and gold crashes at RHIC. The crashes run at a nucleon pair energy of 200 GeV. They use an improved multi-phase transport model for the work.

They give momentum spectra and nuclear modification factors for D0 mesons and Lambda_c baryons. They also give the ratio of the two in both crash kinds. That ratio tests how charm quarks form baryons in hot matter. The work aids heavy-ion physics at RHIC.  The ratio is the key test in their model runs.
arxiv-2601-12387: Jihang Zhu and Chunli Huang study chiral superconductors, a phase that breaks time reversal symmetry. Such phases draw wide interest in physics. One hope is that they could host platforms for topological quantum computation. When time reversal breaks, a clear effect should follow. That effect is orbital magnetization, a magnetic response tied to the motion of electrons.
arxiv-2601-12487:
Caden Drover, R. L. Irvine, and Rachel Wortis study a double quantum dot, a pair of tiny electron traps. Strong Coulomb repulsion in such systems gives rise to a zero bias anomaly. That is a feature in the single particle density of states near zero energy. Its shape and its shifts with settings act as signs of the underlying electronic state.

Disorder plus interactions shape that feature in many systems at once. The team ask a pointed question: how do the leads attached to the dots affect the signs? Leads are needed to measure the dots, but they may distort what they measure. Knowing that effect helps readers trust the anomaly as a probe. It bears on mesoscopic physics and quantum device design.
arxiv-2601-12787:
Ning Sun and Pengfei Zhang connect two measures of quantum chaos in thermofield double states. Under unitary evolution, chaotic systems begun in simple states grow complex very fast. That growth soon blocks any efficient classical description. Chaos is traditionally characterized by spectral traits of the Hamiltonian, most notably the spectral form factor.

A second lens is quantum magic, the hardness of simulation in the stabilizer formalism. Magic can be quantified by the stabilizer Renyi entropy. The team link magic dynamics in these special states to spectral form factors. A bridge between simulation hardness and spectra would unify two views of chaos. It could also guide tests on near term quantum devices.
arxiv-2601-12987:
Evangelos Ntouros and Ewoud J. J. Smeur develop guidance for a tailsitter aircraft under wind disturbances. A tailsitter sits on its tail and flies like a plane, mixing drone and aircraft traits. Their control law is based on a parametric guiding vector field. A vector field approach steers the craft along a path rather than chasing a moving target point.

They integrate the law with a state of the art acceleration and attitude control architecture. The framework enables direct comparison of trajectory tracking and path following guidance. Tests use a realistic tailsitter model under windy conditions. Wind is where elegant guidance laws often fail, so the test is stern. The work serves vertical takeoff aircraft design.
arxiv-2601-13887:
Hong Su sets out a human-inspired frame for AI systems that adapt in 2026. Large language models show strong skill with knowledge and reasoning from text. But text alone limits how they adapt to new settings. It also limits how they verify their own reasoning. Open, dynamic real-world settings expose those limits fast.

Su calls the frame Human Simulation Computation. It aims to mimic how humans sense, check, and adjust in the world. Adaptive systems need feedback loops that text-only models lack. A human-like loop could help AI act with more care outside the lab.
arxiv-2601-14187:
Yaling Ke studies how strong light fields can steer chemical reactions in optical cavities in 2026. Harnessing strong light-matter interactions to control reactions is a promising route. It could deepen our grasp of chemical dynamics at the collective quantum level. It also holds implications for future chemical synthesis paradigms.

Cooperative reactions in cavities show a complex interplay of effects. Mode hybridization, timescale balance, and pathway interference all play roles. A mechanistic understanding of the dynamics is required to reach control. Cavity chemistry may one day let light pick which product forms. The three effects must be read as one play, not as lone parts. That joint read is the hard core of the work.
arxiv-2601-14387:
Songela W. Chen and David T. Limmer study the energy cost of erasing a bit in this 2026 paper. Energy costs of information processing are growing fast. Bit erasure sits at the heart of that cost. Past work set key links between thermodynamic cost and memory storage.

Modern systems, though, work far from equilibrium, where those classic links strain. The authors take on optimal control of bit erasure in stochastic random access memory. Stochastic means the device is subject to random thermal kicks. Their aim is control schemes that erase bits at the lowest true cost in a real, noisy device.
arxiv-2601-14487:
Mrigank Dhingra and Omer San work on forecasting chaotic systems in this 2026 paper. Long-horizon autoregressive forecasting of chaotic dynamics is hard for two reasons. Small one-step errors amplify fast. Rollouts also drift off distribution, so predictions collapse into physically inconsistent states with wrong large-scale statistics.

The team introduces MSR-HINE, a hierarchical implicit forecaster. It augments multiscale latent priors with multi-rate recurrent modules. Those modules run at distinct temporal scales, fast and slow. The design aims to stabilize long rollouts. The point is trust. A long run that stays true to the real system is worth more than a short one that drifts. Readers get a forecaster built to keep the broad statistics of a chaotic system intact over long runs.
arxiv-2601-14787:
Yu Pan leads a team of seventeen authors on a small black hole in this 2026 paper. NGC 4395 is a nearby dwarf spiral galaxy hosting an active galactic nucleus. That nucleus is powered by an intermediate-mass black hole, with a mass of about ten thousand to one hundred thousand suns. Such mid-size black holes are rare finds and key missing links.

The project is the Intermediate-Mass Black Hole Reverberation Mapping Project. Reverberation mapping times how light echoes through gas near the black hole to weigh it. The team reports stable optical continuum lags for the NGC 4395 black hole over years. Stable lags mean the echo delay held steady across long monitoring. Readers get a long-baseline check on a prized small black hole.
arxiv-2601-14887:
Itzhak Goldman looks at turbulence inside a far-off galaxy that is forming stars. His 2026 arXiv paper studies CSWA13, a galaxy stretched by gravitational lensing. The galaxy sits at a redshift near 2, so its light left it long ago.

Earlier work by Goldman found signs of large-scale turbulence in the galaxy's gas. That flow was compressible and of the Burgers type. The new work asks if small-scale turbulence runs alongside the large flow. He probes both scales with multi-point structure functions, a tool that compares the moving gas at set spatial gaps.
arxiv-2601-15087:
Dario Benedetti, Fanny Eustachon, and Omar Zanusso study exotic fixed points of a scalar field theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the Lee-Yang universality class and its multicritical kin. The theory has a complex interaction term, an odd power of the field times an imaginary factor.

These fixed points come from the renormalization group, the tool that tracks a theory across scales. The team works just below the upper critical dimension. They use the local potential approximation to chart critical and multicritical points. The results extend what is known about this odd family.
arxiv-2601-15187:
Noam Soker compares seven rival stories for where the heaviest elements were first forged. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with the r-process, a chain of reactions that builds heavy nuclei in extreme settings. The question is which sites did this work in the early universe.

Soker tests each scenario against the observed traits of r-process elements from that era. He concludes that two sites split the job. A magnetorotational process likely made the elements below the third peak. A common envelope jets supernova likely made the third peak itself in full.
arxiv-2601-15487:
Chandan Kumar Sahu, Premith Kumar Chilukuri, and Matthew Hetrich build a test set for search systems in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework is called MiRAGE. It targets retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, as it moves toward multimodal, high-stakes use. Evaluation tools have not kept pace with that shift. Most datasets use general text or plain documents.

Real enterprise files are harder than that. Key facts hide in tables, figures, and text together. Answering often means joining disjoint pieces of evidence. MiRAGE uses multiple agents to build such questions and answers. The questions are multimodal and multihop by design. For teams that ship RAG systems, a harder, more honest test set is the point.
arxiv-2601-15887:
Piotr Salabura searches for hypothetical particles in a rare decay in a 2026 arXiv paper. Dark matter and new particles may explain effects the Standard Model cannot. Axion-like particles are one candidate family. Their masses may run from MeV to GeV scales. Some versions carry an extra Peccei-Quinn breaking contribution. They couple to Standard Model matter in specific ways. Those couplings make certain decays worth watching.

The search uses the eta meson decay into two pions and an electron pair. The HADES detector collects the data. A rare decay is a clean place to hunt: backgrounds are low, and a new particle could appear as a bump. Null results still matter. They narrow the space where such particles can hide.
arxiv-2601-15987:
Nguyen N. Hung, Gabriel Navarro, and Pham Huu Tiep study character values in finite group theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Characters are functions that summarize a group's representations. Their fields of values collect the numbers characters can take. The authors fix a prime p. For p equal to two, the fields are classified for characters whose degrees avoid p. For odd primes, a conjectural classification has been proposed.

The paper works on that open side of the problem, per its title. Primes enter because degree divisibility shapes character behavior. Classifications of value fields constrain what groups can exist. Group theorists use such constraints in the broader program of understanding finite groups. Incremental progress on a sharp conjecture is how that program advances.
arxiv-2601-16287:
Ryan Lopez and three coauthors use live choice to speed band gap guesses for light crystals. Their 2026 preprint joins a last layer Bayes net with choice by doubt. Light crystals guide light by their gap traits. Guessing gaps by full sums is slow and costs much. A net can guess fast, but needs good train picks to stay true.

Doubt led choice picks the next sums that teach most. An exact form of the net gives doubt marks with no fake draws. Good doubt marks make each new sum count more. Fast, true gap guesses aid design of light gear. The work blends net maths with sum choice.
arxiv-2601-16387:
Hyun-Myung Chun and three coauthors set one law for waver and reply in Langevin flows. Their 2026 preprint deals with flows bent by chance heat noise. Past laws link waver size to reply size at rest. Far from rest, that old link no longer holds in plain form. The team seeks one law that holds in both zones.

They use shared maths in the waver of mass and flow counts. From it they draw one tie that spans rest and non rest. A wide law lets teams read drive from waver in real flows. It also tests if a flow is at rest from data. The work firms up non rest flow maths.
arxiv-2601-16487:
Remi Chierchia and coauthors give wound cuts that stay same across views with field nets. Their 2026 preprint deals with wound care cost and strain. Wards and homes face high cost to track wounds by hand. Pic tools can cut wound zones to track size and heal. One view cuts can clash when the same wound is shot anew.

Field nets hold the wound in a 3D like form from all views. Cuts from that form stay same view to view. Same cuts let teams trust size tracks through time. The work seeks wound tools that cut hand work. It tests field nets on real wound pic sets.
arxiv-2601-16587:
Léonard Polat shares a fresh fine count of a key clash rate for the muon test. His 2026 preprint comes from the BABAR team work. The rate is for electron plus positron to two pions. That rate feeds the sum for the muon odd spin mark. The muon mark is a hot test of the known grain model.

Fine rate counts cut the doubt in that sum much. BABAR data gives one of the most sharp counts to date. Sharp counts let teams tell if the muon mark truly clashes. A true clash would point to new grains past the model. The work is a key part of that long test.
arxiv-2601-16687:
Felix Stoehr and a team of co-authors gauge the reach of the ALMA scope array. ALMA is a set of radio dishes high in Chile. It maps cold gas and dust in space. A space tool proves its worth in part through print. Papers in strong journals show what the data gave. Their 2026 preprint counts and weighs that print record.

The team tracks how many papers rest on ALMA data. They also look at how oft those papers get cited. Trends by year and field come into view. Such counts help funders judge the worth of big tools. They also help the field plan its next grand scopes.
arxiv-2601-16787:
A review sums fresh gauges of a deep split in how matter and antimatter act. When a bit and its anti-twin decay in unlike rates, that split shows. Such splits, timed over full decay spans, test the base theory. The 2026 talk text pulls news from two big labs. LHCb and Belle II both feed the pool.

News spans the CKM angle gamma, a key weak-force mark. It also marks the first clear split seen in baryon decays. Charm meson decays add more fresh cases. These gauges bound how the cosmos kept matter over antimatter. They also point to where new physics may hide.
arxiv-2601-16887:
Oleksii Yanchyshen, Eva Hackmann, and Claus Lämmerzahl track orbits near a black hole with fresh math. Orbits there bend by strong gravity's pull. Small extra forces then nudge the path bit by bit. Gauss-style rules track how path traits shift. Their 2026 preprint builds those rules for Schwarzschild space-time.

No curbs are set on the nudge force's form. Path traits, called osculating elements, shift per the rules. The rules hold in the strong field near the hole. Such math aids probe paths near black holes. It also aids tests of gravity's tale in deep fields.
arxiv-2601-17087:
Preethi Seshadri and a team of four co-authors test fake users in chatbot grades. Bench tests now use chatbot-made users to save cost. Those fake users chat with the bot on test tasks. No one had checked if fakes stand in well for folks. Their 2026 preprint runs a user study on four lands' folk. The lands are the US, India, Kenya, and Nigeria.

Real users did shop-type tasks from a known bench set. Their acts were set next to fake users' acts. Gaps in grade, truth, and fair marks then show. Fake users may grade bots in skewed ways. Bench teams need that truth to trust their scores.
arxiv-2601-17187:
Or Ordentlich and Yury Polyanskiy study fast, compact matrix multiplication. Big language models lean on matrix products for most of their work. Shrinking numbers to fewer bits cuts memory and speeds runs. That shrink is called quantization. The authors study high-rate forms of it, where more bits stay in play.

They cover two cases. In one, both matrices must be shrunk. In the other, only the weights shrink, and the second matrix is known through its covariance. They give both theory and practice for these cases. The work helps teams weigh speed gains against loss of care. It points to where high-rate shrinking is safe to use.
arxiv-2601-17587:
Azza Fadhel and five co-authors use AI to find workable 3D printing settings for metal alloys. Printing quality hinges on inputs like laser power and scan speed. Their links to output quality are complex. Trial and error is the standard hunt, and it is slow and costly. The team uses AI-driven adaptive experimental design.

Adaptive design picks each next test from past results. That steers the hunt toward feasible settings fast. Fewer failed prints save powder, time, and machine wear. Metal printing serves aerospace and medical parts. A smart hunt widens who can print well. The work turns a craft skill into a guided search.
arxiv-2601-17787:
Wei-Ning Chiu, Chuan-Ju Wang, and Pu-Jen Cheng work on teaching recommender systems what matters most in a user history. Their 2026 preprint is about generative recommenders. These systems treat the task of picking the next item as a step-by-step text task. Items are named by semantic codes, and the model writes the code of the item it predicts.

Most training treats each piece of the code as worth the same. The authors say that is a poor match for how the codes carry meaning. They propose two ways to weight the pieces by the information each one adds. A staged training plan, called curriculum learning, supports the scheme. The aim is a model that learns the key signals first.
arxiv-2601-17987:
Ziwei Zheng and co-authors hunt for the smallest neural networks that still do their job well. Their 2026 preprint gives a unified study of minimal deep learning designs. Neural networks excel at classification, yet no one has a clear map of how small a network can be for a set task. The team builds a method to explore that space in a systematic way. They study how three forces interact: convergence, pruning, and quantization.

Pruning cuts parts of a network away. Quantization stores its numbers with less precision. Both shrink a model, but each can break its training. Knowing how the three forces trade off guides lean design. Small, sound models matter for phones, sensors, and low-cost devices.
arxiv-2601-18187: Mabud Ali Sarkar studies the image of the p-adic logarithm on rings of principal units. His 2026 preprint works over a finite extension of the p-adic numbers, with its maximal ideal. The group of principal units, one plus that ideal, plays a key role in number theory. Sarkar examines where the logarithm sends annuli of these units, a question with uses across local field theory.
arxiv-2601-18787:
Saul Baltasar and seven colleagues build a fast path to fit the bent light of far points that pass near a heavy mass. The mass acts as a lens: it splits one point of light into a ring of shots. From the shots, staff can read the lens's mass and the gaps in time between the shots. Those gaps can set the scale of space it-self. Past fits were slow and could miss the true best fit.

Their path runs on graphics chips with a famed lens frame. In tests on made-up shots it reads back the spots, the glow, and the time gaps with care. It also reads the slope of the lens's mass, a hard trait to pin. A fast, true fit could open lens work to far more cases. Bright points like burst stars make the best lens probes of all.
arxiv-2601-19087:
Mohammed E. Eltayeb steers millimeter waves indoors with printed reflectors that use no power at all. Millimeter wave signals are fast but easily blocked, so rooms have dead zones. His reflectors are flat panels whose parts bounce the signal toward a chosen spot, like a mirror shaped for radio.

Each part's bounce is set by the angles of the incoming and wanted outgoing waves, a model the paper works out in full. A switchable pattern of parts, called binary aperture control, aims the beam. Passive panels could stretch indoor coverage without the cost and power draw of active relays.
arxiv-2601-19187:
Aman Desai, Amelia Lovison, and Paul Jackson hunt for a bound pair of top quarks at the Large Hadron Collider. Fresh results from the ATLAS and CMS experiments hint that top and antitop quarks can briefly bind near the energy threshold where they are born. Such a state is called toponium.

The team presents a way to rebuild that state from the debris of collisions, using a method called recursive jigsaw reconstruction. Top quarks decay almost at once, so any bound state hides in fine patterns. A sound rebuild method could turn a hint into a firm find at the collider.
arxiv-2601-19287:
Md. Asif Haider and Thomas Zimmermann study how human reviewers react to code written by AI agents. Past work graded how well agents generate code, but little was known about the review side of real practice. Their large scale study reads code review on pull requests that agents authored.

They map the dominant themes in what reviewers say and ask for. Review is where agent code meets human judgment, trust, and standards. Knowing what reviewers balk at tells agent builders what to fix. It is not just whether the code runs. A human must also accept it into the project.
arxiv-2601-19387:
Lekshmi Murali Rani, Richard Berntsson Svensson, and Robert Feldt study the human side of working with AI coders. Generative tools now support software engineers and their teams day to day. Getting the tools to work well with people, though, is not just a matter of code quality.

The team focuses on the socio-emotional gap: trust, tone, frustration, and the feel of teamwork with a machine partner. Their functional view asks what such collaboration must do for the humans in it. Ignoring that side risks tools that are sharp on paper and draining in practice.
arxiv-2601-19487:
Haonan Zhang and four co-authors untangle the trade between letting attacks through and refusing harmless asks. Safety aligned models fail two ways: jailbreaks that answer harmful inputs, and over refusal that declines benign ones. Past steering methods turn one knob, the size of an answer vector, and trade one failure for the other.

Their method, LLM-VA, aligns vectors in direction instead of just scaling them. A directional fix could cut both failures at once, escaping the seesaw. Models that are both safer and less skittish would serve users better on both sides of the line.
arxiv-2601-19687:
Daniel L. Clarkson and Eduard P. Kontar read the radio static of the Sun for clues about its magnetic field. Type III radio bursts come from beams of fast electrons racing outward along magnetic field lines. The burst's frequency drifts as the beam climbs into thinner plasma. From that drift, scientists infer the beam's speed and path.

The inferred motion does not fit a smooth, straight climb through steadily thinning plasma. Something disturbs the path. The authors argue the bursts carry signatures of large-scale magnetic disturbances and switchbacks, kinks where the field folds back on itself. Reading these signatures turns routine bursts into probes of the solar wind. That helps forecast the space weather that reaches Earth.
arxiv-2601-19787:
Elena Masserini, Diego Clerissi, Daniela Micucci, and Leonardo Mariani build resources for studying task-based chatbots. Chatbots now serve users around the clock in many domains. Yet research on their quality is held back by a lack of large, curated datasets. The authors set out to fix that for chatbots built with Dialogflow, a popular platform.

They present TOFU-D, a snapshot of close to two thousand Dialogflow chatbots gathered from GitHub. From it they curate COD, a validated subset of under two hundred chatbots. A snapshot shows what builders actually ship, flaws included. A curated subset gives researchers a clean base for experiments. Both resources support work on testing and improving conversational software.
arxiv-2601-19887:
Dominic Maggio and Luca Carlone present a system that rebuilds scenes in three dimensions from ordinary colour video, in real time. SLAM systems map a space while tracking the camera through it.
