Their system builds on VGGT, a feed-forward model that estimates scene geometry directly. Version 2.0 substantially improves how incremental submaps are aligned.

Two fixes headline the upgrade. A new factor graph design removes a fifteen-degree-of-freedom drift that plagued the earlier system. It also removes a planar degeneracy, a failure mode on flat scenes. The system still handles the ambiguity that arises when camera settings are unknown. Dense, real-time reconstruction serves robots and augmented reality alike.
arxiv-2601-20087:
A. Tayebi and B. Najafi prove a rigidity result in Finsler geometry. Berwald spaces are a tame class of Finsler manifolds, where distances can depend on direction. Flag curvature measures how those spaces bend. The authors prove that every Berwald manifold with nonzero flag curvature is actually Riemannian, the simpler direction-independent kind.

The result extends classical rigidity theorems of Numata and Szabó. They also show that positively curved constant isotropic Berwald manifolds are Riemannian or locally Minkowskian. Compact cases with strictly positive or negative curvature reduce further. Rigidity theorems are prized because they collapse a wide class to a familiar one. The work sharpens the map of Finsler geometry's landscape. The class looks wide at first sight.
arxiv-2601-20187:
Dingxin Zhang gives a new proof of the Riemann hypothesis part of the Weil conjectures. That landmark result counts points on varieties over finite fields. The proof covers smooth projective varieties. It works by reducing the general case to the case of a hypersurface, using deformation.

The main tool is Artin's vanishing theorem, together with basic facts about perverse sheaves. Shorter or clearer proofs of deep results still matter, since they can expose new links between fields. This route ties arithmetic geometry to sheaf methods in a direct way, and it may help readers who found earlier proofs hard to enter.
arxiv-2601-20287:
Francesco Caravelli presents a framework for memory in classical and quantum systems, seen through hysteresis, where a system's state depends on its past. In his setup, the Hamiltonian at each moment depends on past values of a control Hamiltonian through a causal kernel. This structure fits finite-bandwidth or filtered control channels well.

The framework separates memory that lives in the control signal from true non-Markovian dynamics of the state itself. That distinction matters in experiments, where an apparent quantum memory effect may just be lag in the equipment. The paper gives researchers a clean way to tell the two apart.
arxiv-2601-20487:
Nico Mutzner, Taha Yasseri, and Heiko Rauhut study cooperation when AI agents join small human groups. Most earlier work on human-AI cooperation looked at pairs, one person and one agent. Little is known about how agents affect the rise and upkeep of cooperative norms in groups.

Their title states the headline finding: behavior, not identity, drives cooperation in mixed groups. In other words, what an agent does matters more than the fact that it is an agent. That result shapes how teams should introduce AI members: norms follow conduct, whoever or whatever shows it.
arxiv-2601-20587:
Saifian Farooq Bhat and four colleagues build a hybrid jump-diffusion model for controlling quantum emitters in hexagonal boron nitride. This two-dimensional material is a promising host for stable single-photon emission, thanks to its wide bandgap, high photostability, and fit with nanophotonic devices. The authors study an emitter that is mechanically decoupled from its host.

Their simulation covers temperature-dependent spectral dynamics and optical coherence. Modeling both helps design coherent optical control of the emitter. Reliable single-photon sources are building blocks for quantum communication, so sharpening their control matters. All of this is worked out in a model on a screen, not in a lab test. That keeps the cost low while the team learns what to build next.
arxiv-2601-20787:
G. Chacon-Acosta and two co-authors study a quantum particle that must live on a sphere. Their 2026 paper builds a semi-classical picture of this system. The particle moves on a curved surface. It also feels a force that does not pull toward the center. The team uses a method that adds quantum spread to the classical phase space. The added terms are called moments.

They derive corrected Hamiltonians and paths for the sphere. The new terms show how the particle's own quantum spread pushes back on its motion. Classical theory misses that push. The goal is to keep the ease of classical paths while adding key quantum effects. The work serves studies of particles bound to curved surfaces.
arxiv-2601-20987:
Md Muhtasim Munif Fahim and Md Rezaul Karim bring pretrained AI to child development screening. Their 2026 paper concerns transfer learning in data-scarce settings. Many children face preventable developmental delays each year. Machine learning could flag risk early. Deployment in new countries, though, hits a data bottleneck. Reliable models need thousands of samples. New programs often begin with fewer than one hundred.

The authors use pre-trained encoders to bridge that gap. An encoder first learns from large existing data. It then transfers to the new country with little local data. That transfer enables deployment where training from scratch would fail. The paper targets global child development programs. It offers a path to early screening that does not wait for big local datasets.
arxiv-2601-21187:
Chenyu Huang and six co-authors inject reasoning skill into vision-language models with a finer touch. Their 2026 paper presents FRISM, a model merging method. Enhancing the reasoning of vision-language models by merging them with large reasoning models is a promising direction. Existing methods operate at a coarse, layer-wide level. That often forces a trade-off. Injecting reasoning can erode visual capability. The authors aim to break that trade-off.

FRISM merges at the subspace level instead. Fine-grained reasoning injection targets only the parts of the model that carry reasoning. Visual strengths elsewhere are left intact. The name spells out the recipe: fine-grained reasoning injection via subspace-level merging. Cheaper than retraining, merging reuses models that already exist. The work helps builders who want smarter multimodal systems without starting over.
arxiv-2601-21587:
Abderrahmane Issam, Yusuf Can Semerci, Jan Scholtes, and Gerasimos Spanakis use language models as stand-in learners to study how one language shapes another. Crosslinguistic influence is central to research on bilingual minds. Human studies, though, often clash because no two groups of learners match.

Models offer a controlled learner that can be rerun at will. The authors simulate the influence in a systematic way and isolate its drivers. With noise and background held fixed, the true causes stand out. The approach gives language science a lab bench where classic disputes can be rerun cleanly.
arxiv-2601-21687:
Francesco Alessio, Vittorio Del Duca, Riccardo Gonzo, and Emanuele Rosi work on the theory of gravity at very high energies. Their 2026 preprint builds a systematic framework, based on Regge theory, for scattering where two heavy particles collide and emit several gravitons. The setup also keeps track of spin effects.

The authors work in an ultra-fast limit and keep the leading terms in a standard approximation. In that limit, their results for heavy particles reduce smoothly to the known results for particles with no mass. The framework links three views of the same events: waveforms, shock waves, and unitarity cuts. That gives other theorists a shared language for high-energy gravitational scattering.
arxiv-2601-21787:
Chantale Lauer, Peter Pfeiffer, Alexander Rombach, and Nijat Mehdiyev test whether large language models can draw proper business process models. Building a model in the BPMN notation is complex and slow, since it needs both knowledge of the field and command of strict modeling rules.

Recent models can now generate such diagrams directly from plain text descriptions, building on older text-to-process methods. The 2026 study assesses how competent the models really are at this task. The answer matters for companies that hope to draft process documentation automatically. A fluent diagram with wrong logic is worse than none, so measured competence tells managers where human review must stay in the loop.
arxiv-2601-21987:
J. Christopher Mihos and co-authors peer into the faint outskirts of the spiral galaxy M96. Using deep imaging from the Hubble Space Telescope, they study the stars in the galaxy's extreme outer halo. M96 sits in the Leo I group, a dynamically active neighborhood where galaxies disturb each other.

Their fields lie far from the galaxy's center, at a projected distance given in the paper, and reach very faint stars. The mix of star ages and chemistries there records how the halo was assembled, from swallowed smaller galaxies and scattered disk stars. Their 2026 preprint reads that record. Outer halos are galactic archaeology: their faint stars preserve the merger history that brighter inner regions have overwritten.
arxiv-2601-22087:
Qian Zhang and co-authors build a fairer way to credit power resources for keeping the grid reliable. Capacity accreditation decides how much each generator or storage unit counts toward resource adequacy, the grid's ability to meet demand. Probabilistic assessment is the modern standard for that judgment.

Their 2026 preprint develops a gradient-based framework. Accreditation becomes the directional derivative of a reliability metric with respect to a resource's capacity: how much reliability actually improves when the resource grows. That view unifies two widely used accreditation approaches. Fairer credits matter because they steer billions in investment toward resources that genuinely keep the lights on during the hardest hours.
arxiv-2601-22187:
A short mathematics preprint studies a basic task: solving for a root of an equation. The equation considered takes a simple power form, where an unknown raised to a whole-number power must equal a given positive number. Its real solution is the corresponding root of that number.

The author presents a root finding method whose order of convergence can be chosen freely. The order measures how fast the error shrinks at each step; higher orders reach a precise root in fewer iterations. Methods with tunable order are useful in numerical software, where root finding sits inside countless larger computations. The note keeps its focus narrow: one equation family, one method, and its convergence behavior.
arxiv-2601-22387:
Victor Nikhil Antony and a large team look to plants for a new way to design social robots. Plants are calm, low-demand presences, yet they shape a room's mood and a person's day. Their 2026 preprint contrasts this with most robots, which copy people or pets and demand much heed.

Plant-like robots would act through slow rhythms and soft, subtle cues. They could keep company without nagging for response. The team set out design metaphors drawn from plant life. The work opens a quiet path for home robots. It suits care homes and calm work spaces.
arxiv-2601-22787:
Patrick Putzky and five co-authors tackle a trade-off in shrinking large AI models after training. Fast methods need no extra data and work on any model, but they break down when models are squeezed below four bits per weight. Methods that use extra data keep quality better, yet cost far more compute.

Their method, named in the title, uses entropy coding to store weights in a smarter way. The goal is strong compression to about two bits without needing data for tuning. Small, cheap models matter for running AI on phones and small machines.
arxiv-2601-22887:
Yangyan Li proposes a new way to give autoregressive models more memory without more computing cost. These models, which predict one step at a time, power most modern AI for text and images. Normally, adding memory means making the network deeper or wider, which raises the cost of every step.

The proposal, MoVE, mixes many value embeddings to store knowledge in a new dimension of scale. If memory can grow while active compute stays flat, models could know more for the same price. That trade-off matters for serving AI to millions of users.
arxiv-2601-22987:
Salem Lahlou presents ArabicDialectHub, a learning resource that spans six kinds of Arabic. It covers Moroccan Darija, Lebanese, Syrian, Emirati, and Saudi varieties, plus Modern Standard Arabic. The set holds more than five hundred phrases, drafted with language models and checked by five native speakers.

Phrases are sorted by difficulty and grouped by theme on an interactive web platform. Learners often study the standard form, then struggle with the dialect spoken on the street. A side-by-side resource helps bridge that gap for students and travelers. Stratified difficulty and thematic grouping let learners progress from everyday phrases toward harder, situation-specific language.
arxiv-2602-02587:
Gregg Hartvigsen models how honesty evolves when players can lie about their last move in the prisoner's dilemma, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The spatial model places individuals on a toroidal lattice, each with a default strategy of cooperating or defecting. Strategies tested include tit-for-tat, which copies the other side's last play, and simply repeating the default.

Each player also carries an evolvable probability of telling the truth about its last play. A defector can therefore present itself as a cooperator. The outcomes split sharply. Mixed populations where truth-telling stays high move toward truthful cooperators. Populations dipping below a lower truth threshold collapse into lying defectors. Both end states are stable because each beats mixed middle states. Hartvigsen discusses uses for humans and animals, where reputation and deception coevolve with cooperation itself.
arxiv-2602-02687:
Casey Cartwright and 6 co-authors follow sound waves through a holographic plasma that is expanding anisotropically, in a 2026 paper, mimicking the quark-gluon plasma of heavy-ion collisions. Equilibrium sound speed is a basic property, but a rapidly stretching medium changes how sound propagates. Their model is a strongly coupled supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory studied through its gravitational dual.

Bjorken expansion, the longitudinal stretching pattern of collision fireballs, breaks isotropy and splits sound into two distinct speeds. The speeds range from just below the conformal value up to the speed of light itself. The authors compute speeds, attenuation, and relaxation time numerically from varied initial states under a quasi-static approximation. They construct an anisotropic hydrodynamic description and test where it applies. The results feed back into how experimental heavy-ion data should be interpreted when the plasma refuses to sit still.
arxiv-2602-02887:
Yue Sun and 5 co-authors connect street access to land-use planning in a 2026 paper. Planners often assign land uses and building intensity without a clear, checkable link to how reachable each block is. That gap makes it hard to test policies before adopting them.

Their three-stage workflow starts by measuring street-network access at several radii. Those measures form nested service areas that guide rule-based placement of land uses. Floor-area ratios then follow an access-weighted model that respects total construction targets. A test on a real urban district reproduced corridor-focused shops and industrial belts. Sampling many policies produced efficient plans that balanced access gains against target land shares.
arxiv-2602-03087:
Four-legged robots learn to climb stairs for fire searches in a 2026 paper by Baixiao Huang and 2 co-authors. Quadrupeds perform primary searches early in indoor fires, looking for victims under hazardous conditions. Situational awareness and rapid stair climbing across varied staircases remain the main challenges for such robot-assisted searches in complex buildings with smoke and obstacles.

Their two-stage reinforcement learning approach trains navigation and locomotion together, end to end. A Unitree Go2 robot first learns on pyramid-stair terrain in simulation. The policy then transfers to realistic straight, L-shaped, and spiral staircases. A centerline-based navigation formulation unifies movement and direction without hierarchical planning. Using only local height-map perception, the policy generalized across staircases. The paper analyzes success, efficiency, and failure modes.
arxiv-2602-03487:
Magnetic skyrmions are tiny swirling spin textures that might carry data in future devices. Mathews Benny and 6 co-authors propose an unconventional home for them in a 2026 paper. The hosts are magnets whose ground state is itself noncollinear, with spins pointing in a twisted arrangement. Earlier skyrmion research used ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, or ferrimagnets as the background.

Using first-principles calculations and atomistic spin simulations, the team shows four-spin exchange stabilizes such a state. The hosts are rhodium-cobalt and palladium-cobalt bilayers on a rhenium surface. Both skyrmion lattices and isolated skyrmions emerge on that background. Transition-state calculations find large energy barriers protecting them, which suggests experiments should be able to observe these textures.
arxiv-2602-03587:
A model can ace exam-style reasoning yet fail when the needed knowledge sits in the task's own context. Shihan Dou and 26 co-authors call that missing skill context learning and build a benchmark for it in a 2026 paper. CL-bench gathers 500 complex contexts with nearly 1,900 tasks and over 31,000 verification checks, all written by domain experts.

Each task can only be solved with content supplied in its context: new domain knowledge, rule systems, procedures, or laws fitted to data. Ten frontier language models solve only about 17 percent of tasks on average, and the best reaches under 24 percent. The authors present the gap as a central bottleneck for deploying models on real, context-heavy work.
arxiv-2602-03787:
Removing information from a trained model usually means retraining some of its weights, which can dull its general abilities. Somnath Basu Roy Chowdhury and 6 co-authors move the unlearning to inference time in a 2026 paper. The frozen generative model is paired with a verifier that judges whether each response meets the unlearning requirements.

Responses are refined in rounds from the verifier's feedback, with no parameter updates at all. Conformal prediction enters to cut the computing overhead and to supply distribution-free guarantees on the result. Across hard unlearning benchmarks, the approach reduces unlearning error by up to ninety-three percent against state-of-the-art methods. The approach suits generative models above all, where parameter-editing assumptions often break down.
arxiv-2602-03987:
A safety proof for a simple model may still protect a complex machine. Nikolaos Bousias and 3 co-authors formalize that transfer in a 2026 paper on control barrier functions, mathematical certificates that keep a system inside safe states. Real dynamics are often too messy for direct certificate design.

Their transferred barrier function carries a safety condition from one system to another with different dynamics, even different state dimension. A simulation function plus an explicit margin term absorbs the mismatch. A quadratic-program filter then enforces the condition on the real system. A quadrotor navigation task demonstrates the transfer working end to end.
arxiv-2602-04687:
Yang Tian and 3 co-authors examine how text-to-image models portray people with a disability in a 2026 study. Work on bias in generated images has covered gender and race more and more, but disability has had far less focus.

The team made images with two leading models using a structured set of prompts. They compared outputs for broad disability prompts against prompts naming specific types of disability. They also tested fixes and judged the mood of portrayals through sentiment checks, mixing machine scoring with human ratings. Findings showed lasting gaps in how disability appeared. The authors call for ongoing checks and fixes to generative models, toward more varied and fair portrayals.
arxiv-2603-01487:
Shuairu Zhu, Zhen-Ya Zheng, Fuyan Bian, and colleagues report a distant galaxy that leaks ionizing light in this 2026 study. Such leakers at early times are rare, yet they help explain how the young universe became ionized. The galaxy, named LCEz4-M1, sits at a redshift that marks a very early era.

Two data sets each catch the leaking light on their own, which makes the case strong. A spectral line fixes the distance, and space telescope images pin down where the leak sits in the galaxy. The galaxy is compact and forms stars at a fierce rate for its size. That burst may have blown thin paths in its gas, letting the light escape, and a faint neighbor hints at a mild past clash.
arxiv-2603-02087:
Harikrishnan Unnikrishnan finds the glottis in high-speed throat films with a two-stage pipeline. His 2026 work serves the search for motion signs that show how well the voice box works, a key aid for throat care. Deep models can fake tissue in frames with no glottis at all, and they often fail in new clinics.

A finder first marks a tight zone of interest, which strips out most shape shifts between patients. A cutter then works just in that zone, trained on a small set of marked frames. A time-based check cuts false finds in frames where the glottis is shut or blocked. Top scores land on two test sets, and the skill holds across data sets with no retraining. In a clinic group, the found motion traits match clinic norms, and one spread trait splits healthy from sick voices.
arxiv-2603-02287:
Manjari Dutta, Arnab Mukherjee, and Sunandan Gangopadhyay study a quantum battery in motion in this 2026 paper. The battery is an Unruh-DeWitt detector, a two-level system speeding at a constant rate. It soaks up charge from a classical pulse while feeling particles from a quantum field. Speeding changes what the detector perceives, which makes its charging physics relativistic.

A tool called the quantum regression theorem lets them compute correlations over two times. They first derive the master equation for the battery's state under standard approximations. Single-time averages and two-time correlations are then solved in closed form. Results explain spontaneous emission and show that acceleration speeds up energy loss. A further case covers photon bunching, and they derive the emission spectrum as well.
arxiv-2603-02587:
Samee Ullah, Ye Cao, Ming-Xiao Duan, and colleagues investigate an exotic particle state in this 2026 physics paper. The state, called K star 1680, decays into pairs of lighter particles. In the strange sector, ordinary quark-antiquark states can mix with hybrid states containing gluon content. Charge conjugation parity is not conserved there, which allows that mixing.

Two decay models, the flux-tube model and the quark pair creation model, frame the analysis. The observed two-body decay pattern cannot be explained by a conventional quark-antiquark picture. Strong evidence instead supports mixing between conventional and hybrid components. The authors discuss what that mixing implies for related particle families. Their study guides searches for hybrid multiplets at three major experiments. The strange sector may be a prime hunting ground.
arxiv-2603-02787:
Rui Zhang and Zhichao Lu measure how alike two algorithms really are when machines write the code. Their 2026 paper notes that language-model tools now generate expert-level algorithms on their own. Judging those algorithms by code text or final output alone can mistake a fresh idea for a copy, or the reverse.

Their method, BehaveSim, compares the trail of intermediate solutions each algorithm produces while solving a problem. Aligning those trails with a time-warping measure reveals whether the underlying logic matches. Plugged into two existing design frameworks, the measure pushed generation toward more varied behavior and better results on three tasks. It also groups algorithms by strategy, giving researchers a map of what the machines invent.
arxiv-2603-02987:
Julián Grigera, Steven Costiou, Juan Cruz Gardey, and Stéphane Ducasse show what changes when programmers work with live objects instead of static code. Their 2026 paper draws on Pharo, a Smalltalk environment where objects stay alive and inspectable while development proceeds. Reasoning about programs in the abstract, they argue, makes the underlying model harder to grasp.

The showcase covers custom inspector views for objects, microcommits that undo changes without version-control round trips, and coding directly inside the debugger during tests. Automatic rewriting handles deprecated calls as APIs evolve, and object-specific breakpoints stop the program only for one chosen instance. The authors invite other development environments to rethink their own features along these live lines.
arxiv-2603-03087:
Hartosh Singh Bal adds signs to a classic graph construction and measures how far a graph sits from being bipartite. The line graph turns edges into vertices, and his 2026 antisymmetric version also orients each edge and signs the connections. A signed graph is balanced exactly when the original graph splits into two camps with no internal edges.

The imbalance count, called the frustration index, becomes a stable measure of non-bipartiteness that ignores relabeling tricks. The signed construction also determines the original graph, repairing a famous ambiguity in Whitney's theorem. Bounds tie the new measure to classical ones, and for cubic graphs it equals exactly twice the odd-cycle transversal number. Computing it is provably hard even there.
arxiv-2603-03287:
Alberto Tono and six Stanford colleagues survey a decade of work on turning sketches into three-dimensional models with deep learning. Sketching is a natural way to design, but sketches are abstract and ambiguous, so older software struggled to read them. Their 2026 survey names the new field Deep Sketch-Based 3D Modeling and maps what has been tried.

The map, called MORPHEUS, sorts systems by their human inputs, the model parts and options they output, and how users view and judge the results. Across the map, the authors flag weak spots and open chances for vision, graphics, and interface researchers. Two needs stand out: outputs that carry more information, and controls that follow a designer's intent more faithfully.
arxiv-2603-03687:
Mengyao Wang and six colleagues study the silent audience of online hate speech: the bystanders. Counterspeech, replying to hate rather than deleting it, is known to restrain speakers and support targets, but its effect on watchers was unmapped. Their 2026 team built a strategy framework and a bot, Civilbot, then ran a mixed-method study where bystanders watched it work.

Bystanders generally found the bot credible and norm-setting, though its shallow reasoning limited how persuasive it felt. Effects were subtle and double-edged. A strong performance could guide participation or let bystanders relax while the bot stood in. A weak one could discourage them, or provoke them to intervene themselves. Strategy decided much: reason-appealing cognitive strategies in a positive tone worked best, while mismatched strategies in the wrong context weakened the impact.
arxiv-2605-00287:
Koray Mentesoglu, Rahul Trivedi, and Sara Mouradian design a quantum sensing protocol that measures both parts of a displacement at once. Their setup couples a single helper qubit to a quantum harmonic oscillator, an idealized vibrating system. The protocol needs no complex state preparation and no adaptive control, which keeps it practical.

The qubit meets the oscillator through controlled displacements over repeated rounds of measurement and reset, while the oscillator keeps gathering the signal. Because the displacements do not commute, each round stamps an order-dependent phase that sharpens the estimate fast. The team shows that exact likelihoods for any single measurement record stay cheap to compute, and that simple measurements nearly reach the quantum limit. Regular extraction of information also makes the scheme sturdy against decoherence.
arxiv-2605-00387:
Louis Shuo Wang gives a focused primer on exact penalization for hard search problems, including programs with balance constraints. Penalization folds constraints into the goal as a cost, and an exact penalty reproduces the problem's solutions exactly once the price is high enough. The classic theory leans on smoothness conditions, which Wang recasts as error bounds on how feasible sets respond to small shifts.

Newer results, built on subanalytic geometry and Łojasiewicz-type bounds, push the method beyond those old assumptions. Wang then applies the theory to such problems by rewriting them through their first-order systems and building penalties from leftover terms. Fractional-order penalties, which arise from the new error bounds, get close attention. The paper aims to give both insight into why the method works and help in using it.
arxiv-2605-00487:
Pascal Berrang and 3 co-authors combine two technologies that rarely meet: formal verification of software and zero-knowledge proofs. Their goal is to verify that a secret software system meets a public specification of correct behavior over time, without revealing the system itself. The verifier should be convinced, yet learn nothing about the design being checked.

The method first obtains a formal certificate of correctness, expressed as a ranking function, by deductive model checking. Zero-knowledge machinery then proves the certificate matches the hidden system. One scheme handles systems drawn as transition graphs, using polynomial commitments. The other handles systems written as guarded commands, using a classical lemma to build a witness and efficient protocols to prove it exists. A prototype runs both schemes on temporal logic examples. The authors target domains where safety and confidentiality are both critical.
arxiv-2605-00587:
Martina Russo and 7 co-authors cool overheated gold nanoparticles with flakes of hexagonal boron nitride, a flat material that moves heat well. Plasmonic particles focus light superbly, but the heat they make harms heat-shy uses such as medical sensing and small optics. Plain cooling fails at these scales, where surfaces resist heat flow. The team places the particles on boron nitride flakes over glass, in water.

Models map how flake thickness and surface heat flow govern cooling. Wavefront imaging tests measure the heat around single heated particles. Thin flakes are limited by how much heat they can hold, thick ones by the interface. With the nitride in place, the heat rise fell by up to about sixty percent compared to glass alone. Two cooling paths emerged: straight into the flake, and the long way through the water. Together the work gives design rules for hot tiny devices.
arxiv-2605-00787:
Stavros Orfanoudakis and Pedro P. Vergara present SAVGO, a reinforcement learning method for continuous control, where an agent chooses smooth actions such as joint torques. Earlier similarity methods helped agents learn, but rarely shaped the policy update itself. SAVGO learns a shared space for states and actions where pairs with similar values sit close in angle, and pairs with different values point apart.

That learned geometry builds a kernel over candidate actions at each update, steering improvement toward higher-value regions beyond local gradient steps. Learning, value estimation, and policy change share one consistent objective while keeping off-policy training scalable. On MuJoCo benchmarks, SAVGO beats strong baselines on hard high-dimensional tasks, and ablations isolate each part's contribution.
arxiv-2605-01287:
Stephen Baigent and Janusz Mierczyński study rival species models where growth rates vary over time in a rough, low-regularity way. The models are Kolmogorov-type equations, and the time terms meet only weak Carathéodory conditions rather than being smooth.

A key object is the carrying simplex, a surface of one lower dimension that draws in every nonzero path of the system. The pair define it through the attractor of an extended flow, built as a limit of the solution operator acting on a set. That route has a more dynamic feel than older ones and also gives a way to compute the surface. They prove the motion on the surface matches a system with one fewer species, a fact first noted by Morris Hirsch but largely passed over since.
arxiv-2605-01387:
Małgorzata Nowak-Kępczyk works on maximal commutative matrix algebras, large families of matrices that all commute and cannot be enlarged. For local algebras whose radical cubes to zero, Laffey found a sharp floor for the family's size in terms of three layer sizes, plus one endless family that meets the floor.

Nowak-Kępczyk adds a stacking move that merges algebras sharing outer layers while keeping them maximal and self-centralizing. Stacking yields a standard building block for every pair of outer layer sizes, and turns the hunt for more floor cases into a search over whole-number points on set rays. Over calm fields she settles all minimal blocks on the balanced branch, maps the near-balanced zone, builds a first nontrivial near-balanced root, and solves one full sector. The floor profile is then met for wide runs of matrix sizes and several endless families.
arxiv-2605-01487:
Andrei Tokovinin, Brian D Mason, Rene A Mendez, and Edgardo Costa present two years of speckle interferometry at the 4.1-meter SOAR telescope in Chile. The technique freezes atmospheric blur with very short exposures, letting astronomers measure close double stars far past normal sharpness.

The haul is large: over five thousand position and brightness measures across about three and a half thousand pairs. Typical spacing sits near two tenths of an arcsecond, and the tightest near a hundredth. More than four hundred pairs are resolved here for the first time, beyond even the Gaia satellite, including hundreds of planet-candidate hosts from TESS and dozens of close subsystems and subdwarfs. The measures refine or yield two hundred binary orbits, some with extreme, precisely pinned oval shapes. Calibration pairs are listed in an appendix for other observers.
arxiv-2605-01587:
Hamza Haif, Abdelali Arous, and Huseyin Arslan rank candidate waveforms for 6G under a channel model that refuses to flatter them. Classic grades rest on sparse, near-steady channels, which hide how dense cities, high speed, and mixed deployments actually smear a signal.

Their model adds clusters that are born and die, Doppler spreading, delays that wander, and steadiness that holds only in pieces. Under it, they derive the true input-output behavior of the main waveform contenders, exposing interference patterns the sparse picture misses. A channel-aware priority frame then weighs delay-Doppler resolution, stationarity, effective signal quality, and where users sit in the cell. Simulations with standard channel profiles confirm the split. Two modern waveforms keep their edge only when the channel stays sparse and steady. Tuned classic designs win on reliability when it does not.
arxiv-2605-01687:
Jialin Song and six co-authors build MultiBreak, a large benchmark of multi-turn jailbreaks, the slow conversational attacks that talk a guarded language model into forbidden output. Such attacks mimic natural chat and slip past safety training more easily than one-shot prompts, yet test sets have been small or template-bound.

The team unify a wide pool of harmful intents, then grow the set with an active learning loop. A generator is fine-tuned again and again to draft stronger attacks, steered by an uncertainty signal. The result holds over ten thousand multi-turn prompts across more than two and a half thousand distinct intents, the broadest topic spread to date. Attack success against two current models runs far above the next-best data set. Categories that look tame in one turn turn potent across several, a warning the authors press on safety teams.
arxiv-2605-01887:
Thomas Buc-d'Alché and Luca Lionni study free cumulants for random tensors, where several recent views may or may not agree. Free probability generalises classical independence, and tensors with different invariances need their own version. One approach, for locally unitary invariant tensors, builds finite-size quantities from averages over the invariance group, whose large-size limits should act as tensorial free cumulants.

That programme had only covered certain distributions and part of the needed moments. The authors start a systematic study, link the approach to work by Nechita and Park, and extend results from both lines. Their goal is a fuller account of which moments define such theories and whether competing definitions coincide.
arxiv-2605-01987:
Yexin Zhang, Zhongtian Ma, Qiaosheng Zhang, and Zhen Wang study privacy in graph convolutional networks, which learn from linked data such as social or citation graphs. They use subsampling stability, the idea that training on a random subset can limit how much one record matters. Their goal is a clear link between sampling rate, error, and privacy.

They derive upper bounds on the misclassification rate that depend directly on the sampling probability. A middle range works best. Sampling too often makes the privacy condition hard to meet and gives empty guarantees, while sampling too rarely harms accuracy. The authors present this as the first rigorous frame for subsampling stability in these networks under differential privacy.
arxiv-2605-02087:
Chloe Li and colleagues test a new training step that teaches a language model its own behaviour spec before alignment training begins. Developers often write a Model Spec or constitution for how a model should act. Standard fine-tuning on examples can give shallow alignment that generalises poorly, because examples leave the intended pattern underspecified.

Model spec midtraining inserts synthetic documents about the spec between pretraining and fine-tuning. The model learns the spec's content, which then shapes how it generalises from later examples. In one test, a cheese preference tied in the spec to pro-America values led to broad pro-America generalisation. A spec tied to affordability instead led the other way, showing the step steers generalisation.
arxiv-2605-02187:
Mingyu Luo and colleagues expose a tampering risk in language model agents that use a bring-your-own-key setup. In that setup, traffic passes through a relay the user authorised, which can alter plain-text model replies after alignment checks but before actions run, without breaking encryption. Developers tend to trust the logs and test results in those replies.

A minimal attack rewrites one field that drives execution and regenerates the rest of the reply with the user's key, keeping the model's style. Experiments show false green verification, where harmful code changes pass public tests while quietly defeating security checks. Tests span several benchmarks and five frontier models. The authors propose a provider-signed defence for the response path.
arxiv-2605-02287:
Maksym Nechepurenko compares three methods for detecting informed trading on Polymarket that appeared at nearly the same time in April 2026. One screen by Mitts and Ofir covers more than two hundred thousand wallet-market pairs. A second, by Gomez-Cram and colleagues, uses an event-level sign-randomisation test on the full transaction history to flag skilled winners and likely insiders.

Nechepurenko's own Information Leakage Score measures per-market front-loading of information around a public-event time taken from reporting. The paper argues the three are distinct layers of detection, not rivals on one layer. Sign-randomisation is read as an account-level test of persistent directional skill, given opportunity choice, rather than a direct insider test. Each lens suits a different question.
arxiv-2605-02387:
Binh-Minh Bui-Xuan, Michel Habib, Fabien de Montgolfier, and Renaud Torfs show that the standard graph searches, depth-first and breadth-first, can do more than their textbook uses. Depth-first search has computed strongly connected components since Tarjan's work in the seventies, and breadth-first search gives distances in graphs. The authors prove both searches are strong enough to recognise and certify several well-structured graph classes.

One depth-first pass recognises and certifies trivially perfect graphs, much more simply than a prior method. One breadth-first pass recognises split graphs and bipartite chain graphs. For proper interval graphs, two consecutive breadth-first passes improve on a triple LexBFS algorithm. Characterisations through vertex orderings underpin all of the results.
arxiv-2605-02787:
Anouk Oudshoorn, Magdalena Ortiz, and Mantas Simkus study static analysis for SHACL, a language that states constraints on graph data in the semantic web. Validation, checking one dataset against one document, is SHACL's main service. Comparing two documents, asking whether every graph passing one also passes the other, had no static service, and is the problem taken up here.

The authors treat full documents with recursive shape definitions and targets, beyond earlier work on single shape expressions. Under supported and stable model semantics, the comparison problem is undecidable, even for a modest shape logic. Under the well-founded semantics it flips: the problem is decidable in single exponential time. The bridge is a translation into a rich fixed-point modal logic, with an optimal automata-based decision method.
arxiv-2605-03187:
Fabrizio Berritta, Jan A. Krzywda, Tom Dvir, Paul Buttles, Stanislav Eilhart, Jeroen Danon, and Ferdinand Kuemmeth show how to run a qubit whose frequency jumps between two values. Defects called two-level systems cause those sudden shifts, which spoil gate accuracy in solid-state quantum processors.

Their one-bit feedback protocol guesses the current frequency from a single measurement, reaching the limit set by the qubit's own entropy. Run on a fast classical controller, it suppressed defect-induced beating in a superconducting qubit, cut errors sharply, and held gate quality steady over time. The simple scheme could help large arrays with a few unstable qubits.
arxiv-2605-03787:
Sapna Sachan, Rakesh Kumar Sanodiya, and Amulya Kumar Mahto address a bottleneck in medical image classification. Labeling needs expert time. Also, models trained at one hospital often falter at another, because scanners and protocols differ. Their unsupervised domain adaptation framework aligns a labeled source domain with an unlabeled target domain. That reduces the need for new annotation.

The method combines transfer learning with a Maximum Mean Discrepancy loss computed in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, optimizing class and alignment losses together. On two chest X-ray datasets from different medical centers, adapted models improved strongly over non-adapted ones. A comparison found the kernel version beats standard discrepancy measures at closing the modality gap.
arxiv-2605-03887:
Benjamin Basso, Erkan Kaluç, and Didina Serban compute correlation functions of half-BPS operators in planar N=4 Super-Yang-Mills theory at strong coupling, in the classical limit where operator dimensions scale with the coupling. The kinematics they study correspond, in the dual string description, to strings moving in a product of anti-de Sitter and sphere spaces. Their tool is the hexagon formalism, which tiles correlation functions with hexagonal patches.

They show correlation functions exponentiate in this regime and are governed by the free energy of a set of Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz equations. Those equations are equivalent in structure to the Gaiotto-Moore-Neitzke equations encoding BPS spectra in N=2 theories. Using that correspondence, the authors apply wall-crossing techniques to extend the framework. They formulate a chi-system covering polygonal tilings and closed geometries for single-trace correlators.
arxiv-2605-04387:
Yuichiro Nakai reviews spontaneous CP violation, an idea that could explain why a key angle in the strong force is so small while still producing the matter-antimatter imbalance seen in particle physics. The review focuses on realising the idea inside supersymmetry.

Nakai shows the violation arises along flat directions of the theory and is stabilised by supersymmetry breaking plus strong dynamics, answering worries about scale and unwanted corrections. The framework predicts light new particles that couple very weakly to known matter. It can also generate the cosmic baryon surplus through the Affleck-Dine mechanism at a low reheating temperature, and it predicts a neutron signal within reach of near-future experiments.
arxiv-2605-04587:
Jordi Blanco-Pozo and nine co-authors present a framework for cleaning stellar activity out of exoplanet measurements. A star's own surface activity shifts its measured radial velocity by amounts larger than the signal of an Earth-like planet, and even the best spectrographs cannot remove that jitter alone.

Instead of fitting each spectral line profile with a simple bell curve, they decompose the profile into an orthogonal basis, separating true shifts from shape distortions caused by activity. A time-aware neural network, trained on synthetic distortions from a realistic star simulator, then models how the activity contribution evolves. They validate the method on observations of two active stars from major instruments.
arxiv-2605-04687:
Debabrata Karmakar, Atanu Manna, and Bhakti Bhusan Manna study a scalar field equation on hyperbolic space with two competing power nonlinearities of opposite sign. The equation balances a spectral setting against two terms. One term encourages solutions, and another suppresses them. The question is for which setting values positive-energy solutions exist.

The authors resolve the threshold completely, for every ordering of the two powers. That includes cases where one power is below one. It also includes cases reaching or passing the critical Sobolev power. In one regime the critical spectral value depends on both exponents and the dimension, while in the others it depends on the dimension alone.
arxiv-2605-04887:
Ridho Benedictus Togi Manik and five co-authors predict customer satisfaction for online shopping in Indonesia from comments left under YouTube videos. Sellers now meet customers largely through video-based social media, and the volume of loose, mixed comments is too large to track by hand. The team turns that text into a prediction task.

Their model pairs XGBoost, a boosted decision-tree method, with word-frequency features after careful text cleaning. Word analysis and feature rankings revealed an unexpected pattern in the results. Talk about shopping was heavily mixed with social and political terms, and those terms ultimately shaped whether audience satisfaction read as positive or negative.
arxiv-2605-04987:
Eduard Inozemtsev, Dmitrii Kolupaev, and Andrey Kupavskii study families of permutations that contain no set of pairwise disjoint members of a given size. Two permutations intersect when they send some element to the same value, and a matching is a collection of permutations that pairwise avoid each other in the sense defined by the authors. The central question is how large such a family can be without containing a matching.

The authors characterise the largest families with no matching of a given size and prove a Hilton-Milner type result, which describes the largest non-trivial families of this kind. They also obtain results for the special family of derangements, permutations with no fixed points.
arxiv-2605-05087:
Urshita Pal studies the top cohomology of principal congruence subgroups of special linear groups over Euclidean number rings, a topic linking group theory with the geometry of buildings. Earlier work showed this cohomology vanishes above a degree that grows quadratically with matrix size. For the integers, a question of Lee and Szczarba asked when the top group matches a homology group of a quotient of the Tits building.

Pal generalises that question to Euclidean number rings and proves a natural map between the two objects is always surjective. She also gives sufficient conditions on the prime level that guarantee the map is an isomorphism, extending the earlier integer answer into this wider arithmetic setting.
arxiv-2605-05287:
Francisco Javier Arceo and Varsha Prasad Narsing argue that company retrieval systems have a security flaw at their core: they rank files by relevance, not by permission. In multi-tenant companies, a query can therefore surface another tenant's secret data simply because it scores highest. Agentic systems widen the hole through tool-based disclosure, context build-up across turns, and client-side control tricks.

The authors pin down this relevance-permission gap and propose a layered isolation design in response. Policy-aware intake, search-time gating, and shared inference are joined, with server-side control backing tool permission, state separation, and policy. The design targets vendor-neutral, multi-tenant deployments under legal and cost pressure.
arxiv-2605-05387:
Diffusion models can fill in missing parts of a signal, but only the observed part is pinned down. Ahmad Aghapour, Erhan Bayraktar, and Asaf Cohen study that gap for problems like image inpainting and super-resolution. Samplers that only enforce agreement with the measurements can still place probability in the wrong places.

The authors split the score function into observed and free directions. They bound the error from a natural shortcut by a mutual information term that does not grow with dimension. Guided by the theory, their sampler starts with a projected Langevin step and beat a strong baseline in tests.
arxiv-2605-05987:
Hange Lao, Binjian Nie, and Wei He model solar powered cold storage for open air meat markets. Meat loss is high where power supply is weak, and battery based solar refrigeration is costly to expand. Their study covers five connected meat markets in Abuja, Nigeria, with cooling demand drawn from field data.

The model treats pre-chilled meat itself as a carrier of cooling credit when it moves between markets. Phase change material storage holds cold in place at each market as a second storage form. Shifting storage from batteries to phase change material cut battery capacity by about 67 percent and total cost by up to 15 percent. Letting markets exchange cooling credit cut costs by a further 8 percent.
arxiv-2605-06287:
Davide Bason, Wei Cui, and Lorenzo Ruggeri construct non-invertible duality defects from half-spacetime gauging of a 2-group symmetry. The setting is quantum field theory in two space dimensions plus time, where symmetry structures richer than ordinary groups have become a major theme. The authors start from a parent theory with two discrete Abelian symmetries and a prescribed mixed anomaly between them, then gauge one factor at a time.

Gauging one factor yields a theory with a 2-group symmetry, while gauging the other yields a non-invertible symmetry whose fusion rules they derive explicitly. With three such symmetries in a cyclic anomaly pattern, different gauging choices produce mutually dual theories. The half-spacetime gauging is then carried by a duality defect, illustrated with explicit gauge theory examples and a self contained guide to the cohomological tools.
arxiv-2605-06387:
Nan Jia and eight co-authors study on-policy distillation, a method that trains a student model on its own output with token-level feedback from a teacher. They find three weaknesses in the standard approach: noisy updates, vanishing signals where the advantage is zero, and weak exploration when corrective feedback is thin.

Their fix, Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation, replaces ineffective negative reinforcement with a local divergence penalty in non-positive regions while keeping positive reinforcement. On math reasoning benchmarks it beats standard distillation, keeps higher entropy during training, and retains skills better during later tool-use adaptation.
arxiv-2605-06587:
Shenming Fu and fifteen co-authors measure the projected shapes of galaxy clusters through weak gravitational lensing, preparing methods for Rubin Observatory data. Clusters are triaxial, like squashed three-axis ellipsoids, but sky observations show only a projection. The team stacks lensing signals aligned by each cluster's satellite distribution and expands them in multipoles, going beyond leading order.

Using Dark Energy Survey Year 3 catalogs for a precursor sample with well-centered clusters, they find a projected ellipticity of about zero point three one, with percent-level systematics from miscentering. The value shows no clear dependence on redshift or richness, and mock catalogs verify the measurement. Larger surveys should tighten these shape constraints.
arxiv-2605-06787:
Mario Fernández Navarro, Marta F. Zamoro, Marko Pesut, and Xavier Ponce Díaz map the general structure of multi-axion solutions to the strong CP problem, a puzzle about why the strong nuclear force conserves certain symmetries. Single-axion solutions predict a tight band linking axion mass and photon coupling, and experiments target that band. Adding more axions generically moves predictions off the band in several distinct ways.

The authors identify Peccei-Quinn symmetry breaking patterns and the alignment between quantum chromodynamics and electromagnetic anomalies as the ingredients fixing where axions land. They derive a general sum rule for systems of any number of axions, then exhibit complete theories realizing each regime. An extended experimental search program follows.
arxiv-2605-07287:
Yecong Wan and three co-authors render new views of a scene while spending their building blocks where detail actually is. Feed-forward Gaussian splatting methods usually assign the same number of Gaussian primitives to every pixel or voxel, wasting capacity on smooth areas and starving fine structure. SplatWeaver instead predicts how many primitives each region needs.

Specialist experts each produce a fixed count of primitives, and a pixel-level router coordinates them per location. High-frequency cues guide the router toward textured regions and away from redundancy, with regularization keeping choices stable. Across varied scenarios, SplatWeaver produced more faithful views than leading methods while using fewer primitives overall.
arxiv-2605-07387:
Sebastian Müller and a co-author analyze how validators in DAG-based ledgers choose which transactions to include, using game theory. Validators acting alone with simple rules can produce wasteful outcomes for the whole network. The paper compares two fee mechanisms used in practice: random assignment of each fee to one node, and equal sharing among all nodes.

For both mechanisms the authors derive matching Nash balance points and give a search method to compute them. Test runs show the sharing scheme's balance point reaches higher throughput and rewards, most when fees are lopsided. Oddly, a simple share-based approach sometimes beats the random scheme's equilibrium.
arxiv-2605-07587:
Hexuan Liu and two co-authors attack a counting problem from phylogenetics, about tree-child networks, which model evolution with hybridization. Pons and Batle asked whether the count of bicombining tree-child networks with given leaves and reticulation nodes equals the count of certain constrained words. The identity was an open problem when the paper was written.

The authors confirm the conjecture for networks with a bounded number of reticulation nodes, building families of Young tableaux with walls and holes that biject with the words in question. Projecting the tableaux to decorated Dyck paths yields generating functions, recurrences, and closed formulas. For the single-reticulation case, structural quantities converge to Beta distributions, revealing a probabilistic layer beneath the counting.
arxiv-2605-07687:
Yixiong Jing and five co-authors simplify physics-based digital twins, the spring-mass models used to predict how real objects deform and move for robotics. Twins rebuilt from vision inherit the reconstruction's fine resolution, far more detail than the task dynamics need, which makes repeated simulation rollouts needlessly expensive.

Their method, PhySPRING, uses a graph neural network to learn coarser graph versions of the twin together with their mechanical parameters, merging nodes whose learned dynamic responses are similar. Every reduced layer remains an explicit spring-mass system. On the PhysTwin benchmark it improved reconstruction and prediction accuracy while running up to about two and a third times faster. Substituted into robot policy evaluation, the reduced twins kept manipulation success rates comparable.
arxiv-2605-07787:
Connor J. Gauntlett and David P. Kimsey build a theory of orthogonal polynomials on the unit sphere of the quaternions, the four-dimensional number system. The classical theory on the circle is a mature subject with named theorems. The quaternionic version needs a new notion, the q-positive measure, and coefficient machinery adapted from recent work by Alpay, Colombo, Kimsey, and Sabadini.

Into this setting they carry the Szegő recurrences, the zeros theorem, the Szegő-Verblunsky theorem, and Baxter's theorem. The proofs lean on Verblunsky coefficients and established results for matrix-valued functions. Along the way they develop matrix analogues of Schur's recurrences and of Verblunsky's moment formula, which appear to be new in their own right.
arxiv-2605-07887:
Botond Osváth and two co-authors simulate the controlled movement of parafermions, exotic particles proposed as building blocks for topological quantum computers. Parafermions could support a broader set of protected gates than the better-known Majorana modes, but they are tied to strong electron-electron interactions and are hard to handle. Moving them in a guided shuttling step is a needed step before braiding operations.

Working with an electron ladder model, the team follows the real-time dynamics of the basic shuttling process for Z-4 parafermion edge states. Their runs combine the density matrix renormalization group with the time-dependent variational principle. From the dynamics they assess the adiabatic speed limit, how fast a parafermion can be moved without spoiling it, under conditions relevant to experiments.
arxiv-2605-07987:
Jan Verhülsdonk and five co-authors add uncertainty estimates to deep-learning reconstruction of heart shape, a step clinical use requires. Atlas-based methods rebuild patient-specific cardiac anatomy from sparse, noisy point data, but because they lean heavily on the prior atlas, their errors can be large and, worse, unreported.

Their probabilistic framework couples deep signed distance functions with Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling in the latent space. The functions represent the ventricles' surfaces implicitly through a neural network conditioned on learned latent codes. Reading the reconstruction loss as a log-likelihood gives both a best reconstruction and posterior samples around it. On a public cardiac dataset the method produced accurate multi-surface reconstructions of both ventricles with well-calibrated uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-08187:
Philip Franz, Max von Danwitz, Gregory Duthé, Alexander Popp, and coauthors detect damage in wind turbine blades from air pressure alone. Modern blades are long and flexible, and cheap, non-intrusive monitoring is in demand. Their sensor system, Aerosense, records aerodynamic pressure on the surface without touching the structure.

The underlying experiment mounted an airfoil on a vibrating beam in an open wind tunnel and cut the support in stages to mimic growing damage. A convolutional network trained only on the pressure records learned to detect the damage and grade its severity. The approach offers an interpretable route to blade health monitoring under changing inflow conditions.
arxiv-2605-08587:
Jiaxuan Zou, Ruifeng Ren, and Yong Liu refine how linear attention models update their memory during long texts. Standard attention grows too costly with length, so recurrent designs compress context into a fixed state where the update rule matters most. One popular rule sets its step size by trial rather than theory. The authors return to its regression roots and derive a step size scaled by key size, following the classic Kaczmarz projection idea.

Their Kaczmarz Linear Attention changes one scalar yet keeps the same state and fast parallel training. Tests show the lowest error among linear rivals, stable behavior at very long lengths, perfect single needle retrieval, and faster decoding. Long context modeling gains a principled small change with broad payoff.
arxiv-2605-08787:
Mashrafi Monon, Umaima Rahman, Asif Hanif, Numan Saeed, and Mohammad Yaqub test whether three dimensional medical vision models truly understand anatomy in space, or merely lean on language habits. Their CT-SpatialVQA benchmark draws over nine thousand questions from more than sixteen hundred real radiology reports and CT volumes, checked through an assisted pipeline with strong human agreement.

Questions demand exact anatomical location, left versus right awareness, structural comparison, and relations between structures in the volume. Eight leading models average only about a third correct on the spatial reasoning tasks, often below chance. The gap warns that trustworthy clinical support needs far deeper use of volumetric evidence than current models show.
arxiv-2605-09087:
Aishwarya Fursule, Shruti Kshirsagar, and Anderson R Avila tackle gender bias in systems that detect fake audio. These detectors guard high-stakes security checks, yet few studies ask where unfair gaps between men's and women's voices come from or how to fix them in an orderly way.

Their framework diagnoses the bias source first, then applies a matched fix, testing two detector models on a large spoofing dataset. The gaps, they find, stem not from skewed training data but from sound features, leaked gender cues, and uneven test design. Setting separate decision thresholds per gender cut unfairness by more than half at no cost to accuracy. No single fix closed the gap fully, which is their central warning.
arxiv-2605-09187:
Carla Griffiths and co-author Mirco Musolesi ask whether language models learn semantic roles, the who-did-what-to-whom structure of a sentence, from pretraining alone or only after task-specific tuning. Their 2026 study freezes decoder-only transformers and trains simple linear probes on their inner states. If a probe can extract role information from a frozen model, that information was already present before any adaptation.

Across model scales, frozen representations hold substantial semantic role information, though probing still falls short of fully fine-tuned models. The authors read that as partial emergence: role structure does arise from plain language modeling, but not completely. They also find the inner encoding grows more distributed as models get larger. For interpretability research, the work separates what pretraining gives for free from what fine-tuning adds, and shows how the format of a basic meaning structure changes with scale.
arxiv-2605-09587: Biharmonic tops generalize minimal tops to a fourth-order energy, and one might expect wilder habits. Shun Maeta proves that rotational biharmonic tops in four-sized Euclidean space are minimal after all. The 2026 paper is telling apart shapes with a satisfying punchline.
arxiv-2605-09887: Sparse autoencoders scale in predictable ways; manifold structure predicts the layerwise scaling laws — the geometric wall. Eslam Zaher, Maciej Trzaskowski, Quan Nguyen, and Fred Roosta discover it. The 2026 paper is interpretability research hitting a hard geometric limit head-on today.
arxiv-2605-10187: research reasoning tested across disciplines and modalities — SciVQR is the multidisciplinary, combined benchmark. Longteng Guo, Xuanxu Lin, Dongze Hao, and others build it. The 2026 paper is AI for science, tested broadly. It tests research minds rigorously across truly diverse fields.
arxiv-2605-10287: Electroweak spin-1 resonances — heavy cousins of the W and Z bosons — and their phenomenology at colliders. Ch. Verollet surveys the signatures. The 2026 paper is particle physics beyond the Standard Model. It hunts heavy spin-1 resonances at current and future colliders.
arxiv-2606-00087:
Zhan and co-authors screen for sleep apnea from a face photograph plus clinical data, without letting the AI jump to conclusions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Obstructive sleep apnea-hypopnea syndrome, where breathing stalls during sleep, is confirmed by an overnight sleep study, so cheap pre-screening matters. Asking a multimodal model for a direct yes-or-no proved unstable, swinging between all-negative and excessive positive calls. Their EviOSAHS framework breaks each face image into seven anatomical questions about the neck, chin, jaw, and related features.

Each answer becomes a structured evidence card recording visibility, risk direction, strength, and confidence. Only at the final stage are cards combined with the clinical profile for a balanced decision. On a cohort of over 600 subjects, the system reached accuracy near 88 percent with sensitivity near 95 percent in tests. Auditing nearly 4,500 visual outputs showed structured formatting and visibility rates.

arxiv-2606-04087:
Lachlan Lancaster and co-authors question in 2026 how much trust to place in simulations of turbulent radiative mixing layers, the churning boundaries between hot and cold astrophysical gas. Their title, a nod to Magritte, warns that a simulation of a layer is not the layer itself.

Using high-resolution simulations, they show that a celebrated result, total cooling staying constant as resolution improves, arises from a lucky cancellation. Numerical dissipation and numerical viscosity push in opposite directions and happen to offset. That coincidence has no physical explanation, so converged cooling alone proves little. They identify the scale that truly must be resolved: where an eddy turns over in the same time the gas takes to cool. Resolving it settles the phase structure.
arxiv-2606-04687:
Wang, Yu, Cai, and Fang redesign blockchain consensus to communicate less, in a 2026 arXiv distributed systems paper. Protocols based on directed acyclic graphs achieve high throughput, and recent work pushed their good-case latency toward the theoretical floor. Their protocol, Clownfish, is a partially synchronous DAG-based Byzantine fault tolerant protocol that selectively cuts the number of edges in each vertex.

It also reduces the extra latency suffered in failure cases by optimizing the round advancement rule. And it supports multiple leaders per round to lower average latency while keeping the lower communication cost. The work targets deployments where the network, not computation, limits how many validators a Byzantine-tolerant ledger can sustain.
arxiv-2606-04987:
Zhu, Karadzhov, Stafford, and Vlachos release a dataset of groups thinking out loud together over chess puzzles, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-party dialogue is a critical setting for studying collaborative reasoning. DeliChess contains 107 deliberation dialogues in which participants first solve multiple-choice chess puzzles individually, then discuss them in groups before submitting a revised collective answer. Full transcripts come with pre- and post-discussion choices and metadata on puzzle difficulty and move quality.

Evaluating with three metrics based on chess engine assessments, the authors find deliberation significantly improves group accuracy. Probing utterances, messages that elicit proposals, justifications, or strategic reflection, are analyzed with a classifier trained on prior deliberation data: probing makes post-discussion performance more variable but does not consistently improve it.
arxiv-2606-05087:
Francesca Franzon, Nicolas Rosàs Gómez, and Leo Wanner ask whether language models distinguish light verbs from full verbs in this 2026 arXiv paper. Frequent verbs such as have and make can act as light collocates, carrying little meaning of their own, or as full predicates with concrete meaning. The contrast appears in pairs like make a decision, a light use, against make a cake, a full use.

The team built a large controlled dataset of minimally varying English sentence series in which the same context holds the same verb in both uses. Two probing experiments show that language models do differentiate between the uses even in minimal contexts, and they exhibit separable internal patterns across object types. The authors release the dataset, generation code, and materials as a reusable resource, and the framework extends to broader contexts, more verbs, and other languages.
arxiv-2606-05487:
Pramod Thombre and colleagues present VASTO in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that reconstructs blood vessels and their flow at once from CT angiography data. In the standard workflow, vessel shape is reconstructed first by conventional methods. Flow is computed afterward by simulation, which needs the shape and boundary conditions fixed in advance. Because the shape is frozen first, missing branches or narrowings cannot be recovered even if flow data hints at them.

VASTO instead uses differentiable topology optimization to recover vessel shape and blood velocity jointly, directly from time-resolved projection data. It couples a steady incompressible flow model with a transient transport model for the contrast agent. It maps predictions into measurement space through a differentiable projection operator, so mismatches with the real scan drive the reconstruction. The recovered fields carry hemodynamic information for downstream estimates such as wall shear stress and flow distribution.
arxiv-2606-05587:
Jiang presents a tracker for objects seen from drones in a 2026 arXiv paper. Drone video makes tracking hard: objects look tiny, crowd together, and often hide behind each other. Older graph-based trackers assume one fixed neighborhood size for linking objects. They also treat every object the same, whether fresh, confirmed, or lost. Jiang's network instead adapts its links and node types to the scene.

The system guesses flight height from average object size and widens or narrows its links to match. It keeps three node kinds apart: new sightings, firm tracks, and lost tracks. A gating step stops hidden or lost objects from polluting their neighbors' codes. On the VisDrone2019 test set the tracker scored near ninety-five percent on the main tracking measure. It beat a standard baseline by five points and cut identity switches sharply.
arxiv-2606-05687:
Junheng Li and colleagues make predictive control cheap enough to guide robot learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Humanoid control has two strong tools. Model predictive control plans with physics and respects limits, but it is slow to set up. Reinforcement learning builds rugged skills in simulation, yet without physical guidance. Running the planner inside learning loops has been too costly to justify. The team attacks that cost directly.

A new reward design borrows guidance from planner trajectories built on centroidal dynamics, a reduced model of the robot's mass motion. Their solver runs many horizon plans in parallel on graphics hardware. It skips problem construction and pre-compilation entirely, working straight from changing dynamics. Comparative studies and real hardware tests followed. The guided learner beat baselines on both walking and manipulation skills. Code is public, so other labs can test the recipe on their own humanoids.
arxiv-2606-05987:
Parke and colleagues report the steadiest laser ever locked to a room-temperature cavity in a 2026 arXiv paper, published in Optica. Ultrastable lasers anchor optical clocks and precision measurement. Their stability comes from locking to a Fabry-Pérot reference cavity whose length must not drift. The team's cavity stretches sixty-eight centimeters and sits at room temperature, no cryogenics.

The laser's fractional frequency instability reached four parts in a hundred quadrillion. Its linewidth narrowed to twelve millihertz, a sliver of spectral purity. Both figures are the lowest reported for any room-temperature system. Skipping cryogenic cooling matters beyond records. It puts state-of-the-art stability within reach of more laboratories and field instruments. Thermal noise from mirror coatings, not temperature control, now sets the practical floor. The work reframes what room-temperature metrology can promise. Optical frequency standards gain speed and accuracy from such references.
arxiv-2606-06087:
Aofan Yu and colleagues move an agent's skills out of its prompt and into its weights in a 2026 arXiv paper. Textual skill instructions are reusable, but pasting them in at every step burns context and exposes them as plaintext. LatentSkill converts each text skill into a plug-and-play LoRA adapter. A pretrained hypernetwork performs the conversion, storing the procedure in weight space.

Modular loading, scaling, and composition survive the move. On ALFWorld tasks, success rose by over twenty points on seen splits and thirteen on unseen ones. Prefill tokens dropped by nearly two thirds. Search-QA exact match improved with skill-token overhead down over seventy percent. The adapters form a semantic geometry in weight space. Scaling coefficients tune skill strength, and aligned skills compose through parameter arithmetic. Weight-space skills promise agent libraries that are compact, private, and mixable. The prompt stays clean for the task.
arxiv-2606-06187:
Sandro Franceschi surveys a body of work on reflected Brownian motion in this 2026 arXiv paper on probability theory. Brownian motion is the jittery random wandering seen in pollen grains and stock prices alike. Confine that wandering to a quadrant, a quarter of the plane, with reflecting walls, and its long run behavior becomes surprisingly hard to compute. Queueing networks and other applied models depend on exactly those computations.

The survey organizes results around kernel functional equations, relations satisfied by the Laplace transforms of the quantities of interest. Two regimes get separate treatment: the recurrent case, where a stationary distribution exists, and the transient case, where Green functions describe how often regions are visited. The review also covers Martin boundaries and positive harmonic functions, which encode escape and absorption behavior. Methods from the analytic theory of quarter plane random walks supply most of the solution techniques surveyed.
arxiv-2606-06387:
Lin-Fa Lee and co-authors expose a new attack on AI web agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. WebMCP is an emerging protocol that lets websites hand tools directly to AI agents, skipping the usual interface. Third party scripts on a page can exploit that openness mid session. The authors name the threat Mid Session Tool Injection, and split it into two forms.

Tool Hijacking changes which tools the agent can see, abusing registration races and cancellation signals. Tool Framing instead twists how tools appear, editing names, descriptions, and permission hints so the agent misjudges what a tool does. In their tests, hijacking reached data exfiltration rates up to one hundred percent, though it often broke the task. Framing was stealthier, keeping task completion as high as eighty five percent while still working. The authors recommend binding tool identity to its origin and logging every registration.
arxiv-2606-06787:
Language model agents that use tools still forget: long tasks demand remembering facts, past episodes, and skills that worked before. Wang, Lu, Liu, Dong, and Zhu present AdMem in this 2026 arXiv paper, a memory system built to fix that weakness. Earlier designs stored mostly facts, or replayed past successes while ignoring failures and growth over time.

AdMem unifies three memory kinds, semantic facts, episodic records, and procedural know how, across short term and long term stores. Three cooperating agents do the housekeeping: an actor works on tasks, a memory agent files and fetches records, and a critic grades them. Long term memory is pruned, merged, and scored by reward, so it improves instead of merely swelling. Across several test environments, AdMem agents proved more robust and successful on long multi step tasks than agents using older memory schemes.
arxiv-2606-07587:
Lu and co-authors discover that nearly every method for routing questions among language models hits the same accuracy ceiling, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Routers send easy queries to cheap models, hard ones to expensive models. The field has produced clustering routers, classifiers, ranking methods, and confidence-based rules. Studying 21 methods across 5 benchmarks, the authors find them on a plateau far below an oracle that picks the best model. Even a nearest-neighbor router lands there.

The cause is a predictability bottleneck: routers learn performance per model rather than query-specific signals. They all solve the same easy queries and fail the hard ones needing instance-level decisions. The study maps escape routes, showing training sets, stronger encoders, and end-to-end fine-tuning can push past the plateau. The authors offer the plateau as a diagnostic: if a router lands on it, it has learned averages, not routing.
arxiv-2606-07687:
Yeom and co-authors ask what makes the internal features of a video world model useful for action, in this 2026 arXiv paper. World models learn compressed descriptions of video, called latents, that robots may later use to plan movements. It was unclear whether sharp picture reconstruction or some other training signal creates features that reveal which action comes next.

The team probed many encoder families with one shared inverse-dynamics test, which asks a model to recover the action between two frames. Models with excellent pixel decoding sometimes showed near-zero action recoverability, a striking failure. Encoders pretrained on video itself, especially with temporal context from natural footage, gave the best balance of visual quality and action prediction. Adding feature-level prediction on top helped only a little, and training with action labels made features far more robust when images were corrupted.
arxiv-2606-07887:
Fradelizi, Manui, Meyer, and Ndiaye settle exactly when a classic volume inequality becomes an equality, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Rogers-Shephard inequality bounds the volume of a convex body's difference body, formed by subtracting the body from itself. Extensions to Lp sums, a deformed way of adding shapes, were known for planar bodies and for locally anti-blocking bodies, but equality cases were open.

The characterisation turns out to be the same in both settings. For every exponent p above one, equality holds if and only if the body is a simplex, the higher-dimensional analogue of a triangle, with one vertex at the origin.
