That single shape is therefore the unique extremiser across dimensions and settings. Results of this kind matter because equality cases reveal the rigid structure behind an inequality. They show which configurations a bound is really about, and anchor stability questions about near-extremal bodies.
arxiv-2606-08087:
Hugo Leguillier and co-authors measure the energy bill of voice recognition, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Speaker verification systems use deep ResNet backbones trained on the VoxCeleb2 dataset, and they keep getting deeper and wider in pursuit of accuracy, with their environmental cost largely undocumented. The team trained a family of ResNets varying depth, channel width, and stage distribution, measuring energy consumption and carbon footprint with node-level sensors through both training and inference.

A clear point of diminishing returns emerges. Beyond it, deeper and wider models bring only marginal accuracy gains while energy use grows steeply. Mid-sized networks such as ResNet-50, and variants concentrating capacity in particular stages, achieve favourable trade-offs. The guidelines follow: the greenest competitive model is rarely the largest, and stage distribution matters as much as raw size for the carbon ledger.
arxiv-2606-08287:
Josiah Kunz and Choudhary build a neural network that speeds up engineering stress simulations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Finite element analysis, the standard method for predicting how parts bear loads, is essential for design but expensive, especially across many iterations. Machine learning surrogates can be far faster, yet most struggle to generalize across different shapes. The authors' mesh graph network predicts von Mises stress fields, a combined measure of distortion used to judge failure risk, in flat components with arbitrary holes.

The network treats the simulation mesh as a graph and encodes node types, such as fixed boundaries and hole edges, together with relative distances between neighbors and the applied load. Because it uses relative rather than absolute coordinates, the model is unchanged by shifting or rotating the part, which helps it handle unseen geometries without retraining. It was trained on eleven plate geometries under twenty load conditions.
arxiv-2606-08987:
Kulkarni and colleagues chase the identity of a mysterious glowing point in the Milky Way's halo and rule out the prime suspect, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The WHAM survey mapped the sky in hydrogen-alpha light and found 31 point sources standing out from the Galactic background. For source WPS 46, earlier work suggested the subdwarf PG 0931+691 supplied the ionizing energy. Using the Keck Cosmic Web Imager, the team found nebular emission lines near WPS 46 but no hydrogen-alpha emission near the star itself.

Emission-line ratios and the glow's shape fit an active galactic nucleus or LI(N)ER-like source better than a star-forming region. The authors give reasons the subdwarf cannot power the source. They propose WPS 46 belongs to an intermediate-velocity cloud complex, lit up by shocks. Their follow-up plan pairs a survey instrument with narrow-band images from amateur astronomers.
arxiv-2606-09287:
Pandey, Singh, and Mahdid watch a transformer's internal representations travel through its layers the way neuroscientists track neuron populations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Each layer's output is one step of a trajectory through a high-dimensional space. Instead of probing for pre-chosen features, they measure the trajectory itself: its length, curvature, convergence, layer-to-layer similarity, and stability. The study spans three model families, GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Qwen2.5, across five controlled prompt families.

Semantically related prompts converged in middle-to-late layers, with peak convergence indices from 0.41 rising to 0.58, an attractor-like pull toward shared meaning. Reasoning and analogy prompts curved far more, 0.71 or more radians against 0.31 or fewer for lexical variants, suggesting curvature tracks computing effort. Ambiguous tokens split into separate trajectories, up to 5.6 times the separation by the final layer. Every model also showed the same three phases: encoding, elaboration, and output preparation.
arxiv-2606-09587:
Muhammad Haris Khan and Joel Wester tackle a quiet side effect of writing with AI in this 2026 arXiv paper. Many users ask the same tools for the same tasks, so their drafts drift toward the same phrases and ideas. The authors call this pull the Artificial Hivemind. It can lift average quality while shrinking the range of voices.

Their fix is the Semantic Repulsion Technique. It samples a model twelve times to map its default answer zone, then steers new output away from that crowded centre. Repeated stock phrases are flagged and fined during generation. In machine tests, the method raised semantic diversity by eighty-five to one hundred sixty-seven percent. Consensus phrases fell by forty-three to ninety-five percent. In a study with sixteen regular AI users, the steered text scored higher on usefulness and coherence. Most users said they would use the strong setting again.
arxiv-2606-09687:
Julius Benner builds the dual twin of differential calculus for quantum spaces in this 2026 arXiv paper. Noncommutative geometry treats odd algebras as if they were spaces of functions. A smooth feel comes from a differential calculus, a set of rules for slopes. Codifferential calculi run the same idea on coalgebras, the dual objects, over fields whose trait is not two.

From any first-order codifferential calculus, Benner builds its maximal prolongation, a graded tower with a universal trait. For module coalgebras over a Hopf algebra, he adds a symmetry-respecting flavour. When the coalgebra has a tensor form, those calculi match special right coideals called quantum tangent spaces. In a clean subcase, the tower is a quadratic coalgebra. Worked cases cover the Podleś sphere and quantized projective spaces. One payoff is a fresh proof that a known calculus there has classical size.
arxiv-2606-10287:
Gul and Bhatt tackle a scoring problem in knowledge graph completion, the task of predicting missing links in structured databases, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning testing. Standard assessment relies on single rank-based metrics such as mean reciprocal rank and hits at k. These often yield clashing model orderings across datasets: a model leading on one metric may trail on another. Cherry-picked reporting obscures real progress. The authors reframe scoring as a multi-criteria decision-making problem.

They meta-analyze seven merging methods that combine metrics into one ranking. Each is tested on five criteria: fit with base metrics, cross-dataset stability, freedom under leaving one metric out, strength under noise injection, and reach under leaving one dataset out. Each test is averaged over leave-one-model-out and leave-one-group-out removals so trust scores reflect aggregator conduct broadly.
arxiv-2606-10787:
Rader and Russo make a neurosymbolic learning system practical in this 2026 arXiv paper on artificial intelligence. NeurASP trains a neural network to predict latent concepts, then reasons over them with answer set programming rules; only the final answer is labelled, so learning must backpropagate through the symbolic component. That requires enumerating answer sets and computing probabilities and gradients over them, expensive enough to time out on tasks. The authors re-engineer it with vectorisation, batch processing, and caching of computations.

Speedups reach orders of magnitude on tasks, bringing runs from hours to minutes, and the system handles tens of thousands of answer sets at accuracy. To push beyond digit benchmarks, the authors build a card arithmetic data set around the 52 playing cards, with graded tasks. On it, the accelerated NeurASP outperforms the Embed2Sym framework as the number of latent concepts grows, evidence the bottleneck was engineering, not the idea.
arxiv-2606-10887:
Gupta and colleagues bring a foundation model into audio-visual continual learning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Class-incremental learning adds new classes over time without forgetting old ones, but audio-visual versions are barely studied. The team adapts SAM-Audio, whose rich sound and image features turn out to wobble when classes arrive in stages.

Their fix lets audio features guide the visual ones through attention, so sound tells sight where to look. Dual distillation, at both feature and output levels, fights forgetting. On audio-visual benchmarks the method beats naive fusion of the two streams and the prior state of the art by a wide margin.
arxiv-2606-11387:
Chavarro Polania, a solo author, studies how to promote training recipes cheaply in a 2026 arXiv case study. Short pretraining runs make many recipes affordable, but they can over-promote configurations that only look strong at tiny budgets. His setting is micro-pretraining, a single-GPU runner with staged budgets. From twelve candidates, he runs staged budgets from two minutes to twelve hours on Windows A100 and Linux L40S hosts.

Early screens prove useful but unstable: at five minutes, the best Windows and Linux conditions differ, and the eventual twelve-hour winner is not mean-best at the ten-minute gate. A replicated sixty-minute gate retains the bridge reference, first in all four host-seed cells, repeating that rank in the twelve-hour confirmation across both seeds. The protocol records 169.2 training GPU-hours. Continuing all four sixty-minute candidates would have spent 192 GPU-hours; all nine ten-minute candidates, 432.
arxiv-2606-11587:
Zenghua Zhou leads a team recalibrating the brightness scale of the Sloan Digital Sky Survey in this 2026 arXiv paper. Photometric zero-points are reference settings that turn measured brightness into a physical amount of light. The team uses the Infrared Flux Method, which gets a star's surface temperature from its infrared glow, and runs it in reverse. Temperatures for over 6,000 Sun-like FGK stars reveal what corrections the survey needs.

The r band, one of five colour filters, is already well set, needing a shift under one hundredth of a magnitude. The i and z bands need shifts of a few hundredths, and g needs a small one. The u band shows the largest problem, and its correction depends on which filter curve is used, because of a red leak letting unwanted red light through. Checks against standard stars and Gaia satellite spectra broadly support the new values.
arxiv-2606-11687:
Marius Bayizere presents an open framework for detecting hostile drones in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cheap drones can evade radar, saturate defences and strike targets worth far more than themselves. Existing counter-drone systems lean on one sensor type, react only after detection, and cannot model coordinated swarms, Bayizere argues.

DroneShield-AI fuses six layers: radio signal classification, acoustic motor signatures, camera detection, evidence-weighted fusion, an intent classifier and a swarm module built on graph networks. The intent engine sorts flight patterns into a six-class threat taxonomy and aims to warn operators thirty seconds ahead. The swarm module studies formations of multiple drones as a network. On three public datasets the fused pipeline reaches detection accuracy above ninety-six percent with a false alarm rate near three percent. It runs in well under a fifth of a second on cheap commodity hardware costing a few hundred dollars.
arxiv-2606-11987:
Ragnar Freij-Hollanti, Kirsten D Morris and Patricija Šapokaitė dissect the graphs behind a leading quantum code family in this 2026 arXiv paper. Lifted product codes were the first quantum low-density parity-check codes proven asymptotically good. Their behaviour depends on two parity-check matrices and the Tanner graphs built from them, which link variable and check nodes.

The authors prove the Tanner graphs of the two matrices are isomorphic, structurally identical, for the construction they study. They then establish conditions guaranteeing these graphs are connected, a prerequisite for robust iterative decoding, where a decoder passes messages around the graph. Girth, the shortest cycle length, is also analysed. Most concretely, they characterise and count the minimal absorbing sets of the base graph. Absorbing sets are the small configurations that trap decoders and cause error floors, so enumerating them guides finite-length design.
arxiv-2606-12187:
Hastings rates a voting rule for placing a facility when people may lie about where they live, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents report locations, and a mechanism picks one site for a clinic or depot. The coordinate-wise median takes the middle report on each axis. It is strategyproof: nobody gains by misreporting. Social cost is a p-norm, an average of travel costs stressing the worst-off or the total. The question is how much worse than optimal this rule can be.

For two-dimensional spaces, Hastings pins down the ratio for every pair of cost exponents. The ratio follows a power-of-two formula, settling a conjecture from earlier work. In higher dimensions he proves upper bounds generalizing a recent utilitarian result. The ratio never exceeds three, whatever the dimension or exponents. The median rule therefore stays within a known factor of optimal, even against strategic reports.
arxiv-2606-12287:
Beger and co-authors rebuild the GPT decoder out of brain-style spiking neurons to slash its energy use, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spiking neural networks pass information as brief pulses, firing only when needed, unlike ordinary networks that compute constantly. Swapping in spikes is hard because such networks resist direct training. The authors instead construct SpikeDecoder, a fully spiking version of the Transformer decoder block used for text generation.

Experiments replace decoder parts one at a time with spiking versions, exposing where accuracy leaks away. Residual connections, the skip paths carrying signals around blocks, prove important to keep. The choice of normalization, the rescaling step inside blocks, also matters for spiking versions. Several ways of encoding text into spike trains are compared as well. The finished spiking decoder cuts theoretical energy consumption by eighty-seven to ninety-three percent versus the ordinary baseline.
arxiv-2606-12387:
Chen and co-authors teach database assistants from their mistakes instead of retraining them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Text-to-SQL turns questions into database queries, but production use brings strict dialects like Snowflake, schemas, and shifting user tastes. Fine-tuning is costly and rigid; hand-written prompts do not scale. Their system, Tahoe, stores lessons in a Hint Bank built from debugging traces. Compiler complaints become Syntax Hints enforcing dialect rules.

Execution results and user feedback become Semantic Hints capturing schema and business logic. A Strategy Layer manages user intents as strategies, annotated with success and harm statistics. At query time Tahoe retrieves hints, plans the logic, then synthesizes SQL. On a Snowflake benchmark, pass rate jumps from 61.95 percent to 79.42 percent, syntax checks pass perfectly, and critic rounds per candidate fall from 2.79 to 0.12 on generations. The same bank lifts weaker models without retraining, showing the lessons transfer.
arxiv-2606-12487:
Zhao and co-authors watch a neural network's inner stream across its depth, and spend extra precision only where the stream jumps, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Post-training quantization squeezes language models to four bits for cheap inference. Trouble comes from massive activations, rare huge values that wreck the quantization scale. Existing fixes smooth activations uniformly, ignoring how they evolve layer by layer. The team shows massive activations appear and vanish in phases, causing large changes in the residual stream.

Two new diagnostics, Jump Ratio and Historical Feature SNR, measure the effect. Their DynamicPTQ then assigns eight-bit activation precision only to layers flagged sensitive by this dynamics analysis; weights, caches, and other activations stay at four bits. It plugs into baselines like QuaRot and FlatQuant. On LLaMA models under full four-bit settings, perplexity and zero-shot accuracy improve, with throughput up slightly and modest memory cost.
arxiv-2606-12587:
Shayan Kiyani and co-authors flip decision support upside down: now the AI agent decides when to ask for help, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Classically, models support human deciders. In agentic systems, AI acts on users' behalf while humans and tools form the support crew. Their framework minimizes support usage subject to a safety budget: the chance the agent acts alone on a case where support would have improved its output.

At the population level, the optimal policy is a threshold rule on the value of support: ask when the gain clears a bar. Their online algorithm adapts that threshold, using randomized exploration to control the missed-support error with no assumptions about the data distribution. A calibration-on-the-fly method trims needless calls. The lens covers information gathering, human-AI collaboration, and tool use. Across experiments, the method holds the target error while cutting support usage substantially.
arxiv-2606-13087:
Cavalagli and colleagues map and compute feedback Nash equilibria, where no player can improve alone, in scalar discounted linear-quadratic games with N players, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most numerical methods find only 1 equilibrium, but these games can have many, and the discount factor changes the picture in ways undiscounted studies missed.

With the discount factor in, the authors show that finite-cost equilibria may fail to stabilise the system. That prompts a distinction between feedback Nash equilibria and stable ones, plus a sufficient stability condition. Based on a parametric account of the policies, they propose methods for computing all equilibria, not just one. For the symmetric game they derive a closed-form expression for the symmetric equilibrium. They also give conditions for the existence of up to 2 to the power N, minus 2 equilibria.
arxiv-2606-13287:
Erickson and Johansson give a theoretical explanation for a practical trick in distributed machine learning in this 2026 arXiv paper. Training is often split across many workers that update a shared model asynchronously, without waiting for each other. Slow workers, called stragglers, inject delayed updates that can destabilise training when step sizes stay constant. Practitioners noticed that gradient clipping, capping the size of each update, stabilises this process. The authors prove why: clipping removes the dependence of the method's cost on the maximum delay.

Their analysis models gradient noise with a sub-Weibull distribution, a family generalising the usual light-tailed assumptions to heavier tails seen in deep learning. They prove convergence in expectation, the average behaviour over randomness. They also prove convergence with high probability, the first such guarantee for asynchronous optimisation, meaning bad outcomes are provably rare. The results justify clipping as more than a heuristic.
arxiv-2606-13487:
Mercer connects particle systems to an inverse problem about hitting times in this 2026 arXiv paper. The inverse first passage problem asks the opposite question. Instead of computing when a random process first crosses a boundary, can one design a boundary so that the crossing time has a distribution? Mercer constructs a branching-selection particle system whose limit is governed by a free boundary problem, a partial differential equation with a moving edge. In the system, particles wander as Brownian motions, branch at a set rate, and are removed at a rate depending on their position relative to the boundary.

That boundary is determined by the particles' distribution, closing a feedback loop. Mercer identifies the boundary's limit, as the number grows, as the solution of that problem. The construction gives an existence proof with a mechanism attached. Such inverse problems arise in finance and neuroscience.
arxiv-2606-13587:
Javaid and colleagues design a network for segmenting waste in cluttered scenes in this 2026 arXiv paper. Automated waste recycling depends on vision systems that outline each piece of waste so robots can sort it. Deep learning methods segment well but rely on large backbone networks that are inefficient for sorting plants. Their accuracy deteriorates when backgrounds are cluttered, the case on a conveyor belt. The authors introduce a network that works in two domains. In the spatial domain it captures local dependencies between neighbouring pixels.

In the spectral domain, working with frequency components, it extracts relationships. Alternating between the two lets the network build local and global representations, highlighting the information needed to separate waste from clutter. The design goals are accuracy under clutter and efficiency on hardware. Segmentation in messy scenes is the bottleneck between recycling demonstrations and systems that run in facilities.
arxiv-2606-13687:
Johannes Ellemose and colleagues present the Frustrometer in this 2026 arXiv paper, a system for detecting when users of data visualisations get stuck. Visualisation research knows how to help a frustrated user, through onboarding, help, and guidance. The unsolved problem is timing: trigger help too eagerly and the user's train of thought breaks; wait too long and they have gone astray. The Frustrometer predicts stuckness and frustration by fusing body signals, called biomarkers, with interaction patterns such as clicks and pauses. A convolutional neural network classifier makes the estimate in real time.

The team collected data from a study in which fourteen participants performed tasks on two visualisations while their signals were recorded. That dataset trains and validates the predictor. Real-time frustration detection would let software intervene at the moment of need, with uses from analytics software to education technology. The work treats affect as a measurable interface variable.
arxiv-2606-13887:
Yu reframes a famous open problem about fluid flow as an accounting exercise across scales. The Navier-Stokes equations describe moving fluids, and whether their solutions can form singularities remains unproved. Near the local regularity threshold, certain scale-critical quantities must decay for smoothness to hold. His 2026 arXiv paper defines a reservoir badness from three such quantities and proves a finite-scale supply-versus-tax reduction for suitable weak solutions.

If badness stays outside the decay basin over many scales, the theorem forces an alternative. Either leakage through cutoffs accumulates, or the solution generates positive untaxed critical supply. Supply comes from nonlinear flux and pressure transport; taxes from viscous dissipation and expected decay. Yu is explicit about scope: this is no proof of global regularity and no singular solution. Surviving badness must pay, through supply or leakage.
arxiv-2606-14187:
Chen and co-authors find a hidden flaw in a popular optimizer and fix it by whitening twice, in the right order. Matrix-aware optimizers like Muon orthogonalize momentum matrices via spectral whitening, equalizing singular values. But the Newton-Schulz iteration behind it depends critically on input conditioning, and raw momentum shows severe per-axis scale imbalance. Their 2026 arXiv paper verifies the imbalance with a chi-square test across Transformer layers, then proposes Zeta.

Zeta applies coordinate whitening first, rescaling each axis, before the spectral step. The order is forced, not tuned: the coordinate step creates the isotropy the spectral step needs. They prove the dual pipeline strictly reduces orthogonalization error versus pure spectral methods, by improving the input's condition number. Zeta matched or surpassed strong baselines across language modeling at 0.6B to 8B scale, mixture-of-experts models, and vision tasks, converging faster. Code is public.
arxiv-2606-14287:
Ten Eikelder and Brunk solve a calibration puzzle in multiphase flow simulation: in diffuse-interface models, you cannot simply dial in the tensions you want. These phase-field models replace sharp boundaries with smooth layers, and pairwise tensions emerge implicitly from a bulk potential and a gradient term. For two phases the link is classical, but with N phases, tensions must be matched at once, along paths in the Gibbs simplex. Their 2026 arXiv paper gives a thermodynamically consistent calibration procedure for Cahn-Hilliard-type free energies.

Given a bulk potential and target tensions, it finds a symmetric capillary matrix reproducing the targets via equilibrium profiles. A rescaling step then adjusts interface widths to mesh-resolvable values, preserving tensions exactly. The closure drops into N-phase mixture codes, demonstrated on coupled Navier-Stokes-Cahn-Hilliard flows. Modelers can now start from measured tensions instead of reverse-engineering parameters.
arxiv-2606-14387:
Lolur and many co-authors offer a 2026 arXiv perspective on computing for materials science, the search for new substances with useful traits. Discovery now mixes theory, simulation, experiments, data-driven methods, and early quantum computing. The authors, drawn from universities, industry, and national laboratories, review what each approach can and cannot do today.

Classical simulations scan wide design spaces, while experiments expose decay and uneven behavior that decide real performance. Machine learning speeds the search when datasets are curated with clear provenance and stated uncertainty, and quantum methods may help with strongly correlated electrons. The group calls for reproducible workflows, shared data standards, and honest benchmarks so predictions become reliable enough to shorten the path from idea to usable material.
arxiv-2606-15487:
Baqer and Said study solitary waves for the extended Korteweg-de Vries equation in 2026, a fifth-order wave equation used to model dispersive hydrodynamics such as shallow water waves. The extended equation is non-conservative, which blocks the averaged Lagrangian method that worked for its conservative cousin. Their fix is an augmented Lagrangian, modelled on Luke's Lagrangian, that folds the constraints in through Lagrange multipliers.

Averaging it for a travelling wave yields a solitary wave with the sech-squared profile. The team obtains second-order formulas for the height, speed, and inverse width of the wave from one fixed amplitude parameter. With only first-order terms kept, the formulas fall back to the classical KdV answers. They then predict the lead wave of a dispersive shock from the formulas, and numerical simulations match the predictions closely. The shortcut thus becomes a practical tool for costly shock problems.
arxiv-2606-15587:
Liu and colleagues report a counterintuitive failure mode of robot imitation learning in 2026: perfect demonstrations can be poor teachers. For fine-grained tasks like insertion, stacking, and alignment, a teleoperator compresses the decisive correction moments into a brief window. The learning policy is then flooded with redundant free-space motion and starved of supervision where precision decides success.

Slowing down near alignment and resampling critical segments both help, but mainly by broadening the recovery states the policy sees, not by reweighting familiar frames. The main fix, STAIR, is a compact dynamic feature between the vision-language model and the action expert that distils short-horizon motion into dense supervision. Trained on fluent data alone, STAIR lifts success from fifty percent to about sixty-two percent. That nearly matches the sixty-four percent achieved with deliberately slowed demonstrations. Robot data, they argue, should be designed for machine learnability, not human efficiency.
arxiv-2606-15787:
Dipasquale and Tonegawa study ferronematics in 2026, films made by dispersing magnetic nanoparticles in a nematic liquid crystal. An energy model describes the material with two order parameters: a Q-tensor for the liquid crystal's alignment, and a vector field M from the particles. A coupling term rewards alignment between the two. Earlier work showed that as a parameter vanishes, energy concentrates: the Q-component on finitely many points, the M-component on a varifold.

The open question was whether that varifold has integer multiplicity, what makes it an interface rather than a diffuse measure. They prove it does, provided the coupling exceeds an explicit threshold: after rescaling by a constant, the count is a whole number. That property lets analysts apply minimal-surface and free-boundary machinery to the limit. For ferronematics, strong coupling thus forces a sharp interface between the phases.
arxiv-2606-15887:
Georgantas validates an LLM first-pass manuscript score against peer-review outcomes in 2026, asking whether the number, not the review prose, means anything. AIPR reads a submission and emits five dimensions plus an overall score, by prompting alone, no fine-tuning. The test covers 300 ICLR submissions with public decisions and ratings, under a frozen pipeline with hypotheses registered in advance.

The score separates rejected from accepted submissions with an AUROC of 0.82, rises monotonically across decision tiers, and tracks the mean reviewer rating. Its signal is strongest at the bottom: the lowest-scoring fifth is rejected far above the base rate, with no oral papers in it. A one-paragraph prompt on the same model discriminates almost as well, so the validity comes mostly from the model itself. What the engineering adds is reliability: scores barely move across runs, and each arrives with an evidence-grounded review.
arxiv-2606-15987:
Quattrini and colleagues introduce SCAM in 2026, a line-level dataset for handwritten text recognition in Sahidic Coptic, an extinct dialect preserved in ancient manuscripts. It is drawn from an eleventh-century manuscript, expert-annotated, and gathered from different libraries under varied digitisation conditions. Ink fading, bleed-through, and decay come built in, as do the hurdles of a scarce language with an uncommon alphabet and dialect-specific marks.

Benchmarks show a wide gap from modern-script performance. CTC-based models prove most robust for scriptio continua texts: with no autoregressive decoder, they avoid error cascades and scale better on limited data than hybrid attention models. The two archive subsets transfer unevenly, one direction generalising much worse than the other. Grayscale conversion narrows the cross-archive gap but cannot substitute for diverse multi-archive training data. SCAM gives low-resource document analysis a realistic, historically grounded reference point.
arxiv-2606-16087:
Jaberi studies a network design problem in 2026: keep a directed network strongly connected even after losing certain single vertices, using as few edges as possible. A strongly connected digraph lets every vertex reach every other. Strong biconnectivity adds survival of one vertex removal from a protected set.

Jaberi proves a polynomial-time 7-approximation algorithm exists for this problem, always finding a solution at most seven times the optimum size. The classic minimum strongly biconnected spanning subgraph problem is the special case where the protected set is empty. A bounded variant, limiting b-articulation points, is shown NP-complete in the analysis given. Planners gain a principled fallback with a proven worst-case bound.
arxiv-2606-16187:
Luo and Gao present obliv-clang in 2026, a compile-time checker that helps C++ programs keep secrets from leaking through side channels. Timing and memory access patterns can reveal confidential data even when encryption is sound. Oblivious programming removes that leakage by making run time and access traces independent of secrets. Writing such code by hand is error-prone.

Their tool checks the obliviousness of C++ programs during compilation. It supports rich language features, including arbitrarily nested pointers, so it works with industry-level codebases directly. The checking rules come with a formal soundness proof. Several nontrivial oblivious algorithms serve as case studies to show expressiveness. Programs built with the tool outperform previous solutions in the reported comparisons, with minimum compilation overhead. The checker runs on the clang and LLVM infrastructure programmers already use.
arxiv-2606-16487:
Zapata proves in 2026 large-deviation bounds for sums of heavy-tailed random variables, where the classical Cramér theory breaks down. Cramér's theorem governs sums of light-tailed variables, with a rate function from the moment generating function. For nonnegative variables with regularly varying tails, extremes instead follow the one-big-jump principle: a large sum usually means one huge term. Zapata normalizes at the extreme-value scale and works at the slower speed log n.

At that speed, the resulting rate function is determined only by the tail index, the single number describing how heavy the tail is. The proof transfers a large-deviation principle for the maximum of the variables to their sum, inside the one-big-jump region. The upper-tail probability of the maximum decays like a power set by the tail index times log x, and the sum inherits the same logarithmic behavior.
arxiv-2606-16587:
Ramlau and co-authors replace days of spray simulation with a fraction of a second in 2026, using the simulation mesh itself as the model's input language. Designing spray nozzles means predicting how geometry shapes transient two-phase breakup, but volume-of-fluid simulations with adaptive mesh refinement are far too expensive for design loops. Standard surrogates struggle because both the liquid-gas interface and the adaptive grid evolve. Their geometry-conditioned latent surrogate encodes the adaptive mesh's cell-density field, a compact proxy for where the solver concentrates resolution.

Trained on 797 two-phase nozzle simulations, the model reconstructs transient density evolution and nozzle geometry from that representation, and a lightweight second stage recovers the remaining flow variables. On held-out simulations it captures the key interface dynamics while cutting inference to 0.045 seconds per trajectory, a speedup beyond sixty thousand times against the Basilisk CFD solver, per the report.
arxiv-2606-16787:
Bisht and colleagues study metal oxide clusters in gas giant atmospheres in a 2026 planetary science paper. Before clouds can form on a distant exoplanet, tiny clusters of molecules must survive long enough to grow. Metal oxides are prime seeds, and their stability depends sharply on temperature and pressure.

Using their own thermochemical data, the team tracks eight cluster families, from magnesium oxide to aluminium oxide, across size and composition. Some families win at high temperatures, others at low ones, under solar-like element mixes. Computed spectra show strong mid-infrared absorption features that vary with cluster size, many inside the range of the James Webb telescope's MIRI instrument. Coupling the chemistry to three-dimensional climate models for four known giant planets gives distinct pictures. The hottest worlds destroy large clusters on their daysides, while a warm Jupiter favors bigger cluster growth, linking cluster physics to observable spectra.
arxiv-2606-16887:
Alonso-Tomás and colleagues build coupled optomechanical cavities in a 2026 nanophotonics paper. Mechanical circuits at the nanoscale need compact ways to read out motion, trap it in place and pass it between elements. Flexural modes, which bend sideways at megahertz rates, respond strongly but spread out, making them hard to confine and connect.

Their platform engineers both light and mechanics into the chip pattern. A sideways asymmetry in the photonic-crystal cavity breaks a cancellation that normally hides in-plane bending from the light, making those modes optically bright with no extra parts. Serpentine mechanical links, shaped using complex band theory, act as tiny mirrors and leaky couplers for the flexural waves. In two-cavity devices, the mode splitting falls exponentially as more serpentine cells are added, matching full simulations quantitatively. Coupling strength follows the link design, giving calibrated interconnects for larger optomechanical circuits.
arxiv-2606-17087:
Zivari adds a free information relay to a teaching-learning optimizer in a 2026 metaheuristics paper. Teaching-Learning-Based Optimization improves a population of candidate solutions through teacher and learner phases. Grouped variants split the population into groups that drift apart and stop sharing discoveries.

The relay is simple and costs nothing. At scheduled moments, each group offers its best scored member to the next group in a ring, which swaps out its worst member only if the visitor scores better. Because the copied solution carries its fitness with it, no new function evaluations are spent. Ablation under equal evaluation budgets shows the relay wins far more often than it loses, with a large effect size. In an eight-method comparison it ranks second overall, behind only the whale optimization algorithm. The author scopes the claims carefully: engineering results are mixed, no universal superiority asserted.
arxiv-2606-17187:
Veprev presents a 2026 arXiv paper on eigenfunctions of operators on random networks. The setting is amenable unimodular random rooted graphs, which arise in many fields. Uses range from percolation clusters to graphs built from random subgroups. The question is whether spectral data force eigenfunctions to live on finitely many vertices.

Veprev proves a localisation principle for finite-range operators on such networks. If the expected spectral measure has a positive point mass, a finitely supported eigenfunction exists. That conclusion holds with positive probability over the random network. The result extends a known fact for amenable groups and their Cayley graphs. There, the discrete spectrum is described by local graph geometry, and this paper carries that picture to random networks.
arxiv-2606-17887:
Ali and colleagues studied how staff of a multinational tech firm took up a new AI tool for human resources questions, in a 2026 field study. The firm swapped a legacy HR search system for one backed by generative AI. The authors tracked the live change through search logs. They also ran a staff survey. And they held ten in-depth interviews across the workforce.

Adoption hinged on fit. The tool helped most when its built-in assumptions matched a staff member's role, spoken language, and tenure. Trust in the AI's answers was not automatic. Staff built it by checking sources. They compared systems side by side. They also asked colleagues or HR staff when unsure. The authors argue that fair rollout cannot be judged by access alone. Search skill, content quality, training, and clear accountability all tilted who gained and who was left behind.
arxiv-2606-18087:
Galindo-Silva asks whether living under the threat of earthquakes makes people more national, in a 2026 social science paper. The study separates two margins of national identity. One is distributive, treating membership as a rule for who gets scarce jobs and resources. The other is expressive, covering pride, attachment, and willingness to fight. Survey responses from the World Values Survey across four decades, sixty-three countries, and hundreds of subnational regions are linked to seismic risk maps.

People nearer high-risk zones show stronger national in-group orientation on both margins, with more pride and more priority for nationals when jobs are scarce. Family attachment and out-group hostility do not rise, though religiosity does. The pride response appears only where state and religion are aligned enough to frame disaster as a shared national ordeal, and shocks between survey waves move mainly older, rooted residents.
arxiv-2606-18187:
Mandarapu and Kunkunuru show that a classic database tuning knob mostly tunes nothing, in a 2026 systems paper. Group commit amortizes the cost of flushing a log to disk by batching many transactions into one flush, and a timer or batch-size rule decides when to release the batch. Textbook theory treats arrivals as an open stream and prescribes an optimal waiting time from a square-root rule.

Real database clients, though, form a closed loop: each issues its next transaction only after the last one commits, so the policy's own latency sets the arrival rate. Modeled as a closed queueing network, a greedy rule that flushes the instant the device frees itself lands within a whisker of the best oracle-tuned timer at every load. Above a load threshold set by the device itself, the optimal timer collapses onto greedy, making tuning vacuous.
arxiv-2606-18487:
Aphale and Liu show that training a code model longer in supervised fine-tuning can sabotage the reinforcement learning stage that follows, in a 2026 machine learning paper. The usual recipe picks the supervised checkpoint with the best accuracy before running GRPO training with verifiable rewards, assuming the strongest starter learns best.

Testing depth ladders on two code models across several seeds, they found the opposite on one of them. As supervised training deepened, pre-training accuracy rose while the best post-reinforcement score fell sharply, a rank inversion. Their explanation is entropy collapse: overtraining squeezes the diversity of the model's outputs, and once success rates drop below a threshold, most reward groups become uniform and stop teaching anything. A simple diagnostic pairing pre-training entropy checks with an early entropy monitor flagged risky checkpoints cheaply, while fixes such as label smoothing failed to rescue the collapsed one.
arxiv-2606-18987:
Verde presents a 2026 cosmology study on the ordering of neutrino masses, a long open question in physics. Neutrinos come in three types, and their masses can follow a normal order or an inverted order. Past data gave only a weak lean toward the normal order. New sky data are now sharp enough to turn that lean into a firm model test, the author argues.

The study joins DESI galaxy clustering data with Planck sky data and with neutrino oscillation results. The combined cap on total neutrino mass sits close to the lowest value allowed for the normal order. It sits well below the lowest value allowed for the inverted order. A Bayes factor strongly favors the normal order, and that edge stays strong in wider models and under unlike prior choices. The inverted order is thus pushed into the tail of what the data allow within standard cosmology.
arxiv-2606-19187:
Hajigeorgiou and colleagues show in 2026 that charging energy in a quantum Hall cavity is strongly shaped by its constrictions. Electronic Fabry-Pérot interferometers in the fractional quantum Hall regime probe anyonic braiding statistics. Their signals are muddied by Coulomb charging effects, usually treated as static nuisances set by cavity geometry. The team tests that assumption in a gate-defined cavity tuned to the Coulomb-dominated regime.

The charging energy turns out to vary strongly and non-monotonically with magnetic field, changing by a large share over a small field range. The effect appears only when the quantum point contacts forming the cavity are weakly pinched off, the strong coupling regime. Linking the change to contact magneto-conductance points to field-driven shifts in local compressibility and screening. Incompressible fractional states forming inside the constrictions drive the effect. Constrictions are thus active elements, not passive boundaries.
arxiv-2606-19487:
Cyril Gapp leads a team of nine authors reporting new James Webb Space Telescope views of WASP-121 b in 2026. WASP-121 b is an ultra-hot Jupiter, a giant planet that orbits very close to its star and stays locked with one face in daylight. The team watched two transits, when the planet crossed its star, using the NIRSpec and NIRISS instruments.

As the planet turned during transit, the light curves bent in uneven ways that point to the spin itself. Carbon monoxide absorption grew while water absorption fell slightly across the transit. Gapp and colleagues read that pattern as a sharper heat gradient on the evening edge than on the morning edge. Heat on the east side grows strong enough to split water apart, while carbon monoxide survives. Rotational transits thus give a fresh probe of how heat and chemistry vary across a distant world.
arxiv-2606-19587:
Beichen Wan and Mo Liu train predict-then-optimise models without calling a solver in 2026. In that paradigm, a learning model predicts values that feed a later optimisation task. Training against true decision regret is hard, since decisions jump in steps and gradients vanish.

Smoothing tricks exist, but each gradient step needs an expensive solver call. Wan and Liu derive a surrogate loss from a measure transformation principle. Training then needs no optimisation solver at all. Theory backs the loss with Fisher consistency and excess risk bounds. Tests show decision quality matching leading methods. Training time falls by orders of magnitude at the same time. Decision-focused learning thus scales to larger problems where solver calls once capped progress. Pipelines that retrain often, like scheduling and pricing systems, stand to gain most.
arxiv-2606-20287:
Wei Xia, Jin Wu, Haoran Shi, Xiangyu Wang, and Chanjin Zheng unify essay grading and essay feedback inside one framework called PsyScore. Their 2026 paper notes that automated scoring and feedback usually live apart: neural scorers grade well but explain little, while language-model feedback ignores how proficient the student is. PsyScore ties both to a shared latent ability estimate, through a trait-adaptive neural scorer embedding an item response theory model.

Feedback is then scaffolded to the diagnosed ability, following the zone of proximal development, with multi-agent strategies shifting focus by proficiency level. A third module judges feedback quality through pairwise preferences and simulated revisions. On the ASAP++ dataset, PsyScore matched competitive scoring while giving feedback better aligned with teaching goals. Assessment becomes diagnosis first and grading second.
arxiv-2606-20587:
Swadhin Pradhan, Shazal Irshad, and Jerome Henry ask what matters more for wireless packet foundation models: the tokenizer or the architecture. Their 2026 paper builds on Plume, which introduced protocol-aware tokenization for 802.11 traces. They scale model depth and move the same tokenizer to a different architecture family.

A deeper GPT, Plume-Deep with 24 layers, reaches 98.2 percent top-1 accuracy, gaining 32 points over the original 12-layer design. A Mamba-2 state-space variant, Plume-Mamba, achieves 96.1 percent with 1.7 times the throughput and twice the context length. A controlled two-by-two comparison across tokenizers and architectures separates the two contributions. Protocol-aware tokens, it turns out, travel well across architectures.
arxiv-2606-20787:
Mudit Garg, Alessia Franchini, and Alessandro Lupi simulate in 2026 how gas affects the inspiral of a massive black hole binary that the space detector LISA will hear. A binary of two million-solar-mass black holes sits in a gas disc. Gas torques drive its motion, while gravitational wave emission also drains energy. Their three-dimensional simulations use post-Newtonian corrections to track the live binary.

The binary is followed from 55 to 46 Schwarzschild radii, early in the LISA band at redshift near one. Gravitational and accretion torques are measured with and without wave emission. Accretion patterns change modestly when waves dominate. The gas-induced orbital phase shift is 0.12 radians over 600 cycles. LISA should detect that shift at that distance. Knowing gas effects matters because a phase offset could be mistaken for new physics if the disc is ignored.
arxiv-2606-20987:
Benoît Assi and Pedro Machado investigate composite neutrino models in 2026, where heavy neutrinos form as bound states of a strongly coupled sector. Standard neutrinos mix with these partners through an inverse seesaw. Unusual scaling suppresses light neutrino masses to tiny scales. Matching to low-energy theory yields enhanced dipole operators.

The predicted couplings are far larger than loop-level forecasts in minimal models. An event-level simulation follows production and decay chains that end in a photon. Event rates are computed for the MiniBooNE and MINERvA experiments. Photon energy, angle, and multiplicity patterns are also predicted. Benchmark cases are examined. Large dipole signals would give a sharp probe of whether some particles are bound states, not fundamental.
arxiv-2606-21187:
Sadjad Tavakoli and Saba Alimadadi study change impact recommendation for JavaScript in 2026, drawing lessons from history and runtime analysis. Knowing what a code change affects is key for maintenance and testing. JavaScript makes that hard. Callbacks, events, and shared state hide dependencies. Three practical techniques are built and evaluated.

One technique mines co-change patterns from repository history. Another uses dynamic analysis of runtime dependencies. Dynamic methods capture interactions actually exercised, but miss unexercised links. History methods find coupling, but noisy patterns add false picks. Comparing the two families clarifies when each should be trusted. Such tools guide test selection in large web codebases.
arxiv-2606-21487:
Mark Huasong Meng, Qing Zhang, Weirao Lu, and Chunyang Chen report a sobering audit in 2026 of how Android developers protect their app signing keys. A leaked key lets anyone ship fake updates in a developer's name, and a recent incident hit two major manufacturers. The team mined public repositories for exposed signing credentials, recovered keys using leaked passwords, and matched certificates against more than four thousand apps from stores and manufacturer system images.

They found 5,673 compromised keystores on GitHub and twenty-six certificates tied to 278 real apps, including preinstalled apps from seven manufacturers reaching over ten billion users. A proof-of-concept replacement attack shows the leaks are exploitable, and one automotive head-unit platform in over eleven hundred vehicle models is also exposed. Key mismanagement, they conclude, is a systemic supply-chain risk.
arxiv-2606-21687:
Xuan Qi, Yi Wei, Fanqi Yu, and Manuel Lecha document a paradox of neural network capacity in 2026. Networks with ReLU-style activations split input space into affine regions, one flat rule per region, and the region count proxies expressive power. Theory allows astronomically many regions. Trained networks, they find, use fewer and fewer of them as tasks get harder, a collapse they name expressivity saturation.

Two tools support the claim. A theorem bounds the affine pieces along any line probe by a product of layer widths, yielding a minimum neuron budget for complex signals. Exact enumeration in bounded domains then shows region usage shrinking under growing input-label complexity, with decision boundaries visibly degrading in the hardest regimes. Training footage reveals partitions refining during optimization, then stalling. Bigger theoretical capacity, it turns out, does not mean the trained model spends it.
arxiv-2606-21787:
Ajibode and colleagues tackle missing metadata for pretrained language models in 2026. Model hubs such as Hugging Face host huge numbers of models whose records often omit licenses, model types, or how each model was derived from another. Without that provenance, builders cannot easily check reuse rights or assemble trustworthy model supply chains.

Their method, Semantic Fingerprinting, reads each model's configuration files together with its repository tags to fill in the missing fields automatically. Tested on 317,133 models, it beat propagation-based baselines by up to 31.4 percent and 26.6 percent in prediction accuracy over the two main comparisons. It also labelled 16.6 percent of isolated models that propagation methods cannot reach at all. Applying it to 167,089 unlabelled models expanded traceable reuse chains by 75.9 percent and license chains by 53.6 percent, while revealing 86 previously hidden reuse patterns.
arxiv-2606-22087:
Imran and colleagues propose, in 2026, an index for judging whether a community of homes with solar panels should invest in peer-to-peer trading. Falling feed-in tariffs make exporting solar power to the grid unattractive, while buying stays expensive, so neighbours trading directly is appealing. The catch is structural: if every household is fixed as a seller, a prosumer-heavy community eventually runs out of buyers.

Their Energy Trading Potential Index measures trading potential from data, modelling the market as a graph of buyer-seller pairs over repeated rounds. The key twist is flexible role switching, where prosumers join the buyer side whenever they run an energy deficit. On residential data with solar profiles, a prosumer-heavy mix scored 0.61 under the flexible policy against only 0.15 under fixed roles, a fourfold difference the static model misses entirely. The index is offered as a planning tool for trading infrastructure.
arxiv-2606-22187:
AlMasri recasts, in 2026, Gol'fand's 1964 proposal of discrete time in quantum mechanics as a modern open-systems problem. Gol'fand's extension predicted intrinsic non-unitarity and entropy increase, but it predates the theory of open quantum systems. AlMasri rewrites the discrete evolution equation rigorously as a completely positive trace-preserving quantum channel.

Taking a continuous-time coarse-grained limit yields a specific Lindblad master equation with a fundamental time scale. The step drives decoherence in the energy basis and in a fundamental operator basis alike. Using Spohn's entropy production formalism, AlMasri proves the discrete step forces a strictly positive entropy growth rate. This grounds the arrow of time microscopically, with no coupling to an environment needed. The dynamics also cap the lifetime of discrete time crystals. Precision data bound the time step below ten to the minus twenty-six seconds.
arxiv-2606-22587:
Giovanna Ilardi, Abbas Nasrollah Nejad, and Saeed Tafazolian study how hyperplane sections of a hypersurface vary in this 2026 algebraic geometry paper. Slicing by hyperplanes gives a family of smaller shapes, and the question is whether it really varies in moduli.

For hypersurfaces with at most isolated singularities, the authors use the Milnor algebra to give an infinitesimal criterion for the section map to be generically finite. A local GIT slice argument bridges from the infinitesimal test to the coarse moduli space. The result extends earlier theory from smooth cases to singular ones. For smooth cases it recovers the Lefschetz criterion and generic finiteness in a stated range. In the singular case a new obstruction appears, a linear Jacobian syzygy tied to large automorphism groups. Once excluded, maximal variation is governed by one Lefschetz map being injective. Applications include the Schoen quintic threefold.
arxiv-2606-22687:
Giuseppe Arena, Lourens Waldorp, and Maarten Marsman ask what a prior is worth in this 2026 statistics paper. In Bayesian analysis, a prior's effective sample size expresses its information in units of observations, telling researchers how much data they need to outweigh it. For Gaussian graphical models, networks of conditional dependencies, that number was unavailable.

The obstacle: the Wishart and G-Wishart priors entangle the precision matrix's entries, so their informativeness was never expressed in observation units. The authors formalize that missing number for these models. They adapt five estimators, each computed two ways: globally from a determinant ratio, and parameterwise from a Cholesky decomposition. Two planning strategies follow: one finds the sample size where data dominate the prior, the other the size needed for conclusive edge evidence. Simulations show the strategies target complementary goals, and the estimators differ in sensitivity to network structure.
arxiv-2606-23487:
Amrita Singh and Rishabh Jha adapt medical vision-language models safely in a 2026 paper. Models like BiomedCLIP generalize broadly across medical images. Adapting one to a new clinical service risks two silent failures. The model can forget modalities it already handled. It can also drift from its trustworthy pretrained behavior toward shortcuts in the new data. Their framework, CADRE, freezes the backbone and trains only a low-rank adapter, about a quarter of a percent of the parameters. Two penalties guard the adaptation: a consolidation term bounds lost competence on old tasks, and an anchor term bounds drift from the frozen prior.

Singh and Jha stress-test the method on breast cancer across three very different modalities: histopathology, ultrasound, and chest radiography. Across seeds and adaptation orders, CADRE reached the highest accuracy and backward transfer among adapting methods. Its forgetting was roughly sevenfold lower than the strongest regularized baseline.
arxiv-2606-23887:
Luu generalizes the recipe that predicts particle masses in a family of two dimensional field theories, from one special symmetry element to many more, in a 2026 paper on mathematical physics. In affine Toda theory, the particles correspond to orbits of a Coxeter element acting on the root system, and their masses come from an eigenvector of the Cartan matrix. Variants built on other Weyl group elements show the same orbit pattern. Luu supplies the unified spectral formula for these Weyl orbit particles.

The calculations recast the Cartan eigenvector description for general elements, not just Coxeter ones. As an example, Luu computes the mass spectrum for the D type family built on a non Coxeter element. Parts of the classic Toda spectrum have been observed in quasi one dimensional magnets, so broader spectra guide the search for new realizations.
arxiv-2606-23987:
Basman Monterrubio, Czyzowicz, Stokke, and Thevenot settle when the largest possible collection of clopen sets of a topological group can support a semigroup compactification, in a 2026 paper on topological algebra. Compactifications extend a group into a compact semigroup. Staying inside totally disconnected spaces requires sets that are both open and closed, clopen sets, and the key property is left introversion of the Boolean algebra they form. A predecessor paper asked whether the full algebra of all clopen sets can fail to be left introverted; no example was known.

The authors characterize left introversion of the full algebra using one clopen set and two nets. Applying it, they prove that for a locally compact, first countable, sigma compact, totally disconnected group, the full algebra is left introverted exactly when the group is compact or discrete. Hereditary properties extend the result to further classes of groups.
arxiv-2606-24287:
Damele and Loi prove that two attractive algebraic properties cannot coexist beyond the trivial case. Lie skew braces equip one group with two operations, an additive and a multiplicative structure, linked by a compatibility law. They arise from set-theoretic solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation. A brace that is simple, with no nontrivial ideals, and simply connected, with nilpotent multiplicative group, sounds like a rich object worth hunting.

No such hunt can succeed above dimension one. Damele and Loi show any simply connected simple Lie skew brace with nilpotent multiplicative group must be one-dimensional and abelian. The argument runs through post-Lie algebras, the infinitesimal shadow of the brace. When the additive algebra is solvable, its nilradical is automatically an ideal. When both algebras are nilpotent, a proper ideal with trivial quotient always exists. Lifting those infinitesimal ideals to global ones completes the 2026 proof.
arxiv-2606-24387:
Lee and colleagues release a dataset that teaches software to read car advertisements the way a dealer does. Vehicle listings bury rich data inside free-form sales text. Automotive named-entity recognition, the task of tagging structured facts in text, has few resources. AutoSpecNER, introduced in 2026, contains several hundred advertisements from a popular car-selling website. They carry over ten thousand expert-annotated entities, across fifteen categories including model, engine specification, and battery capacity.

Inter-annotator agreement above ninety percent validates the labels. Benchmarks compare rule-based extraction, fine-tuned transformer encoders, and large language models head to head. A fine-tuned DeBERTa model wins clearly. It posts a micro-averaged score far above the rule-based baseline, and comfortably ahead of the strongest language model. Lee's result is a useful corrective to fashion. For narrow, well-defined extraction, a modest specialised encoder still beats generative giants.
arxiv-2606-24587:
Achituv and Sari write down, in plain formulas, how middleweight stars live and begin to die. Stars between three and ten solar masses burn hydrogen through main sequence life with a convective core. Their 2026 analytical description covers the whole main sequence and the transition toward the red giant phase, regimes usually handled by heavy numerical stellar models.

A simple relation ties the star's total mass to its convective core mass, through the ratio of mean molecular weights in core and envelope. From it, the hydrogen abundance profile outside the core follows analytically, falling as a power of the enclosed mass. Temperature, density, and pressure in that variable composition region become power laws of radius. Core and stellar radii and luminosity emerge as functions of the core's composition. The main sequence hook, a dip in effective temperature, is explained physically and located at a specific small core hydrogen fraction.
arxiv-2606-24787:
A. Ballester-Bolinches, R. Esteban-Romero, and P. Pérez-Altarriba open the representation theory of finite skew braces. A skew brace is a set carrying two group operations tied by a modified distributive law. These structures capture the set theoretic solutions of the Yang Baxter equation, a core equation of mathematical physics. Their representation theory has been a classical open problem. The authors propose a definition of representation and examine its properties.

Representations of the trifactorised groups attached to skew braces turn out to play a fundamental role. The paper develops the definition through that connection. Basic properties of brace representations are established along the way. Ballester and colleagues frame the work as groundwork rather than a finished theory. The hope is that a sound notion of representation will do for skew braces what it long did for groups: turn abstract structure into concrete linear algebra.
arxiv-2606-24887:
Johannes Alt and Sarah Timhadjelt settle where the eigenvectors of a directed Erdős Rényi random graph spread out and where they might not. The graph's adjacency matrix is a sparse non Hermitian random matrix. When the expected degree exceeds the log of the number of vertices, the graph is connected, and the authors show all its eigenvectors are completely delocalised. Below that critical scale the picture needs one qualification.

Under the threshold, delocalisation is proved for eigenvectors whose eigenvalue stays away from zero. The contrast with the undirected, Hermitian world is sharp: there, large eigenvalues come with localised eigenvectors. The results extend beyond the graph itself. They extend to sparse random matrices with independent entries, readable as weighted directed Erdős Rényi graphs. Alt and Timhadjelt thus pin down a clean spectral transition at the connectivity threshold for this non Hermitian setting.
arxiv-2606-24987:
Francisco Andrade, Gabriel Peyré, and Clarice Poon study how many samples unbalanced entropic optimal transport needs before its couplings can be trusted. Optimal transport compares probability measures, but exact balanced transport is rigid: real data has mass that goes missing, is created, or is destroyed. Entropic smoothing and unbalanced marginal penalties fix complementary weaknesses. Rather than bounding only the scalar transport cost, the authors work at the level of the optimal coupling itself. They build a translation invariant dual form of the problem.

For the intrinsic dual variables they prove compactness and strong convexity properties. Those estimates convert into finite sample bounds, holding with high probability, for empirical couplings. The message for practice is direct. Regularisation softens the curse of dimensionality and cuts the samples needed for stable estimation. The outputs also stay compatible with fast Sinkhorn type solvers.
arxiv-2606-25187:
Silting objects are special building blocks inside triangulated categories, a general setting used in modern algebra. Simion Breaz, Andrei Mărcuş, and George Ciprian Modoi study when these objects keep their defining property after moving between two categories. The move happens through adjoint pairs, which are matched functors going in opposite directions. Their 2026 paper works with compactly generated categories, a broad class that includes derived categories of rings.

Breaz and his co-authors prove that the silting property always travels upward through a left adjoint in their tensor setting, and that equivalent objects stay equivalent after the move. Moving the property back down is harder and needs extra conditions, such as a compactness assumption and a new notion they call quasi faithful flatness. One payoff is a downward result that holds under milder hypotheses than earlier work on rings had used.
arxiv-2606-25687:
A dark soliton, a moving dip in a quantum fluid, survives in one dimension but snakes and dies in two, torn apart by sideways instability. Koushik Mukherjee and Hiroki Saito show theoretically in 2026 that a dipolar Bose Einstein condensate can protect its own soliton. Atoms with strong magnetic dipole forces interact over long range and settle into stripe supersolid order, part crystal, part superfluid. A straight dark soliton embedded in that medium feels the stripes as rails: the ordered background itself pins the defect, no external lattice needed.

Excitation spectra explain the protection: the lowest sideways bending branch stays gapped rather than softening into instability, and stripe order stiffens it further, raising the energy cost of bending. Contact only condensates lack this intrinsic suppression. The effect should be reachable with current erbium and dysprosium experiments, offering interaction driven armour for solitons inside structured quantum fluids rather than imposed confinement.
arxiv-2606-26087:
JoungBin Lee and colleagues improve novel-view video generation with a tracking-based training signal. The task turns one reference video into a new video along a chosen camera path. Geometry and motion must both survive the move. Explicit 3D pipelines inherit errors from reconstruction tools. Camera-only conditioning looks great but drifts in geometry and motion.

Attention layers hold the clue. Certain layers already attend to geometrically matching points across views and time. Misaligned attention tracks with motion inconsistency in the output. MVTrack4Gen routes those features into an auxiliary multi-view point-tracking head. The diffusion model trains jointly on video generation and point tracking. Strengthened correspondences make outputs follow the reference motion better. Cross-view geometry holds up more reliably too. Across varied benchmarks, the method reaches state-of-the-art geometric consistency. Camera accuracy stays competitive with the best alternatives.
arxiv-2606-26487:
Defu Cao, Zijie Lei, Muyan Weng, Jiao Sun, and Yan Liu address a mismatch between language models and numbers. Language models read text as discrete tokens. Time series data are continuous numbers, such as prices or temperatures over time. Standard token handling blurs number order and hurts forecasting. Their system, TempoWave, replaces how each number enters the model.

TempoWave turns each value into digit-wise embeddings built from wavelets. An embedding is the list of numbers a model uses to represent an input. Wavelets describe a signal at several scales at once, from fine wiggles to broad trends. The design keeps exact digit identity and fine local detail visible to the model. It also survives common rescaling of the data. Across five forecasting benchmarks with added text context, TempoWave beat standard number handling and rival interfaces. The authors argue the number interface itself is a key bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-26787:
Chennan Ma and five colleagues present AIGP, a pricing framework for online shops that aims at long-term value, not just today's sales. Standard dynamic pricing is hard to interpret and ignores text information like product descriptions and reviews. It also chases short-term metrics. Their framework uses a large language model fed with domain knowledge, structured data, and text context to set prices.

A Long-Term Value Estimator sits at the centre. It is trained by offline reinforcement learning on past data. It scores prices by cumulative merchandise value, return on investment, and milestone goals. For deployment, the language model's skill is distilled into a smaller model by supervised fine-tuning. Decisions stay interpretable because the model reasons in words. The authors report tests on large-scale e-commerce tasks.
arxiv-2606-26987:
Sinie van der Ben, Raphaël Baur, Yannick Metz, and Mennatallah El-Assady search open language models for emotion vectors, internal directions that encode feelings. Prior work on a leading closed model found such vectors shaping behaviour, with geometry echoing human psychology. The authors test whether the finding generalises. Two open-weight models of modest size were examined, using stories the models themselves generated.

Valence, the pleasant-versus-unpleasant axis, was recovered in both models. Its alignment with the top internal direction approached the closed model's reported strength. Where valence lives differed sharply. One model encodes it early and loses it in deep layers; the other builds it only midway. Arousal, the intensity axis, depended on which model's stories supplied the test data. Code and materials are openly released.
arxiv-2606-27087:
Kravitz examines which comparisons between repeated sums and differences of an integer set must always hold. For a finite set of whole numbers, adding it to itself several times gives a sumset, and subtracting gives a difference set. Sizes of these grown sets sit at the heart of additive combinatorics, the study of addition patterns. In the 2026 classification, Kravitz extends a little-known construction of Ruzsa to settle the general higher-order question.

Four counts govern the comparison: sums and subtractions on each side of the claimed inequality. Kravitz characterises exactly which quadruples of counts make the inequality hold for every finite integer set. The answer compares only the smaller and larger count on each side. Both must not decrease from the left side to the right side. Sharp examples show why nothing weaker works, including cases where balanced huge difference sets lose to modest sumsets.
arxiv-2606-27287:
Baxi and colleagues test whether hidden self-promotion can game language models that screen résumés. Prompt injection here means subtle booster text adding no real qualifications, planted to sway the model's ranking. Controlled experiments vary how many candidates inject and how varied candidate quality is. When quality is uniform and few candidates inject, injection reliably lifts rankings. That advantage is the core vulnerability measured, in a hiring study published in 2026.

As more candidates inject, the edge rapidly collapses. Widespread manipulation cancels itself out. With mixed quality, injection works less well on average. Occasionally, though, a weaker candidate still leapfrogs a stronger one, raising fairness alarms. Screening is therefore most fragile exactly when manipulation is rare and quality gaps are small. Employers cannot assume rankings stay clean just because few applicants cheat. Public code accompanies the findings for replication.
arxiv-2606-27387:
Thompson derives an uncertainty principle for nonlocal quantum field theory, where interactions smear across a basic length scale. Under stated assumptions about the detector response kernel at equal times, the observed spread obeys an exact variance addition law. Combining that law with the ordinary Heisenberg inequality yields a nonlocal uncertainty relation. In the infrared, or local, limit the bound reduces to the familiar Heisenberg form. In the 2026 physics paper, at short scales it implies a minimal length set by the nonlocality scale.

Spacetime itself remains a Lorentz-covariant continuum at the manifold level. What dies is pointlike localisation as a realisable notion below that scale. Locality and microcausality must therefore be reinterpreted, not abandoned. The result clarifies what position can mean in a complete short-scale theory. Points become bookkeeping devices, not real places. The short-scale structure of field theory gains a precise working boundary.
arxiv-2606-27587:
Electron ptychography images materials at atomic scale. It rebuilds images from diffraction patterns, but the standard process is slow. Kieran Loehr and seven colleagues present PtyRANNOSAUR in 2026. Their neural network code turns microscope data into phase images within seconds. It runs roughly ten to a hundred times faster than standard methods.

Convolutional autoencoders do the rebuilding. An autoencoder compresses data and then rebuilds it. Each model trains on a large database of crystal structures. Models are tuned to settings such as voltage, beam angle, defocus, and sample thickness. Users need no fine-tuning of their own. The code also handles partial coherence, multiple scattering, and scan position errors. Tests used both experimental and simulated data. The networks recovered atomic structures across many materials. Resolution reached finer than half an angstrom. That matches the best slow iterative reconstructions of the same data.
arxiv-2606-27687:
Language models now generate and label data for hypothesis testing. That convenience makes p-hacking easy. A researcher can tune prompts and settings until the wanted result appears. Maria Thomas, Kristina Gligorić, and Nihar Shah propose a defence in 2026. Their protocol preregisters the experiment. The confirmatory run then uses the first eligible model released after registration.

A model that does not exist yet cannot be hacked against. Hacks tuned on one model also often fail to transfer to the next. The authors tested the protocol on two tasks with known true values. Twenty models from four providers and eleven analysis setups were involved. The protocol would have blocked the hack's transfer in about seventy-four percent of cases on one task and seventy-three percent on the other. The team also preregistered their own experiment. Six of the seven hacking setups failed to carry over to the new model.
arxiv-2606-27987:
Graphs, surface maps, and abstract polytopes are close cousins. Different communities study them with separate tools and databases, though. Katja Berčič and three colleagues argue in 2026 that maniplexes can unify them. Maniplexes capture all three structures in one framework. A single database built around them would help researchers spot shared structures. The authors present a compact storage format for maniplexes as edge-labeled graphs.

The format, lsparse6, is designed so tools can share it. As a first step, two datasets of regular 4-maniplexes are connected outward. Links run to the House of Graphs database and to Potočnik's censuses of tetravalent graphs. Matching uses canonical forms of flag graphs, skeleton graphs, and coskeleton graphs. The RAMP package for GAP encodes the source maniplexes in this form. Future cross-links target the Small Groups Library and map and polytope datasets.
arxiv-2606-28187:
Xiaocheng Yang, Abdulrahman Alrabah, Dilek Hakkani-Tür, and Gokhan Tur address a weakness of systems where several language-model agents work as a team. When the team fails, coarse feedback rarely shows which agent, or which exchange, caused the error, so fixing the team is guesswork.

Yang and colleagues model the team as a computational graph and attach gradient-based weights, numbers that measure how much each agent's output sways the agents after it. Loss signals then flow backward, pinpointing error sources and guiding targeted prompt fixes. Their efficient version, called AgentChord, was tested on two dialogue and tool-use benchmarks. It beat strong baselines, both single-agent and multi-agent, and better blame assignment went hand in hand with bigger gains.
arxiv-2606-28287:
Phong Dang and eight colleagues ask whether the hidden symmetries of the nuclear force govern atomic masses across the whole chart of nuclei, not just in light ones. Ab initio calculations had established two symmetry groups as dominant in small and medium nuclei, but global mass models rarely use them directly.

Dang's team built three interpretable neural networks from the symmetries' Casimir operators, mathematical fingerprints of each nucleus. Operators from one symmetry alone cut prediction error nearly in half against a liquid-drop baseline. Their compact mass formula reached the lowest validation error of the three, rivaling leading models. The networks also spotted physics: the symmetry strengthens near the neutron dripline and gains extra weight among superheavy nuclei.
arxiv-2606-28387:
Adarsh Agrawal and Shashank Indukuri fix the step where natural-language analytics usually fails first: picking which tables a question is even about. Enterprise warehouses hold thousands of tables with abbreviated columns, informal metrics, and hidden joining customs, so a model handed the wrong schema context is lost before any query is written.

Agrawal and Indukuri index the catalog itself, embedding five kinds of objects, tables, columns, metrics, relationships, and past queries, each with its own text template. Vector search, lineage expansion, reranking, workload memory, and access-control gates then assemble the context. On one benchmark of over fifteen hundred questions, table recall topped ninety-six percent. Query history dramatically lifted recall on another, and execution errors fell by more than half on a third.
arxiv-2606-28487:
Andrei Constantin, Seung-Joo Lee, Andre Lukas, and Luca A. Nutricati write down formulas for some of geometry's most wanted objects: Ricci-flat metrics on Calabi-Yau three-folds, the curved six-dimensional spaces at the heart of string theory. Numerical and machine-learned metrics now reach high accuracy, but physics needs to know how the metric changes as the shape's moduli, its size and form parameters, vary.

The team proposes an explicit ansatz for the Kähler potential whose coefficients depend on the moduli.
