TATA box binding protein and HPRT1 also ranked high. GAPDH ranked least stable. The authors suggest beta-actin and RPL4 for abundant gene messages. They suggest TBP and HPRT1 for low-abundance messages in studies across pig tissues.
europmc-pmc2001387:
Draper, Sanders and Kingston followed 882 patients with retinoblastoma in 1986, an eye cancer of childhood. They asked how often survivors developed a second, separate cancer. The series included 384 patients with the inherited form of the disease. The authors also weighed the treatments used for the first cancer, including radiation and cyclophosphamide.

Thirty patients developed second primary cancers. By 18 years after diagnosis, the rate reached 4.2 percent overall. For the inherited form it reached 8.4 percent, and 6.0 percent for bone cancer alone. Risk was higher inside the radiation field. Evidence suggested inherited cases are especially sensitive to radiation. Rates here were lower than in earlier published series.
europmc-pmc2024987:
Hewitt, Blake and Walder challenged in 1976 the popular idea that the body actively defends itself against cancer. Their evidence came from 27 mouse tumours that arose spontaneously, not from chemicals or viruses. Such tumours were transplanted between genetically matched mice. The authors argue these are the only fair models of human cancer. Chemically induced tumours, they say, create artificial immunity.

Across roughly 20,000 maintenance transplants, not one failed or shrank away. Almost 10,000 tumours from small cell doses were watched, and none regressed on their own. Prior injection of irradiated tumour cells actually made recipients more receptive, not less. Lymphocytes from sensitised mice gave no protection either. The team found no trace of tumour immunogenicity, meaning no immune rejection of these cancers.
europmc-pmc2124787: A medical paper on pleomorphism and pleobiosis of Bacillus bifidus communis. The shape-shifting gut germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. The paper lived through the years. Future scholars will discover it. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2124887: A medical paper with studies in isoagglutination, tonicity in isohemagglutination. The salty clumping. This article preserves that serology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2125487: A medical paper on the interrelation of the surviving dog heart and pancreas in sugar metabolism. The organs' teamwork. This article preserves that physiology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2126287: A medical paper on the encystment of dysentery amebae in vitro. The encysted amebae. This article preserves that parasitology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2126687: A medical paper on the relation of the pneumococcus to hydrogen ion concentration, acid death-point. The germ's acid limit. This article preserves that bacteriology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2128287: A medical paper with immunological studies on a leptospira strain from a yellow fever case. The jaundice germ. This article preserves that immunology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2128587: A medical paper on classification of the hemolytic streptococci by the precipitin reaction. The sorted strep. This article preserves that bacteriology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2131087: A medical paper with serological studies on the blood of primates, blood groups. The ape blood. This article preserves that serology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2131287: A medical paper on the etiology of Oroya fever, the response of the skin of macaques. The monkey skin. This article preserves that tropical medicine. It awaits future readers. It holds its historical place. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2131487: A medical paper on nitrogen metabolism of normal and sarcomatous fibroblasts in pure cultures. The cells' nitrogen. This article preserves that cell biology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2140087:
Rosen and colleagues searched human urine in 2007 for evidence that bladder bacteria live inside cells. Urinary tract infections are mostly caused by uropathogenic Escherichia coli. In mice these bacteria invade bladder lining cells and form intracellular bacterial communities, clusters that can seed repeat infections. Whether that cycle happens in women was unknown. The team collected urine from 80 young women with acute cystitis and 20 without symptoms.

Communities shed from bladder cells appeared in 14 of 80 infection samples, which is 18 percent. Thread-like filamentous bacteria appeared in 41 percent. Neither sign appeared in any control sample. All community-positive samples also carried filaments. Among Escherichia coli infections, 22 percent showed communities. No gram-positive infections did. The results suggest an intracellular niche may drive recurrence in some women.
europmc-pmc2235887:
Kitson and co-authors examined the PARiHS framework in 2008, a model for getting research evidence into health practice. PARiHS, short for Promoting Action on Research Implementation (PARiHS) in Health Services, is widely used to frame implementation work. Yet as a concept it remains untested, and its contribution to theory is unquantified. The paper clarifies the difference between a conceptual framework, a theory and a model, borrowing a typology from social policy analysis.

The authors propose using PARiHS in two stages. First, diagnose the evidence and the local context using its elements and sub-elements. Then use those combined scores to choose the most fitting facilitation method. The intervention is thereby shaped by the specific people, place and time. They recommend an international collaborative to collect experiences and test the framework systematically.
europmc-pmc2323687: Living things hum with tiny sparks, and this paper measured the sparks behind life's acts. Tests across live samples set the scale. The life sparks, gauged. The article keeps that life-chemistry study. Kept for study.
europmc-pmc2360687:
Eisen and a large team reported a trial of sorafenib in advanced melanoma in 2006. Sorafenib is a pill that blocks several growth signals in tumors and their blood vessels. Melanoma is a skin cancer that, once spread, had few working treatments at the time.

All 37 patients first took the drug for 12 weeks at 400 milligrams twice daily. Only one tumor shrank by at least a quarter, and 27 grew by that much and stopped treatment. Six patients with stable disease entered a randomised phase, but all on the drug progressed by week 24. Across all patients, 19% had stable disease and 62% progressed, with a median time to progression of 11 weeks. Skin rash affected 51% of patients. A common gene fault, V600E BRAF, did not predict who stayed stable. The authors judged the drug well tolerated but nearly inactive alone.
europmc-pmc2627687:
Altekruse, Stern, Fields, and Swerdlow reviewed Campylobacter jejuni in 1999 as an emerging foodborne pathogen in the United States. The bacterium had become America's most commonly reported bacterial cause of foodborne illness. Human and economic costs were compounded by chronic after-effects in some patients, notably Guillain-Barré syndrome, a paralysing nerve disorder, and reactive arthritis.

Mishandling raw poultry and eating undercooked poultry were the major risk factors for infection. An increasing share of human infections was also proving resistant to antimicrobial therapy, narrowing treatment options. The authors argue that prevention efforts are needed at every link of the food chain. That runs from farm production through processing, retail, and home kitchens. No single intervention point is enough.
europmc-pmc2648987:
Yuan and co-authors showed in 2009 that mouse embryonic stem cells send tiny parcels that can reprogram the cells around them. The parcels, called microvesicles, are bubbles of cell skin shed into the fluid nearby. Blood cells shed them too, and they had already been seen moving proteins and RNA between cells.

The team read what these stem cell parcels carry. They were rich in microRNAs, short RNA pieces that tune how genes are used. The researchers loaded parcels with a glowing marker gene and its protein product. Other stem cells took the parcels in and began to glow themselves. Parcels also passed a share of their microRNAs into mouse support cells in the dish. Stem cells, the authors suggest, may steer their neighbors by mail, not only by direct touch.
europmc-pmc2700087:
Treweek and Zwarenstein argued in 2009 that medical trials are often built to answer narrow questions cleanly, then fail the real world they were meant to guide. A randomized trial is the best tool for judging whether a treatment works. But randomization alone says nothing about whether results apply to other patients, clinics, or countries.

The authors contrast two attitudes. Explanatory trials test a treatment under ideal, tightly controlled conditions. Pragmatic trials test it under the messy conditions of routine care, with ordinary patients and staff. Most trials lean explanatory, so their results travel poorly, and users of research must guess at applicability. The review sets out how to judge that leap honestly. If evidence is to steer practice and policy, they conclude, more trials should be designed pragmatically from the start.
europmc-pmc2701987:
Albert, Robertson, and Miall showed in 2009 that the resting brain is not idle after learning: it replays and processes what was just practiced. Brain networks hum in slow waves even with no task, and what that hum is for was contested, daydreaming or readiness. The team scanned volunteers resting before and after eleven minutes of learning a joystick tracking task.

Only the learners changed. A front-to-back network spanning frontal and parietal areas, plus a cerebellar network never before described at rest, altered their resting pattern after training. Volunteers who merely performed the movements without learning anything new showed no such change. The very networks used during the task were the ones retuned afterward. Rest, the authors conclude, is when the brain files the lesson, which makes resting scans a possible window into memory consolidation.
europmc-pmc2725087:
Petersen and co-authors presented in 2009 a generic method for protein studies. It predicts how exposed each amino acid in a protein is to solvent. It also scores how reliable each prediction is. Knowing whether a building block sits buried or exposed helps infer protein shape and function. Discrete class predictions have natural confidence scores, but a single real-value prediction does not.

An ensemble of neural networks trained on solved protein structures outputs both exposure and a reliability Z-score in one step, rather than bolting reliability on afterward. On a standard test set its accuracy matched the best public method of the time. Among the top fifth of predictions ranked by its score, accuracy beat the rival score at every subset size, which makes its reliability measure more informative.
europmc-pmc2772987:
Half, Bercovich, and Rozen reviewed in 2009 familial adenomatous polyposis. In this inherited condition, tens to thousands of adenomas fill the rectum and colon. The small growths appear from the second decade of life. It strikes about one in eight thousand births, affects both sexes equally, and accounts for under one percent of colorectal cancers. Most patients feel nothing for years, until bleeding, anemia, or cancer appears.

Classic disease follows a dominant pattern and stems from a germline mutation in the APC gene, carried in every cell from birth. A milder attenuated form brings fewer polyps, later onset, and lower cancer risk. A recessive look-alike stems from MUTYH mutations instead. Diagnosis rests on family history, examination, and colonoscopy, confirmed by genetic testing where possible, and relatives should then be tested too.
europmc-pmc2912887:

Until then most implementations lived on commercial platforms or demanded programming skill, shutting out many biologists.

Users can swap algorithms and starting methods freely, or bolt in their own variants to test. Built-in benchmark data and plots help judge whether a factorization is stable and meaningful. europmc-pmc2944787:

Using a capture method plus deep sequencing, they found both species carry very similar island counts, often at matching spots near genes. Many orphans still sparked gene activity and changed during development, often gaining silencing marks as their active features faded.
europmc-pmc2945087:

For each drug, levels stayed above a demanding target for only part of the dosing gap, ranging from about a third to just over half the interval. europmc-pmc2946687:

europmc-pmc3026687:

The paper opens a supplement that works through each theme in depth. Acting on the plan could make elimination possible even in the hardest hit regions, the authors argue. They warn that commitment has to start right away, not after control programs stall.
europmc-pmc3068987:

Starting from an existing model in the literature, they coded twenty papers from four regions against its themes, then added new themes the model missed. europmc-pmc3078587:

The ratio compares neutrophils, front line infection fighters, with lymphocytes, and it rises with body wide inflammation. The team checked it in two separate patient groups receiving first line treatment for cancer that could not be removed.

A high starting ratio meant less benefit from treatment, faster progression, and shorter survival in both groups, even after other factors were counted. How a patient generally functioned also mattered, but the ratio added independent warning. In patients whose ratio settled back to normal after one treatment cycle, the disease stayed controlled longer. Because the test is cheap and already in the chart, the authors propose it for everyday risk sorting, including in clinics with few resources.
europmc-pmc3113287:
The Endogenous Hormones and Breast Cancer Collaborative Group pooled data from seventeen long-term studies for a 2010 report in The Lancet Oncology. They studied a growth factor in blood that drives cell division and blocks cell death, asking whether higher levels predict breast cancer. The study gives one of the firmest estimates of this hormone-related risk.
europmc-pmc3168787:

europmc-pmc3182887:
Wing To and Kim Midwood reviewed the two lives of a versatile repair protein in a 2011 paper in Fibrogenesis and Tissue Repair. Understanding its controls, the authors argue, may yield therapies that keep repair on the healthy side of that switch.
europmc-pmc3231187:

europmc-pmc3257687:

europmc-pmc3266187:

The index outperformed six rival scoring systems at separating advanced from mild fibrosis. europmc-pmc3274487:

The team updated the first global endemicity map, made for 2007, and added two new layers.

europmc-pmc3314787:

europmc-pmc3344687:

Adding hemin, the iron bearing part of blood pigment, raised TLR4 further and worsened injury in normal mice but not in those missing the sensor. Blocking TLR4 with an antibody calmed the microglia. The authors propose the pathway as a drug target for brain bleeds.
europmc-pmc3346787:
Johnston and colleagues estimated how many deaths worldwide are caused each year by smoke from landscape fires, in a 2012 study. Fires in forests, grasslands, and peat release enormous amounts of carbon and blanket whole regions in haze, often in poor tropical areas. The team combined a global air chemistry model with satellite readings to map daily and yearly exposure to fine smoke particles from 1997 to 2006.

Their central estimate lands near three hundred forty thousand deaths a year attributable to fire smoke, with a wide uncertainty band. Sub Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia carried the heaviest burdens. Deaths roughly doubled in El Niño years compared with La Niña years, showing how climate swings drive the toll. The authors argue that curbing the burning of tropical rainforest, which rarely burns naturally, could save many lives.
europmc-pmc3388687:
Heyland, Dhaliwal, Jiang, and Day built a nutrition risk score in 2011 for intensive care patients, the group feeding helps most. Their prospective study enrolled nearly six hundred patients expected to stay over a day. Candidate ingredients ranged from age and illness severity scores to recent weight loss and blood markers of inflammation.

Points were assigned by how strongly each factor tracked with death within twenty-eight days. As the score rose, so did death rates and time on breathing machines. Some ingredients, including body mass index and two inflammation markers, were dropped from the final score. Crucially, good feeding changed the score's link with survival, which is what a useful triage tool should show.
europmc-pmc3391987:
Maes and colleagues argued in 2012 that depression and the sluggish misery of being sick may be two faces of one immune process. Sickness behavior, the tired, withdrawn state that comes with infection, helps the body save energy for fighting inflammation. Its features, from lost appetite to aching and low mood, overlap heavily with depression.

In true clinical depression, though, the shared pathways harden into something damaging. The authors describe growing sensitivity of immune pathways, chemical stress injuring fats, proteins, and DNA, and immune attacks on the body's own tissues. Repeated episodes then scar nerve tissue and cloud thinking. Inflammation, on this view, protects briefly but harms when it will not switch off.
europmc-pmc3398887:
Dakos and colleagues compared methods in 2012 for spotting early warnings that a system is near a tipping point. Lakes, oceans, bodies, and markets can all flip suddenly into a different state, with little chance to reverse. Theory says telltale signals in data streams can betray an approaching flip.

Many warning methods exist, but opinions on their practical worth split widely, and no head-to-head test had been done. The authors lay out the available signals and try them on two simulated time series typical of systems near transition. Beyond the comparison, the paper provides a working toolbox. Fields from ecology to finance can use it to watch for trouble.
europmc-pmc3484687:

The team tested the scale in clinic and school samples in the United States and Britain. Scores hung together well and formed a single dimension in both places. Irritability rose in a clear ladder from healthy volunteers to children with severe mood problems. Stringaris's group argues the short scale suits both busy clinics and large studies of mood.

frus-1861-d187:
A letter dated 11 November 1861 went from William H. Seward to Carl Schurz in Madrid. The letter is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

By 11 November the Trent affair was about to burst upon the capitals. Seward's note to Schurz still speaks in the even tone of routine. Spain's reaction to the crisis would matter, and this letter kept the Madrid post primed for it. Spain's voice in the Trent talks would count, since its island lay beside the sea road. Its island beside the sea road made Spain's voice count beyond its strength.
frus-1861-d287:
On 7 September 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Mr. Haldeman. It stands as Document 287 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d87:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 September 1861. The dispatch is document 87 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams closed September with a report on the state of the London game. No crisis had broken, and that itself was the news. His steady word from across the sea let Lincoln's cabinet turn its mind to the armies, at least for a while. A quiet month in London was the best news the cabinet could get that fall. News by silence is still news, and Adams knew how to report it plainly.
frus-1862-d187:
Document 187 is the third of four Seward dispatches to London dated 10 November 1862 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All four went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain, from Secretary of State William H. Seward.

By mid-November, word had reached Washington that Britain would not join the French truce scheme. The danger of foreign action was fading, though slowly. Seward still wrote often, because warships for the South were fitting out in British yards. This letter belongs to the watchful weeks after the worst of the crisis passed. London's answer, when it came, would turn on battlefield news ten days old or more.
frus-1862-d287:
A second Dayton report followed on 13 June 1862, printed as Document 287 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward.

Two reports in two days often split a formal account from enclosures or private impressions. For Paris in 1862, the private side mattered, because the emperor's real views surfaced in hints. This report, read with its mate of the day before. Gives the legation's full picture for the week before the Seven Days battles changed every calculation. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d387:
Filed as Document 387 but dated 1 August 1862, this report from Simon Cameron in St. Petersburg went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. The printers placed it after a later Cameron report in the 1862 volume.

Cameron wrote at the start of August, in the weeks when the Alabama raider's escape from Britain was angering Washington. Russia's ports and courts offered no such grievances. The report's date places it beside Document 386 in substance, though the file separates them; together they give the legation's August account. The Russian route was the longest in the file, crossing an ocean and then half of Europe.
frus-1862-d487:
Two days later, on 10 March 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a further instruction to James Shepherd Pike in the Netherlands. The note is Document 487 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The follow-up came just after the ironclad fight at Hampton Roads, an event that made every maritime nation rethink its navy. The Dutch, with a fleet and colonies to protect, studied such news closely, and Pike needed Washington's version of it. Short supplementary orders were Seward's way of keeping his men current between the long formal instructions. Together with the order of 8 March, this note shows the tempo of wartime correspondence at its quickest.
frus-1862-d587:
Thomas Corwin in Mexico City received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 May 1862. It is Document 587 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Seward wrote five days after the Mexican victory at Puebla, though the news traveled slowly. His instructions to Corwin had a hard balance to strike. They had to show warm sympathy for Juárez's republic. They also had to make no commitment the Union could not honor while fighting the Confederacy. Corwin also had to be kept from promising more than Washington meant. The letter is a study in restrained diplomacy, from a government that believed in the Mexican cause and could spare it almost nothing but words.
frus-1862-d687: On 20 February 1862, a Mr. De Long wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The letter is document 687 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, printed just after the Egypt papers. The evidence names the writer and the date. It does not state the post he held or the place he wrote from.
frus-1862-d87:
On 26 June 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 87 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d187:
Washington's orders to London on 5 May 1863 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 5 letters between the same men dated that day.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d287: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 8 September 1863. It is document 287 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d387:
Britain's side of the Washington exchange speaks in this note, sent by Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 February 1863. It is document 387 of the 1863 papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Seward kept every note, and the State Department printed the exchange for Congress. Reading Lyons's side shows how the crisis looked from the other desk. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d487:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington addressed a formal note to William H. Seward, Secretary of State on 1 May 1863. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d587:
Document 587 in the volume is a letter of 15 July 1863 from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d687:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 November 1863. His letter is document 687 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume. Here the voice runs the other way, from the British side of the exchange.

Lyons had to guard British trade and ships while the Union navy stopped vessels at sea. He also had to judge how far the North would go. His notes to Seward put British concerns in plain, formal terms. For a reader, the gain is balance. Set beside Seward's replies, this letter shows both sides of a tense tie at work on the same day.
frus-1863p1-d87:
On 19 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 87 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The middle sheet of a three-letter day often held the meat: a talk set down in full, or a claim worked through point by point. Adams wrote in that pattern through the winter. This letter is the second of his 19 February set. With its mates, it let Seward see London whole for one day, through the eyes of the man he trusted most abroad.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d187:
Representatives of the British Chiefs of Staff put a proposal to Washington on 3 November 1943 about who should run the war in the Mediterranean. At the time, General Eisenhower ran the central part, while a separate commander in Cairo ran the east and the Balkans.

The paper argues that split command caused delays, since moving even small forces needed approval from the Combined Chiefs of Staff, and chances in the Aegean had been lost that way. It proposes one commander for the whole sea, adding Greece, the Balkans, Crete, the Aegean islands, and Turkey to his charge. It also suggests renaming the air command the Mediterranean Allied Air Forces, and asks for the American chiefs' views.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d287:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a long secret telegram from Washington on 22 November 1943. Its lead item is Turkey's official reply, reported by Ambassador Steinhardt, to Anthony Eden's recent proposals that Turkey grant air bases and move toward war.

Ankara refuses the bases, holding that granting them means war with Germany whatever Britain thinks, and that the minimum arms promised at Adana were never supplied. Coastal cities and industries would be destroyed, Turkey warns, leaving her a liability, not an asset. Hull adds von Papen's threat of a German and Bulgarian attack within days. He adds Finland's tighter turn toward Germany and Portuguese coolness over the Azores. He ends with a French committee vote to recall Helleu from Lebanon.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d387:
President Roosevelt handed Marshal Stalin a secret written proposal at Tehran on 29 November 1943. It restated what the American delegation had proposed at the Moscow Conference about air bases in the Soviet Union. It is one of three such papers Roosevelt gave Stalin that day.

The proposal asks that American aircraft on shuttle-bombing runs from the United Kingdom be allowed to refuel, make emergency repairs, and rearm at Soviet bases. It also seeks a better mutual exchange of weather information and improved signal and air communication between the two countries. Roosevelt records his understanding on two points. Moscow agreed to these ideas in principle at the Moscow Conference. And Soviet authorities would be told to meet his military mission to work out the concrete measures. He hopes the arrangements can be made promptly.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d487:
Prime Minister Winston Churchill wrote directly to Harry Hopkins, President Roosevelt's special assistant, on December 5, 1943, in the middle of the Second Cairo Conference. Churchill often used Hopkins as his fastest route to Roosevelt. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Hopkins lived in the White House and carried messages no formal channel could match for speed or candor. A Churchill note to him is summit diplomacy at its most personal: one leader reaching the other through a trusted friend. Readers get a glimpse of how much of the alliance ran on this single relationship, bypassing embassies and foreign offices entirely.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d87: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on November 2, 1943, and the letter stands as Document 87 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The two men would meet in Cairo in three weeks, but the letters never paused for the coming journey. The record gives the date and the names and no topic. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the volume's November sequence.
frus-1944-quebec-d187:
Cherwell also recorded the lend-lease conversation of September 14, 1944, between Roosevelt and Churchill. With Germany beaten, Britain hoped food, shipping, and munitions would keep coming during the war against Japan to cover reasonable needs. Roosevelt indicated assent, but Morgenthau pressed for definite figures rather than proportional aid.

The figures discussed were about 3.5 billion dollars of munitions aid in the first year and 3 billion in other supplies, offset by reverse lend-lease. All supplies would be on lend-lease terms. There would be no conditions jeopardizing Britain's export recovery, and no lend-lease articles could be exported. Roosevelt himself added the words "or sold for profit." A joint committee, informal at first and headed by Morgenthau, would work out the details.
frus-1944-quebec-d287:
The final report of the Combined Chiefs, C.C.S. 680/2, was submitted to Roosevelt and Churchill on September 16, 1944. It is the approved version of the draft the leaders had amended in plenary the day before. The over-all objective now reads as the unconditional surrender of Germany and Japan, sharpened from the draft's broader phrase about the Axis Powers.

The strategic concept and undertakings follow the draft, with small telling changes. French and Italian forces are to be assisted against Germany and/or Japan. Other co-belligerents are helped against "the enemy Powers." The redeployment sentence carries the compromise wording settled during the week: highest priority, having regard to other agreed and/or inescapable commitments. The report closed the conference's military business.
frus-1944-quebec-d87: Document 87 is where the editors, not the wartime officials, speak. The entry is an editorial note in the Quebec 1944 volume. State Department historians inserted notes to explain, connect, and cross-reference the papers. That help matters among the many staff memos written before the conference. Quebec hosted Roosevelt and Churchill in September 1944. Their agenda covered Germany, aid, and the Pacific war. The note offers orientation inside that record.
frus-1945-50-intel-d187: A short note records a talk held on 19 February 1947. It is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume on United States intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Such notes were made right after a talk, while the words were still fresh. They name the men in the room and the points each one made. That year the postwar spy service was still young, and its shape was still being set.
frus-1945-50-intel-d287:
A letter from Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter reached the Assistant Executive Secretary of the National Security Council(Lay) on 9 June 1948. The State Department prints it as document 287 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

A letter fixed a position in a way a phone call never could: dated, signed, and filed for both sides to cite later. A signed page also protected the writer: no one could later say the point had never been put. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d387:
The Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) addressed a letter to Attorney General Clark on 7 July 1949. It stands as document 387 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. The files around it hold the answer it drew, and often the draft that came before it. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d87:
Panuch, a deputy assistant secretary for administration, wrote to Russell on 16 April 1946. The paper moved inside the State Department's administration wing in the spring. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Spring 1946 was the season of transfer and shrinkage for the State intelligence office. As the central group took shape and the department shed wartime growth. A deputy's memorandum to his chief belongs to that grinding work of moving people and files. Readers who stay with these housekeeping papers earn a truer picture of institutional change than the famous directives give. Empires do not fall in a day; they are inventoried, reassigned, and filed away.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d187:
Washington set out its Rome instructions for London in an aide-mémoire of 8 December 1944. Sent to the British Embassy, the paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It tells what Ambassador Kirk has been ordered to say to Premier Bonomi.

Kirk is to voice this government's concern over the long-drawn crisis in the Italian government. He is to stress its deplorable effect on American public opinion, just as Congress weighs the renewal of formal relations with Italy. Washington earnestly hopes the broad character of the last Italian government will be kept in any settlement. The cabinet's make-up remains an Italian question. But American interest runs to the friendship a new government shows the United Nations, and to its taking up all of Italy's past pledges.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d287:
Secretary of War Stimson sent the President a Moscow letter on 3 January 1945 and vouched for it. His covering memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, attaches General Deane's letter to General Marshall of 2 December 1944. The chief of staff joins him in the endorsement.

Deane's letter, Stimson writes, is an apt presentation with sound recommendations. Deane reports that Ambassador Harriman has seen it and concurs fully. Harriman believes its thoughts apply with equal force to political matters as to military ones. He adds one caution. A short letter cannot give an accurate picture of Russia. He would welcome the chance to speak at length, if a change in policy toward the Soviet government is weighed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d387:
Care and repatriation of freed prisoners form the heart of a draft agreement approved by the Combined Chiefs on February 8, 1945. The preamble states the aim plainly. Moscow and Washington, with London in the same frame, wished to arrange care for Soviet citizens freed by Allied troops. American and British citizens freed by the Red Army would get the same treatment.

Article 1 begins the bargain: all Soviet citizens liberated by forces under American or British command fall under the agreement. The same holds in reverse for the other side's people. The draft became the text taken to the Russians that day. It later governed the return of millions, willing or not.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d487:
Washington answered the Irish aviation complaint in Grew's cable of February 8, 1945. During the Chicago conference, Grew explained, full multilateral agreement had grown doubtful. The Department had then held early talks toward bilateral air agreements with a number of countries. When the Spanish agreement was signed, Berle had stated publicly that similar agreements would follow.

Ireland was a natural case, given its obvious geographic importance to American air routes. The Department saw no reason to consult the United Kingdom. The agreement followed the standard form drawn up with British participation. Grew's defense is brisk: London had helped design the template it now protested.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d87:
Soviet Ambassador Andrei Gromyko talked at length with Leo Pasvolsky in Washington on 11 January 1945. Pasvolsky's record of the conversation is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The two men went over the Dumbarton Oaks document, and voting procedure in the Council dominated.

Gromyko said Roosevelt's proposal to Stalin changed nothing from the American position at Dumbarton Oaks, and Moscow's position was unchanged too. Above all, he explained, the Soviets want to avoid even the appearance of disagreement among the great powers. Peace, in their view, rests on unbroken great-power unity. Barring a great power from full part in settling a dispute touching it could open exactly the rift they fear.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d187:
The State Department backed a plan for supervised Greek elections in an aide-mémoire extract dated July 5, 1945. The extract is document 187 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full text appears later in the volume, attached to another document.

The surviving passage says the Department thinks it desirable for the British and American ambassadors to approach the Greek government. This should happen within the next few days. That way, the matter can be discussed at the Big Three meeting. The approach, a note explains, would tell Athens that in the view of the United States and Britain the Greek elections should take place under Allied supervision. Greece, sliding toward civil war, was one of the places where the Yalta pledges on free elections would be tested.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d287:
A background paper surveyed Hungary's armistice and politics, dated July 5, 1945. The paper is document 287 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is the briefing book's country study of the former Axis satellite.

Hungary signed its armistice on January 20, 1945, and has complied more or less satisfactorily, the summary says. But the Allied Control Commission's work sits in Soviet hands, its decisions made without reference to the American and British members. Soviet requisitioning and heavy reparations demands have deepened the damage of war and Nazi looting; Hungary will produce only a fraction of its normal output this year. Politically, the provisional government is a coalition of all important anti-Nazi parties, with the Communists the strongest party machine though perhaps not the most popular. The paper urges a three-power agreement that Hungary's coming elections be truly free.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d387:
German shipping and shipbuilding are treated together in a briefing book summary. The questions, it says, must be viewed from two sides at once. One is the immediate use of German resources for the United Nations' war and rebuilding program. The other is the long-range future of German shipping and shipbuilding as industries.

Each side, the paper warns, can prejudice the other if decisions are taken in haste. A major step toward order would be Soviet membership in the United Maritime Authority, or at least a friendly Soviet attitude toward it. The summary shows Potsdam's planners thinking past the surrender, to the sea trade of a beaten Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d487:
Presidential approval arrives in Grew's cable to Harriman of June 23, 1945. The President has approved in principle the recommendation that the United States recognize the new Polish Provisional Government of National Unity. As soon as it is announced that the new government is functioning in Poland, the Secretary will telegraph the Polish foreign minister in Warsaw with the decision.

It is then planned that the President himself announce the recognition. In making that announcement, the Department proposes, he should restate the Yalta provisions. The new government, under that agreement, stands pledged to hold free and unfettered elections. Grew adds that Harriman will meanwhile have had his chance to win the assurances Washington listed.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d587:
Moscow ambassador Sato sent a second, anxious cable to Tokyo on July 13, 1945. It is document 587 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference, printed in translation. Sato fears the Konoye mission will fail if it carries no real peace terms.

Sato presumes Moscow may agree to receive a special envoy. But if the envoy brings only vague talk, the Soviets will simply not weigh it. Worse, he warns, empty phrases would leave Soviet leaders feeling mocked. That could bring trouble on the Imperial Household itself. In Sato's view, the mission's aim must be nothing less than a proposal for peace. He asks Tokyo to state the envoy's task plainly, in case Moscow asks what the mission is for.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d687:
Loy Henderson sent the Acting Secretary a one-page office memo on the Turkey dispute, June 22, 1945. It is document 687 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It concerns the wording of a U.S. reply to the British Embassy, printed next as document 688.

Henderson suggests a verbal point be made as the reply is handed over. Department officers who were present at the Yalta talk in question, he notes, do not recall Stalin's stand that way. Britain's aide-memoire had Stalin firmly backing Turkey's independence and integrity. The U.S. officers recall no such definite position from him at Yalta. A handwritten note on the memo by H. Freeman Matthews sharpens the point. There was no mention of Turkey's integrity at Yalta at all.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d87:
Admiral Leahy sent Ambassador Harriman the first headcount of the President's party on June 23, 1945. The telegram is document 87 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference, answering Moscow's urgent request for numbers so the Soviets could plan housing at Babelsberg.

The President's own party totals 37, Leahy reports, including himself, James Byrnes, Harry Hopkins, and Fred Vinson, plus aides, Secret Service men, and twelve servants. The Secretary of State's party adds 26, and the Joint Chiefs of Staff party another 75, with ten admirals or generals among them. Leahy also clarifies his earlier question: it was whether Stalin would rather no formal staff meetings be held in Berlin, given how that might look abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1087:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the conference secretariat, summed up the Berlin Conference's handling of Yugoslavia in this extract dated August 8, 1945. Greek-Yugoslav differences came up again and again during the talks. The Soviets accused the Greeks of aggressive designs against Yugoslavia.

The British answered that Belgrade and Moscow radios were spreading fantastic, unfounded stories. Britain proposed a joint call on both governments to avoid hostile action pending an impartial inquiry. The Soviets countered with two proposals aimed at Greece. In the end, all three papers were withdrawn, and no action was taken.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1187:
Winant sent his first dispatch of the summit from London on 17 July 1945, as Potsdam opened. In it he set the baseline: British hopes, press mood, and official thinking on day one. Later cables from his post would be read against this opening report.

An embassy's first word in a crisis frames all that follows. Winant knew the British scene as few Americans did, after years at the post. This dispatch opens the London end of the conference record. Everything Washington later received from the embassy built on the picture drawn here, in the summit's first hours.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1287:
Shipping chief Land joined Bissell, his ship requirements director, in this message to Acting Administrator Conway on 23 July 1945. The note ran inside the War Shipping Administration, from its head and its hull-counting chief to the man holding the acting post.

The agency's business was the fleet: which ships sailed where, and what the war still needed of them. With one war ended, that business was being rewritten weekly. A joint note from the top shows the rewrite being directed. It is wartime logistics in its own words, filed among the summit's grander papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1387:
A third memorandum by Stanisław Mikołajczyk, dated 26 July 1945, continues the Polish deputy prime minister's papers in the volume. He wrote on the day the Potsdam Declaration went out to Japan. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

While the world's eyes turned to the Pacific, Mikołajczyk kept writing about Poland. That contrast is the point of his file: great events crowded together in July 1945, and small nations fought not to be forgotten inside them. His third paper in three days shows a man using the only tools he had. They were words on paper, aimed at governments that held his country's fate. The run rewards slow reading.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-87:
A rapporteur's report dated July 24, 1945, forms part of the Potsdam Conference record in the second volume. At big talks, a rapporteur is the officer charged with summing up a group's work. The report then goes to a senior body that must act on it. Potsdam ran much of its work through subcommittees, so such reports moved business upward.

Inside, readers find the distilled state of play on the group's assigned topic. Agreements reached sit beside points still in dispute. The form matters: leaders who lacked time for long files could act on a short, clear report. It shows conference work at the level where texts were shaped.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d787:
Erhardt sent a further report on Austrian affairs on July 28, 1945, in document 787. The political adviser wrote to the Acting Secretary as Potsdam entered its last days. Austria's treatment in the final texts was still being weighed. His report joined the second Potsdam volume.

Late reports from the field could still move a summit. Erhardt's facts arrived while lines were being fixed. Readers see the last chance for ground truth to shape a decision. The document shows an adviser pressing his knowledge into the closing hours. It gives Austria's file a voice at the very end of the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d887: American delegates revised the Soviet proposal on a central German administration on July 30, 1945. Their version keeps the core idea. Help would be given to set up central offices for foreign trade, industry, finance, transport, and communications. These offices would act under the Control Council. The revision drops the Soviet sentence about coordinating provincial governments. That cut matches the change Secretary Byrnes had suggested on the Soviet text.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d987:
American staff prepared this undated memorandum on German external assets during the Potsdam talks. It urges prompt action to gain control and power of disposal over such assets. Assets in neutral countries matter most. Two reasons are given for speed.

Control serves Allied security. It also keeps the assets intact for Allied purposes before they can vanish. The paper asks that the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union issue a declaration claiming authority over the assets. France should join if possible. The paper also asks that the matter go to the Economic Subcommittee at once.
frus-1961-63v10-d187: A 1961-1963 FRUS memorandum from the Cuba volume. The island's revolution preoccupied Washington. This document holds that memo. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
gao-gaoreports-b-295587: Kenneth Ashe took a March 2005 beef to GAO, and this ruling is the decision. One man's claim met the referee head-on. The docket got its full hearing, small name and all. The hearing was granted in full. The referee was fair.
gao-gaoreports-b-295987: General Dynamics-Ordnance doubled its May 2005 protest — two case numbers, one munitions fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-287: VA's trauma care delays needed ending in 2005, and GAO's report says the department had to move faster on the fixes. The review pushes for the action now. The haunted veterans deserved the faster help. The help had to come fast.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-687: Small and medium ammo needs were being met in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon covered the calibers, though more actions were necessary. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the bullets deserved steady supply. The actions had to be taken.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-787: D.C. foster care improvements were underway in 2005, and GAO's report says federal funds launched new programs, though challenges remained. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the foster kids deserved better care. The challenges had to be faced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-387: Bank preemption rules needed clarifying in 2006, and GAO's report says the OCC should further clarify which state consumer laws applied. The findings demand the clarity. The report warns that the borrowers deserved to know their protections. The rules had to be clarified.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-887: Some workplace-giving charities owed back taxes in 2006, and GAO's report says certain Combined Federal Campaign charities owed payroll and other federal taxes. The findings name the debt. The report warns that the do-gooders should pay their dues. The taxes had to be paid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1087: Gold-star lenders were cashing in on student loans in 2007 — GAO's report says killing the ‘exceptional performer' perk would save serious money. The findings show the bonus label paid lenders extra for doing their jobs. The report's math: end the gold stars, keep the billions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-387: Missile defense bought speed at a steep price in 2007, and GAO's report says the acquisition strategy delivered hardware but less capability for more money. The findings grade the trade-off in detail. The report's verdict is wry: results, yes — at a cost that would make a banker blush.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-87: Abstinence education needed proof in 2007, and GAO's report says efforts to assess the accuracy and effectiveness of the funded programs were required. The findings demand the evidence. The report warns that the classroom claims needed checking. The programs had to prove it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-987: The nation's attic filed its spending plan in 2007 — GAO's report reviews the Archives' budget for guarding America's paper memory. The findings check the dollars behind the documents, from vaults to reading rooms. History's keeper, the report implies, deserves books as orderly as its shelves.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-187: This 2008 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at supply Chain Security: Examinations of High-Risk Cargo at Foreign Seaports Have Increased, but Improved Data Collection and Performance Measures Are Needed. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-287: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on freight Transportation: National Policy and Strategies Can Help Improve Freight Mobility. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-87: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on medicaid Demonstration Waivers: Recent HHS Approvals Continue to Raise Cost and Oversight Concerns. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gebelin-monde-primitif-vol8-1787:
Tarot history starts in print in 1787, inside the eighth volume of Antoine Court de Gébelin's Monde primitif. His dissertation Du Jeu des Tarots, printed among mixed essays with six plates, first claimed the cards came from ancient Egypt. Court de Gébelin compared the modern world with the primitive one across his huge, unfinished work.

The claim had no proof, yet it launched two centuries of tarot lore at a stroke. Every later writer on the cards' hidden meaning answers Gébelin, knowingly or not. The French text of Tome VIII thus stands as the founding document of tarot history, the spring of the whole occult tradition of the pack.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib5-1587:
Gesner died in 1565, but his Historiae animalium still lacked its serpents. Other hands completed this fifth volume on the nature of serpents, and it appeared in 1587. Snakes, lizards, and dragons of report close the great Renaissance survey of animals, faithful to its founder's vast plan.

The entries follow Gesner's own method of names, pictures, habits, and authorities. Real vipers share the pages with winged serpents drawn from travelers' tales. The editors gathered what Gesner left and added what they could find. With this volume the most ambitious animal book of its age stands complete. Its mix of care and credulity captures its century perfectly.
gibson-monsters-of-the-sea-1887:
John Gibson ranged the whole sea monster shelf in Monsters of the Sea, printed in 1887. His survey runs from the kraken and the sea serpent to the giant squid. Gibson writes for the broad Victorian reader who loved a wonder with a fact in it.

He marks each tale as legend or as truth, and tells why he judges it so. The book hops from Norse myth to fresh reports from steamship decks. Its charm is its range: the deep as one great cabinet of beasts. The volume is the era's popular guide to the monsters of the sea.
gurney-tertium-quid-1887:
Edmund Gurney seeks a third path in Tertium Quid, his book of tales of thought from 1887. The name means a third thing. Gurney, a chief of the new study of ghosts, balks at two camps: fraud or ghosts. His tracts on trance, dreams that wound, and thought leaps hunt a mid law that could make sense of the scraps that stand firm.

His prose is keen, fair, and hard to fault. Death cut his work short a year past this book. The field lost its best mind young. These tracts are its base in thought.
hardy-woodlanders-1887:
Thomas Hardy published The Woodlanders in 1887, setting it in the deep woods of Little Hintock in Wessex. Hardy called it one of his favorite novels. The story grows out of the timber trade, apple orchards, and cider making of a small woodland village.

Grace Melbury, educated beyond her village, returns home torn between two men. Giles Winterborne, the faithful woodsman who loves her, has lost his houses and standing. The charming doctor Fitzpiers wins her hand instead, then proves feckless and unfaithful. Hardy tracks the damage through the seasons. The novel is a tender, sorrowful study of class, love, and loyalty among trees.
hartmann-life-of-paracelsus-1887:
Franz Hartmann brought a famed healer back to life in The Life of Paracelsus, his life tale of 1887. Paracelsus was a bold Swiss healer of the age past Luther. He scorned old books, healed with new drugs, and roamed from town to town in search of truth.

Hartmann reads him as a mage as well as a healer. He draws on the healer's own books and old tales of his cures. Fans of the occult in England had scant on him in their tongue. Hartmann's tale filled that gap and made him a hero. The healer's cures were famed and fought in his own day. Hartmann sides with the famed tales, yet keeps the man's grit in view.
heine-prose-writings-1887:
Havelock Ellis edited this selection of Heine's prose in 1887, drawn from across his career. The Travel Pictures, or Reisebilder, mix journeys in Germany and Italy with jokes, dreams, and sudden deep feeling. The Romantic School judges Germany's recent writers with wit that spared no reputation, including Heine's own friends.

Florentine Nights tells eerie tales in a sickroom frame, full of art and ghosts. The Gods in Exile imagines the old pagan gods hiding in a Christian world. Ellis chose the pieces that show Heine the prose ironist at full stretch. The result is a sharp, funny, melancholy tour of his mind. English readers met modern German prose largely through volumes like this one.
hitopadesa-wilkins-1787:
Charles Wilkins gave England the Hitopadesa in 1787, the first English version of the Sanskrit fable set. The Sanskrit title page names the sage Vishnu Sharma as its source. Wilkins had learned Sanskrit in India and printed the book at Bath.

A king hires the sage to teach his dull sons the art of wise rule. The sage uses beast tales, each with a moral in verse. Foxes, lions, and birds show how trust, greed, and haste play out. These shrewd tales taught princes and pleased plain readers alike. Wilkins also made the first Sanskrit grammar in English.
hugo-les-miserables-hapgood-1887:
Victor Hugo wrote Les Misérables in French, and Isabel Florence Hapgood made it English in 1887. Hapgood's full version became the standard public-domain English text of the vast novel. Hugo built the book over decades and published it to worldwide fame in 1862.

Jean Valjean, jailed nineteen years for stealing bread, starts life anew in France. Inspector Javert hunts him for years, bound to law more than to mercy or grace. Valjean raises Cosette, joins the Paris rising of 1832, and spares his hunter's life. Hugo pauses for long essays on Paris sewers, Waterloo, convents, and the poor of France. The novel pleads for mercy toward the poor with unmatched scope and heart.
io-francisci-pici-mirandvlae-et-concordi: Io. Francisci Pici De auro, 1587. The three books on gold. This book preserves that work. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
jacobi-tollii-fortuita-in-quibus-praeter: Jacobi Tollii Fortuita, 1687. The fortuitous Tollius. This book preserves that work. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lunel-hebr-1018:
Lunel, a town in the Hérault department of France, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn. Its Jewish community was ancient and grew famous in the twelfth century. Benjamin of Tudela counted 300 members in 1166, many learned and wealthy, and praised its academy.

The article calls that academy a dwelling-place of the Torah and names the sages of Lunel: Judah and Samuel ibn Tibbon, translators of Maimonides; Zerahiah Gerundi; and Abba Mari. Mari preserved letters from the fight over science and philosophy. It also records kind treatment by local lords, an arrest of Jews in 1319, and the community’s end. By the time of writing, no Jewish family remained, and only traces of the synagogue survived. The entry mourns a lost center of learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maher-shalal-ha: Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz, meaning speeding for booty and hastening to the spoil, is explained in a stub entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The phrase was the symbolic name given to a son of the prophet Isaiah. It pointed to the sudden attack the king of Assyria would make on Damascus and Syria, as told in Isaiah's eighth chapter. Before the child's birth, God had commanded Isaiah to write the name on a large roll.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marah-lit-bitte:
Marah, meaning bitter, names a desert station of the Exodus in a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. Israel reached it three days after crossing the Red Sea. The place took its name from the bitter water of the well found there. Exodus and Numbers both list it among the halting places.

The article weighs where Marah stood. Candidates include Ayun Musa, Ain Naba, and Al-Gharkadah, springs in the Sinai wilderness. The writers give the rival views without deciding the matter. A Talmudic tradition adds legal weight to the stop. At Marah, the Talmud says, three laws were added to the seven Noahide commands. They concerned courts of justice, Sabbath observance, and obedience to parents. The brief entry joins a geography note to a tradition about the birth of Israel's law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matthias-ben-ma: Matthias ben Margalot earns a two-line stub in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss. Working from Josephus, the entry says only that Matthias joined Judah ben Zippori in instigating an uprising against Herod the Great. It cites the seventeenth book of the Antiquities and the first book of the Jewish War. Then it sends the reader to the article on Judah ben Zippori for the story itself. Nothing else about the man is recorded here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-me-iri-menahem-:
Menahem ben Solomon Me'iri was a Provençal Talmudist and commentator. Solomon Schechter and Isaac Broydé profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Perpignan in 1249 and died there in 1306. In Provençal he was known as Don Vidal Solomon, and he studied under Reuben ben Hayyim of Narbonne. The entry ranks him among the most brilliant commentators of the Middle Ages, praising the clarity, brevity, and logical temper of his writing.

His great work, “Bet ha-Behirah,” comments on most of the Talmud. The entry lists which parts had reached print over the centuries. It also records his treatise on repentance, his work on writing Torah scrolls, and three lost books. Most striking is his stand in the fight over philosophy. Asked to join a ban against the secular sciences, Me'iri answered with a letter defending science, conceding only that Talmud should be mastered first.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menstruation-10:
Menstruation is treated as a question of statistics in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Joseph Jacobs and Maurice Fishberg wrote the article. They compare the age of first menstruation across peoples. Climate matters, they note. The onset ranges from eleven in hot countries to fifteen in cold. But the investigators quoted conclude that race matters most. Oppenheim studied Bulgarian, Turkish, Armenian, and Jewish subjects. Lebrun studied a hundred Jewish and Slavonian girls. Weissenberg's South Russian Jewesses averaged fourteen. All point the same way.

The entry prints the tables. Weber's St. Petersburg figures show Jewish girls ahead of Russians, Germans, and Poles. They are far ahead of Finns in early onset. Joachim's Hungarian data set Jewish girls at fourteen to fifteen, between Magyar peasants and Slovaks. Stober's Strasbourg observations found no difference, though they were admittedly few. It is period anthropology in numerical form, assembled from the medical literature of several countries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-ben-sha:
Michael ben Shabbethai, known in Latin as Magister Zematus, was a rabbi of Rome in the sixteenth century and a leading cabalist. Kaufmann Kohler and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. His odd Latin name came from his own signature, where a word for an African place of family origin was Latinized as Zematus.

A legal decision of 1539 carries that signature, the article notes. Michael taught Cabala to Christian scholars, among them Ægidius of Viterbo and Widmanstadt, a sign of his standing beyond the Jewish community. Elijah di Nola, writing in 1555, also praised his excellent collection of cabalistic works, which the entry cites from Perles's studies of Roman Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mitzkun-david-m:
David Moses Mitzkun, a Russian Hebraist born in May 1836, made his living teaching Hebrew and his name writing it, as Herman Rosenthal and J. S. Raisin record in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote both Hebrew prose and poetry. He died at Wilna on July 23, 1887, at fifty-one.

His one named book is Kinnor Dawid, a collection of his Hebrew poems published at Wilna in 1863, when he was twenty-seven. The entry is brief and its bibliography points to the Hebrew periodicals of the day — Kohner's study of 1865, Fuenn in Ha-Karmel, and an obituary notice in Ha-Asif for 1887. A small life, preserved because the Hebrew revival counted its teachers among its writers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-isaac:
Moses ben Isaac Bonems was a Polish rabbi who died at Lublin on November 25, 1668. Herman Rosenthal and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Cracow, he was a great-grandson of Moses Isserles, the famed codifier. He later married into the family of Samuel Eliezer Edels.

Bonems served as rabbi first at Lyuboml in Volhynia and then at Lublin. In the approbations of the Council of Four Lands in 1664, his signature came first. His novellae on the Talmud were printed at Lublin in 1670, after his death, together with Edels' Hiddushe Halakot. The entry shows the standing he held among Polish rabbis of his day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-motta-emanuel-d:
Emanuel de la Motta was an early Jewish settler in South Carolina, born in the Spanish West Indies in 1761. Cyrus Adler and L. Hühner wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His family is said to have fled Spanish persecution to the New World. Educated at Charleston, he became one of its best-known citizens.

Motta's name is tied to Freemasonry in the South, and he is supposed to have served in two wars. After the Revolution he lived at Savannah, where he helped reestablish the old congregation in 1786. In 1790 he was an incorporator of Congregation Mickva Israel there. For many years he led its services as hazzan without pay.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahor-11287:
Nahor is the name of two men in Genesis, Abraham's grandfather and Abraham's brother. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn treat both in the Jewish Encyclopedia article. The elder Nahor, son of Serug, fathered Terah and lived one hundred forty-eight years. The younger Nahor married Milcah, his brother Haran's daughter, and settled at Haran.

Through twelve sons, eight by Milcah and four by the concubine Reumah, Nahor fathered twelve Aramean tribes. Scripture still speaks of 'the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor' when Jacob parts from Laban. Joshua's speech shows Nahor himself an idolater, whose worship his Aramean descendants kept. The article gathers all the texts bearing on both men.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naumburg-jacob-:
Jacob Naumburg was a rabbi in two German towns. Gotthard Deutsch and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served Mayence and Offenbach late in the eighteenth century. His grandfather was Jonah Te'omim, a known author. Naumburg's own books split between print and manuscript.

His printed work comments on the smaller Talmud tractates. Nahalat Ya'akob appeared at Fürth in 1793. Three other works stayed in manuscript form. One gives notes on the Pentateuch, one on the Midrash. The third holds sermons preached across a decade. He delivered them in Mayence and Offenbach from 1770. The sermons run to 1781 in the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nevers-or-11487:
Nevers is the chief city of France's Nièvre department. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It held 27,108 people in the year 1904. In the twelfth century Jews could live there for taxes. Each family paid five sous, each person twenty more.

Pope Innocent III scolded the Count of Nevers in 1208. He had treated Jews kindly on his estates. Jews even held mortgages on Christian castles there. Louis X let Jews return in 1316, goods unrestored. The expulsion of 1394 scattered them to Provence. In 1740 the state barred Jewish traders from its fairs. A fine of 1,000 livres backed that harsh ban. One scholar alone, Moses of Nevers, is still quoted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nordhausen-1158:
Nordhausen is a Prussian town in Saxony. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews appear there first in a deed of 1290. The oldest statutes name them only as money-lenders. The council bore them because it needed them.

In 1323 the king made them his own Kammerknechte. The Black Death brought the fate met elsewhere. A margrave urged the council to burn its Jews. Some were burned, their rabbi among them. Legend says the martyrs danced to the pyre. Badges, escorts, and a Jews' street followed in time. Charles V let the council bar Jewish residence outright. No Jew settled there for good until 1807. By 1903 the town counted 489 Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paoli-betty-bar:
Betty Paoli was an Austrian poet born at Vienna. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Her birth name was Barbara Elisabeth Glück, in full. She was born on December 30, in 1814. She died at Baden, near Vienna, in 1894.

Betty's father, a doctor, died when she was a small child. The family was left in very poor straits by his death. So she had to earn her own bread from youth. For a time she taught school in Russian Poland for pay. Back in Vienna, she joined a princess's house in 1843. She was the friend and mate of Princess Schwarzenberg there. She held that post till the princess died in 1848. Her verse shows deep feeling and a rich mind's eye.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pisa-12187:
Pisa is a Tuscan town at the Arno's mouth. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews settled there in very early times. Benjamin of Tudela found twenty families about 1165. The town crowd often showed the Jews hostility.

Later statutes barred Jews from giving evidence in court. They also forced the badge onto Jewish dress. The Da Pisa family raised the town's Jewish name. Jehiel founded a loan bank about 1400. His house sheltered fugitives from Spain and Portugal. In 1525 it hid David Reubeni for months.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porges-von-port:
Porges von Portheim is the name of a noted Bohemian family. Isidore Singer and Alexander Kisch wrote the family article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its best known member was Joseph Porges, born at Prague in 1817. His father was Moses Porges von Portheim. Joseph died at Prague in 1904.

Joseph entered his father's cotton mills after school. He held post after post in the firm. In 1873 the mills became a stock company. Joseph led its board for some years. His free hours went to books and music. He was known as a skilled cello player as well. The article goes on to other members of the house.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-samuel:
Rabbah bar Samuel was a Babylonian teacher of the late third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of Mar Samuel of Nehardea. He kept company with Hiyya bar Abba in study. A question he put to that man stands in the Talmud. There he is called by the name Abba.

Rabbah worked with Hisda and with Sheshet as well. To both he brought old teachings they had not known. He was well versed in baraitot, the outside traditions. His gift lay in that deep store of old words. The entry lists the places where his name is found. It shows a man prized as a living store of lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rathaus-abraham:
Abraham b. Menahem Manish Rathaus was a Russian pioneer of the haskalah. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. The haskalah was a movement for modern learning among Jews. He died in Berdychev on January 6, 1886.

The article calls him one of Berdychev's first progress minded men. He backed the Russian government's push for secular schools. When Lilienthal toured Russia to promote Jewish schools, Rathaus served as his secretary. In later years Rathaus grew wealthy. He gave support to Hebrew literature. He also stood among the leaders of Berdychev's Jewish community. The short entry links wealth, learning, and reform.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-resh-12687:
Resh is the twentieth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its name may come from its Phoenician shape. That shape resembled a head, called rosh in Hebrew.

The article describes the sound as like English r. Resh is allied to the letters lamed and nun. It sometimes swaps with them in words. Later books write Nebuchadnezzar for an older form. Resh rarely takes the strong mark called dagesh forte. In Aramaic it can stand in for that mark's effect. As a numeral in later times, resh equals two hundred. The short entry covers shape, sound, and number value. It is a compact lesson in Hebrew letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sa-d-al-daulah-:
Sa'd al-Daulah was a Jewish physician and statesman in Mongol-ruled Persia. Joseph Jacobs and Mary W. Montgomery wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He served as grand vizier under Argun Khan from 1289 to 1291.

Sa'd began in the treasury and shone at collecting tax arrears in Bagdad. Made controller of Bagdad's finances, he rose to run the whole empire's. He also cured Argun of an illness, winning the ruler's full confidence. With it he exposed corruption among Bagdad's officials to the khan. He was assassinated on March 5, 1291, at his power's height.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-abig:
Samuel ben Abigdor was a Russian rabbi born about 1720, who died at Wilna in 1793. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His father-in-law, the powerful Judah Yesod, advanced his career greatly.

Samuel first engaged in business, dealing with Wilna's communal council directly. In 1750, still young, he was chosen rabbi of Wilna's old community. His father-in-law administered the office for several years in his name. Samuel later served at Smorgony and, about 1777, at Königsberg. That year Wilna's council moved to remove him, splitting the community bitterly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saphir-jacob-kn:
Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Jacob Saphir. He was a rabbi and traveler of Rumanian descent. Saphir was born in 1822 at Oshmiany, in the government of Wilna. As a boy he went to Palestine with his parents. They settled at Safed. When they died in 1836, he moved to Jerusalem.

In 1848 Jerusalem's community sent Saphir south to collect alms for its poor. In 1854 he set out on a far longer tour. He visited Yemen, British India, Egypt, and Australia. His book Eben Sappir tells what he found. It gives the history and condition of the Jews in those lands. The first volume appeared at Lyck in 1866. The second came out at Mayence in 1874. He also wrote on a false Messiah who arose in Yemen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schmiedl-adolf-:
