Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Adolf Schmiedl. He was an Austrian rabbi and scholar. Schmiedl was born at Prossnitz, in Moravia, on January 26, 1821. He served as rabbi at Gewitsch from 1846 to 1849. There he wrote for the journals Kokebe Yiẓḥaḳ and Der Orient. In 1849 he became chief rabbi of Teschen, in Austrian Silesia.

Schmiedl later held pulpits at Bielitz and his native Prossnitz. From 1869 to 1894 he served at Sechshaus, now part of Vienna. He now leads the Leopoldstadt congregation in Vienna's second district. His Sansinim gives sermons on the Pentateuch. His studies treat Jewish-Arabic religious philosophy. One book honors Saadia and his philosophy's merits. Another weighs the struggle for right in Judaism and early Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sefirot-the-ten:
Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It explains the ten Sefirot of the Cabala. The Sefirot are powers through which God showed Himself in making the universe. The word sefirah first meant number or category. In the Zohar it also suggests sphere and light. The Sefer Yeẓirah used it in a deeper sense first.

The full doctrine took shape in the twelfth century. It rests on the Neoplatonic idea of emanation. God, the Neoplatonists held, cannot act or intend directly. So all things flow from Him in stages instead of being made from nothing. The cabalists swapped the Sefirot for those stages. The first three form the world of thought. The next three form the world of soul. The last group forms the world of bodies. All hang like links from the first, hidden in the Infinite.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shalal-sholal-i:
Isaac ha-Kohen Shalal headed Egypt's Jewish community as nagid, following his uncle Nathan. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. One of his duties was naming judges for the community. He chose them from among Spanish refugees of merit.

One such choice stirred long letters and a famous vow. Shalal had sworn to become a Nazarite if forced to name a certain man. Finding no one better, he regretted the vow, and top rabbis answered him. He proved to be the last nagid, since Salim conquered Egypt and ended the office. Around 1517 Shalal moved to Jerusalem, where he died in 1525.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shirah-hadashah:
Shirah Hadashah, A new song sang the redeemed, is a passage in Jewish prayer. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. The passage shows how Midrash shaped synagogue music over time. Its thread starts with rules for the paschal lamb.

Only circumcised men could eat that Passover sacrifice. Old commentators made circumcision the first step toward redemption. That path ended in Moses' song at the Red Sea. Judah ha-Levi's hymn for Passover's seventh day joins both themes. In medieval practice circumcision often happened inside the synagogue. The hymn was then chanted during the morning service. The entry follows one prayer line from law to legend to song.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sirillo-solomon:
Solomon Sirillo was a Spanish Talmudist of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Wilhelm Bacher and M Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was one of the exiles driven from Spain in 1492. He settled at Safed in Palestine. There he debated a ruling on meat with Jacob Berab.

Sirillo wrote a commentary on the order Zeraim. He also covered the treatise Shekalim of the Jerusalem Talmud. He gathered scattered passages into a Gemara on Eduyot. To that work he added comments of his own. Both works are quoted in Solomon Adeni's Meleket Shelomoh. His notes on Berakot were printed at Berlin in 1874.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-philip-:
Philip S Solomon was attorney-general of Fiji, born in Essex in 1830. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Lee on October 15 of that year. Early in life he went to Australia, then New Zealand. He finally settled in Fiji, arriving there in 1870.

He first edited the Fiji Times on his arrival. He then turned to law and joined the Supreme Court bar. In 1889 he became queen's counsel in Fiji. He served as acting attorney-general many times until 1895. He also sat on the legislative council until his death. He was the first warden of Levuka under its new charter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strelisker-mord:
Mordecai Strelisker was a cantor and Hebrew writer born in Brody in 1809. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He served as cantor at Mihăilenĭ in Rumania. In Brody he learned Hebrew literature under Erter and Krochmal. He died in September 1875.

Strelisker placed twelve literary essays in the journal Bikkure ha-Ittim. He also corresponded with Judah Jeiteles in print. His separate works include a lament for Zalman Margulies from 1829. An 1835 elegy mourned Emperor Francis the First of Austria. It was sung in the old Brody synagogue. A later book gives his father's life and an elegy. The entry records a cantor who doubled as a Hebrew man of letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strouse-myer-me:
Myer Strouse was an American lawyer and politician born in Germany in 1825. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on December 16 of that year. His parents brought him to Pottsville, Pennsylvania, in 1832. He studied law and entered the bar there.

In 1848 Strouse founded a farm newspaper in Philadelphia. Four years later he left editing for law practice. Voters sent him to Congress from Pennsylvania in 1862. He served in the Thirty-eighth and Thirty-ninth Congresses. His term ran through the Civil War years until 1867. The brief entry links a farm editor's start to national office. It also notes his name was once Meyer Strauss. Readers get a compact record of an immigrant congressman.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teitelbaum-mose:
Moses Teitelbaum was an Austrian Hasidic rabbi and author. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He signed his name Tamar, meaning palm tree. That name matches Teitelbaum in Yiddish wordplay. He died on July 17, 1841.

Teitelbaum served first as rabbi at Przemysl. In 1809 Sátoralja-Ujhely called him to its pulpit. There he founded an independent Hasidic congregation. It stood apart from Galicia's Hasidic leaders. In 1822 officials suspected him over prison amulets. Prisoners held for libel had received the charms. He said they replaced the mezuzah against demons. Even Moses Sofer paid homage to his name. His homilies on the Torah appeared after his death. Responsa and Psalm commentaries complete his shelf.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tent-11987:
The tent, the portable home of nomads, is described from Bible times onward. Immanuel Benzinger wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Israelite tents likely matched those of Bedouins in Syria and Arabia. Cloth of black goat hair covered rows of poles.

Goat-hair cloth sheds even heavy rain well. Cords and wooden pegs held the cover in place. A hanging curtain split the tent into men's and women's parts. Mats served as both chairs and beds. A hole in the floor made the hearth. Clans pitched their tents in circles or long rows. The article turns a simple shelter into a full picture of daily life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-treason-14487:
Treason in the Bible takes the form of coups and killings of kings. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Strictly, no failed betrayal of country is recorded. Successful seizures of power fill the record instead. Abimelech slew Gideon's seventy sons to rule Israel.

Athaliah wiped out Judah's royal line and took the throne. Saul treated David's rise as treason worthy of death. David himself executed Saul's helpers' killers. Baanah and Rechab murdered Ish-bosheth hoping for reward. David charged them with treason and put them to death. Joab killed the rebel Absalom against David's wish. Shimei cursed David and was pardoned, then later executed. The article reads like a catalog of fallen crowns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-union-of-jewish:
The Union of Jewish Literary Societies linked Britain's Jewish study groups from 1902. Joseph Jacobs and A. M. Hyamson wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A London conference of literary societies created the union. Its aim was spreading Jewish literature, history, and sociology. Israel Abrahams served as its first president.

Member societies span many districts of the British empire. Each keeps complete local independence under the union. The center helps with lecturers and study material. It published a directory of Anglo-Jewish lecturers early on. Illustrated lectures were arranged for member groups to use. Its Jewish Literary Annual records each year's work. The union also brought the Chautauqua movement to England. Summer gatherings at seaside resorts proved successful.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vespasian-14687:
Vespasian was emperor of Rome from 69 to 79. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He founded the Flavian dynasty. Nero gave him command against the Jewish revolt. Rome's earlier defeat had shown the revolt was serious. Vespasian prepared his army at Antioch in the winter of 67.

In spring he marched on Ptolemais with a huge force. His son Titus joined him from Alexandria. Together they led three legions and many allied troops. Galilee was their first target. Gadara fell, and its people were put to the sword. Jotapata then fell after a hard siege. Josephus himself had to surrender there. The entry follows the war step by step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-washington-1478:
Washington is the Pacific coast state admitted in 1889. Cyrus Adler and T. F. Joseph wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was once part of Oregon. Jewish pioneers likely arrived about 1860. Some came from Victoria, in British Columbia. Others came from Portland or Walla Walla.

Seattle drew the first lasting settlement. The Schwabacher firm opened a branch there in 1869. The first congregation, Oheveth Sholom, formed in 1887. Its synagogue was dedicated in 1891. A Reform temple, Temple de Hirsch, followed in 1899. The entry then lists smaller communities statewide. Each town's congregation and cemetery get a brief note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wheel-ex-xiv-25: Wheels appear in the Bible in a few plain settings. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this very short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Ordinary wagons and chariots both ran on wheels. Exodus and Ezekiel name them in passing. A thrashing wheel worked grain on the threshing floor. Proverbs and Isaiah both mention that tool. Potters shaped clay on a wheel or disk, as Jeremiah describes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolff-abraham-a:
Abraham Alexander Wolff (1801-1891) was a German rabbi who led the Jews of Denmark. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Darmstadt, he knew Hebrew well by the age of six. His father, a merchant learned in the Talmud, raised him for the rabbinate.

He studied with rabbis at Mayence and Wurzburg and took a degree in 1821. In 1826 he became state rabbi for Upper Hesse. Two years later the town group at Copenhagen called him. He took the chief rabbi post there in May 1829. He found the Jews of that city split into small groups. Their old synagogue had burned and still lay in ruins. The entry tells how he drew them back into one body.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yimlok-adonai-1:
Yimlok Adonai is the last verse of Psalm 146 in the Bible. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. That verse opens the last set of praise psalms. It serves as a reply at high points in the rite.

It is the last reply in the Kedushah prayer at all times. In the north rite it heads hymn sets in the rite. In the south rite it is sung four times in a row. That chant comes as the scroll goes back to the Ark. Its tune is a quaint strain kept by word of mouth. Men trace that tune to the land of Spain. In the north the verse was once said in one flat tone. On feast days that tone grew into a full tune form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zucker-marcus-1:
Marcus Zucker was a German librarian and author who made art history his specialty. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on May 1, 1841. For some time he served as chief librarian at the University of Erlangen.

Zucker's books follow German and Dutch art across key centuries. They include a study of Dürer's stance toward the Reformation and a life of Michelangelo. He also wrote on Dutch painting of the seventeenth century and a later book on Albrecht Dürer. With J. Merz, he edited the Christliches Kunstblatt, a journal of Christian art.
john-chrysostom-an-exhortation-to-theodo:
When Theodore, a friend of the young John Chrysostom, left the monastic life for marriage and the world, Chrysostom wrote to win him back. An Exhortation to Theodore After His Fall is that letter, in two parts. It survives in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Chrysostom writes in tears rather than anger. No fall, he argues, is final while a person can still repent and return. He mixes grief for his friend with strong hope for his recovery. The letter shows pastoral care at its most tender. It also hints at the heart behind the famous golden mouth of later years.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-1-thessaloni:
Young converts in Thessalonica were grieving their dead when Paul wrote them his earliest letter. Chrysostom's eleven Homilies on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians take up their sorrow directly. The sermons appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Comfort rests on the promise that the dead in Christ will rise. Around that hope, Chrysostom urges clean and watchful living while the church waits for Christ's return. He never lets doctrine float free of the mourners in front of him. The result is tender pastoral care from a preacher who believed theology must console.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-1-timothy-np:
Church order, the marks of good leaders, and the danger of false teaching fill Paul's First Letter to Timothy. Chrysostom, himself a bishop, preached eighteen homilies on the letter. They stand in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A bishop preaching to future bishops gives these sermons unusual weight. Chrysostom spells out how overseers and deacons should live, handle money, and guard the teaching they received. He also warns young leaders against greed and quarrels. Anyone studying how the early Church governed itself will find this series essential reading. Its counsel on prayer and widows' care shows the same care for detail at ground level.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-2-thessaloni:
Persecution, a mysterious man of lawlessness, and idle members fill Paul's second letter to Thessalonica. Chrysostom answers with five compact homilies, printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The letter tries to steady a frightened church, and so do the sermons.

He calms fears about the end times without letting urgency fade. Then he turns practical: those who refuse to work should not expect the church to feed their idleness. Prophecy and plain duty sit side by side without strain. Brief as the set is, it packs in a great deal of pastoral sense.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-2-timothy-np:
Paul wrote Second Timothy from prison, near death, with the famous words: I have fought the good fight. Chrysostom preached ten homilies on that farewell letter. The series appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A dying apostle charges the next generation to guard the faith and endure hardship. Chrysostom, who would himself die in exile, handles those charges with special feeling. He keeps returning to courage, patience, and loyalty to the message. Reading the sermons feels like hearing one tested pastor honor another across three centuries of the same hard calling. Few sermon sets carry quite this much earned feeling in every paragraph.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-colossians-n:
Twelve sermons take up Paul's letter to the Colossians in Chrysostom's Homilies on Colossians. The letter defends Christ's place above every rival power and philosophy of its age. The homilies are given in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Chrysostom unpacks the letter's wide vision with his usual clarity: Christ as head of all creation and of the Church. He warns against empty wisdom that shrinks that claim. The set is short enough to read in a few sittings. It is also deep enough to reward return visits for years, as readers have found.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-galatians-an:
Two very different letters of Paul share one volume in Chrysostom's Homilies on Galatians and Ephesians. Galatians blazes with a defense of grace against legal rules, while Ephesians lifts a soaring vision of the Church. The sermons appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

The Galatians sermons crackle with the preacher's own passion for free grace. Moving into Ephesians, he slows down to admire the picture of Christ's body joined in love. Polemic and poetry pair naturally in this set. Readers get both Chrysostom the fighter and Chrysostom the contemplative in one binding.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-philemon-npn:
Paul's shortest letter pleads for Onesimus, a runaway slave, asking his master to take him back as a brother. Chrysostom needed only three homilies to preach on Philemon, and they appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Small text, large consequences.

The preacher marvels at Paul's tact: no command barked, just love applied with perfect pressure. Master and slave stand as brothers in Christ, a quiet revolution inside a household letter. Chrysostom draws the lesson out gently rather than shouting it. His three sermons remain a lovely guide to the letter's understated power.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-philippians-:
Joy written from a prison cell fills Paul's letter to the Philippians, and Chrysostom preached fifteen homilies on it. The series survives in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Its themes suited a preacher who would suffer for his own preaching in time.

He lingers over the hymn of Christ emptying himself, in Philippians chapter two, and over the call to rejoice always. Contentment, humility, and courage under loss fill the applications. The sermons feel warm rather than combative, aimed at steadying ordinary believers. They remain a friendly way into both Paul's letter and Chrysostom's gentler side.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-st-ignatius-:
Two festal sermons by John Chrysostom honor martyr-bishops of Antioch: Ignatius, thrown to the beasts at Rome, and Babylas, who defied an emperor. The Homilies on Saint Ignatius and Saint Babylas come from the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Both were preached to crowds gathered at the martyrs' shrines.

Chrysostom tells their stories in vivid, dramatic strokes meant to stir courage in his listeners. He also reflects shrewdly on how martyr tales shape the soul of a whole city. The sermons belong to ancient preaching at full stretch. They make the honored dead feel present to the people standing before their tombs.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-acts-of-:
Bold, generous, and united: that picture of the first Church drives Chrysostom's Homilies on the Acts of the Apostles. He preached through Acts to show his own congregation what the Church was meant to be. The sermons stand in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Again and again he sets the apostles' fiery common life beside the lukewarm habits of his own day. Sharing goods, facing danger, and praying together all become quiet rebukes. Yet the tone stays hopeful, since the same Spirit still works. The homilies inspire and convict in equal measure, which was exactly his aim.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-epistle-:
Thirty-four homilies take up the Epistle to the Hebrews, with its claim that Christ surpasses angels, Moses, and the old covenant. Chrysostom's series is printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The golden-mouthed preacher faced a text as lofty as his own gift for speech.

His preaching rises to match the epistle's heights, moving from high priesthood to the heroes of faith. Moral applications cut close to the heart, warning hearers not to drift away. Ancient eloquence here serves a single aim: holding a tired church to its confession. The homilies count among the most powerful of his surviving works.

Thirty-two sermons unpack Paul's letter to the Romans, the weightiest letter the apostle ever wrote. Chrysostom's Homilies on the Epistle to the Romans appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Romans shaped Western theology, and Chrysostom preached it in the East a thousand years earlier.

He unfolds the letter's great themes in order: sin, grace, faith, and the mystery of Israel. A preacher's clarity carries hard doctrine, while a pastor's heart keeps it close to life. His moral applications are famous for leaving no hearer comfortable for long. Generations have ranked these sermons as the classic Eastern reading of Paul's masterwork.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-first-ep:
A divided church, troubled by scandal, received Paul's First Letter to the Corinthians, and Chrysostom preached on it in forty-four homilies. His series includes the well-loved reading of the hymn to love in chapter thirteen. The text comes through the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Factions, lawsuits, and loose morals in Corinth sounded much like problems in Chrysostom's own city. He answers with equal parts rebuke and encouragement, never letting the congregation off easily. His treatment of the resurrection chapter stands out for its hope and force. Few books show practical Christianity preached at so high a level.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-gospel-o:
Ninety sermons work through the Gospel of Matthew verse by verse in Chrysostom's Homilies on the Gospel of Saint Matthew. The set counts as the largest surviving commentary on a Gospel from the early Church. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition presents the full series.

Chrysostom first explains the text with unmatched clarity, then turns it on daily life without mercy. Wealth, pride, and hypocrisy all come under fire from the pulpit. Ordinary hearers were expected to follow long arguments and apply them at home. For fifteen centuries, preachers and readers treated these homilies as the standard guide to the first Gospel.

Eighty-eight homilies guide hearers through the Fourth Gospel, from its soaring prologue to the resurrection scenes. Chrysostom's Homilies on the Gospel of Saint John appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The series was preached to ordinary congregations, not scholars alone.

Signs, long talks, and the farewell words of Jesus all receive patient attention. Against heretics the preacher stands firm; toward seekers he stays gentle and clear. Daily life is never far away, since each doctrine lands in some duty or comfort. This set long held the place of a gold standard for preaching on John.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-second-e:
Paul's Second Letter to the Corinthians is his most personal letter, and Chrysostom answers it with thirty warm homilies. The series is printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. Suffering and comfort run through both the letter and the preaching on it.

Chrysostom draws out the apostle's heart: his hardships, his tears, and his tender appeals to a church that doubted him. Weakness made strong becomes the thread that ties the sermons together. A preacher who knew exile himself handles Paul's pain with special sympathy. These homilies console readers who have known hardship in any century.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-the-statues-:
Riots in Antioch in 387 smashed the emperor's statues, and the city waited in terror for punishment to fall. Week after week, John Chrysostom preached to the frightened crowds, producing the twenty-one Homilies on the Statues. They appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

A political crisis becomes, in his hands, a long lesson on repentance, anger, and God's mercy. He rebukes the rioters, steadies the fearful, and begs the city to change before judgment comes. Preaching rarely gets more urgent than a sermon series delivered under threat of an army. The homilies made his name across the empire.
john-chrysostom-homilies-on-titus-npnf1-:
Crete needed elders appointed, false teachers silenced, and households taught how grace trains people to live well. Paul's short letter to Titus covers all of it, and Chrysostom preached six homilies on the text. They appear in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

From a compact epistle, the preacher draws practical lessons for church life at every level. Sound teaching, self-control, and good works done quietly fill his applications. The sermons move fast and waste few words. They carry the trademark moral energy that made Chrysostom's preaching famous, applied to the ordinary duties of a small island church.
john-chrysostom-homily-concerning-lowlin:
One sermon carries Chrysostom's whole moral medicine in a single dose: the Homily Concerning Lowliness of Mind. Its subject is humility, preached with his trademark directness. The text appears in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

Pride, he argues, sits at the root of nearly every sin. The humble tax collector of Jesus's parable goes home right with God, while the boasting Pharisee does not. Chrysostom aims the lesson at respectable churchgoers who need it most. Short as it is, the homily leaves readers with a clear test for their own hearts. It also shows how much weight one short sermon can carry when the preacher wastes no words at all.
john-chrysostom-instructions-to-catechum:
In the weeks before Easter baptism, John Chrysostom preached a course of sermons to new converts. The Instructions to Catechumens preserve that teaching for those about to enter the Church. They are printed in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

He tells the candidates plainly what they are leaving behind and what life they are entering. Old habits, public shows, and loose speech all come under his warning. A sense of urgency runs through every address, since the hearers stand at the edge of a new life. Few sources show so clearly how the ancient Church formed its members.
john-chrysostom-letter-to-a-young-widow-:
A young woman lost her husband, and John Chrysostom wrote her a letter of comfort. His Letter to a Young Widow, preserved in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, tries to turn raw grief toward hope. It is one of his most personal short pieces.

He grants that grief is natural and does not scold her for tears. Death, he urges, is a kind of sleep, and her loss can become a path to spiritual gain. Alongside deep comfort he gives practical counsel about money and household affairs. The letter shows the great preacher working as a counselor, plain about earth and firm about heaven.
john-chrysostom-letters-of-st-chrysostom:
From lonely exile, John Chrysostom kept writing to Olympias, the deaconess who had stood by him in Constantinople. Their correspondence fills the Letters of Saint Chrysostom to Olympias in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. She had been his closest friend and steadiest supporter in the capital.

The letters mix practical advice, spiritual counsel, and plain news of his sufferings on the road. He thanks her, worries over her health, and urges her not to lose heart. Readers meet the private Chrysostom here: grateful, lonely, unbroken, and tender. Few ancient letter sets show a friendship between a bishop and a deaconess so fully.
john-chrysostom-on-the-priesthood-npnf1-:
John Chrysostom earned lasting fame as a preacher, but On the Priesthood may be his most searched-for book. Written as a dialogue in six books, it asks what it really means to serve as a priest. The 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition carries the text here.

Chrysostom had dodged ordination himself, and he writes honestly about the calling's terrors and dignity. A priest, he says, must answer for the souls of others, a burden few can carry well. Praise and warning stand side by side on every page. Pastors have read the book for sixteen centuries, and it still makes them tremble.
john-chrysostom-select-homilies-npnf1-18:
No short volume can hold all of John Chrysostom's preaching, so the Select Homilies offer a chosen sampler. Festal sermons, moral warnings, and doctrinal talks sit side by side in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition. The choices aim to show his range rather than one theme.

Readers meet the golden mouth in many moods across these pages. He thunders against vice, speaks gently to sinners, and opens scripture with bright clarity. Newcomers to Chrysostom often start here before tackling his long sermon series on whole Bible books. The selection gives a fair first taste of why the ancient world prized his voice.
john-chrysostom-that-no-one-can-harm-the:
Banished from his city and his pulpit, John Chrysostom wrote That No One Can Harm the Man Who Does Not Injure Himself. The treatise, kept in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition, argues that real harm can only come from within. Exile gave its author every reason to test that claim.

No emperor, slanderer, or prison can truly injure a person, Chrysostom insists, because outer losses cannot touch the soul. Only our own sin does lasting damage. He writes with the calm of a man refusing to be crushed by disgrace. The book's inner freedom sustained him in banishment, and readers under pressure have leaned on it ever since.
john-chrysostom-two-homilies-on-eutropiu:
In 399 the fallen court minister Eutropius fled to the altar of Chrysostom's church and clung there for safety. His enemy the archbishop then preached over him, in public, on the emptiness of power. The Two Homilies on Eutropius survive in the 1887 Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers edition.

All Constantinople watched as Chrysostom urged mercy for the man who had persecuted others. Yesterday's ruler, he told the crowd, now trembles before the altar he once ignored. The sermons count among the most dramatic ever preached. They join a plea for compassion to a sharp warning about how fast fortune turns.
kabbalah-unveiled-mathers-1887:
S. L. MacGregor Mathers, a founder of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, published The Kabbalah Unveiled in 1887. The book translates three key parts of the Zohar, the central work of Jewish mysticism, from Latin into English. It was the first English version of any part of the Zohar.

The three books are the Book of Concealed Mystery and the Greater and Lesser Holy Assemblies. They picture the divine nature through the ten sephiroth and vast symbolic faces of God. Mathers adds a long introduction mapping the Kabbalistic system for beginners. The translation fed the whole modern occult revival in the English-speaking world.
king-gnostics-and-their-remains-1887:
Strange engraved gems, stamped with secret names, angels, and symbols, led C. W. King into the world of the ancient Gnostics. The Gnostics and Their Remains, published in 1887, catalogs those magical seals and uses them to explain Gnostic religion. It was the founding English survey of its subject.

King treats the gems as documents, reading whole systems of belief off tiny stones. Basilideans, Ophites, and other sects take shape through their amulets and invocations. Part archaeology and part religious history, the book defined its field for decades. Its plates still fascinate, and its Victorian enthusiasm is catching. Later scholars corrected much, but they all started where King began.
kirwan-essay-on-phlogiston-1787:
Richard Kirwan, an Irish chemist, gave the phlogiston scheme its last great defense in this book of 1787. By then the new French school had strong proof on its side. Kirwan knew that proof well and set out to answer it all. He was no crank, but a sound chemist with a strong name in his field.

He held that phlogiston was a real stuff, bound up with the gas called inflammable air. He dealt with acids too, and how they form and change in his scheme. The book was so strong that the French school felt bound to answer each point in print.
la-vera-dichiaratione-di-tutte-le-metafo: Evangelista Quattrami's Italian book of 1587 promises a true declaration of metaphors, similes, and enigmas. Vincenzo Accolti is also named in its record. The hosted sample shows only a library stamp page. The title alone grounds the work's aim and era. It is a late Renaissance guide to figurative speech and hidden meanings. Such guides helped readers unlock poetry, emblems, and sacred texts.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-1-1887:
Henry Charles Lea was a Philadelphia publisher who became America's great historian of the church's dark side. His History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages appeared in 1887. This first volume lays the ground: the rise of heresy, the church's turn to force, and the building of the tribunal. It is the foundation of modern Inquisition studies.

Lea traces the Albigensian Crusade, the papal inquisitors, and the rules of procedure: secret charges, no counsel, torture by law. He works from the records themselves, in a cool and damning style. France and Italy are his chief ground in this volume. The book made his name on both sides of the Atlantic.
lea-inquisition-middle-ages-vol-2-1887:
The second volume of Henry Charles Lea's History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages, from 1887, follows the tribunal across Europe. Lea wrote from printed records and archives with a lawyer's care for proof. His subject here is the Inquisition at work in Spain's neighbor lands, Italy, and Germany, among other fields.

He treats the Spanish peninsula before its own great tribunal rose, the Italian cities, and the German lands where the inquisitor Conrad of Marburg spread terror. Sorcery and witchcraft enter, as the church begins to hunt them with the heretics. Lea's calm tone makes the burnings and confiscations hit harder. The volume widens his map of fear.
leopardi-poems-townsend-1887:
Frederick Townsend translated the poems of Giacomo Leopardi into English in 1887. Leopardi, who died young in 1837, wrote the lyrics known in Italy as the Canti. Townsend's volume holds that lyric work complete; Leopardi's prose dialogues are staged apart from it in the library.

The poems speak to the moon, to Silvia, to his native village, and to his own heart. Love, boredom, lost youth, and nature's indifference are his great themes. His pessimism is famous, yet the verse itself is full of sweetness and light. Italians rank Leopardi as their greatest lyric poet after Dante. Townsend gave English readers the whole arc of that brief, intense career in one volume.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Motley's second Barneveld volume opens amid the crisis of 1609 and 1610. Its second chapter turns to Henry IV of France and his passion. The king pursued Margaret de Montmorency, wife of the Prince of Condé. The couple fled to the Netherlands, enraging the king.

Spain intrigued around the fugitives while Brussels entertained them splendidly. France sent De Coeuvres to demand their return from the Archdukes. The young Dutch Republic stood in a delicate, dangerous position. Motley weaves private scandal into the machinery of coming war. Spain's intrigues and Spinola's splendid entertainments fill the Brussels scenes. The Republic's difficult position deepens as French rage grows around it.
lotze-outlines-logic-1887:
Ladd translated Lotze's Outlines of Logic, with his encyclopaedia of philosophy, into English in 1887. Hermann Lotze had taught at Göttingen for decades, and his lecture outlines distilled his system for students. Logic comes first in that system, since every other branch of philosophy depends on how we think.

The Outlines present logic not as a bare game of forms but as the study of thought aiming at truth. Lotze adds a survey of the whole circle of philosophy, placing logic, metaphysics, ethics, and aesthetics in their proper order. Ladd's version made the German master's classroom available to English readers. The volume helped form a bridge from German idealism to the new logic being built in Britain and America, and it was widely used as a textbook.
loudun-devils-1887:
Des Niau saw the strange events at Loudun and wrote them down, and his tale reached English readers in 1887. Goldsmid turned the French text into English for this book. The case centers on a group of Ursuline nuns in a small French town.

The nuns said demons had seized them, and crowds came to watch the rites used to drive the spirits out. At the heart of it stands Urbain Grandier, a priest put on trial in 1634 and put to death. Few tales show so well how fear, faith, and law can mix.
mallarme-poesies-french-1887:
Stéphane Mallarmé published his Poésies in 1887, gathering the poems of his career to that date. The text here is the French original. Mallarmé led the Symbolist movement in France, and his poems favor suggestion over plain statement, music over argument.

Among the best-known pieces are 'L'Après-midi d'un faune,' about a faun's drowsy afternoon dream, and the swan sonnet of a bird trapped in ice. His verse is dense, polished, and hard to unlock on a first reading. Patient readers find exact, haunting images of absence, purity, and art itself. The Poésies mark the high point of Symbolist poetry in French.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette:
Volume four of Campan's memoirs opens at chapter eleven, with royal guests. Northern sovereigns took a fancy for travel in those years. The Grand Duke of Russia and his wife reach Versailles in 1782.

They travel as the Comte and Comtesse du Nord for the visit. The Queen greets them on May 20 with grace and dignity. She owns, in private, that queenship is hardest before fellow sovereigns. Dinners, fetes, and much ceremony fill the weeks of their stay. The King of Sweden shares the honours of that season's fetes. Both guests were handled with more stiff form than the Emperor got.
michaelis-majeri-secretioris-naturae-sec:
Michael Maier's searching study of nature's chemical secrets appeared in this edition in 1687. The work had first been published in 1618 under the title Atalanta Fugiens. It is divided into fifty emblems. Each emblem joins a motto, an engraved picture, an epigram, and a discourse.

The plates were engraved by Matthaeus Merian, whose images made the book famous. Maier, a physician and imperial count, wrote for readers born to higher studies. His emblems hide chemical doctrine inside myth, especially the fleeing Atalanta. Scholars of alchemy still treat the volume as one of the art's most beautiful books.
michelson-morley-relative-motion-ether-1:
Albert A. Michelson and Edward W. Morley ran the famed ether test at Cleveland in 1887. Their tool was far finer than the one Michelson used at Potsdam in 1881. They floated the stone base on mercury so it could turn with no jar or shake.

As the base turned, the light bands should have crept if the Earth moved through the ether. They did not creep at all, in test after test, at all times of year. The blank result is the most famed failed trial in physics, and relativity grew from it.
nachtrag-originalschriften-1787:
The Nachtrag of 1787 is the Bavarian government's supplement to its first publication of Illuminati papers. Its long title promises further original writings concerning the Illuminati sect in general. More seized material followed the first volume within the same year, completing the documentary record of the order's suppression.

The supplement prints papers of Zwackh, the order's second figure, and others of its archive. Internal quarrels, membership plans, and the machinery of the grades appear in the members' own words. Published by the men who destroyed the order, the volume is hostile in intent and priceless in content. Together the two 1787 publications give the archive of a secret society, opened by its enemies for all to read.
northwest-ordinance-1787:
The Congress of the Confederation passed the Northwest Ordinance in July 1787, the old Congress's noblest achievement. The law governed the lands northwest of the Ohio River, the young republic's first great western territory. It had to answer hard questions: would new lands be colonies, or equals? Would slavery follow the flag west?

The ordinance bars slavery forever from the territory, a clause that shaped the map of free and slave states for decades. It sets aside land in each township for public schools and promises fair dealing, often broken, with Native nations. Above all, it lays down the path by which territories become states on full equality with the original thirteen. The charter under which the American West was born governed the making of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, and Wisconsin.
openalex-w1557481987:
Adrián Cortés, Matthew Brown, and many co-authors wrote this study. It appeared in Nature Communications in May 2015. Ankylosing spondylitis is a heritable inflammatory arthritis, they note. A gene variant called HLA-B27 is its major risk factor. Its exact role in the disease stays unclear.

The team genotyped thousands of immune gene markers. They studied over twenty thousand cases and controls together. Several other HLA-B variants also changed disease risk, they found. Independent links appeared in three other immune loci. A variant in ERAP1 mattered beyond B27 carriers alone. The results show the genetics are complex and interacting.
openalex-w1997664087:
Ivo Mueller, Simone Widmer, Daniela Michel and colleagues measured malaria infections in Papua New Guinea. Their paper appeared in Malaria Journal in 2009. Standard microscope checks can miss infections. The team asked how much malaria a more sensitive test would find.

They compared microscope checks with a sensitive lab test in fifteen villages. The villages were in the central Sepik area. The lab test found far more infections with all four human malaria species. Mixed infections with more than one species were also more common. Infection patterns also shifted by age group. Nearby villages differed less than microscope results had suggested. Sensitive tests give a fuller picture for malaria control.
openalex-w2120530887:
Catriona Margaret Steele, Woroud Abdulrahman Alsanei, Sona Ayanikalath, and colleagues published this review in Dysphagia in 2014. They asked how changing food texture and thickening liquids affects swallowing. The question matters for people with swallowing problems, called dysphagia. Such changes are a common treatment, yet clinics shared no single set of terms.

The team searched widely and screened more than ten thousand articles. They then reviewed hundreds of papers in full. Only thirty-six directly compared swallowing across at least two textures or thicknesses. Their summary pulled out key trends for thicker liquids. It also showed why the field needs one common naming system.
openalex-w2128360087:
Yan Zhang, Héctor Romero, Gustavo Salinas, and Vadim Gladyshev published this study in Genome Biology in 2006. They traced how bacteria gain and lose the use of selenocysteine, an unusual amino acid that carries the element selenium. Cells insert it by recoding a stop signal, using a special set of machinery.

Comparing bacterial genomes, the authors describe a moving balance. Lineages often lose selenoproteins, the proteins that contain this amino acid. At the same time, new selenocysteine sites can evolve from cysteine, a related amino acid that already handles redox work. The study shows selenium use in bacteria is not fixed, but keeps shifting over evolution.
openalex-w2254226187:
B. Abbott and colleagues in the LIGO and Virgo collaborations published this companion study in Physical Review Letters in 2016. It characterizes the source of GW150914, the first detected gravitational-wave event. The signal came from two black holes merging far away, and this paper extracts what the wave shape says about them.

Data around the event were fitted with a suite of accurate waveform models from general relativity. The pair proved nearly equal in mass, together weighing dozens of times the Sun's mass. About three solar masses' worth of energy was radiated away as gravitational waves. The merged black hole then rang down and settled. Updated values here correct minor errors in the first report.
openalex-w2473397587:
Emiliano Trias, Sofía Ibarburu, and Romina Barreto-Núñez, with colleagues, published this study in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2016. It tests a drug idea for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, a disease that kills motor neurons and causes paralysis. In the rat form of ALS, dying spinal cord tissue fills with abnormal glial cells. The team asked whether blocking those cells could slow the disease.

They studied masitinib, a drug that blocks tyrosine kinase enzymes, in cell cultures and live rats. In culture it stopped harmful microglia from multiplying, moving, and releasing inflammatory signals. Given by mouth after paralysis began, it reduced abnormal glial cells in the spinal cord. It also lessened motor neuron damage compared with untreated rats. The work points to calming spinal cord inflammation as one route worth testing further against ALS.
openalex-w2562375087:
Marcos Deon Vilela de Resende described the Selegen-REML/BLUP software in this 2016 paper in Crop Breeding and Applied Biotechnology. The program uses mixed statistical models to support plant breeding decisions. Estimating variance and predicting genetic values are essential steps in any breeding program. The name combines the REML estimation method with BLUP, a standard prediction approach.

Selegen handles many plant types, from outcrossing species to clonally propagated ones. It covers different experimental and mating designs, repeated trials across sites, and genotype-by-environment interaction. The software estimates genetic values, expected gain from selection, and effective population size. It tests effects using likelihood ratio tests and analysis of deviance. Resende stresses that it is friendly, easy to interpret, and free to download. That makes advanced breeding statistics reachable for smaller research programs.
openalex-w2610193187:
Sachin Gopalkrishna Pai, Benedito A. Carneiro, and José Maurício Mota, with colleagues, reviewed the Wnt/beta-catenin pathway in the Journal of Hematology & Oncology in 2017. This ancient signaling pathway controls cell growth, movement, and stem cell renewal. It goes wrong in many cancers, making it a major drug target. The review focuses on a newer angle: how the pathway shapes anticancer immunity.

Beta-catenin sits at the pathway's core, and its buildup switches the signal on. Recent work shows this signaling also controls whether immune cells enter a tumor. Tumors that shut immune cells out tend to resist immunotherapy. The authors summarize the pathway's role in cancer and the treatment strategies aimed at it. Blocking Wnt signaling might let immune cells back into excluded tumors. That possibility has renewed interest in combining Wnt drugs with immunotherapy, they argue.
openalex-w2767050687:
Sinéad Kelly, Neda Jahanshad, and Andrew Zalesky lead the ENIGMA Schizophrenia DTI Working Group behind this study in Molecular Psychiatry, published in 2018. It pools brain scans to compare white matter structure in schizophrenia. Schizophrenia is a disabling disorder whose brain basis remains partly mysterious. One leading idea blames faulty communication between brain regions, rooted in white matter wiring.

The group combined diffusion imaging data from over four thousand three hundred people worldwide. That scale lets small, consistent differences emerge from noisy individual studies. As its title reports, patients showed widespread microstructural differences across white matter, not one isolated spot. Myelin and fiber-cell abnormalities found by other methods fit this picture. A shared, worldwide dataset like this turns scattered hints into a firm map. It gives future studies solid targets for explaining how wiring goes wrong in schizophrenia.
openalex-w2799873087:
Roman Thibeaux, Dominique Girault, and Emilie Bierque, with colleagues, surveyed environmental Leptospira in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2018. Leptospirosis sickens over a million people yearly, mostly poor rural communities in the tropics. The bacteria spread through water and soil fouled by animal urine. Telling dangerous leptospires from harmless water-dwellers has long been muddled.

For decades, species were split simply into pathogens and saprophytes. A species described in the 1980s broke that scheme, founding an intermediate group between them. The paper reviews the full biodiversity of leptospires found in the environment. Better identification methods could sharpen diagnosis, which often confuses this disease with others. Knowing which species lurk in local water changes risk assessment for whole regions. The authors argue taxonomy here is not bookkeeping; it steers medicine and public health.
openalex-w3000355687:
Carlos Navarro Racines, Jaime Tarapues, Philip Thornton, and colleagues published this data paper in Scientific Data in 2020. It presents a global database of future climate projections, corrected and sharpened for use in impact studies. Raw climate model output is too coarse, at tens to hundreds of kilometers, for farm and species models.

The team applied a bias correction method, called the delta method, to the standard CMIP5 model projections. A careful self-test showed the method cut model bias by half or more. The database holds monthly high and low temperatures, monthly rainfall, and climate indices drawn from them. It is freely available through public climate data portals for agriculture and biodiversity research.
openalex-w3171366087:
Gustaaf Hallegraeff, Donald Anderson, Catherine Belin, and colleagues test whether harmful algal blooms are really growing worldwide. Their study appeared in Communications Earth and Environment in 2021. Such blooms can poison shellfish, kill fish, and close beaches. Reports of them have climbed for decades, but monitoring has climbed too.

Drawing on global event databases built since the nineteen eighties, the authors compare bloom reports with monitoring effort. As their title states, the apparent global rise reflects more intensive monitoring and newly emerging bloom impacts. That finding changes how trend claims should be read. It also argues for steady, standard records before anyone declares a worldwide surge.
openalex-w7204480187:
Victor do Amaral Gurgel Junqueira Azevedo led a Portuguese-language review, in Brazil in 2026, on laparoscopic gallbladder removal in complicated acute cholecystitis. Acute gallbladder inflammation can progress to tissue death, gangrene, pus, or perforation, making surgery harder and riskier. The review searched five sources for medical trials, studies, reviews, and guidelines from 2020 to 2026 in Portuguese and English, weighing safety, technical problems, timing, and results.

Keyhole surgery remains the reference approach even in complicated cases, the authors find, when guided by the patient's condition, anatomy, and safety principles. Heavy inflammation, adhesions, and fibrosis can hide the structures surgeons must identify, so timely rescue plans such as subtotal removal, or conversion to open surgery, are sometimes necessary. Evidence favors operating during the same admission.
openalex-w7204598387:
Nivaldo José de Moura led a Portuguese-language study, in Brazil in 2026, on learning environments for e-learning today. Working qualitatively from the work, the authors lay out what makes online learning environments effective: personalization to each student's needs, collaboration, interaction, engagement, motivation. Inclusion, all driven by the search for new learning that technological resources enable.

Obstacles also abound, they note. Overcoming them requires ongoing improvement plans that include the active agents of schooling: managers, teachers, students, parents, and society itself. Strategic actions to reduce or eliminate the barriers that trouble online schooling are crucial, the authors argue, if e-learning environments are to prosper rather than merely exist.
openalex-w7212178887:
Marcos Saulo Patricio de Sousa leads a team that tests if bend and stretch track with self-reliance in old age. The group was made of seventy older adults in Urupe, Sao Paulo, all of whom train on a set plan. Their ages ran from sixty to eighty. The team used a sit-and-reach bench to score how far each could bend. A standard test set scored how well each did the tasks of daily life.

Both scores, on the whole, looked good. The group could bend well and live with sound self-rule. But the two scores did not move as one. Those who bent most were not the ones who coped best with daily tasks. Bend on its own, the authors conclude, does not set the pace for an active old age. Health in late life rests on more than one trait of the body.
openalex-w7213509987:
Laura Beatriz Sousa Lopes, as named in the sample byline, leads a review of jaw surgery, breathing, and quality of life. Their 2026 integrative review focuses on obstructive sleep apnoea. A PubMed search in September 2026 kept eighteen studies from 2019 onward, out of dozens first found.

Forward movement of both jaws cut apnoea events clearly and improved oxygen levels and daytime sleepiness. Quality of life measures also rose in those patients. Setting the lower jaw back, used for one bite pattern, shrank the airway on scans. Breathing measures stayed stable for most patients, though a small share developed apnoea afterward. Careful selection and follow-up are urged for setback surgery.
openalex-w7213792287:
Giordana Fell Terra and co-authors analyse measles returning to Brazil as vaccination coverage fell. Their 2026 ecological and documentary study uses national immunization and notification data from 2015 to 2025. Measles is highly contagious yet controllable by vaccination, and it re-emerged around 2019.

Almost forty thousand cases were confirmed in the period, peaking in 2019. The outbreak centre shifted from the Southeast before the pandemic to the North afterward. Coverage for the first triple viral dose fell below the World Health Organization safety target, which the analysis names the main driver. Quiet pandemic years reflected social distancing, not lasting control, the authors warn.
openalex-w7214183387:
Marcus Vinícius Aquino Oliveira and Érick Santhiago da Silva Paiva analyse out-of-court compulsory adjudication in Brazil property law. Their 2026 article takes a 2022 registries law and a 2023 National Justice Council rule as its base. The history runs from a 1937 decree-law on purchase promises to a higher court rule dropping prior registration.

Material requirements include admitted deal types, being unable to withdraw, full price payment, and seller default. Procedure turns on a notarial act, a notice cycle, and registrar review at the property registry. Transfer tax and registry continuity are also treated. Judicial and out-of-court routes are compared in tables. Fee costs, free justice for the poor, and uniform procedure close the discussion.
openalex-w7214623487:
Luiz Otávio Menezes Teles and Paula Ribeiro analyzed decision-making in the tile game Rummikub in a 2026 article, treating the game as a small model of scientific thinking. During a match, players build sets, rearrange the table, weigh risks, and plan several moves ahead inside a shifting system of limits and chances. The joker tile, usable as a substitute, adds a special strategic choice.

The authors discuss how building combinations, restructuring the table, anticipating scenarios, and placing the joker depend on one another, and how experience organizes a player's decisions. Playing well, they argue, calls on logical reasoning, working memory, and mental flexibility, the same executive skills used in scientific work. They also suggest that counting probabilities could test how consistent a player's moves really are, linking casual play to formal analysis.
openalex-w7214779887:
Joseane da Silva Ferreira led a 2026 experience report on Pilates in the physiotherapy of a man with a herniated lumbar disc. The patient, aged forty-six, had a lumbar disc protrusion with bone spurs. He arrived in an acute crisis of back and leg pain, rating it near the top of the pain scale, with major functional limits. Early care combined electrical pain relief, manual therapy, dry needling, and exercise therapy.

Pilates was then added, twice a week for about a year. Over that time the team observed progressive pain reduction, stronger muscles, greater flexibility, better lumbar stability, and a return to functional activities. A single case cannot prove a method works, and the authors present it as experience rather than proof. Still, the report suggests Pilates can serve as a useful complement inside longer physiotherapy rehabilitation for lumbar disc herniation.
originalschriften-illuminatenordens-1787:
In 1787 the Bavarian government published Einige Originalschriften des Illuminatenordens, a selection of the Illuminati's own papers. Police had seized the order's archives from its leading members. Printing them was the state's way of exposing the secret society to public judgment, and the volume remains the foundational documentary source for the order's real history.

Letters, statutes, and plans of Adam Weishaupt's order stand here in the original German. The grades, the code names, and the reforming aims all appear without legend's varnish. Conspiracy theory meets the archive in these pages, and comes away changed. Historians build the true story of the Illuminatenorden on this publication and its supplement.
plos-pone-0000087:
Sarah T. A. Roord, Evelien Zonneveld-Huijssoon, and their team tested a combined therapy for autoimmune disease in PLOS ONE in 2006. In such diseases, T cells attack the body's own tissues. Their approach paired a dose aimed at the specific target of the attack with a low dose of drugs that calm cytokine signals.

Each part alone can be weak or harsh. Together, the targeted part steers the calming part where it is needed, so doses can stay low. The authors report control of the autoimmune response in their test system. The design idea, precise aim plus gentle damping, is a template that immune therapy still pursues for diseases like type 1 diabetes.
plos-pone-0000187:
Yesser Hadj Belgacem and Jean-René Martin published this fruit fly genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. A small gland in the fly, the corpus allatum, makes juvenile hormone. The authors show that the gene Hmgcr in that gland controls sex differences in locomotor activity and body size, acting through the insulin pathway.

How males and females grow to different sizes and move differently is a basic question in biology. The paper ties a hormone gland, a metabolic gene, and insulin signaling into one chain. Because insulin pathways are shared across animals, the fly work offers a model for studying sex differences in growth.
plos-pone-0000287:
Scott Smemo and Justin O. Borevitz published this genomics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, on redundancy in genotyping arrays. Genotyping arrays read DNA variants at set positions, and some probes on them overlap or duplicate each other's information. The authors assess that redundancy and what it means for studies using the arrays.

Redundant probes waste money but can also serve as built-in checks. Knowing how much of an array is redundant helps designers trim waste and helps analysts judge data quality. The paper is a practical audit of tools that powered thousands of genetics studies.
plos-pone-0000387:
Jessica Strid and colleagues tested an unusual route to calm arthritis, publishing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Instead of injecting a treatment, they applied type II collagen through the skin, a method called epicutaneous immunization. Collagen is a target of the immune attack in the arthritis model they used, where the body turns on its own joints.

The authors report that skin-based treatment with collagen held back both the start and the advance of chronic collagen-induced arthritis. Teaching the immune system to tolerate its own tissue, through the skin, could point toward gentler therapies for autoimmune disease. The study adds to work on needle-free ways to retrain immune responses.
plos-pone-0000487:
Kevin A. Edwards and colleagues built a reference collection of fly wing diversity, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hawaiian Drosophila are a famous radiation of species, hundreds of fruit flies that evolved on the islands. The team created a database of wing diversity across these species.

Wings record evolution clearly: their veins and shapes vary between species in ways that can be measured and compared. A shared database lets researchers test how wing form evolves and how it relates to each species' way of life. Hawaiian flies are a natural experiment in diversification, and reference collections turn scattered specimens into usable evidence.
plos-pone-0000587:
Eva H. Shang and Irina V. Zhdanova studied how a mother's cocaine exposure affects the unborn child's body clock, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The circadian system runs daily rhythms of sleep, hormones, and activity. Their work shows the circadian system is both a target and a modulator of prenatal cocaine effects. The drug disturbs the system. The system, in turn, shapes the drug's impact.

A two-way relationship is easy to miss if researchers look only at immediate toxicity. Circadian disruption could explain some lasting sleep and behavior problems after prenatal exposure. The study argues for rhythm as an outcome to measure in developmental toxicology.
plos-pone-0000687:
Katsuya Miyake, Toru Tanaka and Paul L. McNeil proposed a new mechanism for a familiar food poisoning, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lectins are proteins found in certain vegetables. Eaten in improperly cooked vegetables, they can cause acute distress in the gut. Exactly how they poison people was unknown, and that gap is what the authors set out to fill.

Gut lining cells live under constant mechanical and other stresses, and individual cells are often wounded and repaired. The team's mechanism ties lectin toxicity to that wound-and-repair life of the gut surface. A clear mechanism matters beyond the kitchen: it could explain other protein toxins and suggest how the gut normally defends itself.
plos-pone-0000787:
Daniel Meulemans and Marianne Bronner-Fraser looked to a humble sea animal for the origin of the vertebrate head, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The origin of the head is central to vertebrate evolution, but paleontology and comparative anatomy struggle with it, lacking unambiguous intermediate forms. Much of the head is built during embryonic development from two ectodermal cell populations.

Amphioxus, a small fish-like creature without a true head, is their window. Studying its development can reveal what came before cartilage, the tissue that scaffolds the vertebrate skull. Insights from amphioxus suggest the head's parts were assembled stepwise, from simpler chordate beginnings.
plos-pone-0000887:
Tero Harkonen, Karin Harding, Thomas Rasmussen and co-authors studied who died in a seal distemper outbreak, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Phocine distemper virus swept through European harbour seals as a new wildlife epidemic. Studies of disease in wild animals often treat every animal as the same, yet age and sex can change the outcome a great deal.

The team broke mortality down by age and sex across the outbreak. Those patterns shape what an epidemic does to a population over years, not just in one season. Their work is a warning against simple averages in wildlife health. It also gives seal managers a clearer sense of which groups need watching.
plos-pone-0000987:
Eric Griez, Alessandro Colasanti, Rob van Diest and colleagues measured how breathing carbon dioxide stirs negative feelings, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inhaling carbon dioxide can trigger a panic like state in people with panic disorder. What it does to healthy people was less clearly charted.

Sixty-four healthy volunteers inhaled four gas mixtures in a double dose setup. The team report the negative affect grew with dose and shifted with age. A safe lab trigger for unease is valuable: it lets researchers test calming treatments under controlled conditions. Age effects also warn against treating all volunteers as one group.
plos-pone-0001087:
Xiaohong Zhang and Hung Tseng studied what happens to the cornea's surface when basonuclin is missing, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The corneal epithelium, the eye's clear front layer, stays healthy through two processes: cells multiply, and cells stick to each other. Wound repair needs both, finely balanced.

Mice with a basonuclin null mutation, no working copy of the gene, let the pair test its role in living tissue. Basonuclin was already tied to ribosome gene control in skin type cells. Its absence impairing homeostasis and wound repair shows a growth regulator's reach. Eye surface healing is a daily clinical concern, from scratches to surgery.
plos-pone-0001187:
Chronic cocaine abuse is blamed for brain changes that make staying abstinent so hard. Deborah Mash and colleagues measured gene expression in the hippocampus of cocaine abusers, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The hippocampus is a brain region central to memory, including the persistent memory of the cocaine rush that can trigger relapse.

The authors report genes that regulate remodeling of the extracellular matrix, the scaffold around brain cells. Changes in that scaffold could physically alter connections between neurons. Their findings link the molecular side of addiction to the stubborn learning that keeps pulling former users back.
plos-pone-0001287:
The visual world is split in two: each half of the visual field is processed by the opposite side of the brain. Cristian Carmeli and colleagues studied interactions between the hemispheres in the visual areas, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Connections between the two sides are abundant near the representation of the visual midline.

The authors describe a novel interhemispheric interaction: modulation of neuronal cooperativity in the visual areas. In other words, activity in one hemisphere tunes how neurons in the other fire together. Coordinating the two halves is essential for a seamless visual field, and this is one of its mechanisms.
plos-pone-0001387:
Peng Gao, Zeyu Xin, and Zhi-Liang Zheng published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how plants balance carbon and nitrogen foods. Plant cells must keep these two in step to grow well. How plants sense that balance was poorly known. The team worked with Arabidopsis, a small plant used in labs world wide.

The authors pinpoint a gene that makes a protein which tags other molecules. They show this gene is key for the plant's response when food balance shifts. Loss of the gene throws the response off. The finding names a core part of how plants tune growth to the food they can get from soil and air.
plos-pone-0001487:
Wei Li and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that maps the human set of E3 ligases. These enzymes tag proteins for removal or for a change in job, and the tag step gives the system its aim. The team listed about 617 such enzymes and their partner parts in the human genome. Most were barely studied.

Among them they found a new enzyme on the cell power unit, which they named MULAN. It shapes how those units move and signal. A full map of this enzyme family gives labs a shared base. It should speed the hunt for drugs that steer protein tagging in disease.
plos-pone-0001587:
Balakrishnan Ramakrishna and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE trial on a drink mix for severe diarrhea in adults. Standard sugar salt drinks seldom cut stool loss beyond what vein fluids and germ drugs do. A starch that resists gut enzymes had shown promise as a swap for sugar. The trial pitted the two mixes head to head.

Adults with acute watery diarrhea got one mix or the other at random. The team weighed stool loss, time to recovery, and safety. Diarrhea still kills widely where care is thin, so a better drink has large value. Even a small gain per case adds up at that scale.
plos-pone-0001687:
Tapio Mappes and co-authors ran a field experiment on how selection shapes life-history choices in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Negative frequency-dependence favors rare types: when a strategy is uncommon, it does well, which keeps variety alive in a population. Population density can also shift which strategy pays, driving cycles in type frequencies over time.

The team tested frequency- and density-dependent selection together in the field rather than the lab. The full text gives the setup and the animal groups tracked. It also shows how success changed as types grew common or rare and as density rose or fell. Field proof matters here because lab cages strip out the crowding, predators, and seasons that make these forces real.
plos-pone-0001787:
Brian L. Fisher and M. Alex Smith revised the trap-jaw ants of Madagascar in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Species inventories are essential for documenting global diversity and for conservation planning. But inventories help only if the taxonomic work of describing and identifying specimens keeps pace. The revision covers two ant genera, Anochetus and Odontomachus, famous for their snapping jaws.

Working through Malagasy species, Fisher and Smith sorted which are distinct, described them, and built identification keys. The full text gives the species accounts, images, and distribution records. Madagascar's ants are found almost nowhere else, so a clean revision underpins every later study of the island's forests and their protection.
plos-pone-0001887:
Nickolay Neznanov and co-authors compared how two viruses react when a key cell machine is blocked, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The machine is the proteasome, which chops up worn proteins, and many viruses lean on it to copy themselves. The two test cases were vesicular stomatitis virus and poliovirus.

The team added drugs that stall the proteasome and watched each virus grow. They report a split result: the drugs strongly curbed protein making by the first virus, while the second fared in a unlike way. That split shows virus families lean on host tools to unlike degrees. It also warns that a drug aimed at one virus may fail on the next.
plos-pone-0001987:
Annalise Paaby and Paul Schmidt studied a gene tied to aging in fruit flies, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The gene, methuselah, was found because mutant flies with a faulty copy live longer than normal. It codes for a cell-surface receptor, and it became a lead candidate for how aging is set.

The pair asked what the natural variety in this gene does in wild flies. Does each form change lifespan, or death rates with age, in a real way? Lab mutants can mislead, since their effects may not match those of common forms. Testing real variants shows whether the gene matters outside mutant lines.
plos-pone-0002087:
Aisha Farhana and co-authors unraveled a two-way iron gate in the tuberculosis bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Iron is scarce inside a host, and TB bacteria use siderophores, small iron-grabbing molecules, to steal it. That uptake is a principal survival strategy and a virulence factor, so its mechanics are a prime drug target.

The team report a novel exporter-importer system in Mycobacterium tuberculosis and show its role in trafficking iron. A gate that both sends the grabbers out and brings loaded ones in is a neat piece of logistics. Blocking it could starve the bacterium in the lung.
plos-pone-0002187:
Stéphanie Bedhomme and co-authors watched fruit fly mating behavior change fast once a conflict was removed, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Males and females often gain from different mating patterns, a tension called intralocus sexual conflict. It can keep each sex from reaching its own best outcome.

In an earlier study the team had removed female selection pressure in the fly Drosophila melanogaster, freeing males from that conflict. Here they report that reproductive behavior then evolved rapidly. The experiment shows in real time how a tug-of-war between the sexes can hold evolution back, and what happens when the rope is cut.
plos-pone-0002287:
Fabian Saenz and co-authors showed that a malaria protein is required for the parasite to enter mosquito salivary glands. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Malaria spreads when sporozoites, the parasite's infective stage, mature in the mosquito gut and then invade its salivary glands. That invasion is thought to depend on parasite surface molecules.

The team studied MAEBL, a protein related to ones the parasite uses to enter cells. They found its transmembrane form is essential for invading Anopheles salivary glands. A step the parasite cannot skip is an inviting target for interventions that stop malaria before it reaches a person.
plos-pone-0002387:
Cabantous and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Stéphanie Cabantous, Yvonne Rogers, Thomas C. Terwilliger, among others. Its subject is new Molecular Reporters for Rapid Protein Folding Assays. The GFP folding reporter assay [1] uses a C-terminal GFP fusion to report on the folding success of upstream fused polypeptides.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002487:
Pechous joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Roger D. Pechous, Travis R. McCarthy, Nrusingh P. Mohapatra, among others. Its subject is a Francisella tularensis Schu S4 Purine Auxotroph Is Highly Attenuated in Mice but Offers Limited Protection against Homologous Intranasal Challenge. Francisella tularensis is a Gram-negative coccobacillus that causes the febrile illness tularemia.

Subspecies that are pathogenic for humans include those comprising the type A (subspecies tularensis) or type B (subspecies holarctica) biovars. The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time.
plos-pone-0002587:
Abrantes led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Patrícia Abrantes, George Dimopoulos, Ana Rita Grosso, among others. Its subject is chloroquine Mediated Modulation of Anopheles gambiae Gene Expression. Plasmodium development in the mosquito is crucial for malaria transmission.

The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002687:
A 2008 study by David S. Boukal and colleagues in PLOS ONE takes up does Sex-Selective predation stabilize or destabilize Predator-Prey dynamics?. Authorship is credited in the record to David S. Boukal and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Little is known about the impact of prey sexual dimorphism on predator-prey dynamics and the impact of sex-selective harvesting and trophy hunting on long-term. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002787:
Basarab G. Hosu and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was reversible disassembly of the actin cytoskeleton improves the survival rate and developmental competence of cryopreserved mouse oocytes. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Basarab G. Hosu, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Effective cryopreservation of oocytes is critically needed in many areas of human reproductive medicine and basic science, such as stem cell research. It goes on to note a further point. Currently, oocyte cryopreservation has a low success rate. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002887:
Wayne P. Wahls, Eric R. Siegel and Mari K. Davidson reported in 2008 on where breaks form in DNA during meiosis in fission yeast. Long non-coding RNAs are transcripts that code for no protein, and their jobs were long unclear. In meiosis, a protein called Rec12 cuts DNA to start recombination, the swapping of DNA between chromosomes.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors show that hotspots for that swapping are directed to places that express non-coding RNA. That links an enigmatic RNA class to a core step in making sex cells. Geneticists get a new clue to why recombination favors some genome sites over others.
plos-pone-0002987:
Elizabeth Musgrove, C. Marcelo Sergio, Sherene Loi and co-authors mapped gene networks tied to estrogen, c-Myc, and tamoxifen response in 2008. Estrogen drives cell growth in normal breast and in breast cancer. Drugs targeting its receptor work, but cancers often resist them from the start or over time.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team identified functional networks of genes responding to estrogen and to c-Myc. They then related those networks to response to tamoxifen therapy. The aim is a mechanistic grip on resistance, so treatment can be matched or combined more wisely. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003087:
Werner Scherbaum, Christian Ohmann, Heinz-Harald Abholz and co-authors randomized blood glucose self-monitoring schedules in type 2 diabetes in 2008. Advice on how often to self-monitor varies widely among physicians treating the disease. The trial enrolled patients with stable metabolic control on oral drugs.

Two testing regimens were compared in a multi-centre randomized controlled trial. Published in PLOS ONE, the design gives the frequency question a direct experimental answer. Finger-stick testing costs money and comfort, so knowing the useful frequency helps patients and health systems alike. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003187:
Manasee Mankar, Radhika S. Joshi, Prajakta V. Belsare and colleagues propose a social view of obesity in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Fat storage has classically been seen as a means of storing energy. Obese people have been theorized as metabolically thrifty, saving energy in times of plenty to guard against future scarcity. Recent research, though, highlighted many brain, behaviour and social aspects of obesity.
