Zongshun Zhou and colleagues in China followed new leaves of the tea-oil tree through three growth stages in 2026. The tree yields a prized cooking oil, but harvests swing widely, and leaf growth may hold clues to better breeding.

Watching shape, internal structure, and gene activity as leaves spread, grew, and matured, the team saw green pigment rise and light capture genes switch on in step. Networks of genes tied leaf form to the making of oils and other compounds. The work lays out how a leaf becomes a working solar panel, giving breeders targets for steadier, richer oil harvests.
plos-pone-0349587:
Thin seams of wet mud between rock layers often decide whether a slope slides. Zumei Zha and co-authors tested how the strength of such muddy seams changes with water content and grain size, in a 2026 PLOS One laboratory study of remade soil samples.

As water rose, the stickiness of the samples first grew, then fell, then steadied, while the friction angle dropped the whole way. Adding coarser grains lowered stickiness but raised friction. Grain mix mattered far more than water in their analysis: how evenly grain sizes spread, and how the size curve bent, pushed strength in opposite directions. The results help engineers judge slope risk.
plos-pone-0349687:
Ye Deng and colleagues used gene databases to test whether flu infection and Guillain-Barré syndrome, a paralyzing autoimmune condition that sometimes follows infections, share a common biological pathway. Clinicians have long suspected a link between the H1N1 flu and the syndrome. The team compared genes switched on in each condition and looked for the overlap.

Shared genes clustered in immune pathways, and network analysis singled out three hub genes, TLR4, TNF, and ITGAM, as likely connectors. The study also mapped the small RNAs that regulate those hubs and possible drug interactions. Database work cannot prove the flu triggers the syndrome, but naming the shared machinery gives laboratory researchers a focused place to test the connection directly.
plos-pone-0349787:
Mohammed Saad Javeed and co-authors combined three kinds of deep learning into one system for understanding city transport data. Traffic networks pour out mixed streams of sensor readings, accident reports, and outside context, and sorting useful resources in real time is hard. Their 2026 design reads sequences forward and backward, weighs long-range patterns with attention, and maps road connections as a graph, all enriched with live data pulled from outside services.

Tested on a Barcelona accident dataset and a highway traffic volume dataset, the combined system classified transport resources more accurately than standard rivals and also spotted anomalies well. Removing either the outside data feeds or the graph component hurt performance, confirming both earn their place. The authors report fast enough responses for real deployment.
plos-pone-0349887:
Hina Hashmi and a large team wired a small quantum circuit into a classical neural network to catch faults on power transmission grids in real time. Grid faults must be found in milliseconds before they cascade, and renewables make flows twitchier. Their hybrid model reads sensor waveforms with a conventional front end, then classifies through the quantum layer. It was tested on two simulated standard grids and on about eight hundred real fault recordings.

Accuracy topped ninety-six percent on simulated faults and just under ninety-five on real recordings, beating the plain deep learning rivals they tried, with decisions inside three milliseconds. Removing the quantum layer hurt performance, their internal evidence that it earns its place. Quantum hardware limits and noise remain honest caveats, but the direction, quantum layers as specialist components, looks practical.
plos-pone-0350087:
Yan Duan and Yun Jiang led a team that built a new wound gel. Bad skin wounds stall when blood flow and growth cues run short. The gel blends two aids in one. Tiny carriers hold genes for two growth factors. They sit in a gel made from platelet-rich plasma. The team tried the gel on full-depth skin wounds in rats.

Wounds with the gel closed faster. Blood flow at the site ran stronger. Skin glands and fibers grew back in denser form. Tests showed the growth genes switched on as planned. Vessel, cell growth, and cell survival marks all rose. So did the early repair type of collagen. The team credits the blend, not one part alone.
plos-pone-0350187:
Rodríguez and colleagues tracked microbes through cheese making at a Danish dairy in a 2026 study. Small shifts in milk handling can change a cheese's taste and texture, which troubles makers who need steady quality. Three milk treatments were compared across fourteen steps of making and ripening a Swedish-style cheese.

One helpful lactic strain dominated the whole process, while other microbes stayed at very low levels. A spoilage germ with tough spores showed up in two treatments but was nearly absent when milk was finely filtered. A new gene-reading method also sped up spotting unwanted microbes early. Makers can use these findings to pick milk handling that guards flavor and safety.
plos-pone-0350287:
Md Habib Ullah Masum and co-authors designed a candidate vaccine on the computer against La Crosse virus, a mosquito-borne infection that can inflame the brain, especially in children. No vaccine or targeted drug exists for it. Their 2026 design stitches together immune-triggering fragments from three viral proteins into one multi-part construct, then runs the construct through a battery of structural and immune simulations.

The design scored as stable and well-formed, folded into a plausible shape, and gripped two immune sensor proteins firmly in docking tests. Simulated immune responses produced antibodies and memory cells, and the gene sequence was tuned for efficient production. The authors stress that everything so far is computational: laboratory, animal, and clinical testing must come before any real-world use.
plos-pone-0350387:
Two blood conditions look alike: carrying the beta thalassemia trait and lacking iron. Telling them apart matters for family counseling in Bangladesh, where carriers are common. Rumana Mahtarin and colleagues compared forty-seven ready-made formulas and twelve machine learning models on this task, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The test used about four hundred seventy people drawn from a larger screened group. Two new formulas blended the best older ones and performed strongly. A ranking method that weighs several quality measures at once picked overall winners. The authors aim for a cheap blood-count screen that clinics can run before costly genetic testing.
plos-pone-0350987:
Zhihao Xie and co-authors tuned how drones should fly to rebuild a traffic accident scene in three dimensions. Investigators photograph crash sites from the air, but altitude and photo overlap decide whether the model is true to centimeters or warped. Using a two-layer analysis that pairs a plain statistical model with a learning model, they tested twenty-seven flight setups against measured errors.

Altitude and overlap worked together rather than separately, and the two analysis layers agreed strongly, which supports the approach. A sweet spot emerged: flying low, roughly twenty to twenty-five meters up, with heavy forward overlap and slightly less side overlap gave centimeter-level accuracy with stable geometry. A trial at a real crash scene backed the recipe. For police and insurers, the settings turn drone photos into evidence-grade models.
plos-pone-0351087:
Diego Santana and colleagues describe a new treefrog species from Brazil's Atlantic Forest, found in the Serra da Mantiqueira mountains of Minas Gerais. The frog belongs to a small group whose members are split between the Atlantic Forest and the Amazon. The team combined body measurements, mating call recordings, and DNA barcoding to make the case that this population is its own species.

They name it Dendropsophus liliae. Small size, rounded toe discs, a spur-like heel flap, a dark red iris, and a white stripe running from snout to eyelid set it apart from its relatives. It is the group's most inland Atlantic Forest record. Finds like this keep rewriting the map of how the two great Brazilian forests exchanged species across drier land over deep time.
plos-pone-0351187:
Employees speak up more when they believe leaders can actually grow. Ziyi Zhang and Michael P Haselhuhn tested that idea across four studies, in this 2026 PLOS One paper on beliefs about whether leadership traits are fixed or changeable.

Workers who saw leadership as developable voiced ideas more often, mainly because they believed speaking up would work. The link ran stronger for suggestions aimed at improvement than for warnings aimed at avoiding failure. The authors extend mindset research, famous in classrooms, into the leadership arena. They suggest organizations that preach leader growth may unlock employee voice as a side effect.
plos-pone-0351687:
Miao Zhang, Huaian Qian, and Tengfei Ma present this 2026 PLOS One study of company data and honest reporting. They ask whether a firm's data holdings stop managers from bending real business choices to hit earnings targets. The authors used deep learning to read company reports. That gave a data score for Chinese listed firms from 2010 to 2023. They compared those scores with signs of earnings tricks run through daily operations.

Firms richer in data showed less of this trickery. The result held up under several checks. The authors trace two routes. Data tools curb managers' short-term thinking. Data-rich firms also draw more analyst attention, which tightens outside scrutiny. The effect was strongest in firms under earnings pressure. It focused on cost-side tricks. The authors argue that digital spending quietly improves the honesty of company reports.
plos-pone-0351987:
Mesafint Kebede and colleagues counted kidney failures after major vascular surgery at Ethiopia's largest referral hospital. The records covered seven years at Tikur Anbessa Specialized Hospital in Addis Ababa. Three hundred seventy-seven adults were included. Kidney outcomes were staged by international rules. The team then modeled which factors around the operation traveled with kidney damage.

Kidney dysfunction followed about one operation in five. That rate is heavy in a system with little spare dialysis capacity. Most published evidence on this risk comes from rich hospitals. A measured local rate does practical work. It tells the Addis Ababa team how large their own risk is, and it gives other hospitals in the region a first mark to beat.
plos-pone-0352587:
Rocco Miazzi and five colleagues review what is known about cocaine exposure before birth. Their 2026 systematic review searched two major databases through August 2025. Twenty-six human studies followed exposed children from infancy into early adulthood. Isolating cocaine's own effects is notoriously hard. Mothers often used other substances too, and poverty and unstable care shadow the same children. The reviewers weighed findings with those confounds in plain view.

Across ages, exposure tracked with a consistent pattern of harm. Babies showed smaller head circumference and motor delays. Older children showed weaker spatial, language, and executive skills. Brain scans found altered white matter and task responses. Growth lagged, and outward behaviour problems ran higher. Yet study quality varied widely, and imaging samples were small. The risk looks real and broad. Honest science must still keep separating the drug's fingerprint from the circumstances around it.
plos-pone-0352687:
Mastrangelo and colleagues, in a 2026 study, look for warning signs that a corneal transplant of a special thin kind will fail within the first years. The operation, used mostly for a swelling disease of the cornea, replaces only the innermost layer. Knowing who is at risk could guide who gets surgery and how it is done.

The team reviewed about one hundred seventy eyes at a regional hospital, followed for at least a year. About one graft in eleven failed. Four factors predicted failure: eyes that were unusually long, grafts from younger donors, trouble unrolling and placing the delicate graft, and major detachment of the graft afterward. Long eyes also had more placement trouble, which may explain part of their risk. Together the four factors explained only a modest share of failures, so much remains unpredictable. The authors urge extra care with long eyes during surgery.
plos-pone-0352787:
Zhao and Yang modeled a digital twin for a smart city drainage system in a 2026 study. A digital twin mirrors a real system live, letting managers test actions safely. Their five-part model adds data and connection layers to a three-dimensional city model, with a light framework for real-time scheduling.

Drainage is the test case, where live sensor data feed the twin and guide pumping decisions. Smart scheduling aims to prevent flooding and wasted energy. City twins attract hype, so working drainage pilots matter: drains are unglamorous, vital, and measurable. Success there would support wider twin use in city services.
plos-pone-0353187:
Lyman, Hanson, and Longo tested how rest breaks affect chest compression quality in a 2026 study. Rescuers tire quickly during resuscitation, and tired compressions grow shallow. Twenty-three young adults each performed nine minutes of compressions under four patterns, from short work-rest cycles to nonstop compressions.

Breathing effort, heart rate, and self-rated strain were tracked alongside compression depth, release, and rate. Comparing patterns shows where quality starts to slip as fatigue builds. Such evidence can guide team rotation rules, so a fresh rescuer steps in before compressions weaken. The lab setup limits direct claims about real arrests, but the fatigue pattern itself is useful for training.
plos-pone-0353287:
Miguel Valério, Fabio Tamburini, and Michele Corazza published this 2026 computational study of lunar calendars across East Polynesia, including Rapa Nui, also called Easter Island. Island communities kept lists naming about thirty nights of the moon. The team compared the wording and structure of forty-eight such lists from every major island group and built a family tree from the differences.

The calendars split into two families matching a proposed split in Polynesian languages. Valério reads the match as evidence that calendar traditions diverged alongside early voyages and language splits across the Pacific.
plos-pone-0353487:
Umair and colleagues, in a 2026 surveillance study, track which types of dengue virus circulated in Pakistan from 2021 to 2025. Dengue returns in seasonal waves, and its four types take turns dominating; a second infection with a different type can be more dangerous. Samples that first tested positive were sent to the national health institute for type testing.

Of more than sixteen hundred positive cases, about seven in ten were confirmed and typed. Type two caused the large majority overall, with type one a distant second and type three almost absent. Type one briefly took the lead in 2023, then type two returned to the top. Cases clustered in the months after the monsoon, and most patients were men in their twenties and thirties. Most reports came from two cities near the testing center, a bias the authors note. They call for year-round, wider molecular surveillance.
plos-pone-0353687:
Li and Pan, in a 2026 language study, test whether a famous idea about translation holds between two very different languages. The idea says traits of a source language shine through into a translation, more so when the source language carries higher prestige. It was built on close language pairs. These authors use a balanced two-way corpus of English and Chinese.

Statistical profiling found shine-through in both directions, but it was stronger when English was the source and Chinese the target, fitting the prestige account since English holds global prestige. Fiction showed the effect more than factual prose. Comparing with studies of closer language pairs, the authors suggest the prestige effect weakens as the two languages grow more distant in structure. They are careful to call that a hypothesis for direct testing, not a settled law, and they frame translation style as a tug among prestige, distance, and caution.
plos-pone-0353787:
Michael Grasdalsmoen and three colleagues use a huge Norwegian student survey to ask whether exercise protects against depression and anxiety, reporting in 2026. More than fifty thousand higher education students reported how often, how hard, and how long they exercised, and a subset completed diagnostic interviews a year later. That forward-looking design lets the team test whether activity today predicts mental disorders tomorrow, rather than merely tracking together.

Students who seldom or never exercised faced a clearly higher risk of a common mental disorder at follow-up than daily exercisers, in both women and men. Risk fell as weekly exercise hours rose, up to about ten hours, and consistency seemed to matter more than intensity or extreme volume. The younger student group showed the most graded pattern. The authors argue campuses should promote regular, attainable activity as part of mental health prevention.
plos-pone-0353887:
Mette Thrane Øhrstrøm and three colleagues follow Danish kidney transplant patients to see how often their original disease returns, in this 2026 PLOS ONE cohort study. The disease, IgA nephropathy, is the world's most common kidney-filter disorder and can destroy a transplanted kidney years later. The team tracked one hundred and eighteen first-time recipients treated at two centres between 1990 and 2020.

Biopsy-proven recurrence struck about one patient in seven, reaching roughly one in six by ten years after surgery. Younger diagnosis, fast progression to kidney failure, and receiving a kidney from a living or related donor each raised the risk. Recurrence sharply increased the chance of losing the graft, underlining the need for closer monitoring.
plos-pone-0353987:
Janbozorgi and colleagues ran a small pilot study, reported in 2026, on whether the time of day for exercise changes gene activity in the bones of diabetic mice. Diabetes can weaken bone and lower the activity of genes tied to cell repair. The team focused on four such genes in bone tissue.

Eighteen male mice were split into healthy, diabetic, and diabetic exercise groups. The exercise groups ran on a treadmill for eight weeks, five times a week, either in the light phase or the dark phase. Diabetes raised blood sugar and lowered the repair-linked genes. Training improved sugar control and partly brought gene activity back. Evening training gave the strongest recovery for two of the genes. As a pilot, the study is early evidence that when exercise happens may shape its benefit for bone.
plos-pone-0354487:
Mauricio Carvache-Franco led a team of four authors on this 2026 survey study of why people use Instagram. Nearly three hundred and seventy users answered questions about their motives, satisfaction, and loyalty, and statistical grouping sorted them into types. Four drives emerged: curiosity and documenting life, self-expression, socializing, and recreation.

Three user segments formed around those drives, differing in background, satisfaction, and loyalty to the platform. Carvache-Franco aims the detailed findings squarely at businesses that sell or communicate through Instagram and need to know which audience they are actually addressing.
plos-pone-0354587:
Duaa Abuarqoub and co-authors test in 2026 a nanoparticle delivery system meant to help stem cells from young tooth tissue become better insulin making cells for diabetes research. Such cells can be converted, but many die along the way. A growth boosting compound was packed into tiny polymer particles made with a microfluidic method and checked for size, charge, and stability.

Treated cells survived better, showed a higher share of healthy cells, and matured more fully, with stronger insulin related markers. In glucose challenge tests the cells released insulin in a controlled way. The authors present the loaded particles as a promising step toward cell based diabetes therapy.
plos-pone-0354687:
Pierre-Yves Robillard led a team of eight authors studying pregnancy risks in a very large birth cohort, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. When the placenta grows a fetus too slowly, some mothers go on to develop preeclampsia, a dangerous rise in blood pressure, but most do not. The team asked what sets those cases apart.

Drawing on records from a long-running cohort of births, Robillard's group compared cases where both problems occurred with cases of slow growth alone. They searched for clinical signs that mark higher risk. A sharper watch list helps doctors focus close care on the mothers most likely to become ill, while sparing others needless alarm.
plos-pone-0354887:
Min Du and co-authors dig in 2026 for genes that raise risk of the most common skin cancer, working at the level of single immune cell types. Large genetic studies had found many risk spots, but averaging across whole tissue hid which cells each spot acts through. Their method joined cancer genetic data with gene control data from a dozen immune cell types.

Cell level analysis found far more linked genes than whole blood analysis, grouped in a few T cell, monocyte, and B cell types. Each type showed its own immune programme. Because the control data came from healthy donors, the authors call the findings leads needing tumour based checks.
plos-pone-0355187:
Mohamed Khalid AlOmar and colleagues improved computer prediction of how deeply buried pipelines have corroded, a measurement that decides when to dig, repair, or replace. Their 2026 study notes that training data for such models is lopsided: mild corrosion cases abound while dangerous deep cases are rare, so models learn to overlook exactly the failures that matter.

The team generated synthetic examples of the rare severe cases, then retrained four kinds of model, including a deep neural network and a gradient boosting method. Every model improved, and the deep network with balanced data cut prediction error by about a quarter. Better corrosion forecasts let pipeline operators spend inspection budgets where the metal is truly thinning.
plos-pone-0355387:
Héctor Hernández-Nuñez and seven colleagues examine how growing cocoa shapes rural life in Colombia, in a 2026 study spanning four departments. Households there have been redesigning how they earn a living, and cocoa has played a different part in each home's mix. The team surveyed and interviewed more than four hundred cocoa-growing households about their assets, strategies, and hopes for the crop.

Five household types emerged, from dedicated cocoa farmers to families mixing cocoa with livestock, coffee, or off-farm work. Santander's households were best equipped for cocoa, while those in Caquetá were least equipped. Families mostly planted cocoa because their land suited it, it paid, and it was easy to manage. Nine in ten saw a promising future in the crop, viewing it as secure income and a cushion for old age.
plos-pone-0355687:
Guanfang Weng and five colleagues redesign the product design process itself around artificial intelligence, using camping cookware as their test case, in this 2026 study. Interest in glamorous camping has raised demand for better cookware, and the team wanted sustainability built into the process from the start rather than checked at the end. They first structured user expectations through structured interviews and expert ranking methods, turning them into a requirements model.

Generative image tools then produced design concepts under structured prompt cards that encoded those requirements, and formal evaluation methods ranked the alternatives and measured user satisfaction. Function and safety, especially usability and ergonomic fit, mattered far more to users than emotional extras like personal flair. The authors report the AI reproduced schemes faithfully and sped creative work, while noting the framework's edge still awaits proof.
plos-pone-0356187:
Minlong Yan and coauthors published a 2026 landscape study in PLOS ONE on mapping feelings along a scenic road, treating emotion as flowing along a route rather than pooling in places. Most emotion maps chop space into plots or zones, missing how a drive or walk unfolds. Combining panoramic imagery, virtual reality sessions eliciting emotional responses, and spatial modeling, the team mapped emotions continuously along a famous scenic road in Wuyi Mountain National Park.

Feelings organized hierarchically, clustering along the main road and thinning into surrounding buffer land. Most strikingly, positive and negative emotions rose together in the most scenic core stretches, contradicting the assumption that a place feels either good or bad. Several landscape features mattered jointly, with sharp threshold effects rather than smooth trade-offs. The framework gives park planners a finer instrument: designing the emotional sequence of a journey, not just its stops.
plos-pone-0356387:
Jennifer Geis and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE exploring an unlikely liquid biopsy for prostate cancer: seminal fluid. The prostate contributes directly to semen, so its shed DNA should be enriched there, but collecting the fluid is awkward and had kept cohorts tiny. Nearly two hundred eighty men scheduled for prostate biopsy mailed in home-collected samples, and the team extracted cell-free DNA and read its methylation, chemical tags varying by tissue and cancer.

All samples held abundant long DNA fragments. Tissue fingerprints showed mostly sperm and white blood cell DNA, but prostate DNA was present at measurable levels. Simple clustering split men into two groups driven by sperm and white cell shares, confounding region-level summaries, so the team used fragment-level methylation features and found signals tied to clinically significant cancer. Seminal fluid, they conclude, is a workable, unconventional biopsy source worth developing.
plos-pone-0356487:
Meihua Sun and six colleagues catalog a family of hormone-response genes in tomato in this 2026 study. The genes, called B-type response regulators, relay signals for cytokinin, a hormone that drives plant growth, and may also mediate drought responses. The team searched the tomato genome and found ten family members. They mapped them across eight chromosomes, sorted them into three subfamilies by shared protein features, and charted where each is most active in the plant.

Some members dominated in shoot tips, others in roots, and one in fruit, while a few were barely detectable anywhere. Control regions of the genes carried drought and stress-hormone response elements, and both simulated drought and the stress hormone abscisic acid switched the genes down. Given the known opposition between cytokinin and that stress hormone, the authors propose these regulators as junction points in drought signaling, useful leads for breeding tougher tomatoes.
plos-pone-0356687:
Victoria C. Nolan, James Harrison, and Jonathan A. G. Cox published a 2026 laboratory study in PLOS ONE on a bee-free artificial honey that fights a stubborn drug-resistant bacterium. Mycobacterium abscessus causes skin, soft tissue, and lung infections and shrugs off many antibiotics, hitting the weakest hardest. Manuka honey works against it, but the team wanted a synthetic version easing pressure on the natural product, so they tuned their vegan recipe with key enzymes and components.

The adjusted artificial honey did more than slow the bacterium: it killed it outright in susceptibility tests. Two ingredients carried the killing power, the compound methylglyoxal and hydrogen peroxide, both familiar from natural medical honey. The authors present the result as proof that a fully synthetic, bee-derived-nothing honey can match the antimicrobial punch needed against this pathogen. A manufactured alternative could make honey-based treatments cheaper and free of supply worries.
plos-pone-0356787:
Yubin Xue, Hongwei Ma, Lin Yang, and Qiang Liu used Global Burden of Disease estimates to track hearing loss caused by otitis media. Otitis media is a middle ear infection common in childhood. Their study covered the whole world from 1990 to 2023. It compared countries by age, sex, and development level. It also separated how much of the change came from population growth, aging, and shifting illness rates.

Age-adjusted prevalence eased downward over the three decades. Yet it stayed highest in poorer regions and among children aged five to fourteen. Boys were affected more than girls. Most cases were mild, and no country showed a clear rise. The results point prevention efforts toward young children in low-income settings, where treatable ear infections still cost the most hearing.
plos-pone-0356887:
Wannes Nauwynck, Karoline Faust, and Nico Boon published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on screening microbes one cell at a time without exotic equipment. Individual cells in a species differ, shaping how communities survive stress, but existing single-cell tools are pricey or fiddly. Their workflow, DE-SWIRL, grows single cells inside uniform double-emulsion droplets made by a simple templating trick, then sorts the droplets with a standard fluorescence cell sorter found in many laboratories.

The team showed droplets of two sizes form reliably, with just under half surviving the process, and they worked out a gating strategy that keeps contaminating particles from corrupting the screen. From a synthetic community they pulled out chosen strains at near-perfect purity, and isolated droplet cocultures from a mixed community. Each run handles around ten million microcultures, making the workflow a cheap route to hunting rare, useful microbes in whole microbiomes.
plos-pone-0356987:
Yusif Gurbanli, Jaron Mohammed, and Francesco Travascio reviewed thirty years of attempts to rebuild the knee in three dimensions from ordinary flat X-rays, avoiding the radiation and cost of CT scans. Their 2026 systematic review gathered twenty-eight studies spanning shape statistics, deep learning, and image registration methods, comparing accuracy, image needs, and speed.

Accuracy improved dramatically over the period, with recent methods landing within roughly half a millimeter to a millimeter of CT truth, and two standard views often sufficed. Processing now takes from under a second to a few minutes. The review's complaints are about evidence quality: small patient groups, few diseased knees, and no shared public benchmark. Still, the trajectory points toward routine X-ray-based surgical planning.
plos-pone-0357087:
Jeremy T Claisse and colleagues produced fine-grained sonar maps of thirteen artificial reef complexes and shipwrecks off southern California, resolving the seafloor into hand-sized cells. Their 2026 study classified 154 reef modules and measured each one's footprint, volume, height, slope, and surface roughness, then asked whether those numbers reflect what the reef was built from.

They do. Quarry rock piles stood tall, steep, and rough within compact footprints, while scattered concrete pieces sprawled flatter with patchier roughness, and their fuzzy edges made footprints harder to draw. Because fish and invertebrates respond to exactly these structural traits, the maps let reef designers match construction materials to ecological goals and give managers a baseline for tracking change.
plos-pone-0357287:
Cecilia Rago led a team of eight authors describing virus tracking dashboards for England, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Family doctors and public health teams need current intelligence on respiratory viruses, not reports that arrive weeks late. The dashboards turn lab results into near-live views of where flu and related viruses are surging.

Rago's group set out how the dashboards serve both primary care and public health users. A GP can see local virus pressure before a clinic fills, and officials can target messages or resources. Timely displays proved their worth during past virus seasons. This work shows how routine lab data, well presented, becomes a daily decision tool.
plos-pone-0357387:
Jetson Lobos, Jeffrey Velasquez, and Fariborz Nasertorabi published a 2026 methods paper in PLOS ONE on making lab-made proteins and peptides easier to purify. Their approach tags a target protein with an elastin-like chain that stays dissolved when cool but clumps when warmed, so filtering can pull the product out without expensive chromatography columns. Two obstacles had slowed adoption: no standard gene cassette for the tag, and no clean way to remove the tag after cutting it free.

The team built a modular, ready-to-use cassette that works under mild conditions, clumping at temperatures only slightly above room temperature and at modest salt levels. After the tag is cut, its tendency to clump at higher concentration lets it be filtered away from the freed product. As a demonstration, they purified a small human antimicrobial peptide, noting the size gap between tag and peptide makes the trick work best.
plos-pone-0357487:
Drissa Sia and colleagues published a 2026 scoping review in PLOS ONE on how pregnant migrant women without medical insurance reach perinatal care. Missed check-ups during pregnancy raise risks for mother and newborn alike, and uninsured migrants face the steepest barriers. The review gathered fourteen studies from Canada, the United States, Iran, and Thailand since 2000, mapping interventions meant to open access, with their strengths, weaknesses, and costs.

A recurring story emerged around policy cuts: trimming services for uninsured migrants looks like savings, but costs resurface later and larger, landing on regional governments covering emergencies. The authors judge several of these shifts politically driven rather than economically sound. Helpful interventions ranged from dedicated clinics to coverage schemes, but coverage stayed patchy. As the first review of its kind, it maps what exists and warns against false economies in maternal care.
plos-pone-0357587:
Luis Pérez-Mañá and four colleagues grade what YouTube tells parents about controlling children's short sight, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Myopia is spreading, treatments to slow it exist, and families increasingly learn about them from videos rather than clinics. The team searched in English and Spanish in February 2025 and kept two hundred thirty-five videos that met their rules, then had three optometrists score each one with three standard quality tools.

Quality and reliability swung widely from video to video. University and professional channels scored best but made up a minority of what parents actually find. Spanish videos edged English ones on one reliability scale, while English videos drew far more views despite no quality advantage. The scoring tools themselves sometimes disagreed with each other. The authors urge eye professionals to publish more evidence based videos, since the popular ones cannot be trusted by default.
plos-pone-0357787:
Jingqi Huang and Wasim Ahmad published a 2026 consumer study in PLOS ONE on how artificial intelligence hosts in live-stream shopping shows nudge people into impulse buying. Working within a stimulus–organism–response framework, they ran scenario experiments varying how human the AI host looked and how socially it chatted with viewers. They measured two inner states that might carry the effect: how much viewers trusted the host's competence, and how emotionally stirred they felt.

Both kinds of humanlike cues raised impulse buying through trust and arousal. Chatty, socially warm conversation moved viewers more than visual humanlikeness. The mechanism worked much the same for men and women, though it differed between product types and between viewers with more or less past AI experience. For sellers designing virtual hosts, the lesson is to invest in conversation style, not just a lifelike face; for regulators, the study names the levers of persuasion.
plos-pone-0357887:
Andrew McKenzie and David Yuzva Clement published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a scoping review on social work's role in preventing and countering violent extremism. Governments increasingly treat radicalization as a social care and public health problem, pulling social workers toward prevention work. Yet research on what social workers actually do there is scattered across countries and concepts, leaving practitioners unsure of their footing.

The planned review will be the first to systematically map that landscape: how roles are described, which theories guide practice, and what experiences workers report. It also aims to name the field's gaps, limits, and openings, separating what is known from what is merely assumed. Because extremism inflicts trauma across generations, a clear map matters for social work's development and for the wider prevention field.
plos-pone-0357987:
Thamonwan Imerbtham led a team of eight authors studying blood vessel problems in a hardening disease, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Systemic sclerosis stiffens skin and organs, and when it also raises pressure in the lung arteries, it becomes far deadlier. The team examined how the vessel lining and platelets behave in these patients.

Imerbtham's work pinpoints where the disease damages vessels most, in the lining that controls flow and in the platelets that drive clotting. Those details suggest where treatments should aim. Pulmonary hypertension is the leading killer in this disease, so vascular insight has direct clinical stakes. Patients need therapies aimed at vessel damage, not only at the skin changes that show first.
plos-pone-0358487:
Sa Huynh Nguyen, Duy Phong Nguyen, and Tat Thang Tran published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies myopia, short-sightedness, in a high-risk cohort of Vietnamese schoolchildren. The authors examine behavioural correlates of higher twelve-month progression, meaning which habits travel with eyes that worsen fastest over a year.

The study also tests how far prediction across schools can go, whether patterns found in one school forecast another's pupils. Myopia is rising steeply in Asian schoolchildren, so knowing which behaviours matter, and whether findings travel, shapes screening advice. Eye health planners in Vietnam and similar countries are the intended readers.
plos-pone-0358587:
Luyao Si, Yi Jia, and Xuye Kang wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about young children's movement. It studies muscle synergy during crawling on hands and knees in children aged four to six. A muscle synergy is a pattern of muscles firing together to produce a movement.

Watching how these patterns work in typical crawling gives a baseline for judging motor development. Children whose crawling uses unusual muscle groupings may need support, and clinicians need normal reference patterns to spot the difference. Developmental specialists and pediatric therapists are the readers most likely to use these characteristics in practice.
plos-pone-0358787: Gheibi and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on judging young doctors' professional conduct. They built a questionnaire to rate how medical residents conduct themselves at work. Then they checked its psychometric properties, the tests of whether a survey measures well. Hospitals need fair tools to spot conduct problems early and to give residents clear feedback on how they act with patients.
plos-pone-0358987:
Wangbing Liang and Haoyu Song ask what makes tourists keen to help keep a folk festival alive, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their case is Shehuo, a traditional celebratory performance tradition from Gansu, China, classed as living cultural heritage. From three hundred ninety valid surveys, the authors tested how the ritual feel of the event and several kinds of authenticity relate to support for passing the tradition on.

Uniqueness, ritual quality, and freedom from practical purpose all predicted stronger support. So did believing the show is genuine heritage and feeling moved by it. Two candidates fell flat: visitor commitment and staged authenticity showed no direct effect. No single ingredient was needed. Six differing mixes of conditions led to high support. Revival efforts, the authors suggest, can reach the same goodwill by several roads, provided ritual distinctiveness and honest history lead.
pmc-10354987:
Uliano-Silva, Ferreira, Krasheninnikova, and co-authors introduce MitoHiFi, a Python pipeline for building mitochondrial genomes. The pipeline uses PacBio HiFi reads, which are long stretches of DNA read with very high accuracy. Such reads have changed genome work, giving cleaner and more complete assemblies than older methods.

Cells that use oxygen carry a small round genome inside their mitochondria, and it is sequenced along with the main genome. MitoHiFi pulls those reads out and assembles that small genome on its own. A clean, fast route to this genome helps studies of species, evolution, and disease that depend on it.
pmc-13191087:
Daan A C Lanser is first author on a 2026 study of sex, drug exposure, and outcomes for a targeted lung cancer drug, alectinib. The drug is first-line treatment for metastatic lung cancers with ALK gene faults. Its effect is tied to how much drug reaches the blood, and real-world data suggest many patients, especially men, fall below the proposed target level.

The authors evaluated two hundred and twelve patients, over half of them women, tracking survival without cancer growth and overall survival against sex, blood drug levels, and gene variants affecting drug breakdown. Follow-up ran for about five years. Their analysis links sex to survival through drug exposure, supporting dose attention by patient traits.
pmc-13191787:
Stefanie Modri is first author on a 2026 retrospective comparison of three risk tools for postpartum hemorrhage, heavy bleeding after childbirth. The condition is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide. The authors re-analyzed data from a parent study at a single United States tertiary hospital, with five hundred and twenty-five participants recruited in twenty twenty-one.

By one definition, about thirteen percent bled heavily; by a lower threshold, about thirty-seven percent. A nursing association tool showed the highest sensitivity and the best accuracy when medium and high risk scores counted together. Yet that tool still labeled about a fifth of those who went on to bleed heavily as low risk. Better predictive models are needed, the authors conclude.
pmc-13198787:
Yi Lung Gan and colleagues present a 2026 case report on heart failure caused by a hidden fast rhythm. A rapid heartbeat kept up for long can weaken the heart muscle, a state called tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy. It can strike fast and mimic other organ failure, delaying the true fix.

Their patient was a 49-year-old man with two weeks of palpitations, breathlessness, and leg swelling. He arrived jaundiced with fluid overload and severe acid buildup, needing intensive care and kidney support. Testing traced the rhythm to a hidden extra electrical path on the heart's left side. A catheter burn procedure cut that path. His heart, liver, and body chemistry then recovered fully. Early rhythm control is the cure.
pmc-13203787:
Dangerously low body temperature is an unusual face of lymphoma, and a 2026 case report authored by Phillip Papayanis argues it can demand faster cancer treatment. The article presents a patient with Hodgkin's lymphoma whose on-and-off hypothermia caused instability severe enough to require intensive care.

Clinicians worked through metabolic, infectious, and other causes before deciding the lymphoma itself drove the heat drops. That judgment prompted urgent inpatient chemotherapy rather than a slower start to treatment. Her temperature swings then settled, which the authors take as proof, and they suggest hypothermia with such swings should push teams toward prompt chemotherapy in similar cases.
pmc-13212387:
Claudio Lucarelli and colleagues ask in 2026 whether high-deductible health plans slow the long-run growth of medical spending, not just its level. Earlier work showed spending drops soon after people switch to such plans, leaving open whether the saving lasts.

Using claims from a national insurer across many employer groups, the team compared people kept in high-deductible plans for four or more years with those kept in low-deductible plans. Long enrolment showed no link to slower growth in total spending or in medical services spending. The result suggests one-off savings from cost sharing may fade as new technology keeps pushing costs upward.
pmc-13212587:
Francesca Larosa and colleagues analyse in 2026 how national climate pledges line up with the United Nations development goals. Governments submit these pledges under the Paris Agreement, but climate action and wider development do not always pull in the same direction.

Using an artificial intelligence framework checked by humans, the team read the first two rounds of pledges from many countries. Richer nations stressed system-wide issues such as health, while poorer nations focused on water, energy, food, and natural resources. The authors discuss what these diverging paths mean for fairness, climate finance, and global governance. Their evidence offers an early warning before new pledges are locked in.
pmc-13212987:
Luheng Tang and co-authors demonstrate in 2026 a solar device that turns seawater into fresh water while harvesting nearly all its salt, leaving no brine to dump. Salt crusting and waste brine have long plagued solar desalination of real ocean water.

A laser-treated black metal panel pulls a thin water film uphill, drinks in sunlight, and sweeps crystallised salt from active zones to collection areas by itself. Run continuously for a week outdoors on real ocean water, the unit evaporated water at a steady rate and collected salt at a matching pace. Efficiency reached roughly three quarters of the sunlight used, with extraction near complete.
pmc-13214087:
Wellington Briques, Débora Maria Russiano Pereira, and Aderbal Silva Aguiar Junior write in 2026 a commentary on how reviewers judge cannabis-based medicines for long-lasting nerve pain. Major reviews call the certainty of benefit low, and the authors accept that verdict while questioning how it gets communicated.

They examine the grading framework reviewers use, the mixing of unlike patients and products, the choice of outcomes, and how directly trial evidence matches real practice. Inconsistent or opaque grading can tilt readers toward overstating or dismissing real effects, they argue. Neuropathic pain trials are short and varied, so context-aware reading matters before clinicians or patients draw conclusions either way.
pmc-13214287:
Stefanie Unger and co-authors track in 2026 how parents bond with their babies across the first two years, using a large German community cohort. Bonding trouble is often treated as fixed once present, yet its course over time was largely uncharted.

Following more than seventeen hundred mothers and over eleven hundred fathers at three time points, the team found three paths in each group. Most parents kept difficulties low and steady, one group started high then recovered, and a third worsened into clinically significant trouble. Anger symptoms, a hard birth experience, and a difficult baby temperament predicted worse paths for mothers. Fathers' paths also hinged on birth experience, temperament, age, and first-time parenthood.
pmc-13216187:
Domenic P. J. Germano and co-authors present a 2026 mathematical framework for simulating systems that mix smooth change with random jumps, such as infections that dwindle to a handful of cases. Pure equation models fail at small numbers, while fully random simulations become impossibly slow.

Their method, called Jump-Switch-Flow, couples ordinary differential equations for the crowded compartments with a discrete random process for the sparse ones, and it lets compartments reach true extinction. The authors show it runs at least ten times faster than existing alternatives while behaving like an exact random simulation. Case studies cover public health intervention analysis and timing viral clearance inside patients infected with SARS-CoV-2.
pmc-13218087:
Justin Haller and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a pilot trial of implant strategies for broken thigh bones near the knee in older adults. These fractures kill more than one patient in five, a toll comparable to hip fractures. The usual single plate or nail often forces patients to keep weight off the leg, which slows recovery.

The pilot will enroll 80 patients aged 60 or older at five US trauma centers. Patients will be assigned at random to one implant or to a doubled construct, a nail paired with a plate or two plates. Everyone will be allowed to bear weight right away. Because the study is a pilot, its measures are practical. They ask whether 80 patients can be recruited within a year, whether treatment follows the protocol, and whether at least 85 percent stay in follow-up. Mobility, function, complications, and deaths are secondary measures for shaping a larger trial.
pmc-13218187:
Laura Antolini and colleagues measure the burden of long COVID in Lombardy, the region hit first and hardest in Italy, in a 2026 cohort study from the PASCNET network. Post-COVID condition remains a major public concern, and its frequency may differ sharply between people treated at home and those hospitalized. The team also checked whether a standard research score can forecast who develops the condition.

The study sampled 1,162 adults with confirmed infection between March 2020 and December 2022, including 546 hospitalized patients and 616 managed by family doctors, and assessed them at a visit in 2024. One year after infection, post-COVID condition had developed in 39.9 percent of the hospitalized group but only 9.1 percent of the community group. Modelled long-term prevalence stayed high among the hospitalized, at about thirty-two percent. The NIH RECOVER score predicted later post-COVID condition, supporting its use for estimating long-term burden, though symptoms varied widely between patients.
pmc-13218287:
Mancang Zhang, Yang Hu, Hao Huang, and Yongyong Shi introduce a 2026 synthesis platform called UCOS for building long and difficult DNA strands. Synthetic biology needs large, complex genes, yet chemical synthesis struggles with strands that are long, full of repeats, or uneven in base composition. Errors creep in, and purifying the correct product is hard.

The platform replaces the porous glass support with nonporous silica microspheres. It adds two quality steps: an enrichment fishing out full-length strands using a flank sequence, and an enzyme that removes error-containing molecules. With those changes, the team synthesized sequences up to 600 nucleotides long, including tandem repeats and skewed base distributions, at high fidelity. Because the strands serve as building blocks, the method should speed construction of genes and custom genetic elements. The authors position UCOS as a foundation for synthetic genomics and metabolic engineering projects that synthesis tools handle poorly.
pmc-13219187:
Pieter L. van den Berg and colleagues tackle how to alert responders to out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in a 2026 study. When a heart stops outside hospital, minutes decide survival, and phone-based systems can summon trained nearby volunteers faster than an ambulance. Alerting everyone burdens volunteers with calls they cannot reach, so many systems phase alerts, contacting more people as time passes.

The design question is how that phasing should adapt to information: where volunteers are relative to the patient, and how long the triage took. Solving the problem with dynamic programming gives insight but runs slowly for decisions. The authors recast the choice as classification and trained it on data from Auckland, New Zealand's first response system. Phasing alerts on information improved performance over a baseline resembling current practice, balancing faster response against burden. The work shows dispatch policy is a lever for survival, not just logistics.
pmc-13220087:
Stefano Vecchia and colleagues count the interaction risks carried by patients starting treatment for pancreatic cancer in a 2026 study. Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma strikes older adults, who arrive with many prescriptions for conditions. Every added drug multiplies the chance of interactions with chemotherapy, yet interaction burden is rarely measured in this population.

The study covered 140 patients aged seventy-five and older who began systemic therapy between 2011 and 2023, with concomitant medicine checked against an interaction database and graded from minor to contraindicated. Seventy percent had at least one interaction. Patients split by pill burden, under five, five to twenty, and over twenty ingredients, showed rising interaction counts at severity levels as the ingredient count grew. The burden did not translate into worse one-year survival, less second-line therapy, or chemotherapy choices. The authors conclude interactions are common and worth managing, even if their fingerprint on survival was not visible.
pmc-13220387:
Hamdah Hanifa and a large surgical team report the removal of two giant hydatid cysts from a man's liver in a 2026 case report from Syria. Hydatid disease is an infection caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus granulosus in its larval stage, and the liver hosts up to seventy percent of cases, silently for a decade or more. Two giant cysts at once, in a system strained by conflict, makes the case a lesson.

The thirty-two-year-old patient arrived with three days of pain, a tense abdomen, and raised white cells. Ultrasound and CT revealed the two giant cysts. At surgery they aspirated both, sterilized contents with a scolicidal solution, removed membranes, and took part of a cyst wall while preserving tissue. He left after three days, started albendazole two weeks later, a six-month course, and at follow-up was symptom-free with normal liver tests and no recurrence.
pmc-13225287:
Zhongfu Tang and colleagues evaluate a 2026 study of astragaloside IV, the main active compound of the traditional herb Astragalus, against lupus nephritis. In this kidney complication of lupus, filtering cells called podocytes can die through ferroptosis, an iron-driven death pathway. Lupus-prone mice received the compound, and a cell model of podocyte injury tested the mechanism directly.

Kidney tissue in treated mice showed less damage, fewer deposits, and lower protein leakage into urine. In injured cells, the compound raised protective factors tied to the PI3K/AKT/Nrf2 pathway and restored several anti-ferroptosis defences. Rescue experiments, which block the pathway again, supported that route as the means of protection, though the work remains preclinical.
pmc-13226687:
Salwa H El-Sabbagh and colleagues turn a 2026 waste stream into a rubber ingredient, building an aluminium hybrid additive from lignin recovered in rice-straw black liquor. Natural rubber needs fillers for strength and antioxidants to resist ageing, and this hybrid aims to do both jobs at once. Microscopy and sizing confirmed nanoscale particles that spread evenly through the rubber.

At low loadings, the hybrid cut the rubber's optimum curing time by about eighteen percent compared with a conventional antioxidant mix. Tensile strength rose by roughly forty-five percent, while stretch at break fell. Ageing resistance also improved, and the composites beat silica and bentonite fillers on strength and ageing at comparable loadings, giving farm waste a high-value destination.
pmc-13226787:
Juliana Albano de Guimarães and Simone Haber Duellberg Von Faber Bison report a 2026 eye case of canaliculops, a rare non-inflammatory cyst swelling of the tiny tear-drainage channel in the eyelid. Most such cysts grow steadily, but their 68-year-old patient had a course that came and went, with repeated swelling at the inner corner of the eye and episodes of watering.

Surgery opened the cyst and placed a fine tube through both drainage channels under endoscopic guidance. Tissue examination showed a multilayered lining without goblet cells, inflammation, or malignancy, and a marker stain supported the diagnosis. The authors note that intermittent symptoms can hide this under-recognised condition and argue for wider awareness among eye specialists.
pmc-13227287:
Guojiang Zhang and co-authors design a 2026 injectable microsphere treatment for osteoarthritis that goes after pain at its source in the joint lining. In patient and mouse tissue, inflammatory M1 macrophages clustered with a nerve-attracting protein called Netrin-1, and removing macrophages eased pain in mice. The spheres are built to home to those lining macrophages and slowly release tannic acid plus tofacitinib, a drug that calms inflammatory signalling.

In mice with surgically induced arthritis, the treatment quieted M1 polarisation, lowered Netrin-1, and kept sensory nerves from growing into the lining. Cartilage breakdown slowed, and walking and pain-sensitivity tests improved. By combining antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and nerve-blocking effects, the spheres aim to relieve pain while also protecting the joint.
pmc-13231687:
Ryuto Abe and colleagues test in 2026 whether testing history can predict tricky drug compounds whose strength jumps sharply with tiny changes. Such activity cliff pairs look nearly identical yet differ hugely in potency, which breaks most structure-based prediction models. Their alternative feeds machine learning with each compound record across many past lab assays.

Under careful splits that block information leaking between training and test sets, profile-based forecasts often failed. A small set of predictions scored very well, and digging into those wins exposed the reason. Success hinged on one or two past assays that closely matched the target test, which a simple nearest neighbor search could find. Profile data help only when a truly similar assay exists in the record.
pmc-13232787:
Emilien Arnaud and colleagues set out in 2026 a study plan to find emergency gut surgery patients who fit an enhanced recovery pathway. Emergency cases die more often and return to hospital far more than planned surgery patients, yet their care stays improvised. Hospital records from Amiens in France will cover four years of emergency department visits.

The team expects roughly twenty-four hundred pathway-ready patients hidden inside several hundred thousand visits. Those patients should skew older and carry acute belly problems such as appendicitis, blockage, or peritonitis. A model will learn to flag them at arrival and predict time to surgery as a second task. Results will shape a live trial of the recovery pathway with remote monitoring.
pmc-13232887:
Ako Azimi and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study on why some breast cancers resist immunotherapy. Working with mouse models of triple-negative breast cancer, the group examined a class of red blood cell precursors called CD71+ erythroid cells. These cells gather around tumors and weaken the immune attack. The team tested curdlan, a yeast-derived sugar that switches on a sensor protein named Dectin-1.

Curdlan unexpectedly made tumors grow faster by boosting the erythroid cells. The sugar caused another protein, Galectin-3, to be shed and deposited onto those cells, where it sat alongside the checkpoint protein PD-L1. Blocking PD-L1 sharply cut the suppressive cells and shrank tumors. Human bone marrow data showed the same cell type, marking a fresh target for treatment.
pmc-13233287:
Niti Mishra, Joan Ballester, and Rodrigo Agerri published a 2026 computational study on detecting flu-like illness in social media posts across languages. Public health teams already mine posts in one language at a time, which limits coverage. The researchers built MuILI, a balanced dataset of 4,284 tweets in five European languages labeled for illness mentions, and tested classifiers across nine flu seasons.

A domain-adapted multilingual model set the benchmark, and cheaper transfer strategies trained only on French data came close behind. Among large language models, only the biggest one tested beat the benchmark, at heavy computing cost. Signals from the chosen classifier tracked official consultation rates closely in real time. The authors present cross-lingual transfer as an affordable path to wider flu surveillance.
pmc-13233687:
Asuka Takayama and colleagues published a 2026 case report of an immune deficiency diagnosed only at age forty-two. X-linked agammaglobulinemia usually appears in early childhood with repeated bacterial infections, because a faulty BTK gene blocks antibody production. This man had no such history, and he came to attention through inflammatory arthritis of the elbow, then inflamed joints and tendons in the hands.

Serious abscesses in the lung and buttock finally prompted immune testing, which showed very low antibodies and few B cells. Genetic analysis found a splice-site variant in BTK that leaked a small amount of working protein, explaining the milder course, and his socially withdrawn life may have limited exposure to germs. Antibody replacement therapy then prevented further deep infections and gradually calmed his joint inflammation.
pmc-13234087:
Mia Bonini and colleagues published a 2026 computational study of hearts kept alive by a left ventricular assist device, a mechanical pump for failing hearts. Their framework welds a three-dimensional flow simulation of the left heart and pump connections to a whole-circulation network model, in one fully coupled, patient-specific package. Valve behavior follows pressure and flow, with leak sizes taken from the individual patient.

Built from one patient's scans, ultrasound, and catheter measurements, the model reproduced clinical targets with a mean error under nine percent. Simulations then tested repairing the mitral valve, the aortic valve, or both. Combined repair gave the largest rise in forward output and eased pressures through the lungs and right heart. The authors offer the platform as a rehearsal space for surgical decisions in device-supported patients.
pmc-13234287:
Felix Preuss and co-authors reported in 2026 on how two kinds of inhibitory brain cells affect a third kind in mouse cortex. The target cells make somatostatin, a chemical signal, and they strongly quiet excitatory neurons. Input arrived either from cells marked by parvalbumin or from cells marked by a gut-related peptide. Earlier anatomy had suggested the two inputs might act quite differently.

Paired electrical recordings measured firing in single target cells while one input cell was stimulated. Both input types reduced the target cell's action potentials to a similar degree. Changing how long the input cell fired did not create a clear difference between the two routes. Microscopy also found no clear difference in where the contacts sat, challenging a simple cell-type rule.
pmc-13234487:
Ravi Maharjan and a large team reviewed in 2026 how freeze-drying can keep fragile biological drugs stable and useful. Demand rose after messenger RNA shots packed in lipid carriers worked during the COVID-19 pandemic. Those carriers are easily damaged by freezing and drying stresses. The review explains how protective parts such as sugars, amino acids, and plastics reduce that damage.

Mixes of sucrose and trehalose receive special focus for keeping particle size and drug encapsulation. Controlling how ice first forms also helped protect the blends. Digital models and in-line light-based tracking cut main drying time greatly in reported work. New part mixes may allow some viral vector products to be kept in a fridge. Faster ongoing freeze-drying methods are also described. The authors offer a roadmap for easing cold chain limits on newer drugs.
pmc-13235187:
Chloé Chavoix and a large team tested in 2026 how a swine-origin flu virus behaves in turkeys and in mice. The virus emerged in French pig farms in 2020, then appeared in breeding turkeys and caused one human infection. Three related viruses were compared: an early turkey strain, a likely turkey-adapted strain, and a pig reference strain. Experiments measured illness, tissue damage, virus amounts, and immune responses.

All three viruses caused only very mild illness and no shedding in experimentally infected turkeys. Mice told a sharply different story across the strains. One turkey strain caused marked illness and deaths with a weak inflammatory response in mice. The pig strain caused mild illness yet stronger inflammation there. Lung virus amounts did not explain the contrast, pointing to immune response as the driver. Only two protein changes separated the most different strains.
pmc-13236687:
Feng Zhou and co-authors traced in 2026 a molecular signal in egg follicle fluid that harms fertility in women with active endometriosis. Tiny vesicles released by cells carry long non-coding RNAs, which regulate gene activity without making proteins. One such RNA stood out as heavily enriched in fluid from patients with active disease. Experiments moved the RNA into granulosa cells, the cells that nourish developing eggs.

Inside those cells, the RNA slowed growth and pushed the cells toward programmed death. Silencing the RNA protected the cells from that fate in the laboratory tests. The RNA binds a helper protein and frees a guardian protein, P53, to enter the nucleus and switch on death genes. Blocking P53 partly reversed the damage caused by the RNA in the experiments. Patients with active disease also showed poorer early embryo quality, matching the cell findings.
pmc-13236787:
Testo and Dumas study how the hormone estradiol shapes brain connections in women at midlife. Midlife brings a sharp hormonal shift for women, and falling estradiol may change how brain regions talk to each other. Such changes could help explain why memory and thinking differ so much between women of the same age.

The team scanned women's brains while they performed a memory task about past events. They linked connection patterns to estradiol, the main estrogen lost at menopause. Mapping this link could clarify who faces higher risk of unhealthy brain ageing, and whether hormone timing matters for protecting memory in the menopause years.
pmc-13236887:
Linsen Zhou and co-authors compared treatment plans in 2026 for proton therapy after mastectomy in left-sided breast cancer. Proton beams can spare the heart and lungs, but shallow chest targets need a device to pull the beam's stopping point closer. The team planned care for 18 patients three ways: with a bolus, with a range shifter, or with both.

All proton plans beat standard photon therapy on heart, lung, and immune-cell dose. The range-shifter plan gave the lowest average heart dose and the best predicted safety for heart and lungs. The bolus plan slightly favored lung dose. The authors favor the range shifter alone, noting it also avoids the fit and hygiene problems of a bolus pressed on skin.
pmc-13237287:
Yifei Ni and colleagues scanned 30 patients with fibrosing interstitial lung disease in 2026 using a special MRI method that maps breathing and blood flow without injected contrast. Each patient was matched with a healthy control of the same age and sex. The imaging numbers were set against lung function tests and high-resolution CT scans.

Patients differed clearly from controls on average perfusion, ventilation, and the share of lung where air and blood flow matched or mismatched. Average perfusion tracked closely with the lungs' gas-transfer capacity and fell as CT showed more scarring and honeycombing. Defect measures moved the opposite way. The authors propose the scan as a repeatable way to grade severity and follow these diseases over time, without radiation.
pmc-13239187:
Dong-fen Geng and colleagues fed one hundred German cockroaches a glowing strain of Salmonella Typhi in 2026 to test experimentally whether the insects can pass the pathogen to mammals through their droppings. Cockroaches are suspected carriers, but fecal transfer had never been measured directly. Fluorescence tracked the bacteria through the insects' guts and feces over a week.

Signals peaked a day after infection and lingered up to seven days, and the glow matched living bacterial counts well. When fecal suspensions from the cockroaches were given to mice, bacterial signals appeared in mouse droppings within half an hour and in gut tissue for up to twelve hours, then vanished. The authors conclude the roaches can mechanically contaminate food and water and deliver a brief, real exposure to mammals.
pmc-13239287:
Yuting He and colleagues built a bioartificial liver in 2026 from gene-edited pig liver cells grown as organoids, and tested it on plasma from patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure. The pig cells had their GGTA1 gene knocked out to lower immune rejection, and human vessel cells engineered to boost growth signals helped them form stable organoids. The device was compared with standard non-biological liver support.

The bioartificial system cut ammonia and bilirubin further than the passive device. Deeper analysis showed it actively repaired metabolism, restoring amino acid balance and raising membrane-repair lipid species tied to calmer inflammation. The authors frame the machine as a biological regulator, not a filter. Their goal is a bridge therapy for liver failure patients who now have almost nothing beyond transplantation.
pmc-13239487:
Konstantinos Ioannidis and colleagues present a 2026 dental case centred on a rare extra bump on an upper molar. The feature, called a parastyle, sits on the cheek side of the tooth and can hide the openings of its root canals, complicating treatment when the inner pulp dies.

Cone-beam scanning mapped the unusual anatomy before root canal work began. Treatment used magnification, modern instruments, activated rinses, and a dressing between visits before the canals were sealed. Two years later the tooth worked comfortably without symptoms, and the dark area of bone damage at the root tip had shrunk. The case shows why imaging matters for odd anatomy.
pmc-13240987:
Chen and colleagues at Taipei Veterans General Hospital trained machine learning models to forecast kidney failure and death. Records covered twenty-nine thousand six hundred seventy-seven chronic kidney disease patients from 2011 to 2021. Sixty-nine routine variables fed five algorithms plus a stacked ensemble. Eighty percent trained the models; the rest tested them.

Only about two percent reached end-stage kidney disease, while twelve percent died. Prediction was strong for kidney failure and more modest for mortality. Calibration and decision-curve checks supported real clinical usefulness. Chen presents the models as practical tools for sorting patients by risk.
pmc-13241487:
Yokoi's team at Hokkaido mapped the idle brain rhythms of medaka fish into distinct repeating states. 32 electrodes took field readings across the sleeping forebrain. 3-second slices of slow delta waves were compared by their matching patterns. Grouping distilled the stream into a handful of network states.

Some states hogged the time while others barely appeared. Back-to-back spells usually stayed in the same state, and shifts retraced known paths. Shuffled data dissolved this structure. Yokoi reads the pattern as self-ordering, echoing rest-state rules seen across vertebrate brains. No task drove the fish.
pmc-13241687:
Motoki Kaneko and Atsushi Sakuraba publish a 2026 network meta-analysis of long-term colorectal cancer screening results. Four strategies were compared: colonoscopy, flexible sigmoidoscopy, and two stool-based tests. Trial evidence on ten-year outcomes guided the analysis.

Looking at everyone invited to screening, colonoscopy and sigmoidoscopy both lowered new cancer cases. Sigmoidoscopy and the older stool test lowered deaths from this cancer, while colonoscopy did not reach that mark in this analysis. No strategy reduced deaths overall. Among people who actually completed screening, benefits looked larger across methods. The authors advise choosing strategies with uptake and health system capacity in mind, since invitation-level effects depend on participation.
pmc-13241987:
Xiaoqing Zhou, Zhen Wang, and Suqun Zheng present a 2026 study of a traditional Chinese yam extract in asthma. Airway remodeling, including new blood vessel growth, drives long-term asthma worsening. The plant rhizome has shown anti-inflammatory hints, but its effect on remodeling was untested.

Chemical profiling of the extract found thousands of candidate compounds with good batch consistency. In an allergen-driven mouse asthma model, the extract cut the airway inflammation score substantially, matching a standard steroid on that measure. Scar-like collagen in airways fell even more sharply. Levels of four linked signaling proteins tied to vessel growth dropped in lung tissue and in vessel cells. The authors propose the extract as a candidate therapy, pending deeper mechanism work.
pmc-13242387:
Dos Santos's team at Alagoas PCR-tested 380 cattle for tick-borne Anaplasma across Brazil's semiarid northeast. Small herds in the semiarid Sertão and Agreste regions were sampled. The msp4 gene flagged infection; a control gene verified the DNA pull. Blood counts were compared between positive and negative animals.

Over 92 percent of cattle carried Anaplasma DNA. Sex, age, breed, production system, and tick burden showed no real link. Infected animals ran sharply lower blood counts. The first gene-based report for two Brazilian states suggests steady local spread in these small regions. Ticks spread the germ.
pmc-13242487:
Brooke Boxrud and colleagues built a depression check-in tool that people with aphasia can actually use. Their paper appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. Depression after stroke is common in aphasia, yet standard questionnaires lean heavily on reading and language. The team ran nine focus groups with fifteen people with aphasia, thirteen care partners, and thirteen speech-language pathologists to choose symptoms and wording.

The final tool asks about six feelings: determined, proud, and interested on the positive side, and sad, like a failure, and angry on the negative side. Each item pairs words with pictures, a picture rating scale, and audio, and participants judged three or four check-ins a day workable. Interviews confirmed the items were understandable, with one picture needing revision. The work shows lost positive feeling deserves as much attention as low mood.
pmc-13242587:
Hossein Bouzarjomehri and colleagues reviewed why Iran's Clean Air Act has failed to clear the country's air. Their scoping review appeared in Environmental Health Insights in 2026. Air pollution remains a heavy burden on Iranian health, yet enforcement of the 2017-era act is weak. The team searched major databases plus policy documents, legal texts, and institutional reports, then sorted the obstacles with a four-part framework.

Barriers clustered into culture and evidence, governance, finance, and technical capacity. Air quality ranks low as a policy priority, public awareness is thin, and agencies work in fragments with little coordination or performance tracking. Funding depends on public budgets with no steady revenue, so projects stall. Monitoring lacks shared data standards and a technology roadmap. The authors conclude the law's weakness lies less in its text than in the system meant to run it, and they propose evidence-based fixes for each layer.
pmc-13243287:
Xianlin Rao and co-authors map how gut microbes may steer immune disease across the whole body in a 2026 review. Autoimmune diseases start when the immune system attacks the body's own tissue. Activity at barriers like the gut can reshape inflammation in skin, joints, lungs, kidneys, and the brain.

The review centers on small chemicals made by gut microbes, such as short-chain fatty acids and bile acid products. These chemicals travel in the blood and act as checkpoints on immune cells in distant organs. The authors also weigh sex-based differences in microbes and hormones. They close by judging tools from diet and probiotics to engineered microbe mixes for future care.
pmc-13244487:
Guanxiong Zhu and co-authors review tiny carriers that deliver immune activators to tumors in a 2026 survey. The activators switch on a cell alarm path called cGAS-STING, which can rally attack on cancer. Free activators break down fast, spread too widely, and can harm healthy tissue.

Carriers made of fats, polymers, metals, silica, or cell vesicles shield the cargo and steer it to tumors. They also release the dose in a controlled way, which sharpens the immune response. The review covers pairings with radiation, chemotherapy, light therapy, and checkpoint drugs. Hurdles that remain include uneven coating by blood proteins and hard scale-up for clinics.
pmc-13245087:
Chouaibi and colleagues, working in Tunisia and Italy, studied how a person's genes shape the bacteria living inside colorectal tumors. Their 2026 Gut Microbes paper focuses on Fusobacterium nucleatum, a mouth bacterium often found in colon cancers, and on SLC22A4, a gut transporter gene already linked to cancer risk.

The team measured two bacterial species in ninety-nine tumor samples and nearby healthy tissue, and also tested cancer stem cells grown in the lab. Tumors carried far more Fusobacterium relative to common E. coli, and the imbalance grew with each copy of the SLC22A4 variant a patient carried. Cells carrying the variant also cleared the bacterium poorly, suggesting the gene helps it survive inside tumors.
pmc-13246487:
Tessema and co-authors review how to stop salt from ruining solar desalination, in this 2026 Global Challenges article. Sun-powered evaporators can turn seawater into fresh water, but in very salty water, salt crystals crust over the surface and choke the process. The review compares six anti-salt strategies, from water-repelling surfaces to designs that walk salt away to the edges where it can be harvested.

For each strategy the authors explain the physics underneath, including capillary flow, back-diffusion down salt gradients, and surface-tension effects. They propose combining approaches, pairing edge crystallization with one-way brine transport, so future systems might produce fresh water and valuable minerals together instead of fighting salt buildup as pure waste.
pmc-13246687:
Pauline Georgees Poless and colleagues pilot a study of thoughts and feelings in firefighters under stress in 2026. Fire work brings repeated danger and strain, yet inner coping during calls is rarely mapped. The team used therapy-style interviews to draw out those inner steps.

Seventy-eight firefighters took part and also filled a standard emotion questionnaire. Fire accidents ranked as the most stressful calls, and mixed emotions were common. Saving people stood out as the top drive during hard moments. Most firefighters saw their own thoughts and feelings as helpful, not as blocks. Reframing a situation was the favored calming habit, while pushing feelings down faded with age.
pmc-13247587:
