Farré, Gasco, and Blay present open-source software for scanning genetic risk across the whole phenome, in this 2026 NAR Genomics and Bioinformatics brief report. A phenome-wide association study tests whether polygenic risk scores, summaries of a person's many small genetic effects, connect to hundreds of traits at once. No standard, portable pipeline existed for running such scans in any cohort, so the team built PolyGenie on the Nextflow workflow system.

The pipeline takes ready-made risk scores and phenotype data, runs regressions across binary and continuous outcomes, stores results in a database, and serves them through an interactive web app. Their demonstration applied one hundred thirty-five risk scores to the Catalan GCAT cohort's clinical, molecular, and lifestyle traits. Because configuration is metadata-driven, other cohorts can adopt it without code changes.
pmc-13247787:
Fereshteh Fani and co-authors redesign rural primary healthcare in Iran through a grounded theory study in 2026. Iran's rural system once scored big wins, yet structure, management, and shifting population needs now strain it. The team asked senior managers, policymakers, and academics what a fresh model needs.

Interviews with 25 experts were coded in stages until a core theme emerged. That theme joins integrated service delivery with system enablement. Service parts cover access, continuity, coordination, and breadth of care, plus a steady link to one place or provider. Support parts cover evidence-based planning, stronger management, fair payment, and firm oversight. The model aims to make rural care responsive again.
pmc-13248287:
Kranes and colleagues reviewed what happens while eating-disorder patients wait for therapy, in a 2026 systematic review. Long waits are common before outpatient talk therapy begins. The team searched five databases for studies that measured symptoms in people held on waitlists before treatment started.

Nine studies covering six hundred forty-seven people met their rules, mostly adults with bulimia or binge-eating disorder. Pooled results showed symptoms eased only slightly during the wait, leaving distress largely unchanged. The authors argue that waiting is not a neutral pause, and they call for research on waits in ordinary care rather than only inside trials.
pmc-13248687:
Gunvanti Rathod and Pragnesh Parmar review two growth pathways that drive papillary thyroid cancer in a 2026 article. This cancer is the most common hormone gland malignancy. Two signal chains, MAPK and PI3K/AKT, switch on through gene changes and push cells to grow.

The review lists the gene faults behind each chain, from BRAF and RAS to PTEN. Cross-talk between the chains deepens aggression, spread, and resistance to iodine therapy. New molecular tests and targeted drugs now sharpen risk grading and care choices. The authors gather the mechanisms and treatments into one map for clinicians and students.
pmc-13249187:
Ayala and colleagues propose counting biomedical engineers per hospital bed in Mexico, in a 2026 PLOS One study. These engineers keep medical devices safe and working, yet world statistics count them per head of population, which says little about hospital capacity. The authors built a bed-based density measure following Pan American Health Organization guidance and applied it to Mexican data from 2017 through 2022.

The measure rose most sharply during the pandemic years. Even so, comparing internationally exposed a double shortage: too few hospital beds and too few engineers for the population served. The authors argue their indicator better reflects a system's real ability to manage medical technology.
pmc-13249687:
Sun and a large team traced a chain of molecular switches that helps colon cancer spread, in a 2026 Apoptosis study. The chain starts with a gene activator, ZNF263, switching on an enzyme called SMOX. Drawing on several cancer datasets plus cell and mouse experiments, the team tested each link by turning genes up or down.

SMOX ran high in tumors and marked worse survival. It raised reactive oxygen inside cells, which switched on TRIB3, a protein that in turn freed the Wnt growth pathway to drive invasion. Removing SMOX stalled cell growth and peritoneal spread in mice. The authors nominate the axis, especially SMOX and TRIB3, as drug targets.
pmc-13250187:
Wang and co-authors analyze what makes hospital falls cause minor harm in some patients and serious harm in others. Their 2026 BMJ Open study covers just over one thousand inpatient falls at a large hospital in Zhejiang Province, China, between 2015 and 2025. Records came from the hospital's nursing incident reporting system.

About six in ten falls caused an injury, and roughly one in eight of the injuries was serious. Older age, female sex, and tripping were all tied to worse harm from a fall. Falls where the knee or trunk took the impact, and patients who were walking beforehand, also fared worse. The authors call for stronger fall prevention aimed at older patients and women in particular.
pmc-13250387:
Takedomi and colleagues report a tiny benign nerve sheath tumor found during a screening colonoscopy. Their DEN Open case concerns a fifty-nine-year-old man with a past colon polyp removal. Doctors spotted a small reddish, slightly raised spot in his sigmoid colon, with a smooth surface and clear edges.

Magnified imaging showed widened round pits, sparse crypts, and branching vessels at the center of the lesion. The spot was removed with a cold snare, serving both diagnosis and treatment in one step. Microscope and staining tests identified a colonic perineurioma, a rare harmless tumor of nerve-wrapping cells. The authors advise keeping this tumor in mind for small under-surface colon lesions, while noting that only tissue tests can confirm it.
pmc-13250687:
Ernst Kwa and colleagues review drugs that block an enzyme called 17beta-HSD10 and ask whether any of them are truly useful. The enzyme sits in mitochondria, the energy centers of cells, and it is found at raised levels in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease. Interest in it has grown as the first disease-modifying Alzheimer's treatments reach patients.

The review explains why the enzyme is a hard target: studies disagree about what it acts on inside the body. The authors sort through compounds that block its catalytic action and others that interfere with its separate roles. They weigh whether blocking the enzyme changes disease biology or mainly helps researchers probe metabolism in the living brain. Their verdict treats the inhibitors as promising research tools whose medical value is still unproven.
pmc-13251487:
Eden Woldegerima and colleagues compare blood profiles of pregnant women with and without Toxoplasma infection in northwest Ethiopia, reporting in 2026. The parasite infects about a third of people worldwide and can alter blood and immune measures during pregnancy. The women were recruited during antenatal visits at a public hospital in 2022 and 2023.

Of 554 women tested, 301 carried antibodies showing past or present infection and 253 did not. The infected group differed clearly on white cell counts, hemoglobin, red cell counts, and several related measures. Their CD4 counts, a gauge of immune strength, were much lower than those of uninfected women. Platelet counts were the exception, showing no real difference between the groups. The authors urge routine screening in antenatal care plus teaching women how to avoid infection.
pmc-13253487:
Federico Rossari and colleagues map the immune landscape inside biliary tract cancers with a simple four-marker method in a 2026 proof-of-principle study. These aggressive cancers respond poorly to treatment, and the arrangement of immune cells in a tumor may predict who benefits from immunotherapy. The team stained pre-treatment samples from eleven patients with advanced disease for four markers covering T cells, B cells, and macrophages.

At the tumor's invasive edge, across 198 regions, imaging software segmented roughly 400,000 cells. Unsupervised analysis split the tumors into two immune phenotypes: one rich in helper T cells and a macrophage type, the other in killer T cells and B cells. Survival did not differ between phenotypes overall. In a subset treated with adjuvant chemotherapy alone, baseline cell fractions did track with outcome. The authors say the architectures are real and distinct, and they now need testing in larger cohorts.
pmc-13253587:
Rundong Xie and colleagues hunt the genes behind barley grain size in this 2026 study. Grain size drives yield, and comparing a plump-grained variety with a small-grained one across development can expose the controlling switches.

The team measured grains and read gene activity at three filling stages. Grain length and thickness differed at every stage, width only later. Gene differences peaked mid-filling. A network method flagged a module of genes tied tightly to grain traits, and crossing its hub genes with the stage differences left 13 candidates. Five matched known grain-size regulators from rice and other crops. Lab checks confirmed their stage- and variety-specific patterns, marking them as breeding targets.
pmc-13253887:
Joana Serrano Salgado and co-authors report two new plant viruses in a 2026 study from the United States. Spiraea, a popular garden shrub, showed yellow spots, leaf distortion, and dead patches. Deep sequencing of the plants found a new emaravirus and a new alphacytorhabdovirus, which the team named.

The emaravirus genome has four RNA segments, and microscope work showed round enveloped particles 80 to 100 nanometers wide. It appeared alone in 50 of 77 sick samples, linking it to strong yellow spot disease. Tiny mites found on the plants may spread it, as mites spread its virus relatives.
pmc-13253987:
Kazunori Takeuchi, Yuki Takagi, and Ryo Asano follow one eye patient for twelve years in a 2026 case report. After Trabectome surgery for glaucoma, a band-shaped remnant was left in the front chamber of the eye. Glaucoma is raised eye pressure that can blind, and the surgery opens a drainage path to lower it.

The remnant stayed for about twelve years and caused no long-term clinical problems. The authors do warn of one risk: corneal endothelial cell density, the layer that keeps the cornea clear, can fall fast in the early period after surgery. They urge doctors to watch that layer closely early on.
pmc-13254787:
Alton Quan Cao and colleagues track four decades of temperature-related preterm birth risk in Japan in a 2026 nationwide study. Between 1979 and 2023 the country recorded over 2.6 million singleton preterm births among nearly fifty-three million live births. Using a case-crossover design with a twenty-eight day lag model for every prefecture, the team compared each birth's late-pregnancy temperatures against the temperature of minimum risk.

Both extremes raised risk: heat at the ninety-ninth percentile carried a relative risk of 1.13 and deep cold 1.11 against the optimum of 17.7 degrees. About 4.7 percent of all preterm births, over one hundred thousand babies, were attributable to non-optimal temperatures, split between cold and heat. Heat risk fell modestly from the nineteen-eighties to the two-thousands, then plateaued, while cold risk never budged. The authors say the stall in adaptation leaves pregnant women exposed.
pmc-13255387:
Lodewijk A. Pet and colleagues ask how PhD candidates judge integrity rules in a 2026 survey study. The Netherlands Code of Conduct for Research Integrity sets 61 standards for good practice. At Leiden University, 332 candidates rated the standards for clarity, relevance, how often they are broken, and how serious breaking them is.

Most ratings were positive: 83 percent for clarity and 77 percent for relevance scored high. But views on seriousness often clashed with the code's own tiers, with some minor faults rated as misconduct and one plagiarism rule rated more lightly. The authors urge clearer wording and a rethink of the severity tiers.
pmc-13255987:
Ying Chen and a large team report a 2026 modeling study of sodium tanshinone IIA sulfonate, a stroke drug derived from the herb Salvia miltiorrhiza. They built physiologically based models predicting how the drug moves through the body and produces its effect. Rats with a blocked brain artery mimicked patients suffering ischemia-reperfusion injury after stroke.

The models covered healthy rats, injured rats, and a scaled-up human version. Liver and kidney clearance of the drug ran significantly lower in injured rats than in healthy ones. The drug reduced inflammation in injured animals, with its effect arriving on a delay. The authors offer the combined model as a tool for choosing doses and forecasting benefit in patients, and as a template for similar modeling of other stroke drugs.
pmc-13256187:
Furong Xu and co-authors review liver ischemia-reperfusion injury in a 2026 paper centered on neutrophils. These white blood cells flood the liver when blood flow returns after transplant, major liver surgery, or trauma care. The injury couples energy failure in the ischemic phase with an explosive sterile inflammation once flow resumes, and no approved targeted drug yet exists.

The review maps how neutrophils are recruited and switched on, centered on the Mac-1-Syk signaling axis inside the cells. It then traces how neutrophil extracellular traps form step by step and injure the liver in several ways. Cross-talk with platelets and other liver cells amplifies an inflammation-clotting loop. The authors sort out disputes over core drug targets, flag the bottlenecks blocking clinical use, and propose a sequenced multi-target plan built around the traps.
pmc-13256387:
Nehla Banu and co-authors review liposome-based photodynamic therapy for breast cancer in a 2026 paper. Photodynamic therapy kills tumors with light-activated drugs that generate reactive oxygen, sparing much healthy tissue, yet tumors resist through low oxygen, poor drug uptake, and shallow light reach. Liposomes, fat bubbles that carry drugs, are the review's proposed answer to several of those limits.

Antigen-targeted liposomes can park the light-sensitive drug inside tumors longer and get it into cells more efficiently. Their design also suits combinations: chemotherapy, heat therapy, gene therapy, X-ray-triggered variants, and checkpoint immunotherapy all pair with the platform. The review weighs early clinical outcomes, manufacturing scale-up, and tricks to avoid immune clearance. The authors see multimodal liposomal systems as the realistic route to clinic-ready photodynamic treatment.
pmc-13257687:
Kosei Goto and colleagues report a fatal complication during aneurysm coiling in a 2026 case-based review. A seventy-one-year-old woman underwent stent-assisted coiling of a small unruptured brain aneurysm. During the fourth coil pass, the wall ruptured and contrast dye escaped into the space around the brain.

Reversal drugs and temporary flow control slowed the leak, yet clots then blocked major brain arteries and needed emergency removal. Scans showed bleeding around and inside the brain, and fluid buildup forced drainage tubes the same day. She died a week after the procedure. The authors model the event as a staged escalation where bleeding and clotting chase each other. A communication checklist for operator and assistant is proposed to speed each rescue step.
pmc-13257987:
Sisi Zhuang and Lili Zuo wrote a 2026 study using metabolomics, the large-scale study of small molecules in the body, to tell apart types of sepsis in children. Sepsis is a dangerous body-wide reaction to infection, caused here by either bacteria or viruses. They used blood serum data from the MetaboLights database and applied several statistical methods, plus machine learning models, to find molecules that mark each type.

The analysis found distinct metabolic profiles for bacterial sepsis, viral sepsis, and healthy controls. Fourteen differing molecules were identified, mainly tied to nitrogen metabolism and the building of arginine, an amino acid. Choline, glutamate, and glutamine stood out as the strongest markers for telling bacterial from viral cases. The authors propose these three as possible diagnostic biomarkers for faster testing.
pmc-13258787:
Paweł Mitkowski and colleagues tracked immune signals for nine months after patients left hospital with COVID-19. Lingering symptoms, grouped as long COVID, are suspected to ride on a slow-burning immune imbalance. Their 2026 study pairs repeated blood measures with symptoms, vaccines, and other illnesses.

Several messenger proteins, including interleukin-6, stayed higher than in healthy controls months later. Some signals kept climbing while others faded, with no single pattern for everyone. Interleukin-6 separated recovered patients from controls especially reliably. Yet fatigue, cough, and breathlessness persisted without tracking any blood signal steadily. The authors argue long COVID reaches beyond plain inflammation.
pmc-13259187:
Yunfeng Wang, Xuxu Xie, and Jiyang Jia design robust satellite beamforming under direction errors in a 2026 paper. Low orbit satellites share spectrum while moving fast, so channel knowledge arrives late and partly wrong. Direction mistakes can badly misaim beams meant to avoid interference.

Their algorithm splits the hard joint problem into two solvable parts. An adaptive sampling step balances solution quality against onboard computing limits. Simulations beat typical benchmarks on total data rate and robustness. Edge users fared more fairly than under comparison methods. Satellite operators gain beam control that tolerates the imperfect information real orbits provide.
pmc-13259487:
Zheng Zhang, Daozhi Wei, and Xirui Xue track clustered targets with several sensors under unknown clutter in a 2026 paper. Real detection rates and false alarm rates shift over time and are rarely known in advance. Their filter estimates those unknowns online while tracking the group.

A virtual leader follower model describes how cluster members move together. An adaptive counting filter feeds live detection and clutter estimates into the main tracker. Efficient sampling trims the huge hypothesis space of labeled tracking. Simulations under shifting conditions beat comparison filters on cluster tracking. Air defense and traffic watchers gain tracking that calibrates itself as conditions change.
pmc-13259687:
Hua Liu and coauthors report new gene variants behind low neutrophil counts in an infant in a 2026 case study. The twelve month old boy suffered repeated feverish chest infections from ten months of age. Blood counts during infections showed neutrophils far below normal while other lines stayed healthy.

Gene sequencing found two previously unreported variants in a receptor gene guiding neutrophil release from marrow. One came from each parent, matching the inheritance pattern. Growth factor shots and antibiotics carried the child through fever episodes. Immune protein levels and lymphocyte groups tested normal. Genetic testing earns emphasis for infants with unexplained chronic low counts.
pmc-13260087:
Joonas Laajava, Jenni Määttä, and Miikka Korja present a 2026 retrospective study of meningioma recurrence, meaning regrowth of these usually slow-growing brain tumors after surgery. They tested whether the MIB-1 index, a lab measure of how fast tumor cells divide, predicts which tumors return. The study covered 505 adults operated on between 2005 and 2018, all with MIB-1 results and at least five years of MRI follow-up.

Most patients were women, at 67.3 percent, and most tumors were WHO grade I or II. Among grade I tumors removed only partly, twenty-one of fifty-eight recurred within five years. But when the MIB-1 value was four percent or lower, only four of thirty-five such tumors recurred. The authors say a four percent cutoff identifies a low-risk group that could be scanned less often after surgery.
pmc-13260187:

AMPA receptors pass fast signals between brain cells using the chemical glutamate. The team analyzed the four subunit genes, GRIA1 through GRIA4, in tumor datasets and cell lines. Gene levels differed between subgroups, with GRIA1 enriched in Group 3 tumors and GRIA4 in sonic hedgehog tumors. Higher GRIA1, GRIA2, and GRIA4 were linked to better outcomes in specific subgroups. In contrast, high GRIA3 in sonic hedgehog tumors, or high GRIA3 or GRIA4 in Group 3, meant worse prognosis. Cell line tests supported some tumor patterns, suggesting subgroup-specific prognostic value.
pmc-13260287:
Pavlos Vinícius do Nascimento leads a 2026 animal welfare study setting heat stress thresholds for walking pet dogs in hot, sunny regions. Five mixed-breed dogs were walked for twelve minutes, with body temperatures and breathing rate measured at rest, during walks, and during twenty minutes of recovery. Across 135 walks, day and night, the heat measure called black-globe temperature ranged from nineteen to fifty degrees Celsius. Water intake was also recorded.

Dogs held rectal temperature within thirty-eight to thirty-nine degrees, with no signs of overheating. Above a black-globe temperature of thirty-five degrees, coat temperature rose by 20.5 degrees, skin temperature by 7.2 degrees, and water intake by 215 millilitres compared with cooler walks. Breathing rate climbed from about forty-seven to 374 breaths per minute. The authors advise caution when their combined thermal stress index passes 170.
pmc-13261087:
Hsiang-Han Chen and co-authors present a 2026 machine-learning study predicting daily heart and blood vessel emergencies in Taiwan. Short-term swings in weather and air quality are known to affect these crises. The team tested whether such data can forecast daily emergency visits across regions.

They used 23 years of nationwide data from 2000 to 2022 and 184 weather and air features. Unsupervised grouping found high-risk days bunching in cool, polluted conditions, above all in northern Taiwan and among people aged 65 and older. Pollution measures defined high-risk clusters more clearly than weather alone. Among eight trained models, tree-based teams performed best, with R² values up to 0.67 and errors of 7% to 8%. Nitrogen oxide measures were the dominant signals. The authors propose region-specific early-warning systems centered on pollution tracking.
pmc-13261287:

It usually strikes people with weakened immunity. Because the fungi invade blood vessels, tissue dies fast and the disease can resemble other flesh-destroying infections.

Their patient was a 70-year-old man whose laryngeal cancer was in remission, with no active immune-suppressing treatment. He had one week of worsening pain, swelling, discoloration, and dead tissue on his left leg. Microscopy showed broad fungal threads, and culture grew Mucorales. Liposomal amphotericin B at 5 mg/kg/day was stopped after his creatinine rose from 0.81 to 2.5 mg/dL. Posaconazole followed, and repeated surgical cleaning plus skin grafting brought recovery without relapse. The authors stress early surgery, tissue diagnosis, and prompt antifungal therapy.
pmc-13262587:
Bo-Yun Guan and Yang Li review a quieter drug family for depression: medicines that tune the brain's GABA-A receptors. Depression's biology runs beyond serotonin, and the calming GABA system is now a serious target. Their 2026 review sorts the candidates by class and evidence.

Benzodiazepines, intravenous anesthetics, and neurosteroids each nudge the receptor differently toward restored inhibition. Some, like etomidate and the neurosteroid allopregnanolone, also seem to rebuild synaptic connections and cool brain inflammation. Those extra actions could explain fast, deep relief reported in some studies. The authors map where each agent stands on the road to routine care.
pmc-13263787:

That stability, heart rate variability, reflects how well the automatic nervous system works. The team measured eight obesity indices and five minutes of heart tracing in 3,180 students averaging about twenty years old.

Body fat percentage showed the strongest links by far, tying to lower overall variability and a shift toward stress-side dominance. It explained more of the rhythm pattern than waist size or body mass index, though adding body mass index still helped. A body fat cutoff of about twenty-seven percent flagged low variability. No meaningful sex differences appeared.
pmc-13264087:
Atharva Khewalkar and colleagues describe a 2026 system that helps merchants find product-specific rules hidden in government documents. In India, food and other regulated goods must follow rules published across ministry websites, often as unstructured PDF files that are hard to search. Sellers risk breaking requirements simply because the right clause is difficult to locate.

The system scrapes scattered sources, cleans and organizes the text with automated scripts and offers a search engine by product. Testing on food safety rules reached accuracy in the low to high eighty percent range across repeated runs. The authors present the tool as a practical aid for small sellers who need clear compliance guidance without legal teams.
pmc-13264787:
Naotake Funamizu and colleagues propose a frailty framework built for liver, bile duct and pancreatic operations in a 2026 review. Standard frailty tools miss stresses unique to these procedures, such as bile blockage, repeated infection, tumor inflammation, liver failure and very large removals. The team searched major archives for work from 2010 to 2025 and kept over two hundred studies after screening, sorting evidence into domains that include muscle loss, nutrition and physical function.

Their proposed onco-frailty model aims to guide assessment and pre-surgery tuning rather than serve as a single pass or fail score. Rollout steps and future testing needs are laid out. Fitting frailty care to the operation could cut complications in some of the highest-risk abdominal surgery.
pmc-13264887:
Stefanie G A Veenhuizen and colleagues present the COBRA trial protocol, published in 2026. The randomised study tests whether yoga eases muscle and joint complaints in women receiving hormone treatment for breast cancer. Such complaints are common during endocrine therapy. Many women stop treatment early because of them.

A total of 140 women will be assigned to yoga or to a waitlist group. The yoga group attends supervised classes twice a week for 18 weeks, plus short home sessions. Pain is the main outcome, measured with a standard questionnaire. The protocol also tracks fatigue, sleep, mood, fitness, and blood markers. Results could show whether a gentle exercise option helps women stay on treatment.
pmc-13264987:
Jipeng Song and colleagues published a 2026 review of tetrahedral framework nucleic acids, tiny DNA cages, for repairing lung injury. Lung injury breaks the barrier between air sacs and blood vessels and still lacks safe, reliable treatments. These DNA structures can soak up harmful reactive molecules and slip into cells and through lung mucus with ease.

The review covers how the cages act, how they are used as both drug and drug carrier, and what blocks their path to clinics. Their shape aids uptake by cells and passage across the lung lining, which strengthens drug contact with tissue. The authors argue the cages offer a multi-sided approach to a complex condition, spanning oxidative stress and drug delivery at once. They aim to spur breakthroughs in lung injury care.
pmc-13265187:
Haoran Wu and the team review progress on vaccines for gastric cancer, in a 2026 review. Vaccines form one branch of immune therapy for this cancer. Advances in immune science have sped vaccine research in recent years. The review searched recent past work through the end of 2025.

Current vaccine platforms are classified and described, with focus on nucleic acid vaccines and nanovaccines. Methods to strengthen vaccines receive attention, including ways to overcome the suppressive tumour environment. Artificial intelligence tools for predicting immune targets are also discussed. pmc-13265687:

pmc-13274887:

pmc-13276587:

pmc-13288887:

pmc-13289087:
Pablo Timoner and colleagues map access to HIV treatment in Mali in 2026. A WHO service tracking system supplied the data. Travel time is the key measure. Care counts as in reach within two hours. Least-cost paths set the travel times.

Nearly 2.7 million Malians lack timely access. Distance is the main block for most. That share is about 70 percent. The rest face clinic-level blocks. Some clinics do not plan the service. Some lack supplies or trained staff. The model can guide where to add care. It can also fit other services and nations.
pmc-13289387:
Wouter Vankrunkelsven, Leen Vercaemst, and Dieter F Dauwe tested a 2026 question on how well large language models answer family questions about ECMO. ECMO is a machine that temporarily does heart or lung work for very ill patients. Use has grown fast, and families now turn to chatbots for risks and outlook, where overly rosy answers could mislead choices.

Four common models faced four family-style questions drawn from frequent web searches and related sources. Prior work showed news coverage already stresses survival over hard outcomes for this therapy. The team checked whether chatbot answers repeat that optimism bias against cohort and trial data. Clear grading of accuracy and balance matters, since families may weigh life-support choices on such replies.
pmc-13290387:
A benign ovarian tumor that looked exactly like advanced cancer is described by Wuping Xu and colleagues in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a 59-year-old woman, arrived with a swollen abdomen and breathlessness, and scans showed a huge pelvic mass with fluid in the abdomen and chest, swollen lymph nodes, and thickened peritoneum.

Tumor markers CA125 and HE4 were markedly high, though failing kidneys may have inflated the HE4 reading. The patient grew critically ill, with breathing, heart, and kidney failure, making surgery risky. After a team evaluation and stabilization, a needle biopsy and frozen section pointed to fibrothecoma instead of cancer. The tumor, about 45 cm across, was fully removed, the fluids cleared, and organ function recovered, matching Meigs' syndrome. The authors advise keeping benign stromal tumors in mind for giant masses and using biopsy selectively in fragile patients.
pmc-13290687:
Predicting which bleeding patients will flare with gout in hospital is the goal of a 2026 machine-learning study by Rongrong Chen and colleagues. Standard gout drugs clash with upper gastrointestinal bleeding, so spotting high-risk patients early matters.

From 718 admitted patients at a Fujian hospital, 158 (22.0%) flared during their stay. Five algorithms learned from admission data, and random forest won clearly, reaching an AUC of 0.951 and accuracy of 0.901 on held-out patients. Explanation analysis named six key predictors: uric acid, creatinine, hemoglobin, blood urea nitrogen, body mass index, and alcohol history. Chen and colleagues offer the model as an early-warning tool so preventive steps can start before a flare complicates the bleeding.
pmc-13290787:
Qiang Lv and a large co-author group report a phase three trial of a new blood pressure pill, sitokiren, in 2026. The drug blocks renin directly, cutting the hormone chain that raises pressure at its source. The trial ran in two stages against valsartan, a standard comparator. Stage one tested three doses over twelve weeks in 129 randomized patients. The middle dose, one hundred milligrams, inhibited renin activity most and cut diastolic pressure best.

Stage two randomized 828 patients to that dose or to valsartan for twelve weeks. Diastolic pressure fell by about six points in both groups, with a small difference favoring neither in practical terms. Side effect rates were similar in each arm. Drug-related reactions actually ran slightly lower with sitokiren. The authors conclude the new renin blocker matches a proven drug for mild to moderate hypertension. Its exposure and safety data support once-daily use.
pmc-13291087:
Two lasers for facial pigment are compared by Ying Wu and colleagues in a 2026 split-face trial. The condition is melasma, a stubborn dark patch disorder. Sixteen Asian women with medium to darker skin took part. Each face got one laser type per side.

Three sessions ran four weeks apart. Pigment, looks, pain, and regrowth were scored for six months. Both sides lightened clearly over time. No clear gap split the two lasers on pigment. Pain after the first session was lower on the picosecond side. Pigment returned at alike rates on both sides. Choice may thus rest on comfort and cost.
pmc-13291187:
A heart tracing that looked like Brugada syndrome hid a deeper disease in a 2026 case from Antonio Scarà and colleagues. Their patient was a 51-year-old man. He fainted during a fever. His tracing showed the classic Brugada pattern, then faded.

First checks found nothing wrong. A day-long heart monitor then caught mixed abnormal beats. Both heart sides seemed to be involved. Heart scans showed a scar outside the usual blood supply pattern. Electrical mapping found more sick tissue in the right chamber. Provoked testing triggered lasting dangerous rhythms. Doctors placed an implantable defibrillator. The case warns against stopping at the first neat label.
pmc-13291887:
Ingrid Glurich's team reports a 2026 case-control study on why people use emergency dental clinics for nontraumatic problems despite living near a safety-net dental network. Records from 2019 identified 1,784 emergency cases and 18,612 controls who came for preventive care within 20 miles of ten clinics. A follow-up survey reached 84 cases and 113 controls.

Risk ran higher for younger adults, men, non-White patients, and those paying alone or through Medicaid or sliding fees. Prior emergency visits in medical or dental settings also raised the odds sharply. Survey answers showed cases more often feared dentists, delayed care, and saw visits as only for emergencies. Cost and missing insurance weighed heaviest on younger patients, and controls attended routine checkups more often.
pmc-13291987:
Yuan Guo and co-authors investigate a 2026 cancer biology study on EBF1, a transcription factor first known for guiding B-cell development, in prostate cancer. Database analyses and tissue staining linked low EBF1 levels with worse disease course. The team then dialed EBF1 down or up in prostate cancer cell lines and in a mouse xenograft model.

Silencing EBF1 made LNCaP and 22RV1 cells grow, form colonies, migrate, and invade more aggressively. Forcing extra EBF1 into PC-3 cells did the opposite, slowing tumor growth and invasion. Molecular assays pointed to EBF1 controlling the gene for ITPR1, a calcium channel receptor, as part of the mechanism. The authors frame EBF1 loss as a driver of prostate cancer progression worth further study.
pmc-13292687:
Haran Yogasundaram and co-authors mine a 2026 heart failure trial dataset, VICTORIA, asking how inflammation and ECG timing jointly relate to sudden cardiac death. They studied 4,391 patients with reduced ejection fraction after a recent worsening episode, all with core-lab ECGs and baseline blood markers. Three markers, high-sensitivity CRP, interleukin-6, and growth differentiation factor-15, were set against repolarization intervals.

A corrected JT interval, not the usual QTc, tied to sudden death, with risk easing slightly per extra ten milliseconds. All three biomarkers predicted sudden death alone, but only hsCRP survived adjustment, carrying a hazard ratio of 1.20 per doubling in the model. Growth factor levels independently tracked both ECG intervals. Adding hsCRP to the ECG model contributed the most new prognostic information. The authors argue inflammation kills through routes beyond electrical prolongation.
pmc-13292787:
Syafwan Syafwan and colleagues tested two heat relief ideas for broiler chickens in a 2026 trial set in tropical semi-open housing. Birds faced daily heat above their comfort range, a common strain on growth in hot climates.

A total of 198 chicks were split across 18 pens into three groups: plain feed, feed with red ginger extract, and ginger plus a cooling perch. Birds on the combined plan had lower body temperature, drank less water, and showed a lower stress ratio in blood cells. Growth did not differ clearly, though feed use looked slightly better. Pairing a plant extract with a cool resting bar may help birds cope with heat.
pmc-13293687:
Camille Dubois and colleagues pair two precision tools to watch how a cell adhesion protein responds to pulling forces, in a 2026 biophysics study. The protein, vinculin, bears mechanical load where cells grip their surroundings, and a built-in fluorescent sensor reports how much tension it carries. Using laser tweezers to hold a coated bead against a living fibroblast, the team could dial up the force the cell had to exert.

Cells held the bead at roughly the same displacement across all trap settings, recruiting more vinculin as stiffness rose. Tension inside vinculin climbed only slightly, and recruitment tracked stiffness rather than the raw size of the force. Occasionally a vinculin cluster slid away from the bead faster than the bead itself moved. The setup reveals force responses that static measurements cannot capture.
pmc-13293787:
Zongying Gui and co-authors pool, in a 2026 review, evidence on whether exposure to bisphenol chemicals raises the risk of polycystic ovary syndrome. These chemicals, found in plastics, can mimic hormones and disturb reproduction and metabolism.

Seventeen studies with 3010 women, found in two databases to December 2024, compared bisphenol levels in women with and without the syndrome. Blood and urine levels of bisphenol A ran higher in women with the syndrome, as did blood levels of its cousin bisphenol S. Spread between studies was high for one chemical and nil for the other. The authors urge exposure cuts and monitoring in care.
pmc-13293987:
Ryan O'Hanlon and Karen Y Wu lay out a 2026 protocol for watching RNA live inside cells with the Spinach family of glowing aptamers. Older tags are bulky, need hard delivery, or drag large proteins that can distort RNA behavior. Spinach tags are small RNA pieces that light up only when bound to a matched dye.

Instructions cover construct design, cloning, dye choice and loading, imaging on standard microscopes, and checks for true signal. Variants named Broccoli, Corn, Squash, and Beetroot allow several RNAs at once. Examples include tracking delivered therapeutic RNA, watching decay after a stimulus, and seeing toxic RNA clumps form.
pmc-13294287:
Daniel J Vermue and coauthors develop X-ray guides to prevent twisted healing in thigh bone nailing for a 2026 cadaver study. Twist errors of 15 degrees or more occur in up to 35% of nailed femur fractures, and no standard imaging routine existed. A mid-shaft break was fixed with an unlocked nail in a full-body specimen, and ten doctors made 150 corrections by eye or by two set views.

Judging by eye missed the true twist by a median of 15.5 degrees in the reported spread. Set views using the lesser trochanter profile or a true side view cut leftover twist to about 4 degrees each, far better than free practice. Doctors favored the trochanter view for speed.
pmc-13294387:
Siying Liu and a large team build a no-touch way to measure okra seedlings under salt stress in a 2026 study. Salty soils curb farm output, and hand measuring is slow and rough. Two camera views fed a lightened PointNet++ model with added attention and feature modules to label 3D point clouds, cluster single plants, and compute height, stem width, and canopy spread.

Seedlings kept growing as salt rose, though rates shifted in the reported trends. The tuned model cut size and compute while sharpening shape capture versus the base network. Fast, harmless scoring can screen many cultivars for salt tolerance and guide planting on salty land.
pmc-13295687:
G A Dakroury, Sh M Abdo, and E A A El Shazly build a green gel that captures zirconium from acid waste in a 2026 study. Zirconium matters for nuclear technology, and recovering it from strong acid streams needs tough, cheap materials. Their blend mixes chitosan, starch, and polyvinyl alcohol into one sorbent.

Lab checks confirmed useful chemical groups and a fine-pored structure in the gel. Uptake peaked under very acidic conditions after two hours and rose further when more metal was offered. Warming weakened capture, showing heat is released as metal binds. The gel survived strong acid, washed clean for reuse, and fits recovery from factory streams.
pmc-13295787:
Simon M Petzinna and colleagues trial an inflammation-specific scan in giant cell arteritis in a 2026 study. Judging disease activity in this vessel inflammation is hard because blood and scan markers lack precision. Their PET tracer targets a vessel protein tied to immune cell entry, aiming for a cleaner signal.

Eight newly diagnosed patients were compared with eight relapsing patients and eight healthy controls. Tracer uptake rose alongside ultrasound-measured wall thickening in a key artery. Steroid exposure dulled uptake, hinting the scan tracks treatment effect. A soluble form of the target protein ran lower in new cases than in relapsing ones, adding a possible blood companion marker.
pmc-13296387:
Barış Erkut Türk and co-authors model, in 2026, custom implants that sit on top of severely shrunken upper jawbone rather than inside it. A three-dimensional jaw model tested one-piece and two-piece designs in titanium and a carbon-reinforced plastic under straight and angled biting loads.

Bone stress barely changed between materials, while design shaped stress inside the implant itself. Two-piece versions stressed more under angled loads but less under straight ones. A combined ranking put one-piece titanium best for angled loads and two-piece titanium best for straight loads. The authors say shape and load direction outweigh material choice.
pmc-13296487:
Maren Umlandt and colleagues probe the layered structure of light-switchable surfactant films on glass in a 2026 study. Such films coat surfaces in water and their inner organisation controls how they behave. A quartz crystal sensor that tracks vibration and energy loss was used to separate stiff inner layers from loose outer ones.

Below a key concentration, the molecules formed compact, rigid layers one to two molecules thick. Above that concentration, extra material piled into a soft, water-rich overlayer that added little firm thickness. The contrast shows the sensor can map vertical structure inside responsive coatings. That ability helps designers of detergents, coatings, and other surface treatments judge film quality.
pmc-13296887:
Chen Huang, Beining Yang and Yan Huo upgrade, in 2026, a wolf-pack-inspired search algorithm for planning drone flight paths. The standard method narrows too fast and settles early, so the team add chaotic starting points, a curved pacing factor and a learning system that switches between exploring and refining.

Leader selection now weighs both solution quality and distance, aiming for steadier convergence. Against five rival algorithms on a standard test suite, the new version performed well on accuracy, speed and robustness. In three-dimensional drone simulations it produced safe routes respecting terrain and obstacles.
pmc-13296987:
Christian Joseph N. Ong and co-authors chart, in 2026, world research on fungus-derived antibiotics against MRSA, the drug-resistant staph germ. Counting 1,666 publications, they trace output growth and shifting themes over time.

Publishing surged after 2010 as fungal products gained ground as alternative germ fighters. Topics moved from broad screening toward biofilm attack, computer docking, fungi living inside plants, production pathways and resistance itself. The authors say the field now blends microbiology, natural chemistry and computing, and they offer their map as a strategy guide toward clinical use against resistant infections.
pmc-13297087:
Jaume Galceran and a Spanish registry network analyse, in 2026, long-term survival and second cancers among childhood cancer patients across sixteen Spanish provinces. Survival has climbed for decades, yet treatment itself raises later cancer risk, and Spain lacked population figures.

The study tracks survival trends by tumour type and measures second cancer risk by time since diagnosis and first cancer kind. It is billed as the country's first population-based look at both questions. The authors aim to guide gentler treatments and smarter lifelong follow-up for survivors, balancing cure today against harm tomorrow.
pmc-13297287:
Jingya Zhang and co-authors upgrade, in 2026, a dhole-inspired hunting algorithm for hard engineering optimisation. The base method explores narrowly and converges slowly, so the team add opposite-guess learning, a borrowed mutation move and curved control of search settings.

Across forty-one standard test functions the modified version beat eleven leading rivals on speed, accuracy and steadiness. It then tackled five real problems, from spring and gearbox design to bearing and column sizing. Paired with a neural network it sharply cut herb moisture prediction errors. The authors call it a robust all-round optimiser.
pmc-13297387:
Losing a neuronal enzyme that builds NAD+ may set off a chain ending in faulty amyloid handling, according to a 2026 laboratory study headed by Andrea Enriquez. Working with cortical neurons, the team examined what follows when NMNAT2 is missing and how the enzyme SARM1 shapes the damage.

Neurons lacking NMNAT2 showed a falling NAD+ balance and a buildup of amyloid precursor protein fragments. Energy failure came in two waves, first in sugar breakdown and later in mitochondrial output, matched by stress signaling inside the cells. Silencing SARM1 restored mitochondrial function and normalized fragment levels, while simply adding NAD+ helped only slightly. The findings nominate SARM1 blockade as a treatment idea worth testing.
pmc-13297787:
Gaogao Dong and colleagues study how entanglement survives in quantum networks as links are cut at random, in a 2026 theory paper. The networks studied grow in flower-like tiers with two knobs that set path lengths. Each link was diluted with a set chance, and the team compared a quantum measure of connection against the classical version.

Quantum connection held on to far lower link densities than classical connection in every layout and dilution tried. Many paths for entanglement, rather than one, compensate when parts of the network fail. The tiered shape adds further toughness. Designers of quantum networks gain proof that multipath entanglement is itself a shield against decay.
pmc-13299187:
Tumors hoard a shield that soaks up the harm from X-ray care, and Haonan Xu and his team review how to drain that hoard in a 2026 paper. X-ray care kills tumor cells in large part by making harsh oxygen forms. The shield, glutathione, mops those forms up, so tumors rich in it stand up to the rays.

The review lays out how the shield is built and how it is reused. It then tours the means to break it. Some drugs block its build path. Some force it to drain. Tiny man-made pods can haul the attack drugs into the tumor. The aim is one: pile harsh oxygen stress on shield-rich tumors so ray care bites again. The team weigh the early proof and the gaps on the road to clinic use.
pmc-13299287:
Marta Calvo leads a team reviewing a rare inherited intellectual disability disorder plus reporting a new case with a hidden structural variant, in a 2026 study. Variants in the TRAPPC9 gene cause the condition, and most known changes are small. Their new patient's two gene copies were disrupted by an inherited deletion and a balanced chromosome swap.

Literature synthesis covered 75 earlier patients, making 76 in total. Intellectual disability appeared in every case, with brain imaging changes, small head size, and motor delay also common. No link between variant type and symptom pattern emerged. Advanced genome mapping proved valuable for finding cryptic structural changes that standard tests can miss.
pmc-13299787:
Statins can physically remodel cell membranes, but turning that trick into a cancer therapy has stumbled, writes Giulio Preta in a 2026 commentary. Beyond blocking cholesterol synthesis, statins slip into lipid bilayers and change how tightly membrane lipids pack, an effect grouped under membrane lipid therapy.

Laboratory studies in model and biological membranes support real potential, including better delivery of chemotherapy drugs into cells. Yet the jump from dishes to patients keeps failing, and the commentary dissects why: dosing, membrane context, and the gap between artificial systems and tumors all conspire. Preta argues the repurposing idea survives, but only with more honest translational design.
pmc-13299887:
Ke Xu and colleagues compare two mulberry leaf powders as the base for artificial silkworm diet, in a 2026 sericulture study. Artificial feeding underpins expansion and automation of silk production, so ingredient quality matters. Chemical profiling contrasted forage mulberry leaves with grafted mulberry leaves across amino acids, fatty acids, and other compounds.

Forage leaves held less of several nutrients, including serine, key fatty acids, and vitamin C, yet far more of one distinctive compound. Silkworms raised on the forage-based diet grew lighter and produced lighter cocoons with a lower shell share. The authors link outcome gaps to metabolite differences and offer guidance for diet formulation.
pmc-13303587:
Sam Hanash, Luigi Buonaguro, and Olivera Finn write a 2026 editorial introducing a research collection on cancer immunosurveillance. The topic covers how the immune system removes tumors, holds them in check, or fails and lets them escape.

Studies in the collection include work on T cells raised by latent Epstein-Barr virus genes that killed varied tumors. Other work covers shared features between virus proteins and tumor proteins that may train protective T cells. A further piece draws lessons from plant defenses against disease. Together the papers link immune watching to therapy, risk judgment, prevention, and outlook for patients.
pmc-13303787:
Fiordaliso Carolina Román-Carraro and Laila Gutiérrez-Kobeh review programmed cell death as an arena of host and microbe conflict in a 2026 synthesis. Orderly cell suicide removes damaged or infected cells without sparking harmful inflammation.

Three main routes trigger this process, all ending in enzymes that dismantle the cell. Viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites have each found ways to block, delay, or hijack these routes at shared control points. Such pressure over long spans likely expanded and complicated the host machinery itself. Framing cell death as part of a joint defense network links daily cell balance with infection outcomes.
pmc-13304987:
Kinga Dulak and co-authors engineer gut bacteria to run a plant enzyme that adds oxygen to flavonoid compounds in a 2026 study. Such plant enzymes make prized products but dissolve poorly in bacteria and need helper partners to work.

The enzyme from a Chinese medicinal herb was paired with a plant reductase, both as separate parts and as one fused chain. Many starter tags, hosts, feeds, and growth settings were screened. Fused versions beat separate ones by about double, and the best linker gave the strongest conversion of chrysin into baicalein. Tag trimming helped, while one added tag hurt output.
pmc-13305287:
Mahisha Jayakody and co-authors gather views on asthma care from migrant communities in Melbourne, Australia, in a 2026 interview study. Deaths and illness from asthma run high nationally, and language-diverse groups face added gaps in knowledge and access.

Forty-seven people with asthma from Vietnamese, Sri Lankan, and Indian backgrounds joined two nurse-led teaching sessions supported by bicultural health educators. Interviews six weeks apart surfaced weak grasp of asthma control, poor inhaler technique, and trouble finding community care. Cultural attitudes and low reading levels shaped management as well, pointing to tailored education needs.
pmc-13305387:
Kui Mao and colleagues pool randomized trials of a moving needle-tip method for placing wrist artery lines under ultrasound in a 2026 meta-analysis. Short-axis views center the vessel well but lose sight of the needle tip, risking failed first tries.

Five databases were searched through January 2026, and thirteen trials with 1,482 adults qualified. Overall first-try success matched the long-axis view across methods. Splitting by technique told another story: the dynamic tip method beat both the fixed short-axis habit and the long-axis view. Time, bruising, wall punctures, and vessel spasm were also compared across trials.
pmc-13306787:
Wajiha Zaheer surveyed self-tuning machine learning for guarding electric car charging networks in a 2026 review. Linked chargers and home devices create shifting data patterns where fixed learning pipelines age quickly and miss new attacks.

Online AutoML adapts to streaming data with little human help, and can learn under tight computing and privacy limits in the authors' account. Attackers can also poison or fool such adaptive systems, so defences must handle drift, scale, privacy and hostile input together. Shared public benchmarks are urged to make competing systems comparable. The team says joint rules will help guard charge nets as they grow in size.
pmc-13306987:
İbrahim Türkmen reviewed fresh behaviour of printable geopolymer mortars in a 2026 survey. Extrusion printing succeeds only while the mix flows, holds shape and bonds between layers, all while the binder reaction steadily stiffens it.

Raw material type, activator strength, liquid share, additives and fibres each shift flow, yield stress and viscosity in the gathered work. Setting pace and early strength decide the printable window and layer joint quality. Missing standard tests and tangled material-process links limit fair comparison across studies, a gap the review maps for future standards.
pmc-13307187: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2016 study claiming naringin drives bone formation in rat marrow cells through the Notch pathway. Concern centred on a control band in one figure that, after squeezing, closely matched a band in another group's paper. Authors did not answer publisher queries, and editors judged results and conclusions unreliable. The notice is short and offers no corrected data, so the bone claims should no longer be relied upon.
pmc-13308387:
Annette M Totten and co-authors scan in 2026 models of person centred care planning for people who live with many long term conditions in the United States. They sifted 966 short records and 187 full papers, and they spoke with experts who run such models on the ground.

They found 40 models that fell into seven broad ways of straying from usual care, from new roles to new pay and tech tools. Most mixed many parts and showed gains on aims that span patient joy and system cost. Lack of time and poor pay fit blocked wide uptake the most. Shared playbooks and ready tools could help clinics adopt what works.
pmc-13308587:
Matthias Van Ginneken and co-authors name in 2026 a fresh subset of cosmic spherules, tiny space grains that melt as they fall to Earth, with odd oxygen marks. About one in ten spherules shows such marks and points to a rock source missing from meteorite stores held on Earth.

The new grains hold settled olivine crystals, sulfur rich glass, and iron nickel sulfur drops, with almost no magnetite at all. Those traits hint at very low oxygen growth and entry paths that fit a tilted, stretched orbit. Modellers link the grains to a primitive, sulfur rich near Earth asteroid of the CY kind. Earth thus gains dust from a parent body that big rocks have not sampled.
pmc-13310687:
Rade B. Vukmir reviews how Alzheimer disease and related dementias are evaluated and managed in acute care in a 2026 article. A patient with memory loss often needs a wide, multi-specialty workup that may start in primary care, an emergency department, or a neurology clinic. Clear sorting of delirium from dementia anchors that workup.

Literature from the national medical database was gathered on diagnosis, imaging, and treatment, favoring primary research over reviews where feasible. Delirium is framed as an acute, fluctuating change tied to sudden illness, while dementia follows a chronic, progressive course. Screening routes, referral triggers, and treatment basics are laid out for front-line clinicians. The author aims to sharpen early recognition and handoffs.
pmc-13310787:
Ignacio Garach Vélez and colleagues review smart computing for the reproductive microbiome in a 2026 paper. Germs in sperm, ovaries, womb lining, and pregnancy affect fertility and birth outcomes. Study data are split and mostly descriptive, so clear clinical use lags behind the volume of results.

Machine and deep learning can clean sparse germ data, compare groups, pick marker germs, and sort patients by outcome. Linking data across sites and methods remains a core task. Clear models that doctors can follow are vital for trust. Joining smart tools with biology know how may move care from description toward prediction.
pmc-13311187:
Pierre Laboudie and colleagues report low early fracture rates for cemented hip stems in weak femurs in a 2026 study. Breaks around implants worry surgeons in wide, thin walled femurs. A stem fixed by the French paradox method through a front approach may suit this high risk group, yet early break rates were unclear.

A total of 670 stems placed from 2017 to 2023 were tracked for about 31 months on average in older adults. Only ten early breaks occurred, split evenly between the two femur types. No severe cement reaction cases arose. Low rates support the method in frail hip fracture care.
pmc-13311287:
Kalina Chupetlovska and co-authors in 2026 report an interview study on how radiologists come to trust or resist AI tools. Most past work asks whether the tools work, not whether doctors will use them.

Eighteen radiologists from two hospitals spoke at length about user, system, maker, ethics, and patient factors. Most felt hopeful about AI for set tasks. Trust rested most on accuracy and time saved, named by nearly all, with easy fit into daily systems also key. Hospital reputation, peer proof, and keeping a human in charge shaped trust too. The study maps what builders must earn.
pmc-13311687:
Xiaoqi Cheng and colleagues detail a 2026 trial of a low-cost hand-worked heat device for blocked oil glands in the eyelids, a cause of dry eye. The device was tested against the Lipiflow machine.

Eighty-four subjects were split evenly between one session of the hand device or the machine and followed for four weeks; 76 finished. Changes in gland scores, tear breakup time, symptom scores, and staining did not differ clearly between groups, pointing to equal effect. No serious eye or device harms appeared. Subgroup work on gland oils and microbes adds clues on who gains most.
pmc-13311787:
Britta S von Ungern-Sternberg, Aine Sommerfield, and Karin Becke-Jakob write a 2026 reply letter distinguishing moral injury from stakes-dependent invisibility at work. Both can distress clinicians, but the harms differ in kind.

Moral injury, in the definition they cite, grows when sustained moral distress hardens into lasting harm or lost function. It centers on acts or powerlessness that clash with a person's own moral compass. Invisibility instead names lacking power, recognition, and voice, so needs go unmet. The authors thank the letter writer for the contrast and agree the two ideas should not be merged.
pmc-13311987:
Giancarlo Ceccarelli and co-authors write a 2026 letter reframing the FIFA World Cup as an epidemiological opportunity, not only a disease risk. The 2026 tournament spans 48 teams and 16 host cities in three countries.

Mass gathering medicine usually asks how to stop outbreaks at crowded events. The authors note this event instead links cities, transport, hospitals, and data systems across a continent for weeks. Millions of fans, workers, and media will move repeatedly between distant hubs. That mesh, they argue, could teach more about disease spread and surveillance than any single-city event, if researchers plan to learn from it now.
pmc-13312487:
Nengjie Yang and colleagues describe, in a 2026 study, a microfluidic-made nanocomposite that carries healthy mitochondria into inflamed joints as a treatment for rheumatoid arthritis. The disease is tied to mitochondrial failure, which stokes reactive oxygen species, immune overdrive, and autoantibody output, so swapping in healthy mitochondria has emerged as a possible therapy.

Their composite, Mito@G3K, forms on a tiny chip where positively charged peptide dendrimers capture mitochondria by charge. Tuning the surface charge higher made them home to inflamed joints quickly, gather there in volume, and stay active for a long time. In cell tests the composite calmed the inflammation that macrophages drive, and in a mouse arthritis model it eased joint inflammation. Gene tests of joint tissue suggested the benefit runs through improved mitochondrial metabolism.
pmc-13312887:
Nathalie de Bouvre and colleagues test, in a 2026 blinded, placebo-controlled trial, whether horse stem cells can ease a painful chronic mouth disease in cats. Feline chronic gingivostomatitis leaves cats with inflamed, ulcerated mouths and few good options in severe cases, so regenerative cell therapy is being explored as a new direction.

Sixteen cats at one veterinary practice received a single intravenous dose of equine peripheral blood-derived mesenchymal stem cells or a control. Owners scored their animals daily, and vets examined them across about three months. Each group reported one ordinary and one serious adverse event, neither tied to treatment, and blood work stayed unremarkable, so the cells appeared safe. But disease activity scores, biopsy results, time to failure, and owner reports showed no significant advantage over control. The authors recommend longer, redesigned studies before judging efficacy.
pmc-13313187:
Rob J Dekker and colleagues study newborn goat kids in a 2026 paper on what happens when a young animal is fed milk from another species. Swapping the mother's first milk and later milk for cow products is common on farms, but how it changes small non-coding RNAs that travel in blood was not well known.

The team used twin kids from six vaccinated goat mothers, with twelve kids in all. One twin got its mother's colostrum and milk, while the other got cow colostrum and a milk replacer. Sequencing of small RNAs in blood, goat milk, and the cow products showed rich mixes of microRNAs and fragments from other RNAs. Handling and storage changed how much of each RNA survived, and blood profiles shifted as the kids grew.
pmc-13314887:
Sebastian Findeklee and colleagues grade a hands-on training block for medical students at a German women clinic, in 2026 work. The Homburg university clinic built a five-day placement that stresses practical gynecology and obstetrics skills over book learning.

Students rated the block on a six-point scale for learning gains and for whether it sparked interest in the field. Of 220 students in the winter term of 2022 and 2023, a total of 205 took part, a share of 93.2 percent as given in the report. Nearly all, at a share of 96.6 percent in the figures shown, rated their satisfaction at the top end, by the account given. The strong marks back skill-first placements as a way to draw students toward women health fields.
pmc-13315187:
Vishal Goel and colleagues used data from a large trial to build prediction models in 2026 for heart failure readmission. The patients had come to 12 emergency departments in South Australia in 2023 with symptoms that led to a heart blood test, and they were followed for 12 months.

Of 14,131 patients, 808 were readmitted for heart failure, at a median of 83 days. An extreme gradient boosting model predicted readmission best in the test set, beating standard logistic regression and three other machine learning methods. Good calibration was also reported. Better early prediction could help teams plan follow-up for patients most likely to return.
pmc-13315887:
Meini Chen and a large team studied in 2026 how two related enzymes keep rod photoreceptors alive as eyes age and face stress. GOT1 works in the cell body fluid and GOT2 in mitochondria, and together they run a shuttle that moves reducing power between compartments, linking them to blinding retinal disease.

Mice missing GOT1 only in rods lost photoreceptors, with NADH buildup and a lower NAD ratio in the retina. Burning off that excess NADH by metabolic or genetic means extended cell survival, pointing to reductive stress as a driver. Mice missing GOT2 instead showed little degeneration, splitting the two enzymes' roles.
pmc-13316087:
Ibrahim S Alshaygy and colleagues pooled evidence in 2026 on how often giant cell tumor of bone turns malignant during or after denosumab therapy. The drug reshaped care for tumors that cannot be removed or would need damaging surgery, yet scattered reports of malignant change raised fear of a causal link.

Searches of three databases to October 2025 gathered trials, cohorts, series, and case reports that carried original patient data. Twenty-four studies entered the qualitative review, and eleven studies with 800 treated patients fed the pooled incidence estimate. Clinical, imaging, and pathology features of affected patients were also charted.
pmc-13316187:
Jerson Mekoulou Ndongo and a large team surveyed university students in Douala, Cameroon, in 2026 on poor sleep and its links with eating disorders, body makeup, and activity. Standard questionnaires measured sleep quality, eating risk, and activity, while body mass index, waist size, and body composition were measured directly in 522 students.

Poor sleep affected 73.7 percent of students and eating disorder risk 35.6 percent of the group, with women at 61.7 percent of participants and higher eating risk. Poor sleep tied to activity level, eating risk, body mass, fat mass, and body water, with patterns differing between men and women in adjusted models.
pmc-13316287:
Gayathri Delanerolle heads a large team behind a 2026 cross-sectional report from the MARIE project, which studies body and mind health around the menopause transition. The work spans 13 countries and draws participants from clinics and communities, including low- and middle-income settings often left out of such research.

Recruitment ran from January 2024 to September 2025 and used digital routes to reach people in peri-, meno-, and post-menopause stages. The report maps symptom load and related health areas country by country, and a smaller subgroup with repeat measures adds detail on changing symptoms, lower-back pain, and daily life quality. By placing rich and poor countries side by side, the project gives policy makers a fuller picture of needs that longer lives now bring.
pmc-13316587:
Rebaz M Ali and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare kidney cancer type, mucinous tubular and spindle cell carcinoma. It was found by chance in a 39-year-old man checked for high blood lipids. The tumor type makes up under one percent of kidney cancers and can mimic other forms under the microscope.

Scans showed two left kidney masses, the larger measuring 26 by 24 millimeters in the scan report. Surgeons removed part of the kidney by keyhole surgery, and tissue study confirmed the rare cancer in the larger mass and a harmless growth in the smaller one. Recovery went smoothly with no return seen on later scans. A short review adds ten recent cases from five reports.
pmc-13316687:
Xiang Ding leads a large team behind a 2026 wound dressing made of plant-based furan polyamide nanofibers with two unlike faces, a Janus design. Early germ growth and biofilms stall healing, so the dressing aims to hit bacteria fast at the wound surface while staying gentle on tissue.

Two near-twin polymers differ by just two carbon links, yet spinning them into fibers magnified that small gap into a strong wetting contrast, with no surface treatment needed. The wet-loving face carried tetracycline, releasing useful levels within four hours. Tests cut bacterial biofilms and lowered germ counts in a pig burn model. The study is the first use of these green polymers as spun wound dressings.
pmc-13317687:
Mads Bertelsen and colleagues describe, in a 2026 methods paper, how computer simulations of neutron protein crystallography can help build the NMX instrument. It sits at the European Spallation Source, set to be the world's strongest neutron facility. Neutrons locate hydrogen atoms precisely, something X-rays cannot do, but beam time is precious.

Monte Carlo models trace neutrons through instrument parts and crystal diffraction before any real beam exists. The team shows how such virtual experiments guide design choices and commissioning of the flagship diffractometer. Honest simulation, they argue, stretches what rare neutron experiments can achieve by rehearsing them in software first. The approach generalizes to other scarce-beam instruments under construction.
pmc-13318587:
Zhenshan Yang and fellow editors introduce a 2026 research collection. The theme is embryo development and the meeting point between embryo and womb lining. That stage shapes implantation, pregnancy, and maternal health. Their editorial surveys the contributions gathered under the theme.

One highlight maps gene activity across the whole human embryo. Pan and co-workers built that resource. A mouse atlas of blood vessel cells names CASZ1 as a guide for lung vessels. Zhang and co-workers add genetic work on eggs and embryos that fail early. A laboratory implantation platform from Molè and co-workers also features. It shows signals between embryo and womb cells. Those signals support early growth after implantation.
pmc-13318787:
Qingmiao Shi and co-authors review, in 2026, the Notch signalling pathway inside the tumour surroundings of digestive cancers. Notch is an old cell-to-cell communication system. Beyond driving tumour growth, it reshapes the neighbourhood that tumours live in. That reshaping helps cancers spread and resist treatment.

The review traces how faulty Notch activity recruits and steers immune cells. Suppressor cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and regulatory T cells all feature. Notch also activates fibroblasts, grows new vessels, and remodels the tissue scaffold. Together these effects build an immune-suppressing environment. The authors summarise Notch-blocking drugs and their pairing with immunotherapy and other targeted treatments. They argue better mapping of these roles could improve outcomes.
pmc-13319387:
Brandon X Lum and co-authors set out a way to track carbon per unit of care in a 2026 report from a Singapore health system. Care sites face more work from aging crowds at the same time as they must cut climate harm. A fair score must weigh both sides at once, not just total smoke output.

One clinic visit was set as one work unit, and other care types were scaled by their carbon weight, with a hospital day counting far more. Scores from 2020 to 2023 showed carbon per unit fell from 16.85 to 16.17 in the units used, even as total output rose. Shifting yearly factors made the math tricky, but the score still aids fair checks across sites.
pmc-13319487:
Chuyu Pan and co-authors sort depression risk by gene pattern in a 2026 study of a large British health bank. Low mood runs in families, but not in one single way for all people. Gene scores grouped by body function were used to split people into types, then health paths were tracked over time for each type.

Three types stood out, one led by immune genes, one led by nerve genes, and one with broad risk across systems. The broad risk type faced the highest chance of new low mood and of later illness after low mood, such as gut disease and low blood counts. Surroundings also hit each type with uneven force, which may guide more personal care.
pmc-13319687:
Konstantinos Kostikas leads a real world study from 2026 on a paired inhaler drug for long term lung disease. Control of this illness means fewer flare ups and steady daily health, yet proof for paired airway openers in daily practice was thin. People whose illness was not controlled on prior inhalers switched to the pair and were followed for 12 weeks.

More than a thousand people joined across many sites, and nearly all finished the follow up. By week 12 a large share, over four in five, reached control of their illness. Lung flow and health scores both improved by clear margins. Low starting lung flow and past flare ups marked those least likely to gain control.
pmc-13320287:
Jianrong Chen and co-authors study a tiny gene scrap that wears out killer immune cells in breast cancer in a 2026 article. The scrap is known to curb tumor cells themselves, yet its work inside the immune crowd around a tumor was unclear. Data bank checks first flagged it as unevenly voiced in breast tumors, then patient samples gave a closer look.

Samples from 32 patients showed higher scrap levels in killer cells inside tumors than in nearby healthy tissue. The scrap latches onto a co start switch those cells need and turns it down, while wear out marks on the cells rose. Tumors rich in the scrap also voiced more call signals that pull killer cells in. The scrap thus both recruits and blunts the same cells.
pmc-13322187:
Lou’i Al-Husinat and co-authors survey organ donation willingness among intensive care families in northern Jordan in a 2026 study. Families hold the key to consent after brain death, yet demand for organs far outruns supply. A structured questionnaire went to 155 adult family members at one referral hospital, covering knowledge, faith views, trust, and campaign exposure.

Only 44 people, or 28.4 percent, said they would donate. Strong trust in the health system was the leading predictor, with odds near eight times higher in adjusted models. A favourable religious stance and strong familiarity with donation also raised willingness. Building trust and clear public teaching look central to closing the gap.
pmc-13322487:
Letícia Pereira Quintaes Godinho and colleagues describe mouth posture in babies with trisomy 21 in a 2026 observational study. Habitual lip and tongue position can shape feeding and later speech, yet norms for these infants were unclear. Videos of 61 infants, with a mean age of 7.4 months, were analysed for resting posture, and records supplied age and health details.

Parted lips were the most common lip posture, at 48.2 percent of observed time, and tongue inside the mouth was the leading tongue posture, at 32.4 percent in the study. Younger age and higher birth weight went with better lip posture, while breastfeeding went with better tongue posture. The links may guide early feeding support.
pmc-13322887:
Aimin Zhou and colleagues compare two chemotherapy routes for colorectal cancer spread to the liver, in a 2026 single-centre study. Records cover 132 patients with liver spread that could not be removed, treated between 2019 and 2023 at a hospital linked to Yichun University.

One group received the triple drug plan FOLFOXIRI, and the other received FOLFIRI plus chemotherapy infused through the hepatic artery. The second group held disease back longer, with median time without growth of 10.3 months against 8.2 months for the triple plan, and had higher rates of tumour shrinkage and disease control. Overall survival looked slightly longer too, though that gap was not firm. Side effects were compared across both groups.
pmc-13323687:
Haihong Zhang and co-authors model online engagement among nursing students in China, in a 2026 survey of 917 undergraduates drawn from five provinces. Scales measured self-directed learning skill, information literacy, self-control and engagement with online study.

Self-directed learning skill predicted engagement directly and also through information literacy, which carried about two thirds of the total effect in their mediation model. Self-control unexpectedly weakened the direct link, a pattern the authors explore in the moderated model. Most participants were women, matching the nursing cohort profile. Findings suggest that teaching students to find and judge information may lift online engagement more than exhorting effort alone.
pmc-13324487:
Naoyuki Ida and co-authors report five cases of advanced cervical neuroendocrine carcinoma treated with pembrolizumab-based therapy in a 2026 case series. The cancer is rare and aggressive, and proof for immune checkpoint drugs in it is thin.

Records from Okayama University Hospital covered care given between November 2022 and April 2025. Each patient got paclitaxel and carboplatin plus pembrolizumab, and all five responded, with one full and four partial responses. Median tumor shrinkage was 78.5 percent and median time without growth reached 10.0 months. Tumors tested as microsatellite stable with low mutation load. Immune side effects stayed grade 2 or lower. In three cases, control later allowed radiation or surgery.
pmc-13324787: Łukasz Lisowski and co-authors issued this brief 2026 item, which is only a correction notice for their scoping review on what shapes the cortical P100 response in pattern visual tests. The notice fixes one label in Figure 2, panel C, where Optics had been printed as Opglalte, and shows the corrected figure. The panel ranks factors that shift P100 timing and size, including age, sex, and blur. Nothing else in the review changes, and the notice states the original article has been updated.
pmc-13325087:
Zhenjie Sun and co-authors model how rock permeability shapes hot water storage in aquifers in a 2026 simulation study. Storing heat underground at high temperature can smooth renewable energy supply, but the rock decides how much heat comes back.

A three-dimensional model coupled heat, water flow, and rock mechanics in a two-well system. Higher average permeability spread heat sideways, cut pumping costs, yet lowered heat recovery. Uneven permeability between directions and patchy rock both hurt recovery, with patchiness the stronger harm. Hot wells reacted more than cold wells because hot water flows more freely. The authors favor rock with weak direction bias and low patchiness for new sites.
pmc-13325387:
Chenglei Wang and co-authors optimize vacuum distillation of hydroquinone and catechol in a 2026 simulation study. The pair are heat-sensitive feedstocks, and standard purification burns much energy for modest output.

An Aspen Plus model with a calibrated NRTL framework simulated the column at a 100 kg per hour feed rate. Single-factor sweeps and response surface tuning then hunted the best settings. The optimum ran at 10 kPa with 16 plates, feed at tray 11, and a reflux ratio of 3.143 for the mass flows. Purity hit 99.2 percent for hydroquinone and 99 percent for catechol, with energy use down 23.7 percent against the plant baseline.
pmc-13325987:
Simone Fezzi and co-authors review how to spot coronary plaques likely to cause future heart attacks in a 2026 article. Many acute events spring from plaques that barely narrow the artery yet carry risky biology.
