Inner imaging tools each add a piece: ultrasound gauges burden, near-infrared reads fat content, and coherence tomography measures cap thickness and calcium. Cost, contrast load, and operator skill limit their routine use. A newer angle reads radial wall strain from standard angiograms to gauge how much a plaque flexes. High strain matched risky features on detailed imaging and predicted later events on its own. Mixing flow, shape, and strain data may refine personal risk calls.
pmc-13326087:
Patrizia Farci and co-authors weigh viral and host traits in hepatitis B liver failure in a 2026 study. Acute infection ranges from mild hepatitis to rapid organ failure, and what tips the balance was unclear.

Samples came from 49 patients: 36 with liver failure in several forms and 13 with ordinary acute hepatitis. Death ran highest, at 82 percent, in subacute failure and failure on chronic infection. Acute failure showed sky-high liver enzymes and a broad type 1 cytokine storm. Genotype A led at 63 percent of cases. Virus populations stayed uniform in fresh failure but varied widely when failure hit chronic infection. Immune tone differed by form.
pmc-13327787:
Natasa Ganea and co-authors track visual pattern learning with brain waves in a 2026 experiment. Fifty-one adults watched image streams grouped in triplets while EEG recorded steady rhythms locked to the triplet rate. Three setups varied how category and single-image information lined up inside each triplet.

Brain responses at the triplet rate were stronger when all images shared one category or when categories played no role, and weaker when categories were mixed inside triplets. Reaction times told the same story, with faster responses to final images in the matching setups. Mismatched category cues thus hinder learning, and the rhythm method offers a live window on learning as it happens.
pmc-13327887:
Jae Won Jo and colleagues compare emergency Hartmann procedures by surgeon specialty in a 2026 hospital study. Staff shortages increasingly push general surgeons to perform this emergency colon operation. Records covered 141 patients treated at one large center between January 2010 and December 2021.

Patients of noncolorectal surgeons were older and sicker on arrival, yet gaps persisted after adjustment. Complications hit 68.5 percent in the noncolorectal group against 36.5 percent for colorectal specialists, and deaths ran 25.8 percent against 3.8 percent between those groups. Noncolorectal operating stayed an independent risk factor for both outcomes, leading the authors to back stronger residency training in the procedure.
pmc-13328187:
Elham Omer Mahgoub and co-authors validate substrates of the liver uptake transporter OCT1 in a 2026 study. OCT1 pulls many drugs, including metformin, into liver cells, and reported partners span a huge affinity range. The team joined computer docking and motion simulations with uptake tests in engineered kidney cells.

Simulations agreed with earlier work that ethidium bromide binds OCT1 tightly, and cells lacking OCT1 barely took it up, while metformin blocked its transport strongly. A fresh finding crowned the work: vitamin K1 potently blocked OCT1-driven uptake, marking it as a high-affinity partner not reported before. Pairing modeling with bench checks offers a sturdy way to vet transporter claims.
pmc-13328487:
Battira M Sharmila and co-authors build an electrochemical sensor for a red food dye in a 2026 study. Carmoisine colors foods, drinks, cosmetics, and medicines, and excess intake harms health, so quick checks matter. Their carbon nanotube graphite sensor was coated with the surfactant sodium dodecyl sulfate to sharpen its response.

The coating grew the active surface from 0.031 to 0.049 square centimeters against the bare sensor on their measure, and detection limits fell to 0.009 μM by cyclic voltammetry and 0.073 μM by pulse methods across narrow working ranges. Repeat readings varied by under 5 percent, marking the device as steady. Cheap dye screening for food safety labs is the aim.
pmc-13329987:
Ognyan Stefanov and co-authors measure record heat direction bias in carbon nanotube films in a 2026 study. Films that spread heat sideways but block it downward can protect stacked electronics. The team tested shop-bought solution-spun films, 20 micrometres thick and centimetres wide, across a wide temperature span.

Heat bias reached a ratio of 1400, with a margin of 160, at room temperature in the reported results. That tops prior records the authors cite. Baking films to remove acid leftovers doubled sideways heat spread speed. Sideways flow also fell with heat in a pattern that points to phonon clashes as the main brake. The authors urge more work on such films for guided heat spreading.
pmc-13330687:
Xueying Bao and colleagues pair two drugs in a targeted nanoparticle to boost lung cancer chemoradiation in a 2026 study. Plumbagin, a natural redox agent, unsettles tumour chemistry and sensitises cells to docetaxel. Dose needs fell sharply in two lung cancer cell lines when the pair was used, the authors report.

A folate-guided liposome carried both drugs together to fix mismatched body handling. With radiation, harmful oxygen build-up inside cells rose well above radiation alone in those tests. In mice, radiation plus the targeted pair curbed tumours by 99 percent in the reported results, with steady weight and no clear blood, liver, or kidney harm. Low-dose gains with safety are the promise.
pmc-13331987:
Albert C Chong and colleagues report a 2026 allergy case in which exercise began triggering anaphylaxis only after a patient started the weight and diabetes drug tirzepatide. The 51-year-old man had obesity, asthma, and allergic rhinitis, and took a weekly 2.5 mg dose.

During weeks six and seven on the drug he had four episodes, starting minutes after half an hour of exercise, with facial flushing, lip swelling, itchy palms, chest pain, nausea, and weakness. The first episodes followed hard CrossFit sessions and sent him to emergency care twice, where fluids and other standard treatment settled him quickly. After tirzepatide was stopped, the exercise reactions resolved. The authors propose the drug acted as a cofactor that lowered his threshold for exercise-induced anaphylaxis, a link they say has not been described before.
pmc-13332387:
Zhenhua Liu and co-authors describe two new beetle species in a 2026 taxonomy paper on the genus Laius, small melyrid beetles that live on seashore rocks. Only three Laius species were firmly confirmed in China, and none had been reported from the mainland since 1921.

Field work on the shore at Xiamen in June 2025 produced a large series of specimens. From them the team names Laius simingensis and Laius xiamenensis, two species found living side by side in Fujian. Two older Chinese listings are argued to belong in other genera based on their original descriptions. The paper also provides a diagnostic key to the valid Chinese species based on males and discusses where Laius flavicornis, recorded in China long ago without a locality, truly occurs.
pmc-13332487:
Bo Lv and colleagues built an explainable machine learning tool in 2026 for early screening of viral encephalitis using only routine blood tests. The brain infection is a dangerous emergency, yet firm diagnosis needs spinal fluid, scans, and EEG, which are slow or missing in small clinics.

Records of 313 patients suspected of the disease from one tertiary hospital were split into training and test sets, and six model types were trained on demographic and blood features. The XGBoost model won, reaching an AUC of 0.949 in cross-checks on the training set and 0.900 on the held-out test set. Explanation analysis named serum albumin and white blood cell counts, plus low neutrophil counts, as the strongest signals, with the pairing of albumin and white cells also influential. The authors offer the model as a front-end triage step for emergency and primary care.
pmc-13332687:
Yen Thi Le and colleagues recount a 2026 case in which lung cancer returned inside the thyroid gland nine quiet years later, masquerading as a primary thyroid tumor. Spread to the thyroid is rare overall, and lung sources account for only about 8.3 percent of such cases.

A 69-year-old woman whose non-small cell lung cancer had stayed stable for 9 years developed a steadily growing lump at the front of her neck. Ultrasound and needle sampling first suggested a harmless thyroid nodule, but its marked growth and her cancer history pushed the team to remove the right thyroid lobe. Tissue study with antibody staining showed metastatic lung adenocarcinoma, and scans found no other spread beyond one small lung nodule of unclear meaning. She was referred for drug therapy. The authors warn that needle results can mislead and that history, imaging, and staining must be weighed together.
pmc-13333387:
Chienhsiu Huang re-examined vitamin D trials in critical illness in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Big randomized trials had failed to show that vitamin D cuts deaths in intensive care. An analysis hinted that patients starting out deficient might benefit, and that dose and route might matter.

Pooling trials in critically ill adults, the analysis found the benefit concentrated in three subgroups. Patients whose starting blood level sat below 20 ng/mL had a 13 percent lower death risk with supplementation, at a relative risk of 0.87 in that group. Patients given no more than 300,000 IU in total did better, at a relative risk of 0.56 in pooled results. Patients dosed by muscle or vein injection gained, at a relative risk of 0.59 by that route. Patients outside those groups showed no gain. Huang concludes the vitamin helps patients rather than all comers, and that trials should enroll by deficiency, dose, and route.
pmc-13333587:
Clare Viglione and a team introduce and test a Circles of Resilience model in a 2026 cross-sectional study of families facing adverse childhood experiences. Early experiences predict poor health, yet health systems lack a framework for building resilience. The model locates protection in circles around the child, from family ties to housing, food, and community conditions.

Parent reports from 156 Latino mother-child pairs at a San Diego health center, collected from 2021 to 2023, fed models linking adversity, maternal anxiety, and child self-regulation. More adversity tracked worse self-regulation. It did so partly through maternal anxiety, which carried a clear indirect path. Vital conditions, housing, food, transport, related directly to better self-regulation. Social connections did not link directly. Yet they weakened the path from adversity to maternal anxiety. The authors read the pattern as support: connections protect the caregiver, conditions protect the child, and each circle deserves a program.
pmc-13333687:
Lisa M. Tereshko, Megan Magrauth, and Mary Jane Weiss authored a 2026 systematic review of training that teaches caregivers to run behavioral mealtime interventions. Children with food refusal, narrow food choices, or disruptive mealtime behavior need support that carries into real family meals.

The review covers 49 articles in which parents or caregivers were trained to deliver a mealtime procedure. The authors judged how well the interventions worked across several dimensions and paid close attention to social validity, meaning whether families found goals and methods acceptable. They close with best-practice recommendations for trainers, an account of gaps in the current literature, and directions for future studies. The work helps behavior analysts design caregiver training that families will actually use.
pmc-13334387: Reda Ebrahim Mohamed Elashram and Liyla Marzouk Alamri issued this 2026 correction notice for their article on graduate students in Saudi special education programs. The article studies how those students use artificial intelligence, and academic resilience and burnout in the group. The notice carries no new findings. It fixes an affiliation for Imam Mohammad Ibn Saud Islamic University in Riyadh, which had been worded wrongly. It also supplies a funding statement that was missing, crediting the university's Deanship of Scientific Research under grant IMSIU-DDRSP2601.
pmc-13336387:
Jiaqi Su and co-authors looked at multiferroic materials as a design principle for batteries in a 2026 article. Ferroic order parameters act as internal dials that electric or magnetic fields can switch, potentially reshaping the electrochemical conditions inside a working cell.

Standard tricks such as doping, coating, and defect engineering freeze in at making. Multiferroic control instead offers live levers: internal biases, adjustable strain, and spin polarization that can fight space-charge buildup, sluggish charge transfer, unstable interphases, and dendrite-driven failure. The review descends from whole-cell behavior to single parts and buried interfaces, tying ferroic responses to measurable electrochemical descriptors. It also weighs design and field-engineering strategies and the measurement tools needed to prove the effects.
pmc-13337387:
Hantian Cheng and co-authors study what helps people with diabetes stay psychologically resilient in a 2026 mixed-methods study from two hospitals in China. A survey of 290 adults with diagnosed diabetes ran alongside in-depth interviews with 15 participants between September and November 2023, all read through Kumpfer's resilience framework.

Social support and easier access to social resources lifted resilience from the outside. Inside, self-belief carried the strongest statistical link among the reported factors, joined by a positive mindset in the interview themes. Numbers and stories were merged in joint displays to show how outer support and inner strengths interact. The findings point to resilience training that builds both community ties and personal confidence.
pmc-13338487:
Nur Amira Adlan and colleagues compare prosthetic knees for walking on soft, uneven ground in a 2026 study. People with transfemoral amputation adjust their gait under physical and mental strain. Passive knee types, polycentric versus fluid-controlled, were compared while walking alone and while doing a listening task.

Groups included 15 able-bodied adults, 6 people using polycentric knees, and 5 using fluid knees in the reported sample. Questionnaires, joint angles, forces, and ground pressure were measured. Both amputation groups reported lower mobility and showed reduced knee and ankle motion. Selected force measures differed by group, showing knee design shapes walking under dual demands.
pmc-13341287:
War's toll on Israeli medical students is measured in a 2026 survey by Jumanah Essa-Hadad and colleagues. Bar-Ilan University students answered an online questionnaire between June and September 2024. They rated their health now against memories of life before the October 7th war, using standard scales for depression, anxiety, stress, well-being, and resilience.

Of 118 respondents, 81.4% recalled excellent or very good health before the war, but only 38.2% said the same currently. About a third met criteria for depression and for anxiety, sleep had worsened for 75%, and well-being fell below the adequacy line for 59%. The authors frame the drop as a training concern, not just a personal one.
pmc-13341587:
A combined heart function index responds to fluid only in patients who benefit, in a 2026 intensive care study by Mircea Tamas Talpoș and colleagues. The secondary analysis covered 59 regular-rhythm patients at a Brussels hospital who received a 4 mL/kg fluid challenge between 2020 and 2023.

Twenty-four patients (41%) raised their cardiac index by at least 15% and counted as responders. In them, the myocardial performance index fell from 0.48 to 0.42 after fluids, signaling better global function. Non-responders showed no significant change. The index, blending squeezing and relaxing performance, may thus separate helpful fluid from pointless or harmful fluid.
pmc-13341887:
A Himalayan plant guards kidneys against a malaria drug's side effects, in a 2026 translational study by Sudip Prasad Jena and Sabina Evan Prince. Artesunate can injure kidneys at high doses, so the team profiled Bergenia ciliata root extract chemically and computationally before animal testing.

Rutin emerged as the lead compound, docking to the PPARγ target at −10.307 kcal/mol with stable simulated binding. The extract left kidney cells over 90% viable in dishes. In rats given 150 mg/kg artesunate, adding extract at 200 or 400 mg/kg lowered urea, uric acid, and creatinine dose-dependently, with tissue sections confirming recovery.
pmc-13342187:
Sexually transmitted infections in Nanjing men are tallied over ten full years by Laiqing Zhu's team, in their 2026 look back. Urine nucleic acid tests from 58,136 andrology clinic patients seen between 2016 and 2025 covered chlamydia, Mycoplasma genitalium, gonorrhea, and Ureaplasma.

Ureaplasma positivity dwarfed the rest at 50.16%, against 2.62% for chlamydia, 2.77% for Mycoplasma, and 0.85% for gonorrhea. Men aged 24 or younger carried the highest rates of the first three, and single infections (93.84%) far outdid mixed ones. The authors caution that an andrology clinic population skews the picture, but the age gradient is very hard to ignore.
pmc-13343887:
Joel Abraham and a large team test the cancer drug sorafenib against pneumococcus in 2026. Streptococcus pneumoniae kills over a million people a year. Resistant strains pushed the World Health Organization to flag it as a priority germ. The team screened a familiar kinase blocker for antibacterial punch.

Sorafenib curbed many pneumococcal types, including multidrug-resistant clinical strains, in dose-dependent fashion. Computer modeling and lab assays pointed to the bacterial kinase StkP, a master switch for division and wall building, as a key target, and adding extra StkP partly rescued growth. Treated germs grew misshapen, leaked more, and invaded lung cells less. In mouse pneumonia, a tenth of the clinical dose cut bacterial loads and delayed death.
pmc-13346187:
Ricardo Jorquera-Gutiérrez and co-authors test how study demands and study supports relate to exhaustion and engagement among Chilean university students, in work issued in 2026. A total of 424 students answered the survey, and a structural model sorted demands such as mental load and career worry from supports such as lecturer help and feedback.

Demands were strongly tied to emotional exhaustion, while supports were strongly tied to engagement, and the two sides also moved against each other. Fit measures for the model were good by the reported cutoffs. The results suggest that stronger teaching support and clearer course information could lower burnout risk on campus.
pmc-13348487:
Kurmashev reviews human brain studies to ask if the many paths into autism meet at shared steps. The review drew on forty-three studies of cortex tissue from donors after death. No single gene pattern showed in all studies. Still, some patterns came back often. Genes for nerve links and synapses ran low. Genes for immune and glial cells ran high. Genes that shape how RNA is cut and joined also ran off track.

Most proof rests on a small core of studies. Many papers reuse the same donor sets. Kurmashev reads the picture as partial overlap, not one cause. Metabolic shifts look like side effects, not core traits.
pmc-13349787:
Peng Dong and colleagues pooled evidence in a 2026 meta-analysis on PTTG1, a gene linked to tumour growth, and its value for predicting outcomes in solid tumours. They searched three databases for studies published up to July 2025.

Twenty-two studies from 21 articles were combined. Patients whose tumours showed high PTTG1 levels had worse overall survival and worse disease-free or recurrence-free survival. The survival link was clearest in kidney, lung, breast, oesophageal, and laryngeal cancers. High levels also tracked with later tumour stage and other signs of advanced disease. Measuring PTTG1 could help flag patients who need closer follow-up or stronger treatment.
pmc-13350187:
Ruxandra Stefania Dragota and colleagues pooled studies in a 2026 meta-analysis on a blood inflammation score in thyroid cancer. The score combines counts of three white cell and platelet types from routine blood tests, and its diagnostic worth and link to lymph node spread were unsettled.

Ten studies were included. Six diagnostic studies with 2,209 participants gave pooled sensitivity of 76.8 percent for detecting cancer, and spread to neck nodes was assessed across the full set. A cheap score from a standard blood count that helps flag cancer or its spread would be handy where advanced testing is scarce, though the authors weigh accuracy carefully.
pmc-13351087:
Pierre J. Magistretti and co-authors reviewed gangliosides in a 2026 article. These are fatty signalling molecules found in large amounts in the brain and spinal cord. They help govern membrane signalling, cell energy use, new neuron growth, and immune responses.

Recent work shows one member, GM1, strengthens energy sharing between astrocytes and neurons. Others steer adult neuron growth through gene programmes. In Huntington's disease models, these molecules calmed inflamed immune cells. They also helped clear misfolded proteins. In spinal cord injury patients, GM1 sped recovery of nerve function. The authors present them as multi-target candidates for repairing the nervous system.
pmc-13351387:
J.R. Taylor and co-authors measured blood ammonia across pregnancy in Thoroughbred mares in a 2026 field study, the first of its kind. New hand-held meters made on-the-spot ammonia readings possible despite the chemical's volatility, which had long blocked such work.

Ammonia levels rose and fell during gestation, and even short spikes threatened the pregnancy, they report. Excess nitrogen in the body can quietly poison both mare and foal, yet the problem is treatable when caught. The authors propose routine ammonia monitoring during pregnancy, and note the lesson extends beyond horses to other species, including veterinary care more broadly.
pmc-13351687:
Areen Y Ibrahim leads a 2026 survey study of family quality of life for parents of children with atopic dermatitis in Jeddah. The itchy, dry skin condition affects about 20 percent of children worldwide and weighs on caregivers too. Caregivers of children aged 0 to 14 years at King Abdulaziz University Hospital were contacted between July 2023 and August 2024.

Family life was scored with the Family Dermatology Life Quality Index, which runs from 0 to 30 with higher scores meaning worse impact. The team expected impaired family life, matching global findings. Results are offered to support care that treats the whole family, and the authors note no earlier Saudi study of this kind exists.
pmc-13354387:
Musab Maqsood leads a 2026 pooled comparison of two self-applied creams for genital warts. Imiquimod and podophyllotoxin are the commonest home treatments for condylomata acuminata. Five studies qualified after screening of two databases plus two trial registers: two randomised trials and three cohorts.

Effectiveness did not differ clearly between creams, with a risk ratio of 0.98, and overall harms were similar at 1.06. Subgroups split by age, though: adults had more harms on imiquimod at 1.22, while children had fewer at 0.51. Clearance speed looked comparable, but warts returned more often and sooner after imiquimod. Choice may hinge on age and relapse tolerance.
pmc-13358487:
Wei Wang and co-authors report a 2026 study on lung cancer that sits at the edge of operable. For non-small cell lung cancer that might still be removed, drug treatment first can shrink the tumor. The team compared plain chemotherapy with chemotherapy plus immune therapy as this first step.

They gathered patients treated at four cancer centers from 2021 to 2024 and matched the two groups so they were alike on key traits. They then compared how many reached surgery, how much tumor was left, and how long patients stayed free of events. The results give real-world support for adding immune therapy before surgery in these border cases.
pmc-13358787:
Yuanyuan Wang and co-authors pool trial results for an immune drug in lung cancer in a 2026 review. The drug, cemiplimab, is given by drip every three weeks for advanced non-small cell lung cancer. Response varies, and certain tumor markers may predict who gains most. The team focused on those marker-defined subgroups.

They searched four databases for randomized trials of the drug against placebo or standard care. They pooled survival, time without growth, and tumor shrinkage, and checked each trial's quality. Sorting results by marker can help oncologists match this costly drug to the patients most likely to benefit.
pmc-13360687:
Emily von Scheven and co-authors explore a new way to link sick children to wellness services in a 2026 paper. Children with long-term illness are rarely introduced to wellness ideas such as movement, calm, and healthy habits. A referral is usually treated as paperwork, sent off with little warmth. The team used human-centered design, which builds services around the people who use them, to rethink the step.

They argue the best referral feels like a real conversation, not a form. It should leave families feeling backed, capable, and hopeful about their child's health. Done that way, the talk itself can spark interest in wellness habits that last for years. With more children growing up with chronic illness, the authors say this human touch could improve lives now and across a lifetime.
pmc-13361187:
Abdulkadir Cidem and co-authors review milk-protein fragments as cancer drugs in a 2026 paper. Lactoferrin is a protein in milk, and digestion cuts it into short pieces with strong cell effects. Best known are lactoferricin, lactoferrampin, and a short piece called LF1-11. Scientists also build altered versions, joining them to chemo drugs or reshaping them for strength.

These fragments favor cancer cell surfaces over healthy ones. Once attached, they can break the cell's skin, reach inner targets, and trigger cell death. The review explains how each fragment's shape drives its action and targeting. It also weighs what blocks their path to the clinic, such as stability in the body. The authors see real promise if these hurdles can be cleared.
pmc-13362087:
Chang-Ling Huang and co-authors measured how vigorous activity links to cancer risk in UK Biobank data in a 2026 study. Wrist accelerometers recorded moderate-to-vigorous activity directly, avoiding the fuzz of self-reports. Gene-based analysis, called Mendelian randomization, added a check on cause and effect, including curved dose patterns. The team tracked total cancer risk and several cancer sites.

Higher measured activity linked to lower total cancer risk and lower risk at multiple sites. The gene analysis suggested a threshold-like pattern, with benefits bending near five hours of such activity per week. Combining device measures with genetic methods strengthens the case that the link is real, not just a marker of healthy lifestyles. The dose shape can guide future prevention studies and public advice.
pmc-13362387:
Abdulmajeed Alfayyadh wrote a 2026 review on a common problem after knee surgery: the thigh muscle often will not switch on. Swelling and pain trigger this block within hours, and if it lasts, weakness and joint wear can follow for years. The review looks at care in the first two weeks after surgery.

Alfayyadh weighs seven options, from electric muscle stimulation and simple thigh exercises to blood flow training and cold therapy. Each helps in some way, but none meets all the needs for home use, patient effort, clear tracking, and rising load from day one. That gap, the review argues, should guide new rehab tools and trials.
pmc-13363187:
Maria Rada and a large team wrote a 2026 review on heart valve disease and heart failure after COVID-19. Heart injury from the virus is well documented, but valve effects have drawn less study. The team searched three major databases for work from 2020 to early 2026 on valve damage, heart failure, and vessel injury tied to the infection. They wove the findings into a clinical summary.

The valve problems that follow infection seem mostly functional, above all leaky mitral and tricuspid valves driven by swelling and strain, rather than direct structural ruin. Patients who enter infection with severe valve disease fare far worse. Blood markers of heart stress and swelling predict decline. The authors stress that direct valve studies are still scarce.
pmc-13367087:
Hope Rugo leads a team that gives in 2026 a plain words sum of a chart study that sets three kin breast cancer drugs side by side. Each drug blocks the cell cycle and pairs with a hormone drug as first care for spread ill. No trial has set the three head to head.

Charts from US care sites show no clear gap in time to ill worse or in life span among the three pairs. The sum backs each of the three as a sound first pick for this ill type. Plain words let patients join the pick talk with their care team.
pmc-13370687:
Carson presents a method that cleans up measurements of brain stimulation responses, in 2026 neurophysiology research. Magnetic stimulation pulses the motor cortex, and the resulting muscle responses, called motor evoked potentials, vary in size from pulse to pulse. Part of that variation comes from background electrical activity in the muscle before the pulse. That activity tracks how excitable the spinal motor neurons are at that moment, even when it sits below standard screening thresholds for a resting muscle.

Carson's regression-based compensation models the link between pre-pulse muscle activity, measured by electromyography over a window such as 100 milliseconds, and the response size, then removes it. When compensation is adequate, he shows, it can change the apparent effect of experimental factors on response size, meaning some published stimulation effects may reflect background excitability drift. The method gives stimulation studies a cleaner yardstick for comparing conditions and tracking treatment effects.
pmc-13378887:
Ruqaiya Al Jashmi and co-authors describe a 2026 case of an extremely rare immune disorder in a preterm baby in Oman. The disorder stems from a fault in a gene called DNASE2, which normally helps cells clear away spare DNA. Without it, the immune system stays switched on and harms the blood and organs.

Signs began before birth, with fluid buildup, poor growth, and heart muscle disease. After birth the baby had low blood cell counts, a large liver and spleen, jaundice, and very high markers of inflammation. Gene tests found two new faulty copies of the gene. Treatment with a targeted immune-calming drug brought clear improvement, despite the baby's small size.
pmc-13381087:
Boyeong Ryu and a large Korean team report a 2026 summary of the first joint national influenza annual report in Korea, covering the 2024 to 2025 season. Two national bodies, the disease control agency and the health insurance service, produced it together. It aims to give a full picture of flu activity and its burden.

The report combined patient and germ surveillance, medical cost data, vaccination coverage, and estimates of how well the vaccine worked. Vaccine performance was assessed with two designs, one mimicking a trial and one tracking changes over time. Pooling these sources in one annual report should help planners judge the season and prepare for the next.
pmc-13381987:
Max Busch and co-authors present a 2026 study of a helper protein that folds a bacterial enzyme before the bacterium exports it. The bacterium, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, causes infections, and the enzyme it exports helps it do harm. The helper, called LipH, sits anchored in the cell membrane, and its working motions were barely understood.

Computer simulations showed the anchored helper is highly flexible, sweeping through many shapes. Its working cavity is sometimes blocked by the membrane itself or by its own linker section. Despite that, lab tests with the helper rebuilt into artificial membranes showed it still activates its client enzyme efficiently. The picture explains how a tethered folding helper can catch and release its target.
pmc-13386487:
Roesch and colleagues ask how many labs must test a disinfectant before its claim can be trusted, in 2026 hygiene standards research. Certification by Germany's hygiene association requires results from two accredited labs. Building probability models from ring trials covering bacteria, yeast, and mycobacteria tests, the authors calculate how false-positive classifications change as one to four laboratories are required. They weigh certainty against the cost and burden each added lab imposes.

Adding a second lab cut the rate of false-positive outcomes in the middle range by up to 90 percent. A third or fourth lab lowered the chance of positive classifications, but the added reliability gain was small against rising cost, effort, and complexity. More labs could even increase disagreement rates. Roesch concludes the existing two-lab rule balances reliability and feasibility, corroborating simulation work. He advises standard-setters to invest in within-lab precision instead of more labs.
pmc-13389487:
Na Zhang and colleagues explore, in 2026, whether the direction of the heart P wave on an electrocardiogram tracks lung function in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. They ask whether this simple heart tracing measure could also help judge outlook for patients.

Records from 407 adults at two hospitals in Henan were split into a control group and a COPD group, with the COPD group divided into five severity levels by predicted breathing capacity. The team applied linear and logistic models, flexible curve analysis, and subgroup checks to link P-wave axis with breathing measures. Heart and lung clinicians gain a low-cost candidate marker, along with a clear account of where the link bends rather than running in a straight line.
pmc-13389887:
Keerthy Ajay Kumar leads a 2026 animal study on whether vitamin D3 can protect the brain against cadmium poisoning. Cadmium is a toxic metal used in industry and spread by mining, fertilisers, and waste, and it can cross into the brain and gather in regions such as the olfactory bulb.

In a two-year experiment in an anatomy department, adult albino rats were exposed to cadmium, with some also given vitamin D3, and their olfactory bulb tissue was examined under the microscope. The authors compare tissue damage across groups to judge any protective effect. Toxicologists and anatomy readers gain tissue-level evidence on a common environmental metal and a widely available vitamin, framed as an experimental test rather than a human treatment claim.
pmc-13391787:
Ana Luisa Rodrigues-Silva, Leticia Pereira Silva, and Rosangela Cristina Marucci review, in 2026, the life history and pest-hunting promise of a South American earwig. Doru luteipes is the most frequently encountered predatory insect in maize fields across Brazil and neighbouring countries.

Over three decades of field and laboratory work have built a scattered picture of its predatory behaviour and efficiency. The review gathers that knowledge and describes rearing methods, aiming to define the earwig's true potential as a biological control agent for release programmes. Integrated pest management researchers gain a consolidated basis for judging whether mass-reared earwigs can cut insecticide use in maize.
pmc-13393887:
Si-Ming Wu, Paolo Fornasiero, and Xiao-Yu Yang comment on a study showing that water squeezed into nanometre-scale cavities can order itself into solid-like patterns at room temperature. The finding upends the belief that such ordering needs deep cold or crushing pressure. Water's shifting hydrogen bond web has resisted tidy models, and confined water matters for catalysis and biology, yet it hides in tiny amounts inside solids where few tools can see it.

The highlighted work paired scanning probe microscopy with diamond quantum sensors and exactly built cavities. The pair mapped local geometry while reading how the water's molecules behave through nanoscale magnetic resonance. That combination finally let researchers measure structure against gap size directly. Wu and colleagues argue the result bridges theory and real catalytic environments, and should change how confined water is modelled in chemistry and biology.
pmc-13394087:
Joers and co-authors test, in 2026, whether brain chemistry measured by magnetic resonance spectroscopy is ready to serve as an endpoint in early-stage trials. The trials target spinocerebellar ataxia types 2 and 3, inherited diseases that erode coordination. Seventy-two participants, 18 with SCA2, 25 with SCA3, and 29 healthy controls, were scanned twice within two weeks at four sites using scanners from two vendors and one harmonized protocol.

Measurements in the cerebellum and pons were highly repeatable across sites, though small vendor-related biases required statistical adjustment. Both patient groups showed lower total N-acetylaspartate and glutamate, and higher myo-inositol and total creatine, than controls in those regions. Several chemical levels differed between SCA2 and SCA3 with strong effect sizes, meaning the genotypes leave distinct signatures. A ratio of N-acetylaspartate to creatine tracked clinical severity scores best, with correlations of 0.5 or stronger, supporting its use in multisite trials.
pmc-13394387:
Jeong-Ki Kim leads a 2026 study that tackles rust in magnesium alloys, the lightest metals used to build things. Iron specks in cheap, low-purity magnesium start rust fast, so makers often pay for costly pure metal. The team instead grew grains with an iron-rich core wrapped in a shell low in iron. Those grains sit inside the metal like tiny guards.

The shell walls off the iron core and stops it from sparking rust. Metal made this way resisted rust about as well as metal from ultra-pure stock. The authors say the trick could cut costs for cars and planes. Light parts would last longer without pricey refining.
pmc-13394587:
Lila Dudley heads a 2026 review of sex gaps in leg artery care in the United States. Peripheral artery disease narrows leg vessels and causes pain or worse. Doctors often reopen vessels from inside, using balloons, stents, or scrapers. The team searched major databases for United States studies from 2016 to 2024 on women with symptoms.

Nine studies passed the screen, and their results clashed. Five found more problems such as vessel tears or bruising in women. Four found women needed repeat work more often, while one found no gap. On limb loss and death, reports split both ways. The authors call for shared measures so future work can settle the question.
pmc-13395187:
Tong Yang and co-authors turn, in 2026, red blood cells into tiny tweezers that move objects inside living vessels. A fibre probe makes a long light field that catches red cells as they flow past. A caught cell bends the light again and forms a second, stronger trap. That trap holds small particles far better than the probe alone.

Trapped particles moved against the flow at three times the plain probe speed. Immune cells switched on within seconds of contact. Chains of red cells also acted as guides that carry light over distance. Computer models backed the stronger grip and range. The authors pitch the trick for drug delivery and immune control in the body.
pmc-13395387:
Lei Bao and co-authors report, in 2026, a light-driven trick that moves two chemical groups at once. Swapping groups on a molecule's frame can shortcut drug making. Moving two at once demands tight control of which group goes where. Their method uses a light catalyst that passes energy, not electrons, to start the swap.

Radical sorting sets the order of moves and the final coupling. The path runs through a split pair, a phosphate group hop, and a joining step. The trick worked on both lively and plain carbon chains. The team also extended it from nitrogen-oxygen pairs to nitrogen-nitrogen pairs. The authors pitch the method as a broad editing tool.
pmc-13396087:
Jean Lopes da Silva and co-authors tested two natural preservatives together against the spore-forming bacteria that spoil orange juice, in a 2026 food science study. Alicyclobacillus species survive pasteurization and acid, and their growth gives juice an off taste that costs producers money.

The pair under test was D-limonene, the citrus peel compound, and nisin, a bacteria-made preservative already used in foods. Five strains were challenged in lab media and in processed orange juice. Checkerboard tests mapped how the two interact, and disc, dilution, and kill tests set the doses needed to stop growth or destroy both active cells and their tough spores.
pmc-13396187:
Levy and colleagues map, in 2026, how DNA repair enzymes called glycosylases recognize damage depending on the letters surrounding each lesion. Cells suffer thousands of DNA lesions daily, and base excision repair sends glycosylases to find them, yet the surrounding sequence context was largely unexplored. Their high-throughput platform, BER-Map, measured binding across thousands of lesion-containing sequences for three human enzymes: UDG, TDG, and MBD4.

Binding depended strongly on context reaching several bases beyond the lesion, and neighboring positions interacted in non-additive ways, so simple letter-by-letter scores cannot predict recognition. Analysis and simulations pointed to DNA shape, especially minor groove width, as part of the signal the enzymes read. Nearest-neighbor preferences resembled known cancer mutational signatures from cytosine deamination, tying repair choices to mutation patterns. The authors present BER-Map as a platform for decoding how repair specificity shapes the genome's mutation landscape.
pmc-13396487:
Yuqi Meng and co-authors built a motion sensor out of light circuits etched on a chip, and tested it in 2026. Photonic accelerometers promise fine sensitivity for navigation and vibration work, but earlier versions were hard to read out and saturated over a narrow range.

The device counts interference fringes on the chip itself to unwrap the light signal, which widens the range it can measure while keeping fine detail. Bench tests gave a noise floor of 2.0 micro-g per root hertz. The authors outline how more optical power and more loops of waveguide on the moving cantilever could push that floor toward 10 nano-g, near the limit set by photon noise.
pmc-13396687:
Patrick Forster and co-authors revisited whole brain radiation for lung cancer that has spread to the brain, now that immunotherapy has changed the outlook. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 147 patients with non-small cell lung cancer and brain metastases treated between 2017 and 2020.

Median survival from diagnosis was 9.7 months. Patients who received immunotherapy lived a median of 31.5 months, against 14.7 months for those who did not. Outcomes for whole brain radiation, alone and combined with immunotherapy, were compared with survival models that adjust for other factors. Whole brain treatment carries real costs to memory and thinking, so knowing where it still adds life matters.
pmc-13396887:
Xindi Wang and co-authors followed 64 patients through the first year after CAR-T cell therapy to learn why natural killer cells, a front-line immune patrol, come back slowly in some people. Their 2026 study links the delay to the storm of inflammation the therapy can trigger.

Killer cell counts and their surface receptors were tracked over time, since these cells help guard against infection and relapse after the engineered T cells do their work. Recovery lagged in the first month for most patients. High levels of the calming signal IL-10 during cytokine release syndrome, the feverish reaction many patients suffer, tracked with poorer killer cell return, and lab assays probed how IL-10 suppresses them.
pmc-13398187:
Kunitaro Watanabe and co-authors describe lasting relief for a young office worker with hamstring tendon pain at her sitting bone. Their 2026 case report follows a woman in her twenties whose buttock pain grew during desk work. The condition is often mistaken for piriformis trouble or spine disease, since scans of her lower back looked normal and nerve blocks helped only briefly.

Tenderness at the ischial tuberosity, pain on sitting and provocation tests pointed to the hamstring origin, and ultrasound showed a faintly darkened patch at the tendon root. Guided injections of anaesthetic and steroid every two weeks (18 in all) joined stretching, hip-lift exercise and less sitting. Step by step the pain settled, showing non-athletes can share this athlete's injury.
pmc-13398487:
Somnath Bar, Shu Li and Tirtha Banerjee build a model that explains, not just predicts, wildfire damage to California buildings. Their 2026 study learns from more than 100,000 damage inspection records gathered between 2013 and 2024. Inputs span land shape, vegetation, human footprint, live weather and a new composite flammability rating for each building.

Rigorous checks kept nearby records apart by a 200-metre dead zone so the model could not cheat on location. The full model scored 88 percent accuracy in its main test, dropping to 82.9 percent without the flammability rating and 74.5 percent without weather as well. Grid-based checks varied widely by place, a honesty check on how far one statewide model can stretch.
pmc-13398787:
de Jager and colleagues build, in 2026, the first atlas of cortical sulcal imprints on endocasts of the genus Pan, our closest living relatives, chimpanzees and bonobos. Fossil brains never survive, so palaeoneurologists read the grooves brains pressed into skulls, and a reference atlas for Pan was missing. The team micro-CT scanned 21 dry crania of Pan paniscus and Pan troglodytes. They reconstructed virtual endocasts automatically and mapped the density of detected sulcal imprints statistically.

Key sulci debated in fossil interpretation, including the lunate sulcus, were detected across all 21 endocasts, as were grooves of the frontal, parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes. The sulcus rectus appeared on 90 percent of left hemispheres and 100 percent of right hemispheres in the sample, while accessory features like the fronto-marginal sulcus showed lower detection rates. The authors offer the density maps as a baseline for judging which imprints on hominin fossil endocasts reflect real brain anatomy.
pmc-13398987:
Qi Fang and colleagues pair light-sensitive cell loss with vessel leakage to grade diabetic eye disease. Their 2026 study images 50 eyes from 32 patients who had never been treated for diabetic retinopathy, spanning mild non-proliferative disease to the proliferative stage. Adaptive optics cameras count individual photoreceptors, the light-catching cells whose slow death steals sight.

Dark patches in the photoreceptor mosaic grew stepwise with severity, from an average of 1.86 percent at the mild stage to 5.92 percent at the proliferative stage in the values listed. The macular leakage index climbed in parallel, reaching 8.98 percent at the worst stage, and the two measures correlated positively. Together they may stage disease more honestly than either alone.
pmc-13399187:
Linda Hoffmeister and a large team tested whether blood that patients collect themselves and post to a laboratory matches ordinary venous samples, in a 2026 study. Regular checks of blood sugar control, kidney function, and cholesterol matter for diabetes care, yet clinic visits are hard for many patients. The team examined five measures: HbA1c, creatinine, and three cholesterol-related values.

In a general practice setting, 105 participants used a Tasso+ device to collect capillary blood from the upper arm. Each also gave two venous samples, one posted and one couriered straight to the lab. Posted capillary results agreed very closely with couriered venous results for HbA1c, with a concordance coefficient of 0.999 in the reported analysis. Creatinine and lipid values also matched well. The authors conclude that mailed self-sampling is reliable enough for remote monitoring of these measures.
pmc-13399287:
Marcia Bucco, Juliana Ollé Mendes, and Jorge Vinícius Cestari Felix describe a training exercise held inside a working hospital ward in 2026. The drill tested how staff respond when a fire breaks out during trauma care. Hospital fires are rare but can turn catastrophic when teams lack practice. Running the drill in the real workplace exposes weak points in routes, equipment, and communication.

The exercise took place in October 2024 at a large philanthropic hospital in the capital of Paraná, Brazil. The scenario opened with a maintenance worker who received an electric shock from shorted wiring. He fell about 1.5 meters, suffering facial trauma plus an exposed leg fracture made up with moulage. Six fire brigade members, three rapid response team members, and seven emergency professionals took part, then joined a debriefing. The study is qualitative and exploratory. It gathers participants' perceptions to judge in situ simulation as a teaching strategy.
pmc-13399887:
Pablo Gelber, Eduard Ramírez-Bermejo, and Gonzalo Caviasso describe a mini-open reconstruction of both layers of the medial collateral ligament using one graft and an adjustable femoral button, in a 2026 technique paper. The authors blame lingering looseness on grafts fixed at points that stretch unevenly through the bend, plus too little control of tension at fixation.

Two incisions of two centimeters each, one up by the medial epicondyle and one below the joint line, frame the work. A folded soft-tissue graft of eight to nine millimeters is looped over an adjustable-loop button that is flipped onto the far side of the femur. Shortening the loop draws the graft into a thirty-millimeter tunnel to a marked depth. The adjustable loop then allows final fine-tuning of depth and tension before stability is tested.
pmc-13400387:
Efthymios Triantafyllou and colleagues look, in 2026, at a hidden late effect of radiation for throat cancer: failure of the reflex that steadies blood pressure. Survivors can face swings in pressure, racing heart, light-headedness and fainting. The same radiation can injure lower cranial nerves, which are checked at routine follow-up visits.

Records for 414 survivors treated between 2016 and 2019 were reviewed again. About one in five showed signs linked to reflex failure. Among the small group with cranial nerve injury, the share was 39 percent, nearly three times the odds seen in others. The authors urge a low threshold for dedicated testing in that subgroup.
pmc-13400487:
Luigi Cerbone and colleagues survey, in 2026, Italian specialists on genetic testing for pleural mesothelioma, a rare cancer of the lung lining tied to asbestos. Inherited mutations appear in up to about one in eight cases, and guidelines advise testing all patients for them. Practice, the team suspected, lagged behind advice.

Forty-five doctors from a national network answered a 24-item survey sent in 2025. Access to inherited testing was fairly high, yet very few routinely offered it. Tumor gene sequencing, by contrast, was almost universally available and used mainly to screen for trials. Cost, scarce genetic counseling and low awareness were the top barriers named. The authors call for better pathways so guideline advice reaches patients.
pmc-13400587:
Valquiria Maria de Carvalho Aguiar and a Brazilian team track, in 2026, a nature-based cleanup of the Maricá Lagoon on the Rio de Janeiro coast. The lagoon suffers from excess nutrients, and from late 2021 a mix of helpful microbes was applied regularly in one of its main inflow basins. Water and sediment were monitored from 2020 to 2023.

Algae pigment levels in the treated basin fell sharply by 2023. In lagoon sediments, organic carbon dropped from close to eight percent to under three percent, and phosphorus trended down despite one spike. A trophic index improved from heavily over-enriched toward mid-level states at several stations. Nitrogen patterns varied strongly by shore, showing the system remains uneven.
pmc-13401287:
Sonsoles Salto-Alejandre and many co-authors report a 2026 effort to build the VIRA score, a risk tool for predicting death within 30 days when a patient is diagnosed with COVID-19 pneumonia. The score folds the familiar CURB-65 pneumonia scale together with SARS-CoV-2 RNAemia, meaning virus genetic material circulating in the blood.

Earlier work had tested CURB-65 in COVID-19 but not in cohorts that included immunocompromised patients, even though RNAemia is tied to worse outcomes. The developers drew on two multicentre cohorts: 539 immunocompetent patients and 280 immunocompromised patients. Vaccination coverage differed sharply between them, at about 35 percent in the first group and about 86 percent in the second. The score is meant to flag high-risk patients right at diagnosis.
pmc-13401787:
Xi-Tong Zhu and a large team of co-authors investigated fusion transcripts in plants in a 2026 study, asking whether these joined RNA messages are real biology or laboratory ghosts. Fusions were first characterized in cancer, and plant reports have multiplied with modern sequencing, but their meaning is hotly debated.

Combining several high-quality long-read RNA datasets from rice, the team found that almost all detected fusions come from technical and analytical artifacts rather than real events. The main culprit is template switching during reverse transcription, guided by short matching sequences and worst in PCR-based workflows. Misalignment, reference genome bias, and gene misannotation add more false fusions, and recurring artifact hotspots explain why signals cluster non-randomly. Redesigned validation experiments in vitro and in living tissue showed the common fusion signals do not reproduce and do not reflect real transcription.
pmc-13402687:
Shuo Wang and co-authors build an electrode surface that delivers protons and electrons in step, turning nitrate waste into cyclohexanone oxime, a valuable chemical building block. Making nitrogen chemicals with electric power could rebalance the human-perturbed nitrogen cycle, but proton and electron timing at the surface usually drifts apart, wasting charge. Their interface layers protonated polyaniline over graphite sheets as a combined donor system.

Nitrate then reduces toward hydroxylamine by two paths at once, one chemical and one electrochemical, and pairing with cyclohexanone closes the ring product. Output reached 67.1 micromoles per hour per square centimeter at 69.9 percent Faradaic efficiency, holding steady from pH 3.0 to 11.0 in the reported runs. A solar-driven version and machine learning predictions support wider use. The team frames interface donor design as the lever that steers selectivity.
pmc-13402887:
Mohammad Amin Bafandeh and co-authors describe rebuilding a full jaw with a subperiosteal implant in a patient whose ridge had wasted too severely for ordinary implants. These frame implants sit on the bone under the gum rather than inside it. The design is an old idea revived by modern imaging and digital fabrication, for cases where grafting is long, risky, or likely to fail.

The team stresses four lessons in their summary. Surgeon and prosthodontist must design together. The prosthetic plan should drive the implant design. Converting to an overdenture can rescue the bite when abutments come out non-parallel. And structured follow-up must watch the soft tissue closely. Their case applies those rules across a whole jaw rather than a single tooth. For patients out of standard options, the report offers a workable route back to a functioning denture.
pmc-13403387:
Obasanjo Bolarinwa wrote a 2026 commentary on unfair gaps in UK maternity care, tied to a national report on mothers' deaths. Black, Asian, and migrant women still die around birth at far higher rates than white women. The author argues that the gaps stem from how services are planned and run.

Cultural awareness, he says, should sit at the core of safe care rather than at its edges. He urges that it be built into care rules, service contracts, and staff training. Real work with affected women and local groups should shape the changes. Without bold action, he warns, poor outcomes and lost trust will persist.
pmc-13403887:
Florian Stubenrauch and colleagues showed in 2026 that light plus heat can strip hydrogen from methanol far past normal chemical limits. Making formaldehyde this direct way has long been a dream goal, since it skips the hazards and emissions of the standard route. Pure heat alone stalls at low yields.

Their flow reactor shone UV light on a coated plate while heating it from behind. Over 70 hours of steady running, the target product share hit 95 percent of output. Conversion rose up to 60 times above the plain heat limit. Tiny oxygen doses lifted output more, by refilling key surface sites.
pmc-13404787:
Chebly Dagher and colleagues test whether simple breathing measures during light exercise can flag hidden vessel disease in lung patients, in 2026 work. Their patients had non-severe pulmonary hypertension tied to interstitial lung disease. Full cardiopulmonary exercise testing with catheters can reveal pressure problems, but it is complex and invasive.

Records from 16 patients who had both light exercise testing and invasive testing were reviewed. Two breathing-derived markers were checked: GXCAP, an estimate of vessel stretch capacity, and VE/VCO2, a measure of breathing efficiency. Patients had earlier been split into those whose vessel resistance rose with exercise and those whose stayed stable. The analysis asks how well the simple markers separate those two groups.
pmc-13405087:
Dinh-Dien La and co-authors release a large Vietnamese dataset for finding named items in government documents, in 2026 work. Automated reading of administrative text needs training data, and existing Vietnamese sets cover news or medicine rather than official paperwork. Their corpus, PAP_NER, fills that gap.

The set holds 162,801 sentences with 205,807 labelled items in five classes, including agencies, legal documents and dates. Human annotators agreed strongly, with a kappa of 0.85 in the reported checks. A hybrid model joining PhoBERT with a CRF layer scored 97.95 percent micro F1 on the test set, beating several baselines. Ablation tests show which parts of the model carry the gain.
pmc-13405587:
Vanessa dos Santos Viana, Juliana Schaia Rocha Orsi and Regiane Cristina do Amaral track low birth weight across Sergipe, Brazil, in a 2026 spatial study. Babies born underweight face higher death risk in the first month and lasting health effects. Sergipe carries high social vulnerability, which shapes maternal nutrition and care.

Most health regions showed a steady trend in low birth weight rates over the years studied. The state's share of underweight births rose in 2015, 2018 and 2023, the highlighted years. Mapping pinpoints which health regions hold the densest clusters of cases. The authors read the pattern against prenatal care quality, income and maternal age to guide regional action.
pmc-13406687:
Xin-Yue Tang and colleagues test nicotinamide, a vitamin B3 form, against sun-aged skin in mice, in a 2026 study. Sunlight ages skin through cell senescence, where worn cells linger and spread inflammatory signals. Multi-omics work first suggested ageing skin struggles to make NAD+, a molecule nicotinamide feeds.

Supplemented mice showed restored NAD+ machinery and healthier skin barrier proteins, including collagen in the reported measures. Senescence markers such as p53 and p21 fell, and the inflammatory secretions of aged cells were suppressed. The dual action, delaying cell ageing while muting its harmful signals, is the authors' central claim. Results come from mice, so human benefit awaits testing.
pmc-13406787:
Joel Quarnstrom and co-authors, publishing in 2026, describe a wearable device meant to ease shoulder strain during lifting work in factories and warehouses. Repeated overhead tasks tire shoulder muscles and raise the chance of injury. Existing spring-based aids help lift but resist lowering, while fully powered devices drain energy and can drop a load if power fails.

Their design mixes both approaches, pairing an elastic element in parallel with a motor-driven helical actuator that can be adjusted. The paper works through movement and force calculations, lays out the electrical control system, and tunes the mechanical advantage profile. A working prototype was built and tested to check whether the concept holds up in practice.
pmc-13407887:
Periklis Paganos and co-authors use, in 2026, a sea star to ask how the ovary's cell types evolved. Egg production needs germline cells and supporting body cells working together. The sea star Patiria miniata is a non-chordate relative of ours. It produces millions of eggs across its life. That makes it a practical window on ancient arrangements.

Single-cell RNA sequencing combined with sharp 3D imaging catalogued the sea star ovary's cell types and their layout. The team found candidate egg stem cells plus supporting cells resembling mammalian granulosa and theca cells, along with plausible signalling conversations between support and germline cells. Most intriguingly, the ovary may run its own hormone-like control system, suggesting hormone-like control of reproduction predates the vertebrates.
pmc-13408187:
Masataka Sakashita and a team from 55 Japanese institutes asked in 2026 whether shrinking a molecular risk score before transplant helps people with myelodysplastic syndromes. These blood disorders can progress to acute leukaemia, and stem cell transplant remains the only cure. A newer scoring system reads mutations across many genes to grade risk more precisely.

The group calculated scores before and after bridging therapy for transplant patients drawn from more than three thousand sequenced cases. Lowering the score before transplant did not translate into better outcomes afterwards, which suggests that the biology present at diagnosis drives prognosis more than short-term score movement. Clinicians weighing extra pre-transplant treatment gain a caution against assuming that an improved score means an improved outlook.
pmc-13408587:
Zucheng Wu, Hao Wei, and colleagues report in 2026 a record-setting kesterite solar cell made from cheap, earth-abundant elements. This copper-zinc-tin sulfide-selenide technology stalls because a selenium bake makes crystals grow in two layers, leaving seams, voids, and stray phases inside the film. The team traced the damage to an early reaction at the film's back face, where selenium forms a low-melting copper phase that seeds uncontrolled growth.

Their fix shapes the selenium supply into a vertical gradient during the first stage, keeping selenium away from the temperature window in which the rogue phase forms. Single, column-like grains then grow from the top down, carrying charge better and wasting less of it. Devices reached a certified efficiency a shade above fifteen percent, and the strategy also suits a related solution-processed solar technology.
pmc-13408987:
Kunio Kaiho, Jeroen Sonke, Stephen Grasby, and Li Tian read mercury isotopes in 2026 as a seismograph of the worst mass extinction in Earth history. The end-Permian crisis, a quarter of a billion years ago, is blamed on Siberian flood volcanism, yet the eruption's pulse-by-pulse rhythm has been blurry. Mercury, spat out by volcanoes and preserved in sediments, carries isotopic fingerprints that might resolve it.

Across several rock sections, two mercury isotope measures moved in lockstep opposition, but only inside three crisis intervals totalling about one hundred fifty thousand years. During those windows, samples from land, sea, and volcanic sources converged on the same signature, while background samples scattered. Mercury loading tracked the same pattern. The authors argue that crisis times brought overwhelming source control from volcanism, and they offer the coupled isotope structure as a tool for dissecting eruption pulses in deep time.
pmc-13409087:
Onurkan Alkan and colleagues test in 2026 whether a chore-like functional circuit can judge everyday ability in people with atrial fibrillation better than a corridor walk. The Glittre test has patients carry a backpack through a loop of sitting, standing, stepping, and moving objects on shelves, mimicking real daily tasks that the six-minute walk test misses. Thirty-nine patients and thirty-nine matched healthy controls completed it.

Patients finished the circuit about nineteen seconds slower than controls. Repeating the test an hour later gave excellent agreement, and slower times tracked shorter walking distances strongly, plus weaker muscles and worse quality-of-life scores on related measures. Analysis also identified a cut-off separating patients with heavier symptom burden. The authors endorse the test as valid, reliable, and clinically useful for this population.
pmc-13410087:
Bartosz Ogłaza, Małgorzata Kalandyk-Kołodziejczyk, and Piotr Wegierek describe in 2026 three fossil aphid species preserved in Canadian amber. The amber dates to the Late Cretaceous, when these tiny plant-feeding insects already lived in varied forms. Naming new species from amber adds pieces to that old record.

Alongside the three new species, the team describes a wingless form of a species called Alloambria infelicis. They also re-examined the original type specimens of aphids already known from this resin. Careful study of body shape in the trapped insects grounds each new name. Together, the finds widen what is known about aphid variety near the end of the age of dinosaurs.
pmc-13411287:
S. M. Yasir Arafat and co-authors review in 2026 suicide across eleven Muslim-majority countries in the World Health Organization's African region. Stigma, criminal law, and religious prohibition hide the problem from view, which makes these countries a blind spot in global research. Rates, culture, and data quality all come under review.

Reported rates ranged widely, from a low in Algeria to the region's high in Burkina Faso. Male rates beat female rates in every country listed. Undercounting is likely where suicide is a crime or a disgrace, so figures may understate the truth. Prevention, the authors argue, must pair sound mental health care with legal reform and approaches that respect local faith and custom.
pmc-13411787:
Noufel Alshadood and colleagues present in 2026 a pancreatic tumor that refuses a single label: part hormone-type cancer, part duct cancer. A 68-year-old woman carried cystic spots across the pancreas, a widened main duct, and a raised tumor marker, all pointing first to a mucus-producing growth. Full removal of the pancreas followed team review.

Pathology split the mass roughly two-to-one between duct cancer and a slow-growing neuroendocrine tumor, with a separate high-risk cyst beside them. The mix fits the formal criteria of two rival categories at once, mixed tumor and collision tumor. Without gene data on shared ancestry, the team could not settle which story is true, a gap they flag for the sparse literature.
pmc-13413787:
Lucia Angelini and co-authors sort symptoms into clusters in 2026 for patients seen at a joint radiotherapy and palliative care clinic in Italy. People referred for comfort-focused radiation rarely suffer one symptom at a time, and clusters may guide treatment better than single complaints. Records from 215 patients seen between 2017 and 2020 carried Edmonton scale scores for ten symptoms at the first visit, analysed two ways: by statistical components and by patient grouping.

One method found four clusters: a tiredness and breathlessness bundle, a mood pair, a nausea and appetite pair, and pain standing alone. Grouping patients instead yielded three mixed clusters in their analysis. Worse physical performance tracked the physical clusters, while patients dominated by mood symptoms were less likely to receive palliative radiation. The authors say cluster thinking can personalize symptom care.
pmc-13415887:
Yingwei Xie and colleagues analyze two decades of United States cancer registry data for racial gaps in death among clear cell kidney cancer patients, in 2026. Records from 2000 to 2019 show Black patients with the highest five year death incidence, near 22 percent, just above white patients. Mortality fell over time for everyone.

Gaps still persisted, with hazard ratios near 1.15 for Black patients and 1.25 for American Indian and Alaska Native patients versus white patients. Death from cardiovascular disease drove a widening Black and white gap. Stage at diagnosis, surgery access, income, and geography explained part of the pattern.
pmc-13415987:
Animaw Lingerew Dagnaw and colleagues describe a fourteen-year-old boy with tuberous sclerosis complex who was also born with a single right kidney, in a 2026 case report. Tuberous sclerosis grows benign tumors in skin, brain, kidney, and heart, driven by faults in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. Facial skin lesions brought the boy to a dermatology clinic.

His skin signs began at age three, followed by brief whole body seizures for a few months at age four. A solitary kidney raises the stakes sharply, since kidney growths typical of the syndrome threaten the only working organ. Lifelong watchful monitoring and kidney sparing care are essential, the authors emphasize.
pmc-13416487:
Mairi Ziaka reviews the gut microbe brain axis in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2026 narrative review. The axis links gut germs with the brain through immune, hormone, and chemical signals. Past work from three databases covers the axis in health, in Alzheimer's, and in care attempts aimed at gut germs.

Changed gut mixes in Alzheimer's track with brain swelling and faster decline in the gathered findings. Probiotics raised mind test scores and calmed swelling in some studies. Prebiotics and stool swaps are also weighed as ways to fix gut germ imbalance. Stronger trials of microbe based therapy are the stated need.
pmc-13417187:
Xueping Su and co-authors test a helpful fungus plus a plant hormone copy against cadmium stress in wheat, in a 2026 greenhouse study. Cadmium in soil stunts wheat, harms leaf function, and builds up in grain tissues. Pots varied cadmium level, hormone dose, and fungus presence, with five repeats per setup.

Under cadmium, the paired treatment raised shoot growth and plant mass by roughly half or more. Damage markers in leaves fell, protective enzymes rose, and cadmium in roots, shoots, and leaves dropped by about two fifths to over half. The pairing looks promising for safer wheat on polluted ground, pending field trials.
pmc-13417287:
Balakrishnan S Anju and co-authors trace how nitrite changes at a nickel centre, in a 2026 chemistry study. Nitrite links to nitric oxide, a key signalling molecule in the body, and controlling that flow matters for health. Well defined nickel complexes let the team follow each step between nitrite, nitric oxide, and nitrate.

Adding a thiol converted nickel bound nitrite into a nickel nitric oxide species through a short lived acid intermediate. Hydrogen sulfide gave the same product, showing crosstalk between the two signals. An oxygen donor then pushed the species stepwise toward nitrate. Small ligand changes altered stability, guiding future catalyst and sensor design.
pmc-13417487:
Perez-Cullell and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study from France linking community pharmacies to skin doctors through a secure online platform. France has a long-standing shortage of dermatologists, and patients wait about three months on average. Pharmacists in 40 urban and rural pharmacies were trained in clinical photography and sent 731 cases to 12 volunteer skin doctors over one year.

Doctors completed 714 reviews, and reply times improved until most answers came back within two days. Cases ranged from suspected skin cancers to eczema, rosacea, and shingles, and doctors flagged dozens of likely cancers for fast follow-up. Most pharmacists were pleased, and they reported most patients were too. Gaps remain: prescriptions cannot yet be sent through the system, and family doctors sit outside the loop. A second pilot now tests fixes for those gaps.
pmc-13418287:
Xiaowen Hu and colleagues present a deep learning system for predicting how mutations change drug binding, in a 2026 study. Mutations drive drug resistance, yet lab testing each one is slow, and mutant protein structures are scarce. Their base model learned from 1.5 million data points using sequences alone, without needing three dimensional structures.

A fine tuning method then teaches the model to sense small binding shifts between normal and mutant proteins despite near identical sequences. Gains held across regression and classification tests and across targets from coronavirus, HIV, and cancer. The tool could prioritise which resistance mutations deserve urgent lab attention.
pmc-13418487:
Xin-Yi Nie and colleagues identify a master switch for development and virulence in Aspergillus flavus, the mould that poisons crops with aflatoxins, in a 2026 study. The switch, a heat shock factor called HsfA, exists in two copies. Silencing it stopped spores germinating, which blocks colonisation at the first step.

Six direct target genes were confirmed, each switched on by the factor at defined promoter sites. Restoring any one target partly rescued germination, growth, and infectivity in switch deficient strains. The fungal switch differs structurally from its human counterpart, explaining why human targeted inhibitors failed. Blocking the fungal switch could cut aflatoxin contamination at source.
pmc-13418787:
The editors-in-chief of Cancer Cell International retract a 2016 paper by Youguang Pu and colleagues on a gene target in bone cancer drug resistance. Concerns reached the journal about a figure panel that looked much like a panel in a related paper. A second concern involved images suggesting that lab animal care fell short of journal rules.

Pu and the co-authors accepted that the images looked alike yet gave no account of why. None of the authors answered later letters from the publisher about the notice. Citing the missing answers and the animal welfare breach, the editors state that trust in the results is gone. The record now carries the retraction in full, with the reasons set out for any reader who finds the paper.
pmc-13419287:
Phatcharaphon Whaikid and colleagues build a care system for muscle loss in older adults who once were homeless and now live in supportive housing. This group ages early and faces stacked health and social burdens, placing it at high risk of sarcopenia, the loss of muscle strength and mass. Standard diagnosis needs body scanners that community sites often lack.

The team joined interviews with a review of prior work to design a system fitted to this setting. Early use was then checked for feasibility, quality as users saw it, and user satisfaction. Muscle-wasting risks like low activity and poor diet can be caught in daily housing life if staff have the right tools. The system gives housing programs a practical route to spot decline early.
pmc-13420087:
Yuanyuan Zhang and colleagues hunt for shared gene patterns between COVID-19 and psoriasis, two diseases that meet in clinic more often than chance suggests. People with psoriasis on immune-suppressing drugs catch the virus at higher rates than the general public. The team reworked two public gene data sets, one for each disease, to find genes that shift in both.

Shared shifting genes fed network analysis that named hub genes at the center of the overlap. Three hubs, named EGF, SERPINA1, and CD8A in the report, scored well as possible markers for both diseases at once. Shared molecular routes could explain why the two conditions aggravate each other. The findings offer testable targets for lab work on combined treatment.
pmc-13420187:
Maximilian Gimbel and colleagues test a decision aid meant to help cancer patients judge homeopathy with clear eyes. Homeopathy enjoys wide use and acceptance despite a want of proof that it works beyond placebo effects. The study used a before-and-after survey with no comparison group, in 123 adult cancer patients recruited at German cancer centers.

The aid explained what homeopathy is, how its products are made and approved, what studies show, and how insurance treats it. Most participants felt well informed afterward, reported fresh insight, and said they would pass the material on. Results varied with traits the study did not measure, such as prior belief. The authors propose tailoring later aids to gender and starting knowledge.
pmc-13420487:
Rui Xiang and colleagues name a scaffold protein that drives high blood pressure by switching the energy style of artery wall muscle cells. About one billion adults live with hypertension, and the muscle switch in vessel walls is a core part of how it hardens. The protein, RIMKLA, was found to grab two partners: an enzyme that strips phosphate tags and a sugar-burning enzyme called PKM2.

By seating the two together, the scaffold triggers a tag change that wakes PKM2 and flips the muscle cells toward their harmful state. Artery tension was measured on vessel rings, and blood pressure by tail cuff and by remote radio tracking in the animal work. A drug blocking PKM2 lowered both vessel tightness and blood pressure in the tests. The chain gives drug hunters a fresh, specific lever against a disease usually treated broadly.
pmc-13421287:
Lauren F Collins, Casey Chmura, Morgan M Philbin and Jonathan A Colasanti review, in a 2026 paper, how long-acting injectable HIV treatment can reach people who struggle with daily pills. The approved injection pairing of cabotegravir and rilpivirine was tested mainly in people already stable on treatment, which limited its official use.

Frontline staff and community advocates have pushed access wider, and newer evidence shows people who start injections while the virus is still detectable reach suppression at rates similar to those starting suppressed. The authors stress that injections alone are not enough: support programmes, funding and delivery models decide whether the benefit holds. Costs in money and staff time remain the main barrier they identify.
pmc-13421387:
Tuan K. Nguyen and five colleagues create, in a 2026 paper, a composite material that mimics an enzyme and anchors a glucose sensor. The material pairs iron vanadate crystals with reduced graphene oxide, grown together in water with a soap-like agent that spreads the crystals evenly across the carbon sheets.

Acting like the enzyme peroxidase, the composite detected hydrogen peroxide at very low levels, with a detection limit reported at a fraction of a micromole per litre and strong sensitivity. Coating it with the real enzyme glucose oxidase produced a glucose sensor covering the range relevant to diluted samples, again with a very low detection limit. Tests showed stability and little interference from common substances.
pmc-13422087:
Andrea Corsonello leads a large European team examining, in a 2026 secondary analysis, whether a blood protein called endostatin helps explain anaemia in older people with kidney disease.
