Anaemia is common and draining in chronic kidney disease, and endostatin — a vessel-suppressing fragment that rises as kidneys fail — might blunt red blood cell production.

The SCOPE cohort contributed 2,008 participants aged seventy-five and over. At entry, about twenty percent were anaemic, and higher endostatin tracked with lower haemoglobin after extensive adjustment. Among 1,394 initially non-anaemic participants followed for two years, the analysis modelled new anaemia with death handled as a competing event. Kidney function was tested as a modifier of the relationship. The authors present endostatin as a candidate contributor to anaemia's origins.
pmc-13422287:
Ali Mussa leads a sixteen-author review, published in 2026, of immune-based treatment for breast cancer, from checkpoint drugs to engineered cells. Checkpoint inhibitors that release the PD-1 brake have become standard for some triple-negative cancers, yet most breast tumours resist them, hide in suppressive surroundings, or exact heavy side effects.

The review sweeps across checkpoint blockade, adoptive cell therapies — including CAR-T, CAR-NK and tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes — and newer immune modulators. Pivotal trials are weighed critically, and recurring obstacles get their own treatment: finding predictive biomarkers, overcoming resistance and manufacturing living cell products at scale. Combination strategies and a framework for personalising therapy close the survey. The authors aim it at researchers and clinicians planning the next trials.
pmc-13422587:
Alexandra Stefani leads a six-author team trialling, in a 2026 study, a phone app that calculates the maximum safe dose of local anaesthetic for each patient. Overdose can kill, the arithmetic mixes weight, drug and patient factors, and most existing calculators have never been validated — some propose unsafe doses.

Fifty anaesthetists at a Geneva hospital were randomised to the LoAD Calc app or their usual methods, then worked through ten clinical vignettes covering three anaesthetic drugs. The trial's main measure was the overdose rate: how often a calculated dose exceeded the safe ceiling. Calculation speed, confidence, usability and agreement between practitioners were also scored. The authors present the design as a template for validating clinical calculators.
pmc-13422887:
Jing Wu and four colleagues present, in a 2026 paper, a faster algorithm for nonnegative matrix factorisation. That method splits a table of nonnegative numbers into two simpler tables. Their product approximates the original table. The technique pulls sparse, useful features from large datasets, and speed decides whether it is usable at scale.

Their hybrid alternates between two solvers for the subproblems, steered by a loosened line-search rule whose slack is controlled by a tunable parameter, plus a step-size trick that speeds convergence. They prove the method settles globally under mild assumptions. On synthetic and real datasets it beat leading alternatives. The authors aim the algorithm at high-dimensional data analysis generally.
pmc-13423087:
Chauvin and colleagues identify a turncoat cell type in this 2026 study of ovarian cancer, which spreads across the abdominal cavity. The cavity's lining cells, mesothelial cells, are the first tissue the cancer touches, and the team traced how tumors recruit them into service using lineage tracing, three-dimensional models, and spatial gene profiling.

The recruited cells start on the tumor surface, burrow into its core, and morph toward a fibroblast-like state. A subgroup marked by the protein SERPINB2 turned strongly immunosuppressive, dialing down inflammatory signals and raising IL-10, TGF beta, and a T-cell attractant that favors regulatory cells. In mouse ovarian tumors, these cells tracked with faster growth, fewer helper T and B cells, more suppressive regulatory T cells, and outright resistance to combination immunotherapy. The authors propose targeting the converted lining cells to restore antitumor immunity.
pmc-13423487:
Cheng and colleagues reveal traffic control for mitochondria in this 2026 cell biology study, showing how contact sites between the endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria organize the organelles' journeys around the cell. The reticulum protein atlastin-2, ATL2, turns out to recruit the transport machinery exactly where the two organelles touch.

ATL2 pulls an adaptor protein, TRAK1, onto the reticulum membrane, strengthening its grip on the mitochondrial motor adaptor MIRO1 and promoting outward mitochondrial movement. Cells missing ATL2 end up with mitochondria clustered around the nucleus instead of spread through the cell. ATL2 also stabilizes the contact sites themselves by binding the fusion protein MFN2. Under low oxygen, an enzyme tags ATL2 at one specific site for destruction, collapsing the distribution system, a detail that may matter in stressed tissues.
pmc-13424587:
Gu and colleagues reported in 2026 on gene changes in mouse kidney and liver after daily exposure to e-cigarette vapor. The long-term body effects of vaping are still unclear, so early warning signals in organs matter. Male mice breathed room air, vapor without nicotine, or vapor with nicotine for one hour a day over three months, and the team then read gene activity in both organs.

Gu found that vapor-exposed groups clustered apart from the air group in the kidney. Nicotine drove more of the gene changes in the kidney, while the base vapor chemicals drove more in the liver. Changed genes pointed to oxidative stress and inflammation in the kidney, and to disturbed fat handling and immune signalling in the liver. Overall, the pattern fits early moves toward fibrosis, stiff scar-like tissue, plus metabolic upset from chronic vaping.
pmc-13424687:
Salimian and colleagues check whether standard heart-risk calculators work in people with chronic lung disease. Their 2026 paper tests three North American risk equations in adults aged 40 and over with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, drawn from five community cohorts. Recent evidence suggested a widely used British tool badly underestimates risk in this group, raising doubts about its counterparts.

The newest equation, PREVENT, discriminated best, with an accuracy measure of 0.76 against lower scores for the older tools. Yet PREVENT still underestimated actual risk by about a quarter, while the Pooled Cohort Equations and Framingham score overestimated risk by roughly 30 percent. Errors varied with age and sex, with underestimation worst in younger adults. The authors warn that none of the three tools can be trusted as-is for lung disease patients.
pmc-13425587:
Tatsuki Fukumitsu and colleagues test whether a palm-sized wireless ultrasound device can measure thigh muscle size as well as MRI does. Their 2026 study uses an extended field-of-view technique, which stitches images into a wider picture, to measure the cross-sectional area of the quadriceps muscle.

In the first experiment, 100 young adults were scanned with both methods, and agreement was strong, with a correlation of 0.98 and reliability scores above 0.99 for both men and women. In the second, 11 men completed eight weeks of resistance training, and both methods detected significant muscle growth. The ultrasound-measured gain exceeded the smallest change the device can reliably detect, and changes tracked MRI closely. The authors conclude the pocket device validly monitors muscle growth for sport and clinical use.
pmc-13426487:
Jacob Surber, Randy M. Morgenstein, and Erin Goley show that a bacterial sugar transport system controls cell length and width by separate routes in a 2026 study of Escherichia coli. Cells grown in rich medium grow larger and wider than starved cells, yet how metabolism sets size stayed partly unsolved. Mutations in the phosphoenolpyruvate phosphotransferase system, which phosphorylates sugars as they enter, produced both shorter and thinner bacteria.

Length control ran through production of the messenger cAMP, while width control ran through levels of phosphoenolpyruvate or pyruvate inside the cell. Two semi-independent pathways let one metabolic system tune cell shape dimensions separately.
pmc-13427087:
Mayeesha N. Khan, Nicole Asamoah, and Smitha Kacheri Pathayappura present pyoderma gangrenosum in a 26-year-old woman in a 2026 clinical article. This rare neutrophilic skin disease typically erupts as a rapidly expanding, painful ulcer and often imitates infection or vascular disease, delaying correct management. Pathergy, an exaggerated skin reaction to minor trauma, offers a useful diagnostic clue in such cases.

First-line treatment is immune suppression with corticosteroids, with cyclosporine and other suppressants plus careful wound care as adjuncts. Recognizing the pattern early spares patients harmful debridement aimed at presumed infection, a key practical lesson of the case. Cuts and scrapes can spark fresh sores in this ill state, so wound care must be soft, slow, and free of harsh steps that tear the skin.
pmc-13427487:
Elisa Zavattaro and a nationwide group of Italian dermatologists report data from the 2024 Vitiligo Week awareness campaign in a 2026 letter. Vitiligo is a chronic disorder of progressive melanocyte loss producing visible white patches, frequently accompanied by other conditions, particularly thyroid disease. Although neither life-threatening nor contagious, its conspicuous appearance shapes patients' daily experience and care seeking.

Campaign data profile clinical features, patient experience, and current management across Italy's participating centers. Awareness week encounters reach many people who might otherwise delay specialist care, giving the specialty a national snapshot for planning services. White patches draw eyes in a way few skin signs do. Most of those who came were women, and most had lived with the signs for years by the time they sought help at these free weeks of care. It was a full week of free care.
pmc-13427687:
Shaopeng Chen and colleagues raised the efficiency of silicon solar cells by adding a thin acid layer at the electrical contact. The cells use molybdenum oxide to collect positive charges, a design that avoids the costly doping steps of standard panels.

The added layer, phosphomolybdic acid, forms a strong electric push at the contact and lowers the barrier charges must cross. Contact resistance fell by about 24 percent, and the finished cell converted 24.9 percent of sunlight into power, up from 23.6 percent without the layer. Voltage and fill factor, two quality measures, both rose as well. Chen presents the tweak as a record for this cell family and a cheap route to better panels.
pmc-13427787:
Karekezi and colleagues describe how the IRCAD Africa center in Kigali built skull base surgery training for Sub-Saharan African surgeons. The field is held back across the region by scarce gear and support systems, and by little planned teaching. Skull base work demands fine detail knowledge of neurovascular and craniofacial anatomy. It also takes joined-up, many-field skill.

The center's 360-degree course launched in May 2024 and repeated in May 2025. It trained 75 surgeons drawn from 12 African countries in total. Hands-on teaching ran across 11 wet-lab stations with preserved bodies. Six modules spanned the antero-lateral corridor through wider endonasal routes. Trainees filled in daily reflection forms, alongside lectures, live demos, and guided dissection. Trainees rated both theory and hands-on training highly. The authors offer the model as a framework for skills labs in resource-limited settings.
pmc-13428987:
Anna Bottiglieri and Punit Prakash model, in a 2026 study, which tissue properties most sway computer predictions of heat treatment for lung tumors. Microwave ablation cooks a tumor through a needle antenna, and results vary more than doctors like. Their computer model placed a standard antenna inside a 2-centimeter tumor and varied tissue properties across realistic ranges. Properties tested covered electrical behavior, heat storage and conduction, and blood flow at the tumor's edge, which carries heat away.

Heat capacity and blood flow changed the predicted kill zone the most, shifting coverage margins by several millimeters. Electrical properties mattered least, moving results only slightly. Those millimeters decide whether a safety margin around the tumor gets fully treated. The authors argue that measuring thermal properties and perfusion in real tissue deserves priority, since planning software is only as good as those inputs.
pmc-13429987:
Jonathan H. Chin, Matthew T. Sanders, and Robin G. Stanley report, in a 2026 veterinary case, a swollen cataract in a diabetic cat, a combination almost unheard of in house cats. The Australian domestic longhair was referred for a cloudy lens. One eye held an early cataract, while the other held an intumescent cataract, a lens swollen with fluid, whose capsule had split at its edge. The cat was under treatment for diabetes, and earlier eye redness had been blamed on surface infection.

pmc-13440787:

pmc-13443187:

pmc-13444487:

pmc-13445187:

pmc-13445787:

pmc-13446887:

pmc-13447487:

pmc-13448087:

pmc-13449387:

pmc-13463087:

pmc-13464287:
Stormy Keppel leads a team that reports a catheter-based tricuspid valve replacement guided by ultrasound from inside the heart. An eighty-one-year-old man with carcinoid syndrome, a hormone-secreting tumor state, faced a severe tricuspid leak and cardiogenic shock. Standard throat ultrasound gave too weak a view for safe placement.

The team slid a three-dimensional ultrasound probe through the neck vein instead, which placed the camera beside the valve with nothing in the way. Live views from that route steered the EVOQUE valve into place. The neck route, the authors argue, deserves a place beside standard imaging when throat views fail. Patients too sick for open surgery gain most from such options.
pmc-13464887:
Syed Atif Hasan Naqvi and four co-authors use DNA barcoding to read how cover crops reshape soil nematode groups in a Canadian carrot field. Cover crops rest soil between cash crops, and nematode worms mirror soil health in their mix. Alfalfa, sorghum, and a blend of the two were grown, then folded into the soil.

Half the plots got nitrogen fertilizer after the covers went in, which let the team split crop effects from feeding effects. Crop type, more than fertilizer, drove which nematodes ruled each plot. The blended cover gave the most balanced result: fair pest worm control, the heaviest single carrots, and the soundest soil food web. Seasons reshaped the web strongly under every treatment as well.
pmc-13465287:
Bardoe and colleagues studied in 2026 why pregnant women in Ghana's Bono East Region miss hepatitis B vaccination. The virus can pass from mother to child at birth, so the gap matters. The hospital-based study mixed methods. Blood screening, questionnaires, interviews, and focus groups covered 1,430 pregnant women. Statistical models then linked beliefs and circumstances to actual infection.

About 74 of every 100 women had not taken the vaccine or not finished the series. Actual infection was uncommon, at about 18 per thousand women. The reasons women gave blended the spiritual and the practical. Fear of divine punishment and beliefs about spiritual poisoning stood out. Cost and time pressure also featured. Women citing spiritual poisoning beliefs had nearly nine times the odds of infection. Concern about burdening family nearly tripled the odds, and perceived cost raised them roughly sixfold.
pmc-13465487:
Alejandro Cornejo Müller leads a team that establishes ΔCN60, a mouse liver tumor cell line with two genes left switchable. Caspase-8 and NEMO steer liver cells between death and survival under TNF signals, a core inflammatory cue. Tumors were raised chemically in mice bred so both genes could be deleted on command in the dish.

The line keeps its genetic switches intact and its chromosome set stable across passages. Flipping both switches slowed growth, cut the survival signal's move into the nucleus, and pushed cells toward a stem-like state. Youth markers AFP and CD133 rose, while albumin, the liver's workhorse protein, fell. The line lets labs run mouse-grade genetics on a bench, trimming animal use.
pmc-13465587:
Ziang Song and co-authors examine whether a drug called 4-phenylbutyrate can rescue faulty brain receptors tied to severe childhood epilepsy conditions, in work published in 2026. The faulty part is the alpha1 subunit of the GABA-A receptor, changed by variants in the GABRA1 gene. The team combined computer modeling, cell tests, and mouse work to follow the idea.

In lab-grown cells the variant protein lowered both total and surface levels of the subunit, leaving fewer working receptors on the cell surface. Recordings of electrical currents, chemical tagging of normal and mutant copies, and tests in Gabra1 mutant mice let the group track how the drug affected expression and function across models.
pmc-13465787:
Zhang and co-authors probed in 2026 the two-way traffic between gut microbes and bile acids in liver fibrosis, using rats. Liver fibrosis is the scarring that can harden into cirrhosis. A chemical injury model produced the scarring. The team profiled stool microbes and measured bile acids precisely. Two rescue strategies were then tried: transplanting stool microbes from healthy rats and giving probiotics.

The scarred rats' gut communities shifted markedly. Clostridia and kin rose, while Bifidobacteriales and kin fell. Nineteen bile acids ran significantly higher in the blood of scarred rats. Both rescues pushed the microbe mix back toward normal, each in its own way. Both also trimmed excess bile acids such as TUDCA. Most importantly, the degree of liver scarring eased under both treatments. The authors present the microbe–bile acid loop as a workable treatment target.
pmc-13466287:
Bofeng Pan, Adam Maalal, and Dake Hao review how scaffold materials coax stem cells into becoming bone, in a 2026 article on bone repair. Large bone gaps from injury, disease, or birth defects still challenge surgeons. Mesenchymal stem cells offer a promising cell source, and the material around them can steer their fate.

Two cue families get equal billing. Chemical cues include growth factors, small molecules, gene cargo, peptides, and tiny cell-made packets loaded into scaffolds. Physical cues include stiffness, surface texture, pore layout, and stretching forces. Safety worries and approval hurdles around loaded agents push interest toward materials that guide cells by feel and structure alone.
pmc-13466587:
Salim Bin Ghouth, Ozkan Cigdem, and Valentina Mazzoli ask whether thigh muscle shape and inner architecture, read from MRI, can predict leg strength better than size alone, in a 2026 study. Strength fades with age far faster than muscle mass does, so quality must matter. Twenty-four healthy adults aged thirty to seventy-nine, evenly split by sex, were scanned.

Models compared volume alone against shape alone and shape combined with fiber architecture from diffusion imaging. Only features that reached statistical strength stayed in the final models. The work tests whether detailed imaging of the quadriceps can explain force that a simple size measure misses, a question with direct bearing on fall risk in older adults.
pmc-13466887:
Sadanori Akita and colleagues report outcomes for custom-made elastic compression garments fitted to patients whose limbs standard garments cannot fit, in a 2026 case series from four Japanese institutions. Compression is first-line care for slow-flow vessel malformations and for swelling disorders, yet limb overgrowth, asymmetry, and unusual body shapes defeat ready-made sizes.

Patients treated between mid-2023 and late 2025 received garments tailored to their bodies for vessel anomalies, edema, varicose veins, and post-injury or post-surgery swelling. Success was judged two ways: measured change in limb circumference and the patients' own satisfaction. Real-world series across several centers remain scarce for tailored garments, which is the gap this report addresses.
pmc-13467887:
Seong Jae Cho and co-authors test in 2026 a plant-based glue helper that lets polypropylene plastic bond with natural lignocellulose fibers. Polypropylene and plant fiber normally refuse to mix, so makers add a compatibilizer, usually a petroleum-based one. The team made a bio-based rival by grafting itaconic acid onto polypropylene in a melt process, then blended it into composites with raw and water-repelling treated fibers.

The bio-based version produced the strongest composite of all, reaching a tensile strength of 23.5 megapascals with untreated fiber. The authors credit better grip at the fiber surface, which let the long untreated fibers carry load as they should. Treated fiber helped even without any compatibilizer, but once the helper was added, fiber length became the dominant factor. The work offers plastic makers a greener route to stiff, fiber-filled parts.
pmc-13468287:
Natalia Lisiecka and colleagues ask in 2026 a deceptively simple question: once ionic liquids leave the bottle and enter water or soil, do they still behave as ionic liquids at all? These designer salts are praised for low volatility and tunable properties, yet environmental behavior may split them apart. The article focuses on ion pairing, the tendency of the positive and negative ions to travel together, versus each ion going its own way.

Evidence from herbicidal ionic liquids, their ordinary precursor salts, and mixtures suggests the ions often act as largely independent species under real conditions. Greasy cations drive most of the sorption to soil and the microbial toxicity, while herbicidal anions keep the mobility and breakdown patterns of their conventional salt forms. If the pair does not survive contact with the environment, safety assessments built on the paired liquid may misjudge both halves, which is the authors central warning.
pmc-13468887:
Stefanelli and colleagues propose a model linking gut microbes, vitamins, and skeletal degeneration, in a 2026 Perspective article on bone and joint disease. Their argument starts with dysbiosis, an imbalance in gut bacteria that can weaken the intestinal barrier. A leakier gut exposes the immune system to more microbe products, keeping low-grade inflammation going. The authors focus on vitamin D signals and on menaquinones, forms of vitamin K gut bacteria produce.

In the proposed chain, immune messengers including IL-6, TNF-alpha, and IL-17 tip bone balance toward breakdown through the RANKL pathway, which controls the cells that dissolve bone. Vitamin D normally calms such immune activation, while bacterial vitamin K may feed into the same control circuits. Diet patterns enter the model as levers on microbe ecology. Stefanelli stresses the menaquinone contribution to human vitamin K status remains unproven, and presents the model as a research agenda.
pmc-13470487:
Raj and colleagues in India told in 2026 of a man's hip that fell apart in months after two strong steroid shots. The rare ill is called rapidly destructive osteoarthritis. The man, 55, had mild to fair wear in his left hip. He got two high dose shots, set six months apart, each led by live X-ray to the joint. He was young and male, not the type this ill most often strikes.

Six months past the last shot, his pain had surged and his use of the leg had shrunk. Films showed the joint gap gone and the ball of the thigh bone caved in. He went on to a full hip swap, which went well. The authors warn that repeat high dose shots may feed this fast collapse, and urge teams to tell patients of the risk up front.
pmc-13470687:
Villő E. Bécsy-Jakab and colleagues study in 2026 how recovery conditions change the lignin pulled from plant processing streams. Lignin, the woody polymer left over from biorefining, varies so much in behavior that industry struggles to use it. The team acidified liquors from corn stover and hybrid poplar that differed in recipe, solid content, and holding temperature before filtering.

A clear transition temperature emerged, set by the liquor source and its strength. Below it, lignin filtered slowly and came out dark, brittle, and smooth surfaced. Above it, the same liquors gave fast filtering, lighter, powdery lignin with rougher grains. The authors explain the flip through cluster growth patterns that shift with heat and concentration. Knowing the threshold should help producers tune recovery for the material they actually want.
pmc-13471187:
Girma and co-authors audited antibiotic prescribing for acute diarrhea in 2026 at a teaching hospital in central Ethiopia, where most diarrhea needs no antibiotic at all. The team reviewed charts of 302 patients treated in the first half of 2023, judging each prescription against Ethiopia's standard guidelines. Nearly half the patients were children under five, sampled systematically across ward records.

The numbers were stark: about three quarters of patients received at least one antibiotic, most of them a single drug. Metronidazole led the list at about 18 percent of prescriptions, followed by cotrimoxazole and ciprofloxacin. Judged against the guidelines, about 77 percent of the prescribing was inappropriate. Watery diarrhea, which is usually viral and self-limiting, made up about 58 percent of cases, yet antibiotics flowed anyway. The authors link the pattern to rising drug resistance and urge strict adherence to the national guidelines, with stewardship oversight on the wards.
pmc-13471387:
Elkhodiry and colleagues reviewed the evidence for screening young children for autism at home using eye-tracking, technology that follows where a child looks on a screen. Their 2026 scoping review searched PubMed and Scopus for studies from 2015 to 2025 and mapped devices, methods, and results.

Most published work still comes from clinic or laboratory trackers, which account for 82.4% of papers, while wearable devices make up 8.8% and ordinary webcams just 5.5% of the literature. Studies devoted to home use remain rare at 3.3% of papers, even though home screening could reach families far from specialists. One large included study followed 1,089 toddlers and measured social visual engagement from videos. The reviewers say validation, regulation, and deployment hurdles still stand between promising results and routine clinical use.
pmc-13471487:
Li and co-authors investigated what governs dynamic visual acuity, the ability to read moving targets, in young adults with myopia. Their 2026 study tested 30 healthy volunteers with a mean age of 23.0 years, measuring acuity at target speeds of 20 to 80 degrees per second plus optical quality and retinal structure scans.

Acuity changed significantly across speeds, worsening as targets moved faster. Performance at 20 and 60 degrees per second correlated negatively with the eye's mean spherical prescription, with correlation values of −0.537 and −0.430 respectively at those speeds. Optical quality measures across 5 to 30 cycles per degree also tracked acuity, while specific wavefront aberrations, labeled Z7 and Z9, showed their own significant associations.
pmc-13472887:
Liu and colleagues surveyed 346 taekwondo athletes in China in 2026 on mindfulness, stress handling, brooding, and psychological distress. Athletes face hard training, competition pressure, and injury stress. The team tested whether mindfulness protects mental health through two routes: better stress self-management and less brooding, meaning repetitive negative thinking.

Mindfulness was linked with stronger stress self-management and with less brooding. Good stress self-management in turn predicted both less brooding and less distress, while brooding predicted more distress. The combined indirect path from mindfulness to lower distress was statistically clear. Together the model explained about 29 percent of the differences in distress between athletes. The authors suggest mindfulness training could be a practical mental health resource in demanding sports programs.
pmc-13473087:
Domaradzki and Koźlenia asked whether the clock time students habitually train at changes their injury risk, surveying 454 recreationally active university students. Their 2026 study classified training into morning, midday-afternoon, and evening-night habits and modeled lower-limb injury counts and occurrence against sex, body composition, load, and experience.

Injury frequency differed significantly across timing groups, with the heaviest burden among evening and night exercisers, at a significance of p 0.004 for the timing contrast. Men were injured more often than women, and higher fat mass index also raised counts, while older age within this young sample protected. The prediction model reached an AUC of 0.74 for injury occurrence. Sex and timing acted independently, with no interaction between them.
pmc-13474587:
Liu and co-authors pooled nine randomized trials covering 252 people with chronic ankle instability. They tested blood-flow restriction training, exercise performed with a cuff that partially limits circulation to force adaptation at light loads. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis measured balance reach, ankle strength, muscle activation, and self-rated ankle function.

Restriction training improved dynamic balance: the Y-balance anterior reach gained a standardized mean difference of 0.57 against controls, and the composite reach score gained 0.31, though the certainty ratings were low and very low respectively. The clinical backdrop is large: roughly 40% of people who sprain an ankle once go on to develop chronic instability with repeated giving-way. The authors endorse the method as a safe, cheap option while demanding standardized protocols in future trials.
pmc-13474787:
Ghods and co-authors studied 58 men held as forensic psychiatric inpatients at Razi Psychiatric Hospital after homicide offenses, asking what shapes their quality of life. Their 2026 study measured self-esteem, meaning how much a person values himself, and hope, meaning a sense that goals can still be reached. They used standard questionnaires and tested whether hope carries part of the link between self-esteem and daily well-being.

Both traits tracked with better quality of life, and the link from self-esteem ran largely through hope in the team's mediation analysis of the survey answers. The indirect path through hope scored 11.2 points on the quality scale, while the direct path left after accounting for hope was small and not significant. Together, self-esteem and hope explained 47 percent of the differences in quality of life scores across these patients.
pmc-13474987:
Hu and colleagues ran a trial in 2026 comparing hard interval training with gentle steady training for stroke survivors who cannot walk. Keeping the heart and lungs fit after stroke aids recovery, but the best training style for non-ambulatory patients was unclear. Forty patients were split at random into two groups for four weeks of training, five days a week.

Both groups improved on daily-living and leg-function scores. Peak oxygen uptake, the main fitness measure, rose by about the same amount in both groups, so interval training was not better overall. Subgroup checks told a finer story: patients who started with fair daily-living scores, and those of normal weight, gained more fitness from the hard intervals. The authors say longer, larger trials are needed before intervals can be recommended for this group.
pmc-13475687:
Mengistu and colleagues pool global evidence on azithromycin resistance in Salmonella, the foodborne bacterium behind typhoid-like fevers and gut infections, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Azithromycin is a key antibiotic when other drugs fail. The team combined studies of resistant isolates worldwide and examined how many shrugged off several drugs at once, plus which genes drove it in each region and bacterial subtype.

Across the pooled studies, 9.12 percent of Salmonella samples shrugged off azithromycin, with a confidence interval running from 6.53 to 12.07 percent in the pooled estimate. Among those, 31.10 percent resisted many drugs and 19.30 percent resisted nearly all drugs in the reported shares. The toolkit included efflux pumps, enzymes that alter the drug, and class 1 integrons. Rates ran highest in Southern Asia and Eastern Europe. Mengistu urges tighter tracking and drug discipline across human and animal care.
pmc-13476187:
Marta Albanell-Fernández and co-authors review real-world use in 2026 of a broad antifungal drug for cryptococcosis, a severe fungal infection. Eight patients at one large hospital received the drug, most with weakened immune systems. Lung and whole-body forms led the case mix. The drug mainly served after two weeks of stronger starter therapy, and twice as a salvage try.

Treatment ran six to twelve months and was tolerated well in this small group. Blood levels sat in the target range where checked, while spinal fluid levels were too low to detect. That gap matters for brain forms of the disease. More data are needed before this drug anchors care.
pmc-13476387:
Joost J. M. Simons and co-authors price routine baby vaccination against meningococcal B disease in the Netherlands in 2026. The germ causes nearly all Dutch cases of invasive meningococcal disease, a fast and deadly infection. A dynamic spread model compared three baby doses with no program over full lifetimes. Costs and quality-adjusted life years were counted from a societal view.

The program prevented more than two thousand cases and over one hundred deaths in the base run. Cost per healthy year gained sat just under a common Dutch threshold line. Modest rises in disease rates or modest price cuts pushed it below that line. Outbreak risk keeps the case finely balanced.
pmc-13477387:
Jacqueline Maya and colleagues present a 2026 study from a United States academic center on mild high blood sugar in pregnancy that falls short of a diabetes diagnosis. The center tested all pregnant patients with a two-step glucose process. Pregnancies were classed as normal tolerance, gestational glucose intolerance with zero or one abnormal test value, or gestational diabetes.

Among more than 41,000 pregnancies, about 12 percent had glucose intolerance and about 4 percent had diabetes. Intolerance with one abnormal value carried clearly higher odds of pregnancy blood pressure disorders, close to the risk seen in untreated diabetes. Intolerance with zero abnormal values showed no such rise. The authors raise the possibility that treating this milder sugar problem could lower blood pressure complications, a question that needs trial testing.
pmc-13478487:
Olivier and colleagues tested a new flexible injection knife in 2026 for endoscopic submucosal dissection, a technique that lifts and cuts away early digestive tract tumors through an endoscope. The knife injects fluid at high pressure to raise the tissue while it cuts, aiming to simplify a hard procedure. Five trainee operators alternated between the new knife and a standard one in anesthetized pigs, performing 41 stomach and 59 bowel dissections.

In animals, the knives performed alike on technical measures, but operators rated their satisfaction significantly higher with the new flexible knife. The team then compared 379 human bowel procedures at an expert center, 70 done with the new knife, and matched 69 cases per group by difficulty. Complete removal with clean margins reached 95.52 percent with the new knife against 82.35 percent for the standard knife, and curative removal also led, without more perforations.
pmc-13479987:
Engels and co-authors systematically reviewed studies from 2019 to 2023 on how hospital staff adapt to and innovate with electronic health records after the systems are already installed. Most hospitals now run these records, and the gains depend on staff who keep adjusting workflows and finding new uses. The team searched four databases and screened the results against set criteria with two independent reviewers.

From 3,585 records found, only 14 studies qualified for the synthesis, and most of them covered adaptation rather than genuine innovation by staff. Factors fell into four families: psychological, work design, technological, and organizational, spanning mindset toward change, time pressure, and record design itself. Innovation leaned mostly on psychological and work design factors, and the authors assembled everything into one framework meant to help hospitals squeeze full value from systems they already own.
pmc-13480087:
Chuanzhi Wang and co-authors report a 2026 study of a mixed exercise plan for women whose weight looks normal but whose body fat runs high, plus women with obesity. Sixty-seven women aged 22 to 45 finished twelve weeks of supervised training and body scans at both ends. The plan mixed aerobic and resistance work, aiming at fat and fitness rather than scale weight alone.

Fat mass fell in both groups, while lean mass rose. Belly fat deep inside the abdomen dropped in both groups, and fitness scores climbed by a like amount. Weight and body mass index fell only in the obesity group. Blood markers for heart and metabolic risk shifted little once strict corrections were applied. Since the study had no control group, cause and effect stay uncertain, yet the results argue for judging health by body makeup rather than weight alone.
pmc-13481687:
Montecalvo and colleagues reviewed in 2026 what is known about the Indian Medical Association as a political actor in Indian health policy. The association, among the world's largest doctor bodies, has long engaged national and state policy, yet its stances and influence had never been synthesized. Searching nine databases for English studies from 1974 to 2024, the team screened the record of its policy work.

Thirty-seven papers qualified. The association has been active in seven arenas, from violence against doctors and private sector regulation to curbing traditional medicine and defending professional autonomy. It reacted against new laws in every arena except doctor safety, and through inside and outside tactics it often influenced, stalled, or shrank legislation. Its weight rests on membership size and deep ties to administration and business, though its tactics lack coherence. The authors call for more open routes into health decisions.
pmc-13481987:
Massimiliano Cantinotti and co-authors present a 2026 expert consensus guide on speckle tracking ultrasound for children with heart disease. The technique follows tiny echo speckles in heart muscle to measure squeeze strength before plain scans show trouble. The paper gathers the imaging group of a European paediatric cardiology society to set shared practice.

Sections cover how the method works, normal values for children, and its use across birth defects and acquired disease, from repaired Fallot cases to single-chamber hearts after staged surgery. Worked examples show where strain readings add insight beyond standard measures. Gaps get plain treatment: no shared thresholds, loose timing rules, and thin proof on outlook value. The guide aims to steady daily use while spurring joint studies that can close those gaps.
pmc-13482287:
Torres-Reveron and co-authors test a non-hormonal drug target for endometriosis pain in rats. Their 2026 paper builds on evidence that corticotropin-releasing hormone, a stress signal boosted by estrogen, drives inflammation and pain in endometriotic lesions. They blocked its receptor CRHR1 with pexacerfont, a pill-form drug, and compared it with vehicle and with the hormonal drug elagolix.

Rats received treatment in week-on, week-off cycles starting 25 days after disease induction. Pexacerfont cut mechanical pain by about a third and inflammatory pain by slightly more. Within lesions it lowered nerve growth factor, blood-vessel growth signals, a proliferation marker, and two inflammatory messengers. Unlike elagolix, it left hormone ratios largely undisturbed. Adhesion scores, rating internal scar tissue, fell by half, an effect the comparators did not show.
pmc-13482387:
Wang and co-authors film spraying drones over rice paddies in 2026. They study how rotor downwash, the wind blasted downward by the blades, moves the crop canopy and the pesticide droplets falling through it. No standard method existed for watching the canopy ripple, so they combined aerial photography with machine vision, then checked droplet deposition with simulations and thrust tests. The goal was practical, finding flight settings where the disturbed canopy zone and the droplet landing zone overlap.

That overlap peaked at flight speeds of 3 to 4 meters per second, where the wind-opened canopy received the spray most evenly across the plants below the drone. Faster flight broke the match, blowing droplets sideways into drift and leaving landing zones misaligned with the canopy the wind had opened for spraying. Slower passes wasted chemical the same way, and the authors offer the speed window as a field-ready setting.
pmc-13482587:
Celik and Karadag Celik measure a stress protein in children's urine in 2026, asking whether lipocalin-2 betrays early metabolic trouble in pediatric obesity. The cross-sectional study compared 43 children with obesity against 32 healthy controls, all aged 11 to 16, collecting full-day urine samples. They normalized the protein to creatinine, a correction for urine concentration, and checked insulin resistance with a standard index.

The corrected ratio ran significantly higher in the obesity group than among controls, even though raw protein amounts alone did not separate the groups in this sample. Within the obesity group, children classed as insulin resistant carried higher urinary lipocalin-2 concentrations than those without resistance in the exploratory analyses. The authors suggest the marker reflects early metabolic or kidney stress in obese children, while calling for larger prospective multicenter studies before it guides care.
pmc-13483187:
Trung and colleagues worked out, with pen-and-paper style mathematics, how rubidium atoms respond to light under a special condition called electromagnetically induced transparency. In that condition, laser beams make an otherwise opaque gas briefly see-through at certain frequencies. Their 2026 study modeled a six-level atomic system, meaning atoms with six relevant energy states, driven by just two control lasers. Both common rubidium isotopes were modeled, in cold and hot gases.

The setup produced four separate transparency windows, four frequencies where light passes instead of being absorbed. That doubles as four channels for steering or storing light in one cloud of atoms. The authors also mapped how the gas bends light and slows it down under each condition. Trung offers the results as predictions to guide experiments on slow light and quantum memory devices.
pmc-13483487:
Amanuel Mesfin Oljira and co-authors share a 2026 case report of the youngest known throat leech infestation, in a six-month-old boy from rural Ambo, Ethiopia. The baby arrived after two days of mouth bleeding, blood-stained vomit, dark stool, and poor feeding. His blood count showed severe anaemia, with haemoglobin at 7.3, yet his breathing stayed clear.

Doctors spotted a dark mass in the throat and pulled out a living leech about 2.5 centimetres long with forceps under direct view. Bleeding stopped at once. Transfusions, antibiotics, and iron followed, and the boy recovered fully. The family had fed him untreated spring water from three months of age, against guidance to breastfeed alone for six months. In regions with unsafe water, the authors urge, unexplained infant bleeding should prompt a search for parasites.
pmc-13483687:
Caitlin R Williams leads a 2026 mixed-methods study of why global guidance on heavy bleeding after childbirth often fails to reach practice. Surveys gathered views from 102 international stakeholders and 246 frontline workers in three high-burden countries, checked against more than two thousand direct observations of care. A preset threshold marked when a barrier counted as severe.

Oxytocin, the standard preventive drug, enjoyed strong policy backing on paper, while other uterus-contracting drugs lacked the same support. A clot-supporting drug, tranexamic acid, was underused because several barriers stacked together. Care for bleeding that resists first treatment faced the widest set of obstacles. The mapping shows implementers where policy, supply, and training fixes must land together rather than one at a time.
pmc-13485087:
Christy and colleagues presented in 2026 guidelines for cortical and cerebral visual impairment in children, a disorder where brain damage to visual pathways harms sight even when the eyes may be sound. It is a growing cause of childhood vision loss in India and similar countries. The authors drew on world best practice, existing assessment tools, clinical experience, and expert agreement to set out how to assess children and plan help.

Christy lists common causes such as oxygen loss around birth, low blood sugar, head injury, and infections of the brain. Children with this impairment often also have cerebral palsy or delays in movement, thinking, and speech, which makes their needs complex. The guidelines pair clinical and functional assessment with rehab strategies shaped to each child. They also stress telling this condition apart from delayed visual maturation, a milder early pattern that resolves on its own.
pmc-13485287:
Jing Zhou weighs whether opening blocked heart arteries improves long-term survival for kidney patients after a heart attack. Published in 2026, the prospective cohort nested in the Kailuan Study follows kidney disease patients who had a heart attack between 2006 and 2020. Matched groups compare 452 patients who received the artery-opening procedure with 745 who did not.

Receipt of the procedure was linked to lower death risk overall, with the advantage concentrated in the first five years and fading afterward. No clear differences appeared for new heart failure or for worsening of kidney disease itself. Kidney patients are often excluded from the trials behind heart guidelines, so real-world matched evidence carries weight. Timing matters for counseling, since benefit appears front-loaded rather than permanent.
pmc-13486787:
Qahiti and team built a mathematical model of the gut-brain conversation in autism that remembers its own past. Standard models assume inflammation fades as soon as its trigger leaves, which clashes with how symptoms linger. Their 2026 model uses fractional-order equations, mathematics with built-in memory, across five linked compartments from dietary triggers to behavior, with two-way influence between gut and brain.

The analysis found a tipping threshold where the system flips from healthy recovery into chronic pathology. Sensitivity testing named the microbiota recovery rate the most powerful lever against that flip. The behavioral recovery rate, by contrast, governed how severe symptoms settled at steady state. Simulated treatment plans combining three interventions outperformed single approaches in the control exercises reported. Qahiti argues therapy timing matters because past inflammation keeps steering the system long after triggers fade.
pmc-13487987:
Are Fjermeros, Geir Vegard Berg, and Jos Benders follow a stroke improvement effort at a medium-sized Norwegian hospital in a 2026 case study covering 2013 to 2024. Quick clot treatment matters greatly after stroke, so a cross-disciplinary team tracked door-to-needle time, the delay from arrival to treatment. Sources included observations, internal documents, performance data, and interviews with team members.

Early gains came with a shared care pathway, regular feedback, and team-based working. Performance later slipped as staff changed and improvement work faded. Simulation training and renewed engagement revived the effort. The authors conclude that lasting improvement needs both committed practitioners and structures that keep good habits visible when people leave.
pmc-13488187:
Thallysson Hebert da Silva and colleagues track heart attack hospital care and deaths across Brazil during the COVID-19 years in a 2026 study of national health databases. Hospitalizations from 2015 to 2023 and deaths from 2015 to 2022 were compared with averages from the five years before the pandemic, and trend models looked for changes over time and place.

Admissions for heart attack rose every pandemic year studied, with the largest jump in 2022 at nearly thirty-seven percent above the earlier average in the reported figures. Deaths dipped slightly in 2020, then rose in the next two years. Growth was strongest in the Central-West and North regions for both measures. The authors highlight regional strain that outlasted the first pandemic year.
pmc-13488287:
Alaa Elmetwalli and colleagues compare noninvasive prenatal testing platforms for Down syndrome screening in a 2026 meta-analysis described as AI-guided. The tests read fetal DNA fragments floating in the mother's blood, or, in newer approaches, capture whole fetal cells. Ten high-quality studies from 2010 to 2023 were analyzed under standard review rules, covering sequencing-based, targeted variant, digital PCR, and cell-based platforms, with accuracy judged by sensitivity and specificity.

Sequencing-based cell-free DNA testing pooled at very high sensitivity and near-perfect specificity for trisomy 21 in the reported synthesis. Cell-based testing looked promising yet somewhat less accurate in the studies available. AI risk models sharpened calls in complex cases, such as low fetal DNA share. The authors keep sequencing as the standard.
pmc-13488587:
Pedro Alcantara da Silva, Carla Branco, Sibila Marques, and Joao Limao test what predicts student mental well-being in Portugal in a 2026 survey study. The sample was drawn to represent students at thirty public higher education institutions in the 2021 to 2022 academic year, with 9,611 respondents. Well-being was scored with the World Health Organization five-item index, and predictors were entered in blocks covering background, health, lifestyle, self-esteem and life satisfaction, studies, relationships, and leisure.

Health, lifestyle, self-esteem, and life satisfaction carried the most predictive weight in the reported models. Background factors, leisure and cultural activity, academic factors, and relationships added smaller contributions in that order. Missing answers were filled through repeated imputation across fifteen datasets. The authors argue campuses should target the strongest blocks first.
pmc-13489787:
Caballero and a chemistry team in Spain tested in 2026 iron based catalysts that turn carbon dioxide into cyclic carbonates, ring shaped chemicals used as solvents and in batteries. Their one part iron compounds join CO2 with epoxides, simple ring shaped starter chemicals, in a reaction that wastes no atoms. The work asked how the iron charge state, iron two versus iron three, changes the speed and yield of the run.

The iron catalysts worked under mild heat and normal air pressure, with no solvent and no added helper chemicals. The iron three forms beat their iron two twins by a clear margin. The authors link that edge to stronger Lewis acid pull, the grip the metal uses to wake the epoxide ring. Rate tests showed the pace rose in direct step with catalyst dose, a sign that the two iron centers in each unit act as a pair.
pmc-13490487:
Gandini and colleagues assembled 350 colorectal cancer patients whose tumors carried a specific repair defect and tested every tumor for amplification of the HER2 growth gene. The two traits guide different treatments, and case reports had hinted they never coexist. Their 2026 study gathered cases from two Italian referral centers spanning 2016 to 2024, staging each tumor and profiling its common mutations alongside the HER2 testing.

Not one patient in the cohort carried HER2 amplification, a clean zero across all 350 repair-deficient tumors tested. Most tumors were stage two or three, and sixty percent carried a BRAF mutation among those with molecular data available. The authors call this the largest series aimed squarely at the question. Gandini concludes co-occurrence is extremely rare and likely anecdotal, so testing resources should be allocated with that rarity in mind.
pmc-13491687:
Shihong Zhang and four co-authors pool in 2026 the trial evidence on electrical stimulation for leg recovery after surgery to rebuild a torn anterior cruciate ligament. Several stimulation types exist, and patients and therapists need to know which adds most to standard rehabilitation exercises. The reviewers searched five databases through March 2026 and combined results directly and through a network analysis.

Eleven randomized trials covering 629 patients met the criteria. Adding stimulation beat exercise alone on pain scores and knee range of motion, though not on a standard knee function questionnaire. Neuromuscular electrical stimulation ranked first for both pain relief and motion in the network rankings. The reviewers recommend pairing that stimulation type with rehabilitation, while noting the limited gain in overall knee scores.
pmc-13491787:
Zhen Liang leads a thirteen-author team hunting in 2026 for genes that tie immune control to bone metabolism in liver cancer. The disease is often found too late for current treatments to work well. Mining single-cell and bulk gene data from tumors, the researchers sorted nine cell types. They screened for genes that predicted patient survival while also tracking with immune activity.

Seven genes passed the screen, and one, APLP2, stood out for being switched on mainly in cancer tissue. Silencing APLP2 in liver cancer cells slowed their growth, invasion, and movement while increasing cell death, and it weakened two major growth pathways. The silenced tumor cells also stopped suppressing bone-forming cells and let immune cells release more attacking signals. The authors nominate APLP2 as a fresh treatment target.
pmc-13493087:
Mengmeng Pu, Yijun Chen, and Dewei Ouyang trace in 2026 a protective RNA circuit that fails in diabetic kidney disease. Blood from seventy-four kidney patients, one hundred four diabetics without kidney damage, and eighty healthy volunteers showed the long non-coding RNA RAD51-AS1 running low in the kidney group. Its level tracked with worse filtration and heavier protein leakage.

In kidney cells bathed in high glucose, restoring RAD51-AS1 revived growth, curbed cell death, and lowered both oxidative damage markers and inflammatory signals while boosting antioxidant defenses. The RNA works as a sponge for a smaller RNA, miR-154-5p, freeing a mitochondrial gene called MPC2 from its suppression. Adding the small RNA back erased the protection, confirming the chain. The authors propose the circuit as a therapeutic target.
pmc-13493187:
Zolkiewski and colleagues map how small changes to a drug's shape change its risk of seizures. Some drugs block ion channels in the brain by chance. That block can set off toxic effects. The team picked eighty-eight test compounds from a large open library. Each sat close in shape to a known risk drug. They tested all of them on four human ion channels in lab cells.

Twelve shape traits linked to action at one channel, a nicotinic receptor. Four of those traits also linked to a second channel. In human stem cell neurons, changed compounds gave changed seizure-like signals. The map gives designers clear traits to avoid early.
pmc-13493787:
Xu and co-authors ask what happens when two common pollutants reach lung cells together. One is ultrafine carbon black, a soot particle found in fine air pollution. The other is amisulbrom, a widely used farm pesticide that can travel through the air. Using A549 cells, a standard human lung cell line, the 2026 team dosed the cells with each substance alone and combined, then checked results with three statistical models built for mixtures.

Both substances harmed cells more as the dose rose, but the soot was the stronger poison, needing a far lower dose to kill half the cells over 24 hours. All three models agreed the combined effect was simply additive, meaning the harms stacked without amplifying each other. Carbon black drove almost all of the joint harm, while the pesticide's share stayed weak and unstable across models. Combined exposure did raise cell stress markers and programmed cell death.
pmc-13495187:
Jacinta Chibuzor Ene, Nkechinyere Patricia Onyishi, and Lum Perpetua Tanyi study, in a 2026 paper, how family caregivers in Enugu State, Nigeria, manage care for older adults and cope with the load. Ageing brings frail health and changed food needs, and Nigerian custom places care in the family, not in homes for the aged. The team ran group talks and long interviews with 54 caregivers and health workers.

Caregivers named steep hurdles: the older person's age, ills, and attitude, plus their own money and schooling gaps. Most coped through ties with people or through inner resources such as faith, a hopeful outlook, games, and music. Village communal support, once a cushion, is fading. Few knew that social workers could help with care planning. The authors urge bringing social work services into family care, since demand grows as elders age and caregivers say they are in dire need of help.
pmc-13495387:
Jinyoung Jeong, Jae-Ran Seol, Seo-Hee Choi, and Seheon Lee present a 2026 report of three cases where shock wave therapy was tried as a salvage path for stubborn upper arm fractures. The humeral shaft sometimes heals slowly or not at all, and the standard fix, revision surgery with fresh hardware, adds tissue damage and nerve risk. The problem grows harder when screws loosen or fixation is in doubt.

Shock wave therapy, sound pulses aimed at the bone, can stir healing without cutting, and guidance bodies accept it for delayed healing after checks. Its catch is that it stirs biology only; it cannot steady a loose construct. The authors chose patients whose hardware, though flawed, still held the bone, expecting renewed callus growth toward union. They present the cases to mark where this non-surgical option may serve and where loose, failing fixation still demands the operating room.
pmc-13498587:
David Bertram leads a 2026 team presenting ActiTect, a free computer pipeline that screens for a sleep disorder from wrist movement records. People with this disorder act out dreams during the rapid eye movement stage of sleep, and the condition often precedes Parkinson disease and related disorders. Wrist sensors could support large-scale screening, but recordings differ between devices and centres, which has limited earlier tools.

ActiTect standardises the data, detects sleep and wake periods on its own, and extracts motion features a learning model can read. Trained on 78 people, it separated cases from controls strongly in internal checks. Performance held up on a blinded local test set and on two outside cohorts from other centres, and key features stayed stable across datasets, supporting wider testing of the shared model.
pmc-13498887:
Mohamed Ahmed Hamed, Talal Abdullah Ahmed Alnajjar, and Ziyad Daifallah Alsubhi compare in 2026 two fluid types for treating diabetic ketoacidosis, a life-threatening complication where the body produces excess acids. Standard saline has long been the default fluid, yet its high chloride content can add a separate acid problem. Balanced fluids, whose salts sit closer to blood plasma, might avoid that drawback, so the authors searched four databases for direct comparisons from 2021 onward.

Nine studies covering 1,416 patients qualified, mixing randomised trials and other designs. Balanced fluids consistently lowered excess chloride and improved an acid-base measure compared with saline, and insulin infusions ran shorter in two studies. Hospital stay results were mixed, with no clear difference in kidney injury or death, leaving the effect on full recovery time uncertain pending stronger trials.
pmc-13500087:
Christos Tsironis and co-authors examine in 2026 how oral health shapes quality of life in later years and how that experience ties to loneliness, sleep, and dream recall. Their cross-sectional study enrolled 609 community-dwelling adults aged 60 and older in Greece. Standard scales measured oral health-related quality of life, plus emotional loneliness, while brief self-report items covered sleep quality, sleep sufficiency, napping, and how often dreams were remembered.

Better oral quality of life went with clearly lower emotional loneliness, the strongest link in the analysis, and with modestly better sleep appraisals and less daytime napping. Lonelier participants reported poorer sleep yet no difference in dream recall. A small link between oral quality of life and dream recall appeared in adjusted models. The authors themselves flag it as exploratory and possibly a chance finding, urging caution given the single unvalidated dream question and many comparisons.
pmc-13500487:
Gozansky Einav, Weissman-Fogel Irit, and Okon-Singer Hadas test in 2026 whether two brief cognitive trainings change how healthy women respond to experimental pain. One training teaches acceptance of pain sensations, while the other retrains attention away from pain-related images, and both are proposed as chronic pain tools whose benefits vary unpredictably. Eighty healthy women each completed one active and one control session in random order, with emotional questionnaires, attention tasks, and standardised sensory testing before and after.

At group level, both active trainings dulled sensitivity to the exact heat level used in training yet beat their control conditions on nothing, and no other pain modality improved. Individual starting points mattered more, since women who began with stronger attentional capture by pain images and higher fear of pain gained the largest heat sensitivity reductions from acceptance training. Personalised matching is the authors' takeaway.
pmc-13500687:
Ali and colleagues built lightweight detectors for fake text, audio, and images, three separate problems gathered under the deepfake label. Most detectors are heavy models that smaller newsrooms and police units cannot run quickly. Their 2026 framework trains one specialist pipeline per format, using heavy data augmentation to harden the models. It includes three home-grown compact networks named VerbaFake for text, EchoFake for audio, and PixelFake for images, alongside well-known efficient architectures.

Trained on tens of thousands of samples per format, the text models scored near-perfect accuracy in the reported tests. The best image models reached the high nineties, and the audio trio climbed just below that mark. The authors' scratch-built audio model beat two famous imported networks in their comparison. Because each detector works on one format alone, the system stays small and fast enough for real-time screening.
pmc-13500787:
Tiller and co-authors review how Streptomyces bacteria control production of their specialised chemicals. Their 2026 paper surveys recent advances in a field built on a puzzle. These soil bacteria make many valuable compounds, including antibiotics. Yet when and why they make each one is often unclear, and much of their capacity stays untapped.

The review describes a layered control system. Regulators inside each production gene cluster interact with genes elsewhere in the genome. Broad-acting regulators compete with each other and with proteins that organise the chromosome. Together they integrate many signals into production decisions. The authors also highlight production in cell types and growth stages not previously linked to these chemicals. Finally, they describe containment strategies the bacteria use to handle their own potent enzymes and distribute the products safely.
pmc-13500987:
Ibrahim M. Alzuheir leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 cross-sectional study of MRSA carriage among people who work with dairy cattle in Jordan. Nasal swabs came from 100 cattle-exposed individuals and 100 non-exposed controls. The team identified Staphylococcus aureus by a gene test for nuc and confirmed methicillin resistance via the mecA gene. Multiplex tests screened the isolates for drug resistance, toxin, biofilm, and immune evasion genes.

S. aureus grew from 41.0 percent of all swabs, and 76.8 percent of those isolates were MRSA, split almost evenly between the two groups. The resistance gene blaZ appeared in every exposed-group isolate, and biofilm genes icaA and icaD were universal. Several virulence genes differed significantly: selr, hlg, and etd were commoner in exposed isolates, and etd appeared only there, in 50 percent of cases. The authors call for ongoing molecular surveillance at the livestock-human boundary.
pmc-13501687:
Elias Amarneh leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 Palestinian case of a rare vena cava clot alongside two autoimmune conditions. A 33-year-old healthy man arrived with fever, acute right-sided flank pain, and other symptoms. Early checks suggested a urinary stone, but pain persisted and inflammation markers stayed high, prompting more imaging. Scans revealed thrombosis of the inferior vena cava, the great vein returning blood from the lower body, an unusual site for a clot.

The pattern pointed to suspected antiphospholipid syndrome, an autoimmune clotting disorder, coexisting with relapsing polychondritis, an autoimmune attack on cartilage. That pairing has rarely been reported. The authors suggest antiphospholipid antibodies may feed the vascular inflammation seen in the cartilage disease, hinting at a shared mechanism. They call for suspecting the clotting syndrome early when a vena cava clot appears without provocation, and for more study of the overlap.
pmc-13503687:
Amelia C Corona leads a 2026 study of a new smell test battery for pet dogs, called dogSIT. Older tests often use one scent, need the dog to walk, or let sight affect the result. The new battery uses pairs of scents held in steel tea balls while the dog rests.

Dogs met each scent four times in a row, then a new one, and staff timed how long each dog engaged. Repeat tests with 25 dogs gave steady scores, and raters agreed well. In 65 dogs, age, weight, and sex shaped how dogs met new scents. Older dogs engaged less with new scents, which fits known aging effects and may aid work on food drive in old dogs.
pmc-13503887:
Sandeep Kumar, Ramesh Gupta Burela, and Arpit Kumar Srivastava model how the shape of a magnet-driven rubber tube changes its motion, in a 2026 study. The material mixes iron grains into soft rubber, so a magnetic field can pull it into new shapes. Such tubes suit soft robots and adaptive parts.

Their computer model couples magnetic pull with large bending, using a custom material rule in a standard solver. Two shape ratios were varied: width against length, and wall thickness against length. Bigger ratios widened the tube's sideways bulge but piled stress near the fixed base, a likely spot for first failure. Shape and field strength interact in curved, nonlinear ways. The results give design hints for safer, stronger soft actuators.
pmc-13504787:
Rémy Coulomb leads a team reviewing whether a keyhole hip operation harms the results of a later full hip replacement, in a 2026 systematic review. Keyhole surgery now treats joint pinching and cartilage tears in many young, active patients. Some of them later need a full artificial hip, and surgeons worry the first operation could complicate the second.

The review gathered eighteen comparison studies with more than twenty-eight thousand replacement patients, about a third with prior keyhole work. Surgery-day gaps were small, though operating time ran longer in some studies. Infection, fracture, and leg-length issues showed no clear gap. Reports on later revision and dislocation split both ways, with higher risk flagged when replacement came within a year. Function gains stayed strong in both groups.
pmc-13506587:
L M Delgado and colleagues compare, in a 2026 review, two extents of colon surgery for colonic Crohn disease in the era of strong modern drugs. A smaller operation removes only the diseased segment, while a larger operation removes more bowel. The review pooled five studies with 1095 patients, 501 with the smaller operation and 594 with the larger one.

Rates of return disease, repeat surgery, complications, and death looked broadly alike between the two choices. The smaller operation linked to a much lower chance of a permanent stoma, a surgically made opening for waste. The authors advise weighing a possible small rise in return risk against the clear benefit of avoiding a stoma.
pmc-13507087:
Zhihuang Chen, Wen-Yan Tong, Jiye Shu, Junliang Zhang, and Xiaodong Xiong present a 2026 chemical method to make sulfur-centered chiral molecules with high precision. The products, sulfonimidoyl fluorides, act as click linkers that join other molecules and matter for drug design. Direct control of handedness at a sulfur-fluorine bond has been hard to achieve.

Their one-pot route runs fluorination, water treatment, and a second fluorination under mild conditions. A phosphate partner guides handedness through size and hydrogen bonds. Many products formed with high selectivity for one handed form. Those products can then convert into varied sulfur-chiral motifs, which widens access to new drug and materials building blocks.
pmc-13508787:
Nicole Cady and colleagues built a gut model that lets oxygen-loving human colon cells grow beside oxygen-hating gut bacteria. Organoids are lab-grown mini tissues, and their setup keeps air on one side of the cell sheet and no air on the other.

Colon sheets grown in the system behaved more like living gut lining than sheets grown in normal air. A common gut bacterium, Bifidobacterium adolescentis, shielded the sheets from damage by inflammatory signals. Its protective product was a compound called indole lactic acid, which guarded the barrier in proportion to dose. Fed to mice, that compound eased treatment-triggered colon inflammation in females, and the system now fits 96-well plates for faster screening.
pmc-13509287:
Beatrice De Santes leads a fourteen-author team testing an extract from the Ghaf tree, the national plant of the United Arab Emirates, as a natural anti-aging skin ingredient, in 2026 work. Ghaf survives harsh desert life, which hints at protective chemistry. Detailed profiling found the extract rich in polyphenols, led by catechins and flavonoid relatives. Three standard assays measured its power to neutralize the reactive molecules that age skin. Enzyme tests covered four enzymes that break down skin structure or drive pigmentation.

The extract scored exceptionally high on every antioxidant assay, in step with its rich phenol content. It also blocked all four aging-linked enzymes at levels the team judged biologically relevant. As a practical proof, the group blended the extract into preliminary emulsion creams and checked the result. The authors present Ghaf extract as a multi-action candidate for future skin products.
pmc-13509387:
Kareem and colleagues built a tool to predict survival for cardiac sarcoma, a rare, fast-growing heart cancer, using United States registry data, in a 2026 methods study. Prediction is hard because cohorts are tiny, follow-up is incomplete, and risk factors act in curved ways. Their tool fuses a neural network learner suited to patterns with the classic Cox proportional hazards model, weighted together, with safeguards against information leakage.

Kareem found 727 patients and kept 27 predictors after screening. In leakage-free cross-validation the combined model ranked patients' risk better than the Cox model alone. But the Cox model's risk estimates matched real outcomes better, a trade-off the authors state plainly. Follow-up summaries described which factors drove the combined model's scores. They stress the high scores are likely too rosy and that the tool is a research aid that needs outside validation and recalibration before any clinical use.
pmc-13511087:
Camaleta Boothe, Arianna Rossi, Jenniffer Kalil, and Jean J. Latimer review tiny RNA strands called microRNAs as a possible biologic route to treating cancer, in 2026 work. These strands tune gene activity after genes are read, and cancers can lose the ones that hold growth back or gain extra copies of growth-pushing ones. Lab-made copies of the missing strands, called mimics, have curbed spread, growth, and cell survival in dishes, animals, and early trials.

A single mimic can strike several genes in one pathway at once, and some can restore response to drugs that had stopped working. Bare strands break down fast, so chemical tweaks add staying power, and carrier particles help them cross cell walls, though carriers can stir inflammation. A tweak swapping one building block for a drug-like version also eased entry. The authors trace lessons from an approved sister therapy as a roadmap.
pmc-13514787:
Lee and colleagues present a 2026 study of an explainable AI framework that grades radiation pneumonitis, lung inflammation after radiotherapy, from CT scans. The data came from 46 lung cancer patients, yielding about twenty-four hundred images with and without the condition. A generative network extracted image features, and heat maps showed which areas the system attended to.

Attention maps guided the choice of feature layers, and statistical trimming cut the feature set from over twelve thousand to 730 values. A stacked ensemble, several classifiers feeding a final judge model, then made the call. The design prizes interpretability and speed alongside accuracy, so doctors can see the inflamed regions behind a grade rather than trust a black box. Early, visible grading of this side effect helps teams adjust care before breathing worsens.
pmc-13518787:
Chuanjia Yao leads a ten-author team proposing a 2026 blockchain system for settling disputed medical insurance claims inside hospital groups. Insurers and hospitals often clash over whether a charge was legitimate, partly because each side sees different information. Slow, contested settlement then strains the whole consortium.

Their design pairs an isolation forest algorithm, which flags unusual expenses automatically, with smart contracts that let an anonymous expert panel vote on disputed cases using a Fleiss kappa agreement measure. Tests reached a peak of 229.64 transactions per second and cut some transaction costs sharply. Yao and colleagues present the setup as a scalable way to govern insurance funds more fairly.
pmc-13520187:
Subeen Kim leads a seven-author cross-sectional study in 2026 on how frailty severity relates to diet quality and food security among older Korean adults. National survey data from 2013 to 2020 supplied 9,263 adults aged 65 or older, scored on a 41-item frailty index and a Korean healthy eating index.

Frailty affected 14.1 percent of men and 23.8 percent of women, clustering with low education, low income, and living alone. Eating index scores fell steadily as frailty worsened in both sexes. Severe food insecurity carried far higher frailty odds, especially in women, where the odds ratio reached 9.03. Kim and colleagues urge sex-specific nutrition programs plus stable food supply for aging populations.
pmc-13520287:
Zi-Wei Li leads a nine-author umbrella review in 2026 that stacks 30 existing meta-analyses of bullying prevention programs for children and adolescents into one comparison. Four databases were searched to October 2024, yielding 4,740 records before screening. Seventeen distinct interventions were sorted by who leads them: families, schools, communities, health services, or collaborations.

Every statistically significant result favored the programs, spanning behavior change, mental health, and attitudes. Effect sizes ranged widely. Music-based work posted the largest behavior-change estimate, martial arts led collaborative efforts, and sports led for mental health gains. Li and colleagues caution that effectiveness varies sharply by design, so program choice should follow the outcome a school or service actually wants to move.
pmc-13520387:
Yu-Wei Fan and colleagues investigate in 2026 autistic traits among children with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, asking whether a subgroup shows extra behaviour difficulties. Traits were measured with screening questionnaires in 154 children split across healthy, ADHD-only and combined diagnosis groups.

Children with ADHD scored higher than healthy peers on most trait measures, while scoring lower than the combined group. Within ADHD, 29 children met the trait threshold and showed wide behavioural differences that the full analysis details. Early results point to more rule-breaking and aggressive behaviour in that subgroup. Clinicians may need to screen for such traits rather than treating ADHD as uniform.
pmc-13520487:
Griffin and colleagues published a 2026 study on a prostate cancer risk report patients can actually read. Polygenic risk scores blend many small gene effects into one cancer risk figure. Clinics increasingly order them, yet reporting styles vary wildly and confuse patients. The team built a summary report plus a question page inside a screening trial.

Eight men eligible for screening reviewed the materials in interviews. Picture arrays showing absolute risk landed best of all the graphics tested. Color and bold type steered eyes to the key facts well. Bell curves and incidence curves, though, were often misread or skipped. Tailored plain reporting matters as scores enter routine care, they conclude. Simple visuals beat dense charts for lay readers, the men said.
pmc-13521887:
Sania Khan and colleagues study in 2026 a cosmetic allergy that darkens the face over time. Care took place at a hospital in Ghaziabad, India. The illness mimics other causes of facial darkening, so it is often missed. Patch tests can unmask the trigger scents and dyes.

The study held 55 patients over 18 months. Most patients were women aged 31 to 40 years. Brown-black colour was the main look. Skin scope views showed grey-brown tones, globules and pore plugs. Two patch sets were read at set times by global rules. Full trigger lists follow in the results. Avoidance plans rest on those lists.
pmc-13522787:
Shenghao Huang leads a randomized trial of augmented reality guidance for locating small lung nodules before surgery in a 2026 study. One hundred sixty-eight patients with peripheral nodules no larger than two centimeters received either augmented reality navigation with dynamic tracking or standard CT-guided localization. Accuracy was the main outcome, with time, radiation, needle adjustments, and complications also tracked.

The augmented reality group had lower average localization error, at about four and a half millimeters versus six and a half in the standard group. Procedures were shorter, radiation exposure was lower, and fewer needle adjustments were needed. Success rates were high and complication rates similar in both groups, with no severe events. The authors support augmented reality as an efficient alternative to CT guidance.
pmc-13522887:
Georg Semmler, Jan Embacher, and Mattias Mandorfer reply to a letter about two noninvasive liver tests in a 2026 response concerning fatty liver disease and liver cancer surveillance.
